questionText: Assess the effectiveness of the options available to organic and biodynamic grape growers to control pests and diseases.
body:
## Defining effectiveness

Effectiveness cannot be assessed without a yardstick, so I set three. First, agronomic efficacy: does the option hold the pest or disease below the threshold at which crop and quality are lost, and does it do so reliably in a bad year rather than an average one? Second, economic effectiveness: what does it cost per hectare in materials, tractor passes, labour and yield forgone, and — the more important figure — what is the cost of the downside when it fails? Third, durability: does it degrade the soil, select for resistance, or fall foul of tightening regulation?

The second test governs the answer, because the fundamental constraint on the organic or biodynamic grower is not the absence of any single product but the absence of a systemic curative option. A conventional grower who misjudges a downy mildew infection can spray a penetrant fungicide and recover the crop. The organic grower cannot, so every decision must be taken earlier, with less information, and with the full loss on the table. That asymmetry — prophylaxis with no rescue — is what makes organic disease control an exercise in risk management by a grower with fewer resources than the neighbour over the fence.

## Two different logics

Organic and biodynamic control are conceptually different, and blurring them produces a weak answer. Organic control is substitution: prohibited synthetics are replaced by permitted contact materials, and the aim is containment — keeping inoculum below the damage threshold, spray to spray, through the season. Biodynamic control is preventive: the aim is a vine in balance, with moderate vigour and an open canopy, on the premise that a balanced vine is less susceptible, so that the contact treatments are needed less often and at lower rates. Biodynamics is organic plus a preventive philosophy, not an alternative toolkit; every biodynamic grower still uses copper and sulphur.

## The organic toolkit assessed

Copper against downy mildew and sulphur against powdery mildew are the load-bearing treatments, and their efficacy is genuinely good in dry, low-pressure climates — Mendoza, the Douro, inland Australia — where I would rate organic control as fully effective and barely more expensive than conventional. In Atlantic and maritime climates the assessment changes sharply. Both are protectant and non-systemic: they wash off, so they must be reapplied after each rain event, which in a wet Loire or Bordeaux season can mean fifteen or more passes against a conventional programme's six. The cost is not the material, which is cheap, but the diesel, the labour, the soil compaction from repeated passes and the physical impossibility of getting a tractor onto saturated ground at the moment cover is most needed. Durability is also poor: copper accumulates in soil and is toxic to soil biology, and the EU has progressively cut the permitted copper rate to a few kilograms per hectare per year averaged over several seasons. Effective, then, but climate-contingent and under regulatory pressure.

Bacillus thuringiensis against lepidopteran larvae is a genuine organic success: cheap, specific, and as effective as the conventional alternative. Pyrethrum is the weak point — permitted, but broad-spectrum, killing the beneficial predators the system depends on. Where flavescence doree, where insecticide treatment is compulsory in designated zones and the organic grower's only permitted option is pyrethrum, the organic grower is forced into the least selective material available. That is a real and under-discussed failure of the system.

I would not credit pheromone mating disruption against grape moth or raptor perches against birds as organic control at all. Both are now standard practice across sustainable and much conventional viticulture, so they neither distinguish the organic grower nor demonstrate the system's effectiveness.

## Canopy management: the most cost-effective lever

The cheapest and most durable control is cultural, and it is the one most growers underweight. Fruit-zone leaf removal shortly after set, shoot thinning to reduce shoot density, careful shoot positioning and timely trimming all lower humidity in the bunch zone, improve spray penetration to the fruit, and cut botrytis and powdery mildew pressure directly. Reducing vigour through a permanent inter-row cover crop does the same by producing a smaller, more open canopy. The economics are attractive: the cost is seasonal labour, incurred once, against a saving of several spray passes and a lower chance of catastrophic loss. This is where biodynamic prevention is genuinely vindicated — its emphasis on balance produces the canopy that makes the sprays work.

## Biodynamic preparations

Assessed against my three tests, the specifically biodynamic materials — the horn preparations, and the herbal teas and decoctions of horsetail, nettle and willow used as preventive tonics — have weak evidence of direct fungicidal efficacy, and I do not think a candidate should claim otherwise. Their cost is low, so a grower loses little by using them, and the practices that surround them (close observation, timely intervention, low vigour) plausibly deliver the benefit attributed to the preparations themselves.

## Assessment

Effectiveness is a function of climate before it is a function of philosophy. In dry climates organic and biodynamic control is effective and economically competitive. In wet maritime climates it is effective in most years and can fail completely in the worst, and the honest assessment is that the system works there only for growers whose margins absorb the occasional lost vintage. Ranked by return on cost, I would put canopy management first, copper and sulphur second as necessary but constrained, biological insecticides third, and the biodynamic preparations last on evidence — while conceding that the discipline they impose may be worth more than the materials.

questionText: What practical options does a viticulturist have at his or her disposal to address long term changes in climate in an established vineyard?
body:
## Defining long term, and what is already fixed

I take long term to mean 30 to 50 years — the productive life of a single planting, and the horizon over which a mean growing-season temperature shift of one to two degrees is a reasonable planning assumption. That definition does the work in this answer, because it separates seasonal adaptation from structural adaptation: anything reversible within a season is a buffer, not a solution, and only decisions that persist across decades count as addressing long-term change.

The question also confines me to an established vineyard, so site, altitude, aspect, row orientation, spacing, rootstock and variety are already in the ground and are not on the table in the way they would be for a new planting. What remains available is the canopy, the soil, the water, the plant material through grafting and progressive replanting, the wine style, and the regulations. I take them in ascending order of how long they last.

## Canopy and soil: the annual buffer

The canopy is the fastest lever and the shortest-lived. Over decades the direction of travel in warm regions reverses forty years of orthodoxy: instead of opening canopies to ripen fruit, growers will retain leaf area and lateral growth to shade the bunch zone against sunburn, remove leaves only on the morning side, raise the fruiting wire away from radiating soil, and trim later and less. Higher bud loads and larger crops slow sugar accumulation and delay harvest. Delayed winter pruning, and in hot regions double pruning to push the cycle into a cooler autumn, shift the ripening window by weeks. These are real and worth doing, but they are re-decidable every season and therefore buffers.

Soil is the more durable half of the same problem and the one most often omitted. Raising soil organic matter through compost and permanent cover crops increases water-holding capacity measurably over a decade or more; under-vine mulch cuts evaporative loss; reduced tillage preserves structure and rooting depth; and correcting compaction restores the root volume a vine needs to survive drought. Below-ground water retention is a slow, cumulative investment, which is exactly why it belongs in a long-term answer and not in a list of seasonal fixes.

Where irrigation is legal, the long-term option is not simply to irrigate but to install monitoring and move to regulated deficit irrigation, and to secure the water right — which over 40 years is a bigger constraint than the equipment.

## Plant material: the structural lever

The decision that actually matches the time frame is plant material, and it can be taken inside an established vineyard in two ways. Top-grafting converts existing trunks and root systems to a later-ripening or more heat- and drought-tolerant variety or clone, keeps the mature root system, and returns to production in two or three years rather than five. Progressive replanting — replacing a few per cent of the vineyard each year as vines reach the end of their lives — allows rootstock change towards drought-tolerant selections such as 110R or 140Ru without ever taking the block out of production. Over 40 years, progressive replanting will have renewed the whole vineyard, which means the rootstock decision is available on a long horizon even though it is unavailable next season.

Style change follows from this and is the option most candidates miss. If a site can no longer make the wine it was planted for, the long-term answer may be to change the wine rather than fight the climate: picking a proportion earlier for a sparkling base, moving a red from a ripe, extracted style to a fresher, earlier-picked one, or converting a warm block to rosé. Grafting and style change are the same decision viewed from two ends.

## Long-term change is not only warming

An answer confined to heat would be wrong. Earlier budburst extends the spring frost exposure window even as mean temperatures rise, so long-term frost defence — wind machines, and the water supply that sprinkler protection requires — is an adaptation investment, not a legacy one. Rainfall is becoming more concentrated, so erosion control on slopes, permanent inter-row cover, drainage capacity and terrace maintenance all need designing for larger events than historical records suggest. Hail frequency is a genuine long-term risk, and netting is the only intervention with reliable evidence, though hail netting is restricted or prohibited under some appellation rules.

## The regulatory option

Over 30 to 50 years the rules are as movable as the vineyard, and lobbying is a practical option. The abandonment of legal restrictions on irrigation in European appellations is the clearest case, and permitted-variety lists are already changing: Bordeaux has authorised a small list of additional varieties, among them Touriga Nacional, Marselan and Alvarinho, for use within its regional appellations. Rules on harvest dates, minimum and maximum alcohol, enrichment, acidification, netting and shade cloth are all candidates for revision, and a viticulturist who is not engaged with their appellation body has surrendered a lever.

## Conclusion

Ranked by how long the effect lasts, the priorities are soil water-holding capacity and plant material through top-grafting and progressive replanting, then style change, then the regulatory framework, with canopy work as the buffer that carries the vineyard between structural decisions. The mistake to avoid is treating the annual buffer as the answer: shading a bunch zone helps this season, but only grafting, soil and the rulebook operate on the timescale the question sets.

questionText: Can Cabernet Sauvignon and Riesling be successful in the same location?
body:
## Definitions and position

Two terms decide this question. By same location I mean a meso-area: a sub-region of the order of tens of kilometres across, sharing one broad mesoclimate but containing real variation in altitude, aspect, soil and exposure. That is the scale at which the question is interesting. A single vineyard block is too small to be worth asking about, and a country or a large region is too coarse to mean anything — saying that Australia grows both varieties answers nothing.

By successful I mean commercially viable: fruit that ripens reliably to the typical style of its variety, at a yield and quality that pays its costs and finds a market. I deliberately do not restrict this to great wine. Reading the question as being about world-class examples of both varieties would set an artificial bar and change the answer.

My position is yes. The two can be successful in the same meso-area, and routinely are — but only where topography or maritime influence supplies enough internal variation for the grower to allocate each variety to a different site within that area.

## What each variety needs

Cabernet Sauvignon buds late and ripens very late, so it needs a long season and a high heat accumulation, and above all a warm, dry autumn to finish. It performs best on stony, free-draining, heat-retaining soils that keep the root zone warm. Its failure modes are cool-site herbaceousness from unripe methoxypyrazines and hard, dry tannin when the season runs out before the fruit is ripe. It is drought-tolerant, hard-wooded and durable.

Riesling buds early, which exposes it to spring frost, but it has exceptionally cold-hardy wood and survives winters that would kill Cabernet. It ripens early to mid-season, retains acidity strongly, and its quality argument depends on a long, slow, cool ripening period that builds aroma while the acid holds. Its failure modes are the reverse of Cabernet's: in a hot site it ripens too fast, loses acidity and aromatic delicacy, and its thin skins sunburn and rot.

So the varieties sit perhaps 200 to 300 growing-degree-days apart in requirement and prefer opposite ends of a temperature range. That is the apparent conflict.

## Why the conflict dissolves

It dissolves for two reasons. First, both varieties are unusually adaptable. Both have hard wood that overwinters well, both tolerate a wide range of soils, and both are grown commercially across a broader climatic span than most varieties — which is why they are among the most widely planted grapes in the world.

Second, and decisively, a meso-area is not climatically uniform. Within twenty kilometres, a rise of 300 metres in altitude, a change of aspect, or proximity to a lake or ocean can shift mean growing-season temperature by more than the difference between the two varieties' requirements. Co-existence is therefore achieved not by compromise but by allocation: Cabernet on the warm, low, stony, sheltered sites, Riesling on the higher, cooler, more exposed ones. Diurnal range is the other enabling condition — hot days ripen the Cabernet while cold nights preserve the Riesling's acidity.

## Where it happens

Clare Valley is the clearest case: Riesling on the higher, cooler Polish Hill and Watervale sites, Cabernet on the warmer, lower ground, both regarded as regional benchmarks. Washington's Yakima Valley does the same, with Riesling on cooler sites and Cabernet concentrated at the warm, low-rainfall eastern end. British Columbia's Okanagan Valley runs the split along its length — Riesling in the cooler north near Kelowna, Cabernet in the desert-like south around Osoyoos. In Western Australia, Great Southern combines Riesling at Mount Barker and Porongurup with Cabernet in the warmer Frankland River sub-region, and Margaret River grows both under maritime moderation. Oregon's Umpqua Valley, Alto Adige — Riesling at altitude, Cabernet on the valley floor — and the Northern Galilee hills all show the same pattern. Even the Pfalz, warm enough to ripen Cabernet marginally on its best sites, is a plausible case.

## The viticultural work that makes it possible

Allocation is not sufficient on its own, and this is where good viticulture earns the result. Riesling planted in a warmer meso-area is managed for acid retention: fuller canopies to shade fruit, minimal leaf removal on the afternoon side, higher yields to slow ripening, and earlier picking. Cabernet in a cooler one is pushed the other way: open canopy, exposed fruit, lower crop load, warm free-draining soils, low-vigour rootstock and every device that advances ripening. Row orientation, rootstock choice and irrigation timing can be set differently for each block. High-quality viticulture will produce good results even where the climate is marginal for one of the two, which is exactly why the answer is yes more often than the raw climate data suggests.

There is also a practical advantage in the timing. Riesling and Cabernet are typically separated by four to six weeks at harvest, so a single grower can pick, press and process both without competing for tank space, labour or attention — which is one reason the combination survives commercially where it exists.

## Conclusion

Yes. Cabernet Sauvignon and Riesling can both be successful in the same location, provided location is read as a meso-area with genuine internal variation and a wide diurnal range, and provided the grower allocates sites deliberately and manages each variety towards the opposite objective. They cannot both succeed in a uniformly hot or uniformly cool place — that is the real limit, and it is a limit of topography rather than of the varieties.

questionText:
Compare the main vine training systems used in the following wine regions:

a. Mosel
b. Alsace
c. Marlborough
d. Châteauneuf-du-Pape
body:
## The comparative frame

These four regions occupy the extremes of two axes, and comparing them along those axes is more useful than describing each in turn. The first axis is heat: the Mosel must gather every available degree, Chateauneuf-du-Pape must shed heat and conserve water, and Alsace and Marlborough sit between. The second is vigour and water: Marlborough has too much of both, Chateauneuf-du-Pape too little, and the training system in each place is largely a solution to that imbalance. Topography then overrides everything in the Mosel, and variety complicates the picture at Chateauneuf. I take these drivers in turn.

## Slope and mechanisation

The Mosel is the only one of the four where terrain, not physiology, dictates the system. On the steepest slate parcels — the steepest Mosel parcels exceed sixty per cent gradient — running wires across the slope is impractical and a tractor is impossible, so vines are trained individually on a single tall stake and worked up and down the slope on foot or by monorail. The cane is bent into the characteristic Mosel arch around the stake, which concentrates the shoots into a compact plume, holds the fruit low against slate that radiates stored heat at night, and keeps the canopy presented to the sun on a slope where light is the scarce resource.

The other three regions have terrain that permits wire trellising, and all three use it. That is the first real comparison: the Mosel's stake training is not a stylistic preference but the only option on ground the other three do not have, and where Mosel slopes are gentler or have been reconfigured into wider terraces, growers have moved to conventional wire-trained vertical shoot positioning precisely so they can mechanise.

## The same system doing different jobs

Vertical shoot positioning appears in the Mosel, in Alsace and in Marlborough, and it is doing something different in each. In the Mosel it serves mechanisation and uniform ripening on the accessible sites. In Alsace it is a disease and frost solution: on the fertile lower slopes and valley floor, VSP lifts the fruit clear of frost-prone ground and opens the canopy for air movement and spray penetration, which matters for thin-skinned, rot-prone Riesling and Gewurztraminer in a region whose dryness is not a guarantee. Alsace also varies the system within itself — single or double guyot with a straight or arched cane on vigorous sites to fill the fruiting wire and even out budburst, spur-pruned cordon on the poorer granite and limestone hillsides, with different leaf-removal and trimming strategies for the aromatic whites.

In Marlborough, VSP is a vigour-management system. Deep, fertile, well-watered alluvial soils on the Wairau plains produce far more shoot growth than the crop needs, so the answer is a tall trellis, long four-cane pruning to spread that vigour over more buds, wide rows — Marlborough's row spacing is commonly around 2.4 metres — to admit light into a big canopy, and full mechanisation of pruning, trimming and harvest to keep cost per tonne low. On the most vigorous blocks growers divide the canopy vertically, using systems of the Scott Henry type, to expose more leaf area without shading the fruit. The comparison with Alsace is direct: the same VSP skeleton, but Alsace uses it to open a moderate canopy and Marlborough uses it to house an excessive one.

## Heat, wind and water at Chateauneuf-du-Pape

Chateauneuf inverts the Mosel's problem. Free-standing gobelet needs no wire, which matters where the mistral would flog a trellised canopy; the low, self-supporting head of old wood is stable in that wind; the bowl of shoots shades its own fruit against sunburn and slows ripening; and the low, unirrigated vine on galet-covered, drought-prone soils has neither the vigour nor the water to fill a trellis in any case. Where the Mosel arch is designed to expose fruit, the gobelet is designed to hide it.

But Chateauneuf is not simply bush vines. Grenache, with upright growth and strong wood, suits the free-standing head; Syrah has a trailing habit, needs support, and is generally trained to guyot on wire; Mourvedre, needing heat and late ripening, is usually kept as gobelet. The best comparison in this question is therefore internal: one appellation running two systems because two varieties have different growth habits.

## Why the alternatives fail

Test each system in the others' conditions and the logic closes. Gobelet in Marlborough would give too little leaf area for the crop, trap humidity in a wet maritime spring, and forfeit mechanisation in a high-labour-cost country. VSP at Chateauneuf would expose fruit to sunburn and the mistral and demand water the site does not have. Bush vines in Alsace would hold humidity around thin-skinned aromatic whites and block the tractor in narrow rows. And wire systems on the Mosel's steepest slate simply cannot be installed or worked.

## Conclusion

Ranked by force, the drivers are topography first — it removes all choice in the Mosel — then the vigour-and-water balance, which explains why Marlborough spreads a canopy and Chateauneuf contains one, then variety, which is why Chateauneuf runs two systems at once. Heat management cuts across all of them, and it explains the sharpest contrast in the group: the Mosel arch and the Provencal gobelet are opposite answers to the same question about where the sun should fall.

questionText: What steps can a viticulturist take to provide and maintain proper vine nutrition?
body:
## What proper nutrition means, and what I am leaving out

Proper vine nutrition is not maximum nutrition. It is supplying each element in the right proportion at the stage the vine needs it, so that the vine achieves moderate vigour, sets and ripens a balanced crop, and enters winter with adequate reserves. Excess is as much a failure as deficiency: over-supplied nitrogen produces vigour, shading, poor fruit set, botrytis and dilute fruit, while excess potassium raises must pH and costs the winemaker acidity.

The temptation with this question is to survey every element in turn, and I am deliberately not doing that. I take three steps in order — understand the soil as a delivery system, diagnose before intervening, and then intervene with the cheapest durable lever available — because that sequence is what separates growers who correct nutrition from growers who merely fertilise.

## The soil is the delivery system

Almost every nutritional problem is a problem of availability rather than of absolute quantity, and availability is set by three interacting processes.

Physically, the soil determines how much root there is. Depth, structure, drainage and the absence of compaction control root volume, oxygen supply and water movement, and a vine on a compacted headland will show deficiency symptoms in a soil that analyses as fully adequate. Water is the carrier: dry soil is nutritionally unavailable soil regardless of what it contains, which is why irrigation scheduling is a nutrition decision as much as a water one.

Chemically, pH governs the availability of nearly everything. High-pH calcareous soils immobilise iron and induce chlorosis; acidic soils release aluminium and manganese to toxic levels and lock up phosphorus and molybdenum. Cation exchange capacity determines how much a soil can hold against leaching — a sandy soil cannot store an annual application, so the same total dose must be split.

Biologically, mycorrhizal associations extend the effective root system and are the principal route for phosphorus uptake; organic matter mineralisation supplies most of a vineyard's nitrogen; and soil fauna maintain the structure the physical side depends on. The point that matters is that these three interact, so a chemical correction applied to a compacted or biologically dead soil will not deliver.

## Diagnose before intervening

The step most often skipped is measurement. A full soil analysis before planting and at intervals thereafter establishes pH, organic matter, texture and base saturation. Petiole or leaf-blade sampling at flowering and again at veraison is the more useful annual tool, because it measures what the vine has actually taken up rather than what the soil holds — which is precisely the distinction that availability makes important. Visual symptom diagnosis is fast but unreliable, since deficiencies mimic each other and mimic virus. Must analysis at harvest, particularly yeast assimilable nitrogen, closes the loop retrospectively and tells the grower whether the vineyard programme worked.

Modern technology mostly serves targeting. Aerial and satellite infrared imagery maps vigour variation across a block so that sampling is directed at the anomalous zones rather than averaged into meaninglessness; soil conductivity mapping does the same for texture and depth; neutron and capacitance probes track soil moisture through the profile, which matters because uptake follows water. The gain is not new information about the vine so much as the ability to manage a block in zones instead of as a unit.

## The interventions

Structural corrections come first because they are made once and last for decades. Lime raises pH on acid soils, gypsum addresses sodicity and structure, deep ripping and drainage restore root volume. Where soil pH is high and calcareous, the decisive step is rootstock: rootstocks selected for lime tolerance, such as 41B and Fercal, prevent lime-induced chlorosis in a way no annual foliar programme can match, and that choice is made once at planting.

Annual supply then follows. Mineral fertiliser applied to the soil is precise, fast and easy to calculate against yield removal. Fertigation is more precise still where irrigation exists, allowing small doses timed to demand at flowering and post-set, and minimising leaching losses. Compost, manure and legume cover crops build organic matter, feed the biology and release nitrogen slowly, but they are imprecise and slow to act. Foliar application is the tool for rapid correction of trace elements — zinc, boron, magnesium — where soil chemistry prevents root uptake.

## Choosing between routes

Different approaches work, and the choice is agronomic rather than ideological. A dry-farmed, low-vigour hillside with no irrigation cannot fertigate and must build fertility through organic matter and mulch; a high-yielding irrigated block can dose precisely and should. A vigorous, nitrogen-rich site needs the opposite intervention entirely — under-vine or inter-row vegetation to compete for water and nitrogen and bring the canopy back into balance. To claim that only composting or only mineral fertiliser is correct is to mistake a site-specific decision for a principle.

## Maintaining it

Maintenance is a cycle rather than an event: sample annually at the same phenological stage, keep records long enough to see trends rather than noise, match inputs to the nutrients removed in fruit and prunings, and re-test after any structural change.

Ranked by return, the highest-value steps are the durable ones — drainage, pH correction and rootstock choice — followed by a genuine diagnostic programme. The annual fertiliser decision, which is where most attention goes, matters least of the three.

questionText: When and how can hail cause damage at various stages of vine growth? What methods are most effective for preventing or responding to such damage?
body:
## When

Hail forms when a strong updraught in a deep, unstable convective cell carries water droplets repeatedly above the freezing level, accreting ice until the stone outweighs the updraught that supports it. That is as much mechanism as the question needs; what matters viticulturally is when and where those conditions occur.

They occur where warm, moist air is forced over relief or meets a cold front — the Rhone valley and the Bordeaux and Burgundy edge of the Massif Central, northern Italy and the Alpine foreland, the Andean foothills at Mendoza, the continental interiors of North America and South Africa's Breede River valley. The season is late spring through summer, with a strong afternoon and early-evening peak, and events are highly localised: a corridor a few hundred metres wide can be destroyed while the adjacent commune is untouched.

Hail becomes a serious issue at two moments in particular: the spring window from budburst to fruit set, and the run from veraison to harvest. Between those, the vine's capacity to compensate is greatest and the loss smallest.

## How

The timing dictates the damage. At budburst and early shoot growth, hail strips swelling buds and snaps soft green shoots. The primary buds carrying this season's inflorescences are destroyed; secondary and latent buds push, but they are less fruitful, later and uneven. Because the vine also loses the leaf area that builds carbohydrate reserves, and because next year's inflorescences are initiated in this year's buds, severe spring hail carries quantitative repercussions for up to two years — the delayed effect most candidates miss. Burgundy and Chablis have repeatedly lost consecutive vintages this way.

At flowering, hail knocks off inflorescences and directly removes yield, with no possibility of compensation. Between set and veraison, the dominant damage is to leaves: shredded canopy reduces photosynthetic capacity, so ripening is delayed and sugar accumulation depressed even where fruit survives. Bruised berries either desiccate and drop, or scar. Wounds on shoots and trunks are entry points for botrytis and, over the longer term, for trunk-disease pathogens.

From veraison to harvest, hail is at its most damaging commercially. Softened, sugar-rich berries split, and if warm humid weather follows, the vineyard converts to botrytis and sour rot within days; a crop can move from healthy to unsalvageable in under a week, and mouldy or earthy taints follow into the wine. Post-harvest hail matters least, though damage to canes reduces bud quality for the following spring.

## Prevention

Assessed on evidence rather than popularity, the options separate sharply.

Netting is the only physical prevention with reliable efficacy, and it is what I would fund. It is proven, and in hot regions it doubles as sun protection — the reason it is close to standard in parts of Mendoza. The costs are real: high capital outlay, annual labour to deploy and retrieve, some shading of the canopy which is a disadvantage in cooler regions, and the fact that netting is restricted or prohibited under some European appellation rules on landscape and typicity grounds. That prohibition is worth challenging: the rationale appears to rest more on appearance than on evidence about wine quality, and it deserves proper study.

Anti-hail cannons are widely deployed and have no robust evidence of efficacy; they are also a source of neighbour disputes over noise. I would not invest in them. Cloud seeding with silver iodide is more credible in principle and regional cloud-seeding programmes operate in Mendoza, in parts of France and in Alberta, but effect sizes are genuinely hard to demonstrate against natural variability. I treat seeding as a collective, quasi-insurance measure rather than something a single estate can rely on.

The most effective prevention is not meteorological at all. Because hail is so localised, dispersing holdings across several parcels and communes — the pattern Burgundian growers arrived at by inheritance and now defend deliberately — is genuine risk mitigation. Crop insurance, where a market exists, is the other real instrument, and in many regions it is the only one that reliably converts a total loss into a survivable one.

## Response

Response is where most answers stop short, and it is where the recoverable value lies. The first step in the days after an event is triage: assess severity block by block, then apply a protectant fungicide, typically copper-based, to wounded tissue, because open wounds on green tissue in warm weather are a botrytis and bacterial infection route.

After early-season damage the key treatment is re-pruning: cutting damaged shoots back to a clean node to provoke an even secondary flush, rebuilding leaf area to restore reserves for the following season, and accepting a token or zero crop this year. Modest nitrogen and water support that regrowth without inviting excess vigour.

Mid-season damage calls for the opposite of protection: open the canopy by leaf removal to speed drying, drop damaged bunches in a green harvest so rot does not spread, and move to more frequent, gentler botrytis control. Close to harvest the response is commercial — pick early, sort ruthlessly in the vineyard and again at the winery, and consider declassification, bulk sale, or diverting fruit to rosé or a sparkling base where the style permits.

The following season, expect reduced bud fruitfulness, prune to more buds to compensate, and monitor for trunk disease entering through old wounds. Ranked overall: netting and parcel dispersal for prevention, speed of response afterwards, and insurance behind both.

questionText: It is often noted that some wines are not perfectly clean, and have low levels of potentially faulty aromas, sometimes referred to as "funky". How can a winemaker best manage a desirable element of "funkiness" in his or her wine?
body:
## Defining the terms: funk, desirable, manage

Funkiness is best defined as the grey area between fault and complexity: aromatic and textural characters produced by compounds that are unambiguously faults at high concentration, but which at low concentration, and in a style that can carry them, read as savouriness, depth and individuality. Desirable is a judgement made against a style brief and a market, not an absolute — the struck-match note that makes a serious white distinctive would be a fault in a supermarket Sauvignon Blanc sold on primary fruit. Manage is the operative word, and the one that sets the shape of this answer: the task is not to remove these characters but to arrive at a chosen level of them, deliberately and repeatably. Controlled funkiness and random spoilage can produce the same molecule; they are wholly different acts of winemaking, because only one of them is specified in advance and stopped at a defined point. I take the question to run across still, sparkling and fortified wine at all price levels, not only low-intervention wine.

## The characters in play, and their mechanisms

*Ethylphenols.* Brettanomyces bruxellensis decarboxylates and reduces hydroxycinnamic acids to 4-ethylphenol and 4-ethylguaiacol — spice and leather at low levels, animal and medicinal above. It works on trace residual sugars after fermentation, favoured by high pH, warm cellars, low free SO2 and oxygen ingress at racking or topping. 4-ethylphenol is detectable in red wine at of the order of 400 micrograms per litre, which is the number that defines the target.

*Reduction.* Hydrogen sulphide, mercaptans and thiols give struck flint, smoke and, past threshold, drains. They arise from nitrogen-stressed yeast and from lees held without oxygen.

*Oxidation.* Acetaldehyde gives bruised apple and nuttiness; flor yeast additionally generates sotolon-driven curry and walnut notes. Acetobacter, needing oxygen, converts ethanol to acetic acid and thence to ethyl acetate.

*Volatile acidity.* Acetic acid and ethyl acetate, from acetic acid bacteria working aerobically, read as lift and perfume just below threshold and as vinegar and solvent above it — the grey area with the narrowest margin of all.

*Skin, solids and lees.* Extended maceration on white grapes brings phenolics, grip and a savoury oxidative edge; high fermentation solids and long lees ageing bring cheese and yeast-derived reductive notes.

## Managing to a target, not eliminating

Four disciplines convert this from luck into method.

First, set the target before harvest, as a sensory specification with an analytical proxy — a 4-ethylphenol ceiling, a free and molecular SO2 regime, a dissolved oxygen band.

Second, generate the character on purpose. Reduction is created by high fermentation solids, low assimilable nitrogen, a sulphide-producing yeast strain and reductive handling. Oxidative character is created by deliberate ullage, cask ageing without topping, or a flor veil. Phenolic funk is created by skin contact time and temperature. These are process settings, not accidents.

Third — and this is the single most useful lever — build the character in a fraction and blend. Fermenting one parcel reductively, or ageing one cask oxidatively, and blending it back at a chosen percentage gives a continuous dial and a repeatable result, where treating a whole tank gives one irreversible shot.

Fourth, arrest at the target. Sterile or 0.45 micron membrane filtration, molecular SO2 of roughly 0.6 mg/L, and dryness to trace sugar stop Brettanomyces where it stands. Reduction is adjusted downward by racking, aeration or copper — residual copper is legally capped at around 1 mg/L — and, importantly, copper additions strip thiols permanently, so this is a decision to take late and small. Oxidation is arrested by topping, inert gas and SO2, and volatile acidity has a hard stop in the EU ceiling of roughly 1.2 g/L for red wine.

## Across the styles

The grey area is not the property of one category. In sparkling wine, reductive base-wine handling and long lees autolysis are used deliberately in Champagne and increasingly in English and Tasmanian sparkling; low dosage exposes those notes rather than hiding them. In fortified wine funk is the category: flor-aged Sherry is built on acetaldehyde, Madeira's canteiro ageing on controlled heat and oxidation, Rutherglen Muscat on decades of oxidative solera. Among white table wines, Jura Savagnin aged sous voile, and skin-contact whites in Georgian qvevri, Friuli and Slovenian Brda, all trade on characters the same examiner would fail in a Chablis. Among reds, traditional Northern Rhône Syrah and old-school Rioja carry ethylphenols as part of their identity, while a modern Napa Cabernet built on fruit purity cannot. The counter-example matters: Amarone and other appassimento reds carry volatile acidity that would condemn a Beaujolais, because concentration, sweetness and dried-fruit character absorb it. Style context, not the molecule, decides.

## Conclusion

Funk is manageable in proportion to how reversible it is. Reduction and oxidation are chemical and can be dialled both ways; skin contact is a decision taken once and blended afterwards. Brettanomyces is alive, and a population that is merely tolerated will keep growing in bottle. So the best management is to generate the character deliberately in a defined fraction of the blend, measure it against a numeric target, and then kill or arrest the mechanism — never to leave it running and call the result complexity.

questionText: Shape, size and material of a vessel used for fermentation and maturation are important factors in determining style and quality. Discuss with particular reference to Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.
body:
## The three physical variables

Shape, size and material act on wine through four measurable physical properties, and the whole argument follows from them.

*Surface-area-to-volume ratio.* As a vessel gets smaller, each litre of wine touches more wall. That governs three things at once: oxygen ingress through the material, extraction of whatever the wall is made of, and the proportion of lees in contact per litre. A barrique — 225 litres in Bordeaux and 228 in Burgundy — admits of the order of 20 to 30 mg/L of oxygen into a wine over a year; a 5,000-litre foudre of the same wood, far less per litre, and a 500-litre puncheon sits between.

*Thermal behaviour.* Stainless steel conducts, so temperature is externally controlled and can be held anywhere. Wood and concrete insulate, so a fermentation self-buffers and peaks are slower and broader; a small barrel also loses heat fast because of the same surface ratio, which is why barrel-fermented whites run cool without refrigeration.

*Geometry.* In red fermentation the ratio of cap surface to wine depth decides extraction. A wide, shallow, open-top vat gives a large cap surface, low hydrostatic pressure and gentle, even extraction by punching down; a tall narrow tank concentrates the cap, raises pressure and demands pumping over. In whites, a concrete egg or a rounded tank sets up convection that keeps fine lees suspended without stirring.

*Permeability.* Oak transmits oxygen and gives lactones, vanillin and toasty volatile phenols. Concrete and unglazed amphorae give micro-oxygenation with no flavour of their own. Stainless is inert on both counts.

## Cabernet Sauvignon

*Fermentation.* Cabernet is thick-skinned, high in anthocyanin and in tannin that is coarse if over-extracted, so vessel choice is an extraction-control decision. Open-top vats in Bordeaux and Napa allow punch-down and cap-wetting with low mechanical stress; taller stainless tanks with pump-over give a more aggressive, oxygenative regime that suits fruit needing tannin softening. Concrete and wooden fermenters buffer the temperature peak, which matters because Cabernet ferments hot and hot extraction pulls hard tannin.

*Maturation.* Here small oak is doing chemistry, not decoration. The steady low-dose oxygen of a barrique drives anthocyanin-tannin polymerisation, stabilising colour and softening the palate, while oak tannin adds to the structure the variety already has. Cabernet's weight and phenolic load tolerate new oak that would smother a lighter red, which is why the classed growths, Coonawarra, Maipo Alto and Ningxia's premium reds converge on small barrels — not fashion, but a variety with the substance to absorb them.

## Chardonnay

*Fermentation.* Chardonnay is neutral and phenolically light, so the vessel largely writes the style. Stainless steel preserves primary fruit and acidity: Chablis, unoaked Australian and Chilean Chardonnay. Barrel fermentation, by contrast, integrates oak far more seamlessly than post-ferment oak ageing does, and the yeast metabolises some of the harsher wood aldehydes. The larger 500-litre puncheon, now widespread in Margaret River and the Adelaide Hills, gives the textural benefits of wood with roughly half the oak signature per litre — a direct consequence of surface ratio, and a response to a market that moved away from heavy oak.

*Maturation.* Lees contact is the second lever, and small vessels maximise it per litre. Burgundian pièce ageing with bâtonnage builds mannoprotein-derived texture and mouthfeel; concrete eggs and amphorae in Limarí and elsewhere deliver that texture with micro-oxygenation but no oak flavour, which is the point of choosing them.

*Alternative materials.* Concrete and amphora are now used for both varieties, and for the same physical reason in each: slow oxygen ingress with no wood flavour. For Cabernet that means colour stabilisation without oak masking a site; for Chardonnay it means texture without vanillin. Large old oak — foudres and ovals — behaves differently again, giving low oxygen and almost no extractable flavour per litre, which is why it survives for wines wanting slow evolution and neutrality.

## Where the choice is variety-specific

The divergence is real. Chardonnay is routinely fermented in the vessel it matures in; Cabernet almost never is, because red fermentation needs cap access that a barrel cannot give. Chardonnay uses the vessel to add what the grape lacks; Cabernet uses it to moderate what the grape has too much of. And new oak levels that flatter Cabernet will erase Chardonnay.

## The commercial end

Most of both varieties is made far from this. Rotary and autovinifier fermenters extract Cabernet colour and tannin in two to four days rather than ten, which is precisely the right tool for a wine that must be bottled within months; large temperature-controlled stainless tanks with oak staves or chips deliver oak character at a fraction of barrel cost and with far better batch consistency. These are competent engineering answers to a genuine commercial specification, and plenty of excellent wine is made in unfashionable vessels — old large oak in Rioja and Barolo among them. Chardonnay at volume is fermented cool in large stainless tanks and, where oak character is wanted, given staves; the resulting wines are clean, consistent and exactly what the price point requires.

## Conclusion

Shape, size and material matter because they set oxygen exposure, thermal profile, extraction geometry and flavour transfer. They determine style directly; they determine quality only insofar as they are matched to the fruit, which is why the same barrique makes a great Cabernet and an oak-drowned Chardonnay.

questionText: How can a wine's tannin profile be managed during vinification?
body:
## Introduction

Tannin profile means the quantity, the size distribution and the origin of the phenolic polymers in a wine, and therefore how it is perceived: grippy or supple, drying or fine. It is managed by controlling three things — how much is extracted, from where, and how it is subsequently polymerised or removed. Grapes must arrive at phenolic ripeness for any of this to work, but the question is about vinification, so I take that as read and run through the process in order: pre-fermentation, fermentation and cap management, pressing, post-fermentation operations, additions and oak, and then the other wine styles and the commercial end of the market.

## Before fermentation

Destemming decides whether stem tannin — greener and coarser, but firming — is in the vat at all; whole-bunch inclusion is a deliberate tannin decision as much as an aromatic one. Crushing sets skin surface area. A cold soak at 8 to 12 degrees Celsius extracts anthocyanins and aroma in water, but very little tannin, because condensed tannin needs ethanol as a solvent; that asymmetry is exactly why it is used. Pectolytic and maceration enzymes break down cell walls and raise the rate of extraction thereafter.

## During fermentation

Ethanol is the main variable: as it climbs, tannin extraction accelerates and shifts towards seed tannin, which is harsher. Temperature is the second — fermentation at 28 to 30 degrees Celsius extracts far more than a cool ferment. Time on skins is the third.

Cap management determines how much of the potential is realised. Punch-down submerges the cap with high wine-to-skin contact and, done gently by hand or firmly by pneumatic ram, is the most controllable tool. Pump-over irrigates the cap from above; it extracts less per operation but adds oxygen, which helps yeast and starts tannin polymerisation early. Délestage (rack and return) empties the tank, aerates strongly, and lets the seeds settle out so they can be removed — a targeted way of cutting harsh tannin. A submerged cap gives slow passive extraction. Rotary fermenters achieve in two to three days what a static vat takes ten to do; they are the right tool where throughput and consistency matter and they extract efficiently by design. The timing decision matters as much as the technique: working the cap hard early, while alcohol is low, favours skin tannin and colour; working it late favours seed tannin.

## Pressing

Pressing is where much of the profile is actually decided, and it is under-used as a lever. Free-run is softer and lower in tannin, phenol and potassium; press fractions rise steeply in tannin, and in pH, with pressure. Keeping fractions separate — light press, hard press — gives the winemaker discrete blending components to taste and assemble, and hard press fractions can be fined with gelatin, egg albumen or PVPP to strip aggressive tannin before any is blended back. Free run itself can be fined for the same purpose. Pressing off before dryness leaves the last, harshest extraction in the marc.

## After fermentation: polymerisation

Extended maceration of two to four weeks continues extraction but, more importantly, allows tannins to polymerise and to bind with anthocyanins, so the wine tastes softer despite containing more phenolics. Micro-oxygenation does the same job deliberately, dosing of the order of a few millilitres of oxygen per litre per month, higher during the post-fermentation phase and far lower after malolactic fermentation. Barrel ageing supplies the same slow oxygen ingress, plus oak ellagitannins, plus lees that adsorb tannin. Fining pre-bottling is the final subtractive step, and it is selective: gelatin binds the largest, most astringent polymers, egg albumen polishes gently, PVPP removes the small bitter phenolics, and casein or plant proteins serve vegan specifications. Blending is the last lever of all — assembling free run, press fractions and differently handled lots to a target profile.

## Additions

Oenological tannins are the most neglected tool. Added at crush, condensed and gallotannin preparations bind and stabilise anthocyanins and inhibit laccase; added post-fermentation they restore structure and mid-palate to thin or early-pressed wines. They are legal, widespread and cheap, and no serious answer on tannin should ignore them.

## Other styles

In white wine the object is usually to avoid tannin: whole-bunch pressing, low press pressures, cutting hard fractions, and PVPP or casein fining. Skin-contact and orange whites invert that, extracting deliberately. In sparkling the press regime does the work — Champagne takes only 2,050 litres of cuvée from a 4,000 kg marc precisely to leave phenolics behind. In sweet wine botrytised fruit brings laccase, and gentle pressing plus protective handling limits phenolic pick-up. In Port, extraction must be complete before fortification arrests it, hence lagares, robotic treaders and autovinifiers working the cap intensively over two or three days.

## The commercial end

Judicious tannin management arguably matters more at entry level, where the wine has no time in bottle to resolve. Early pressing before dryness, thermovinification and flash détente to get colour with minimal tannin, rotary fermenters, oak staves for a little ellagitannin, oenological tannin for structure and gelatin fining for smoothness are all standard, and all deliver a soft, approachable profile to specification.

questionText: Discuss the impact of malolactic fermentation, or its absence, on wine style.
body:
## What malolactic fermentation is

Malolactic fermentation is the bacterial decarboxylation of the dicarboxylic L-malic acid to the monocarboxylic L-lactic acid, with the release of carbon dioxide, converting one gram per litre of malic acid into roughly 0.67 grams per litre of lactic acid. Because one acid group is lost, the wine becomes both less acidic and softer in the mouth: lactic acid is perceived as rounder than the sharp, green malic acid it replaces. Titratable acidity falls, typically by 1 to 3 g/L, and pH rises, typically by 0.1 to 0.3 units. It is not a fermentation in the yeast sense at all — no sugar is consumed and no alcohol produced.

The organism is Oenococcus oeni, a lactic acid bacterium renamed from Leuconostoc oenos in the late 1990s. It occurs naturally on grapes and in cellar surfaces and equipment, and spontaneous MLF is entirely normal; winemakers also inoculate with cultured strains for speed and control. It is preferred over the other wine lactic acid bacteria, Lactobacillus and Pediococcus, because it tolerates pH below 3.2 and ethanol to around 14 per cent while producing fewer off-flavours.

## Controlling it

MLF is conducted at 18 to 22 degrees Celsius; below about 16 it stalls, and there is no wine bacterium working happily at 36. It requires low free SO2, a pH above roughly 3.1 and warmth. Conversely, blocking it is achieved by cold, by free SO2 held above roughly 15 mg/L, by lysozyme, and finally by sterile filtration at bottling. Blocking is not free: it commits the producer to a microbially fragile wine that must be filtered and kept cool, so the style decision carries a handling cost.

## White wines and sparkling bases

This is where the largest stylistic swing occurs, and where most of the marks lie. In a barrel-fermented white, full MLF lowers acidity, adds body through the bacterium's own metabolism, and generates diacetyl from citric acid — the buttery, hazelnut note that defines the style. Diacetyl is perceptible from around 1 to 4 mg/L, and it is not fixed: extended lees contact reduces it to near-odourless acetoin and butanediol, so the same completed MLF can taste buttery or merely creamy depending on what follows it.

Blocking MLF is the default for aromatic whites — Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, Albariño, Grüner Veltliner — because the crisp malic acidity and the volatile thiols and terpenes are the product. Partial MLF, on a fraction of the blend, is the most useful tool of all: it gives a continuous dial between the two poles, widely used in Chablis, Sancerre and cool-climate New World whites.

In sparkling base wines the decision is different again, because acidity is structural. Full MLF is used to soften a lean base and, crucially, to guarantee that MLF cannot occur in bottle after tirage, which would cause haze, extra gas and off-flavours. In warm-climate sparkling production, and by producers seeking maximum tension and ageing potential, MLF is deliberately blocked and the wine sterile-filtered instead.

## Red wines

It is wrong to wave reds through with "all reds go through MLF", even though most do. In red wine MLF is as much a stability decision as a style one: because the wines are usually bottled with low SO2 and higher pH, removing malic acid is the only practical way to prevent a bottle refermentation. The stylistic gain is softer acidity and a rounder texture; conducted in barrel, it also integrates oak better than tank MLF does.

The exceptions are real and instructive. Nouveau and other carbonic-macerated styles bottled within weeks of harvest do not have time for MLF and rely on sterile handling instead. Sweet reds — a growing commercial category — must have both malic acid and residual sugar protected from bacteria, so MLF is blocked and the wines are sterile-filtered. Some producers in hot regions block MLF to avoid pushing an already high pH higher, since above about pH 3.8 the wine becomes microbiologically vulnerable, and acidify instead.

## Fortified wines

In Port and other mutage styles the addition of spirit arrests yeast and bacteria alike, so the wine keeps its malic acid; the resulting freshness under high sugar and alcohol is part of the style, and the absence of MLF here is a structural rather than an incidental fact.

## Impacts beyond flavour

MLF also carries risks that shape whether it is used at all: volatile acidity if Lactobacillus or Pediococcus dominate, biogenic amines including histamine, mousiness, and geranium taint if sorbate meets lactic acid bacteria. Against that, a completed MLF is a microbiological insurance policy: a wine with no malic acid left has nothing for lactic acid bacteria to act on in bottle, which is why it can be bottled with less SO2 and looser filtration than a malic-retaining wine of the same style. That trade-off — flavour freedom bought with handling cost, or handling freedom bought with flavour change — is the real substance of the decision.

## Conclusion

MLF changes style in three ways at once — it lowers and softens acidity, it adds or masks aroma through diacetyl and lees, and it settles the wine's microbial fate. Its absence is an equally deliberate stylistic act, bought with sulphur, cold and filtration.

questionText: What are the winemaker's options and challenges in colour management for different wine styles?
body:
## Introduction

Colour management means hitting a target hue and intensity for the style, and then holding it through bottling and shelf life. It runs across every category — pale whites, rosés at a commercially specified shade, deeply coloured reds, amber skin-contact whites, blanc de noirs sparkling, tawny fortified — and the target may equally be maximum colour, minimum colour, or a particular oxidised colour. I take the options first, by style and in process order, then the harder half: the challenges of fixing the colour and of defending it against rot, oxygen, fining and time.

## Where colour comes from

Anthocyanins sit in the hypodermal cells of the grape skin; the pulp is colourless in almost all varieties, the teinturiers such as Alicante Bouschet and Saperavi being the exception that proves the rule. Extraction is therefore a skin-contact decision. Anthocyanins are water-soluble and extract early — within the first few days — whereas tannin needs ethanol and extracts late, which is the asymmetry every red winemaker exploits.

## The options, by style

*White wines.* The task is to prevent colour. Whole-bunch pressing at low pressure, cutting hard press fractions, and SO2 at crush of the order of 50 mg/L to inhibit polyphenol oxidase all limit phenolic pick-up. The counter-intuitive option is hyperoxidation: deliberately oxidising the must so that browning precursors polymerise and are removed as solids, leaving a wine that is paler and more stable thereafter. PVPP and casein fining remove existing browning.

*Rosé.* Three routes, and the choice sets both colour and structure. Direct pressing of red grapes gives the palest wines, in the Provençal manner. Short maceration, typically two to twelve hours, gives more colour and more phenolic weight. Saignée bleeds juice off a red ferment, giving a deeper wine and, as a by-product, a more concentrated red — but the rosé is a residual, not a designed wine. Blending red and white is prohibited for still rosé in the EU, and permitted for Champagne.

*Red wines.* Cold soak at 8 to 12 degrees Celsius extracts anthocyanin with little tannin; warmer ferments, longer cap contact and more frequent pump-overs extract more of both. Pectolytic and maceration enzymes raise the extraction rate. Thermovinification and flash détente, heating the must to around 70 to 80 degrees Celsius, deliver colour with very little tannin, which is exactly the specification for a soft commercial red.

*Skin-contact whites, sparkling and fortified.* Extended maceration of white grapes makes deliberately amber wine. In sparkling, a blanc de noirs depends entirely on press fractions taken gently enough to leave the skins unbroken. In fortified wine, Port fixes colour by extracting hard before spirit arrests everything, while tawny and Madeira styles pursue the opposite: colour deliberately oxidised to amber over years in cask.

## Fixing the colour: pH, tannin and stability

Extracting colour is the easy part. Free anthocyanin is unstable and its colour is pH-dependent: at typical wine pH of the order of a quarter of free anthocyanin sits in the coloured flavylium form, the rest being colourless or blue-shifted. Acidification with tartaric acid therefore brightens and intensifies colour directly, and it also improves microbial stability — one adjustment doing two jobs.

Lasting colour is polymeric. Anthocyanins condense with tannins, often via acetaldehyde bridges, into pigments that are stable and no longer bleached by SO2. This is why tannin management and colour management are the same problem: adding oenological tannin at crush supplies condensation partners, controlled oxygen through pump-over, micro-oxygenation or barrel ageing supplies the acetaldehyde, and co-pigmentation with colourless phenolics stabilises colour in the short term. Oxygen is therefore not the enemy here but a tool, dosed deliberately.

## The challenges

*Rot.* Botrytis-infected fruit brings laccase, which oxidises anthocyanins rapidly and, unlike the grape's own polyphenol oxidase, is not controlled by SO2. It causes oxidasic casse and irreversible colour loss. The answers are sorting, rapid processing, heat treatment to denature the enzyme, and bentonite.

*Oxidation post fermentation.* Uncontrolled ullage, sloppy racking and high dissolved oxygen brown a white and turn a red from purple towards brick. Deliberate oxidation is a style; accidental oxidation is a defect, and the difference is whether it was measured.

*Subtractive losses.* Fining is the commonest cause of unintended colour loss: gelatin and egg albumen strip pigmented tannin, PVPP strips browning but also colour, and over-fining cannot be reversed. Tight pad and membrane filtration removes colloidal colour. Colouring-matter deposit in bottle, metal casse from iron and copper, and light strike in clear rosé bottles complete the list.

*SO2 bleaching.* Free anthocyanin binds SO2 reversibly and loses its colour, so a young red looks markedly paler immediately after a sulphur addition and a rosé can appear to have lost its shade. The winemaker must know this is temporary and partial, and must not respond by re-extracting or by cutting the SO2 the wine needs for protection — a real trap when colour is being judged against a specification.

*Measurement and consistency.* All of this is only manageable because colour is quantifiable — absorbance at 420, 520 and 620 nm, or CIELab coordinates — against a specification that a retail buyer will hold the producer to, vintage after vintage.

questionText: Examine the pros and cons of skin contact during the winemaking process.
body:
## Definition and approach

Skin contact is any period during which juice or wine is in contact with grape skins, and with the seeds and pulp fragments that accompany them, from the moment the berry is broken until the solids are separated by pressing or draining. It therefore covers pre-fermentation maceration, fermentation on skins, post-fermentation maceration, and the incidental contact that occurs inside a press. The first summary point worth making is that every wine experiences some skin contact: even a whole-bunch-pressed Champagne base has juice moving across skins under pressure. The question is not whether, but how long, how warm, how vigorous and how oxidative.

I examine it by wine category, because the extraction chemistry is broadly common but the risks and the commercial consequences differ sharply between colours and styles.

## White wines

The gains are aromatic and textural. Bound terpene precursors in Muscat and Gewürztraminer, and thiol precursors in Sauvignon Blanc, sit in the skin, so a short cool maceration of six to twelve hours before pressing raises aromatic intensity and adds mouthfeel and body — routine in Marlborough and for Pinot Gris in Alsace.

The costs are real. The same contact extracts phenolics that read as bitterness, raises potassium and therefore pH, picks up colour, increases protein and so the bentonite requirement, and exposes the must to oxidation and, on any rot-affected fruit, to laccase. It also slows the press cycle at the busiest point of vintage. The judgement is variety-specific: what flatters Gewürztraminer would coarsen Chablis.

## Skin-contact and amber whites

Taken to weeks or months — Kakheti in qvevri, Collio and Brda in a range of vessels — skin contact converts a white wine into a structurally tannic one. The pros are genuine: tannin and oxidative stability let these wines be made with very little SO2 and age far longer than their fruit alone would allow, and they are commercially distinctive. The cons are bitterness, loss of primary fruit, elevated volatile acidity and Brettanomyces risk under long unprotected maceration, and a narrow market.

## Rosé

Here skin contact is the whole design. Direct pressing gives the palest, most delicate wines of the Provençal type; a short maceration of a few hours gives more colour and more phenolic weight; saignée bleeds off a red fermentation, giving the deepest rosé but subordinating it to the red it was drawn from. The con is that colour and phenolics move together, so a producer chasing extra flavour risks both a shade the market has moved away from and a bitter finish.

## Red wines

Red winemaking cannot be waved through simply because skins are always present, because the whole craft lies in how much contact and of what kind. Skin contact delivers anthocyanin, tannin, flavour and the polymeric pigment that gives colour stability and ageing capacity. Different routes reach the same place: gentle punch-down in a small open vat, pump-over in a tall tank, and a rotary fermenter can each arrive at a soft, well-coloured wine, the last in two or three days rather than ten. The same technique can serve opposite ends — punching down infrequently and gently for a delicate Burgundian infusion, or hard and often for maximum extraction from the same fruit.

The risks are equally specific: over-extraction of hard seed tannin once alcohol is high, acetic bacteria and ethyl acetate on an exposed cap, Brettanomyces during a long post-fermentation maceration, potassium-driven pH rise, and the plain capital cost of tank time.

## Sparkling, fortified and sweet wines

In traditional-method sparkling the object is to minimise contact: whole bunches, gentle low-pressure pressing and discarded later fractions, because phenolic bitterness is merciless in a bone-dry, low-dosage wine and because black grapes must give white juice. The exception, Champagne rosé by saignée, shows contact used deliberately for colour.

In Port the extraction window is tiny — everything must be pulled from the skins in two or three days before spirit arrests fermentation — which is why lagares, foot treading and robotic treaders exist. In Tokaji, macerating aszú berries in must for of the order of twelve to thirty-six hours is skin contact under another name, extracting sugar, flavour and phenolics; in Sauternes the opposite choice is made, whole bunches pressed gently to keep laccase-borne oxidation and bitterness out. Two sweet wines of comparable stature, and opposite answers to the same question — which is the point about context.

In Sherry the fruit is pressed quickly and lightly, because Palomino's phenolics would coarsen a wine that must then spend years exposed to oxygen or to flor; extraction here would be the enemy of a style built on what happens after fermentation.

## Conclusion

Skin contact is the winemaker's principal lever on structure, and its pros and cons are the same phenomenon read in two directions: everything it adds — phenolics, colour, aroma precursors, potassium, ageing capacity — it adds together, along with exposure to oxygen and to microbes. The notable trend of the past decade is that whites have moved towards more extraction and reds towards less, which suggests the profession now treats skin contact less as a default setting and more as a dial to be set per wine.

questionText: What are the most common causes of bacterial spoilage in wine? What effect do they each have, and what measures can be employed to guard against them? Your answer may consider the whole grape growing and winemaking process.
body:
## Definition and scope

Spoilage is microbial activity that produces a sensory or compositional defect making the wine less palatable, unstable or unsaleable. It is not the same as microbial presence: *Oenococcus oeni* conducting a clean malolactic fermentation is not spoilage, while the same genus of organism working on residual sugar in a stuck fermentation is.

The question asks specifically about bacteria, so I exclude the fungi and yeasts that are commonly confused with them. *Brettanomyces* is a yeast; botrytis, powdery mildew and downy mildew are fungi; TCA arises from fungal methylation of chlorophenols; reduction is a chemical, yeast-derived phenomenon. The bacterial causes that matter in wine are two, with a third minor case: acetic acid bacteria, lactic acid bacteria, and *Zymomonas* in sweet fortified wines.

## Acetic acid bacteria

*Organisms and mechanism.* *Gluconobacter oxydans* dominates on damaged fruit, *Acetobacter aceti* and *A. pasteurianus* in wine. They are obligate aerobes: they oxidise ethanol to acetaldehyde and then to acetic acid, and esterify acetic acid with ethanol to ethyl acetate.

*Effect.* Volatile acidity gives vinegary sharpness and, more damagingly, ethyl acetate, obtrusive from roughly 150 mg/L, gives nail varnish and glue. At low levels VA can lift a wine; past threshold it is a fault, and past the EU limit of 1.2 g/L for red wine and 1.08 g/L for white and rosé the wine cannot legally be sold. Acetaldehyde additionally binds SO2, so a spoiling wine needs ever more preservative to stay protected.

*Measures.* Oxygen exclusion is the whole defence, because these bacteria cannot work without it: keep tanks full, top barrels, gas headspaces with nitrogen or CO2, avoid a dry exposed cap during long macerations, and check dissolved oxygen at transfers. Maintain molecular SO2 of 0.5 to 0.8 mg/L, which at pH 3.4 means about 20 to 32 mg/L free SO2 and at pH 3.7 roughly double that - a reminder that pH control is a microbiological measure. Add cellar hygiene, clean and sulphured barrels, cool storage, and regular VA analysis so a rise is caught while it is still blendable.

## Lactic acid bacteria

*Organisms.* *Oenococcus oeni*, *Lactobacillus* species such as *L. brevis* and *L. hilgardii*, and *Pediococcus damnosus*. All are tolerant of alcohol and low oxygen, so they are the harder problem: unlike acetic bacteria, they thrive in a sealed tank.

*Effects.* Where sugar remains — a stuck or sluggish fermentation — heterofermentative LAB ferment it to lactic and acetic acid, the classic *piqûre lactique*, and metabolise fructose to mannitol, giving a viscous sweet-sour wine. *Pediococcus* and *Lactobacillus* produce exopolysaccharides that make a wine ropy and oily. Both genera, and *Oenococcus* too, can produce the tetrahydropyridines responsible for mousiness, which is undetectable on the nose and appears retronasally as the mouth's higher pH releases the volatile base. Excess diacetyl overwhelms a wine with butter. Tartaric acid degradation, *tourne*, produces gas, haze and a flat palate. Biogenic amines — histamine, tyramine, putrescine — carry health and export consequences rather than sensory ones. And if sorbic acid has been added, LAB convert it to the compound responsible for geranium taint.

*Measures.* The primary control is denying them a substrate: ferment cleanly to dryness with adequate yeast assimilable nitrogen and sound temperature control, so no sugar is left for them to spoil. If MLF is wanted, inoculate a large, healthy *Oenococcus oeni* population to outcompete *Lactobacillus* and *Pediococcus*, and sulphur promptly on completion — a wine sitting post-MLF without SO2 is the single most vulnerable state in the cellar. Keep pH down; above about pH 3.5 the spoilage species become competitive and SO2 becomes ineffective at the same time. Lysozyme, typically dosed at 250 to 500 mg/L, is active against these Gram-positive bacteria and is the standard tool for blocking MLF or arresting a spoiling one, though it does not touch acetic bacteria. Never use sorbate in a wine that may see LAB. Finally, filtration: a 0.45 micron membrane removes them at bottling, backed by a sterile filler.

## Zymomonas

In sweet and fortified wines *Zymomonas mobilis* ferments residual sugar, producing haze, gas and hydrogen sulphide. It is controlled by sterile filtration and sound SO2, and it is worth knowing because it is the one bacterium that survives conditions designed to stop the others.

## In the vineyard

The vineyard contribution is narrow but decisive: the bacterial load arriving at the winery comes almost entirely from damaged fruit. Botrytis, sour rot, hail, bird and insect damage and split berries carry high populations of acetic acid bacteria and already-elevated VA and gluconic acid, and no cellar practice fully recovers from that. Canopy management for airflow, timely spray programmes, careful harvest, sorting, cool transport and SO2 at reception are therefore microbiological measures, not merely quality ones.

## Conclusion

Bacterial spoilage reduces to a short list of controllable variables: oxygen, sugar, pH, SO2, temperature and hygiene. Acetic bacteria are beaten by excluding air; lactic acid bacteria by leaving them nothing to eat and then removing them.

questionText: What should a winemaker's main considerations be when preparing a finished wine for bottling?
body:
## Scope

Preparing a finished wine for bottling is the process of making a wine that is already stylistically complete into one that is safe to seal: stable in the bottle for its intended shelf life, analytically within specification, and legally saleable in its destination markets. The bottling line, its hygiene and the dry goods are a separate discipline, and I set them aside deliberately; my subject is the thinking about the wine. Three questions govern it — is it stable, what do the numbers say, and is it legal — and behind all three sits a fourth, which is time, because several of these operations have lead times of days or weeks.

## Stability

*Microbiological.* The wine must not referment or be spoiled in bottle. That means confirming it is dry and that malolactic fermentation is either complete or securely blocked - below the enzymatic detection limits of roughly 0.1 g/L of residual sugar and 0.05 g/L of malic acid - and then deciding the filtration specification. A 0.45 micron membrane retains yeast and most spoilage bacteria; a cleaner wine destined for early drinking may go through at 0.65 micron to avoid stripping. Any wine bottled with fermentable sugar must be sterile-filtered and filled aseptically. The plating result and any *Brettanomyces* count drive that decision.

*Protein.* Whites and rosés must pass a heat test, otherwise a haze appears on a warm shelf. Bentonite trials establish the dose, and the addition must be made and settled before the final filtration, not after.

*Tartrate.* Conductivity or a cold test establishes the risk. The decision is between cold stabilisation, which occupies a chilled tank for days, and an in-line addition of carboxymethylcellulose, metatartaric acid or potassium polyaspartate. CMC is not compatible with a protein-unstable white, so the two stability decisions interact and must be taken in the right order.

*Oxidative and metal.* Dissolved oxygen at filling, and total package oxygen, determine how the wine ages; iron and copper are checked for casse risk and as pro-oxidants. Colour stability, and pinking potential in a white, are assessed at the same point.

## Chemical analysis

Analysis is a decision tool, not a record. Free and total SO2, read against pH, set the addition made immediately before filling: the target is molecular SO2 of about 0.5 mg/L in a dry red and 0.8 mg/L where sugar is present, so the required free SO2 roughly doubles for every 0.3 rise in pH. Alcohol, residual sugar, titratable acidity, pH, volatile acidity, malic acid, turbidity and dissolved oxygen complete the standard panel. Each figure is compared with three references: the legal limit, the customer's specification, and the producer's own house style. A supermarket buyer's analytical specification is frequently tighter than the law, and a wine failing it is rejected on delivery.

## Legal conformity

SO2 is where an MW candidate is expected to be exact. The EU permits 150 mg/L total SO2 for a dry red and 200 mg/L for a dry white or rosé, rising by 50 mg/L once residual sugar reaches 5 g/L and to 400 mg/L for the sweetest categories; the United States sets a single total ceiling of 350 mg/L; organic wine in the EU is held some 30 to 50 mg/L below the conventional figures. Volatile acidity has its own ceiling, 1.2 g/L for reds in the EU, and alcohol must be within a labelling tolerance of 0.5 per cent abv.

Beyond that, the winemaker must confirm that every additive used is permitted in the destination market — the permitted lists differ between the EU, the US and Australia, and an additive legal at home can make a shipment unsaleable abroad. Allergenic fining agents from egg, milk or fish must be declared unless residues are below the threshold, and contaminant screens for ochratoxin A and, for some markets, heavy metals and pesticide residues, are part of the release decision.

## Additives beyond sulphur dioxide

SO2 is the one candidates always know; the others are where the marks are. Ascorbic acid is used with SO2 on whites to scavenge oxygen at filling, and is actively harmful without adequate SO2 because its own oxidation product is hydrogen peroxide. Dimethyl dicarbonate at up to 200 mg/L and sorbic acid at up to 200 mg/L are the two microbial insurance options for an off-dry wine — DMDC hydrolyses away and leaves no residue, sorbate persists and risks geranium taint if lactic acid bacteria are present. Gum arabic protects colour and mouthfeel; copper is capped at 1 mg/L and metatartaric acid at 100 mg/L; nitrogen and CO2 are adjusted, since dissolved CO2 of a few hundred milligrams per litre lifts a crisp white and coarsens a soft red.

## Conclusion

The main considerations are therefore stability, analysis and legality, taken together and in the right sequence. The discipline that distinguishes a good winemaker here is planning backwards from the bottling date, because bentonite, cold stabilisation and a rejected analysis all cost time the calendar may not have.
