questionText: Consider the key issues for storage of wine after packing is complete.
body:
## Scope, and the one variable that dominates

Once a wine is packed it stops being a winemaking problem and becomes a physical asset with a shelf life, held in a warehouse, a distributor's facility or a retailer's back room. I am concerned here with static storage and deliberately not with transport, which raises its own issues of transit temperature and handling. Six issues matter: temperature, humidity, light, taint, closure behaviour over time, and stock management. They are not equal, and I will argue that temperature is the dominant one and that light and taint are the two most commonly neglected.

## Temperature

Temperature acts twice over. Chemically, wine ageing is a set of oxidative and hydrolytic reactions whose rates follow the Arrhenius relationship — as a working rule, reaction rates roughly double for every 10 degree Celsius rise. A wine held at 25 degrees is therefore ageing at something like four times the rate of the same wine at 5 degrees, losing fruit, gaining aldehydic and cooked-fruit notes and browning. This is why the industry standard for long-term storage is 12 to 15 degrees Celsius: cool enough to slow the reactions, warm enough to avoid tartrate precipitation and the cost of deep refrigeration.

Physically, warmth expands the wine faster than the glass, raising internal pressure until liquid is forced past the closure. Repeated cycling pumps wine out and air in, so the ullage grows and oxygen ingress accelerates — which is why fluctuation is more damaging than a steady moderate temperature. Weeping capsules and stained labels are the visible symptom, and they render stock unsaleable long before a consumer tastes anything.

## Humidity

Relative humidity of roughly 60 to 75 per cent is the working target, and the reasoning is more about packaging than about wine. Below that, exposed cork surfaces dry, labels curl and cartons lose rigidity. Above it, mould grows on labels, corrugated board loses compression strength and pallets slump — a genuine warehouse safety issue as well as a stock write-off. The often-repeated claim that low humidity dries a cork through and admits air is weaker than it sounds: the wine-facing end of a cork in a bottle stored on its side stays saturated regardless of room humidity. The honest position is that humidity is primarily a packaging integrity variable.

## Light

Light strike is the most under-managed storage risk because the damage is invisible until the bottle is opened. Riboflavin absorbs light in the near-UV and blue range and, in the presence of methionine, drives the formation of methanethiol and dimethyl disulphide — cooked cabbage and drains. Champagne and other low-phenolic whites in clear or pale green glass are the most vulnerable, which is why the fault has long been known in Champagne as goût de lumière. The evidence is unusually good here: the effect is reproducible within hours of supermarket fluorescent exposure. Controls are cheap and effective — dark warehousing, keeping cartons closed, UV-absorbing glass and dark bottles, and limiting display time under retail lighting.

## Taint from the storage environment

A warehouse can contaminate wine it never touches. Chlorophenols and bromophenols from treated timber, pallets, packaging board and fire-retardant coatings are methylated by moulds to chloroanisoles and 2,4,6-tribromoanisole, which migrate through closures and cartons into the wine at parts-per-trillion levels. There are documented industry incidents of whole warehouses being condemned this way. The controls are strict: no chlorine-based cleaning, no treated timber, no solvents, fuels or agrochemicals stored alongside wine, and periodic air and packaging testing. This risk is entirely avoidable and entirely disastrous when ignored.

## Closure behaviour and orientation

Storage duration must be matched to the closure. Natural cork has substantial bottle-to-bottle variation in oxygen transmission, which is the mechanism behind random oxidation and the reason two bottles of the same wine can differ after five years. Screwcaps with tin-saran liners transmit very little oxygen and can leave a reductive wine reduced; Saranex liners transmit more. A warehouse holding stock for a decade is therefore making a different decision from one turning it in six months. Orientation follows from this: horizontal storage is necessary for cork and irrelevant for screwcap and most synthetics, so the received wisdom needs qualifying rather than repeating.

## Stock management

Finally, the commercial issues. Strict rotation on a first-in-first-out basis, because a wine's value falls as its remaining shelf life shortens; accurate batch traceability and retained samples, so that a fault found in the market can be isolated to a pallet; stack heights within the cartons' compression rating; and, in bonded storage, duty-suspension compliance and security.

## Conclusion

The key issues, ranked, are stable cool temperature first, because it governs the rate of everything else; then protection from light and from environmental taint, both cheap to control and catastrophic to ignore; then humidity and closure-matched storage duration; and throughout, disciplined rotation, since the commonest reason a stored wine disappoints is simply that it was kept too long.

questionText:
Evaluate the prevention and correction of the following problems:

a. Pinking in a white wine made for drinking early
b. Phenolic bitterness in a red wine
c. High levels of volatile acidity in a full bodied red wine
body:
## a. Pinking in a white wine made for drinking early

*Mechanism.* Pinking is a salmon or onion-skin blush that appears in white wines made from certain varieties — Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Gris, Sémillon and Grenache Blanc among them. It is important to get the causation the right way round: pinking is a consequence of protective, reductive handling, not of oxidative handling. Colourless phenolic precursors related to the anthocyanidins survive a strictly anaerobic vinification, and then colour up when the finished wine meets a small amount of oxygen — at bottling, or on the shelf. A wine handled oxidatively at the juice stage has already lost those precursors to polymerisation and settling, and does not pink.

*Prevention.* The primary lever is therefore juice-stage oxygen. Deliberate must oxidation or full hyperoxidation on a susceptible variety precipitates the precursors before fermentation and is the most reliable prevention available. Beyond that: maintain adequate free SO2 after fermentation to keep the precursor reduced, avoid ascorbic acid, which is a documented aggravating factor, minimise oxygen pick-up at bottling, and screen the wine before bottling with a pinking susceptibility test, in which a small hydrogen peroxide addition is followed by an absorbance reading at 520 nm.

*Correction.* PVPP is the specific tool — it binds the low-molecular-weight phenolics responsible — at doses of the order of 10 to 50 g/hL, established by bench trial. Casein and activated charcoal also work, charcoal at real cost to aroma. Blending with an unaffected lot is the cheap answer where volumes allow.

*Verdict.* Prevention is cheap and correction is effective, so this is the least serious of the three problems. Because the wine is made for early drinking, the small aromatic loss from PVPP is a fair price and there is no ageing requirement to protect. My judgement is that the essential discipline is the pre-bottling test: an untested susceptible white is the one that pinks in the trade.

## b. Phenolic bitterness in a red wine

*Mechanism.* Bitterness is a taste, distinct from the tactile astringency with which candidates often conflate it, and it comes principally from low-molecular-weight phenolics — flavan-3-ol monomers such as catechin and their small oligomers. The sources are seeds, stems, unripe skins and hydrolysable tannins from new or poorly seasoned oak. High alcohol and low residual sugar sharpen the perception.

*Prevention.* Everything here is a vinification decision. Harvest at phenolic rather than merely sugar ripeness; destem where stems are green; avoid extracting seed tannin late in fermentation when alcohol is high, and use délestage to remove seeds from the vat; keep fermentation temperature and cap work proportionate to the fruit; press before dryness and keep hard press fractions separate; and choose oak by seasoning and toast rather than by newness alone.

*Correction.* Fining is the main route, and selectivity matters: PVPP targets exactly the small bitter phenolics; gelatin binds larger, astringent tannins and strips colour with them; egg albumen is the gentlest polish for a fine red; casein, and pea or potato protein for vegan specifications, sit between. Every one of these requires a bench trial, because over-fining removes colour and mid-palate and cannot be reversed. Micro-oxygenation and extended barrel and lees ageing help by polymerising phenolics into larger, less bitter forms. Gum arabic and a few grams of residual sugar mask rather than fix. Blending is usually the most efficient remedy of all.

*Verdict.* Correction is genuinely limited here — every subtractive treatment takes something else with it — so prevention carries far more weight than in part a. If the wine is already bitter I would blend first, fine with PVPP second, and accept a repositioned wine rather than fine it into hollowness.

## c. High volatile acidity in a full-bodied red

*Mechanism.* VA is chiefly acetic acid, produced by acetic acid bacteria acting on ethanol in the presence of oxygen, and by lactic acid bacteria on residual sugar; the associated ethyl acetate, which becomes obtrusive from roughly 150 mg/L, is what makes the fault smell of solvent. The sensory threshold in a full-bodied red is around 0.7 to 0.9 g/L, and the legal stop is the EU ceiling of 1.2 g/L expressed as acetic acid. Full-bodied reds are the vulnerable case: high pH, high alcohol, long maceration and years in barrel.

*Prevention.* Sound, unsplit fruit; rapid processing; adequate yeast assimilable nitrogen so fermentation finishes cleanly; never a dry, exposed cap; molecular SO2 at 0.5 to 0.8 mg/L maintained after malolactic fermentation, which is the moment of maximum vulnerability; disciplined barrel topping and barrel hygiene; cool cellars; and routine VA analysis so a rise is caught while the wine is still blendable.

*Correction.* Genuinely poor. The bacteria must first be removed by filtration and SO2, or the VA simply returns. Blending down against a low-VA lot is the practical answer and the arithmetic is simple. Reverse osmosis coupled with an anion-exchange resin does remove acetic acid, but it is costly and its permissibility varies by jurisdiction.

*Verdict.* This is the most serious of the three, because it is progressive and barely reversible. Prevention is effectively the only real answer, and a modest VA that lifts a big red is a judgement, not a licence.

questionText: Who is making money in the wine industry and why? Discuss in detail three specific examples of profitable wine businesses from different parts of the wine industry supply chain.
body:
## How I am measuring "making money"

Revenue is not profit, and profit is not return. I judge each business below on operating margin and on the return earned on the capital it employs, because this industry's characteristic trap is a respectable margin earned on an enormous asset base — land, oak and slow-moving stock — that destroys the return. Two propositions frame the answer. First, money is made where there is either a structural barrier to entry or ownership of the customer relationship; it is almost never made by growing grapes. Second, my three examples sit deliberately at different points of the chain — an input supplier, a brand owner and a retailer — and each earns its money by a different mechanism.

## Inputs: Corticeira Amorim

Amorim is the world's largest cork producer, listed in Lisbon and therefore publicly accountable. It runs a high-teens EBITDA margin, on trade estimates, on annual sales in the hundreds of millions of euros, sustained through a decade in which its customers' own fortunes swung violently.

Three things explain that. Supply is structurally constrained: cork oak takes decades to reach first harvest and, under Portuguese conservation law, may be stripped only roughly once a decade, and the forest is concentrated in Portugal and Spain, so no competitor can buy its way into the position at any price. Demand is fragmented: Amorim sells to tens of thousands of wineries, almost none of which has purchasing leverage over it. And it answered the screwcap threat by investing in TCA remediation and then segmenting a commodity into a graded range with a premium technical tier, converting a price-taker into a price-setter.

This is the picks-and-shovels position, and it is the most dependable profit in wine: sell *to* the industry rather than *in* it and you are indifferent to which brand wins.

## Brand ownership: LVMH's Wines and Spirits division

Moet Hennessy reports a recurring operating margin of roughly 30 per cent — several times what a good branded still-wine business earns, and earned on Champagne and cognac rather than on any technical advantage.

The mechanism is legally guaranteed scarcity plus ownership of the route to market. Champagne's appellation area is fixed by law, so the raw material cannot expand with demand; LVMH owns a large vineyard holding, contracts much of the rest, and releases stock against demand rather than clearing it. It then owns distribution in most significant markets, so it captures the importer's and often the distributor's margin as well as the producer's, and it controls how the price is presented at the point of sale rather than surrendering that to a third party. Marketing spend at a scale no independent house can match defends the price. Return on capital stays high despite very heavy ageing inventory because the price per bottle carries it.

Costco is widely regarded as one of the largest wine retailers in the world by value, and it repays close reading because it does not make its money on the wine. It is widely reported to cap its mark-up in the mid-teens percentage range on branded goods and its own Kirkland Signature label - well below a supermarket's typical wine gross margin.

Wine is therefore a traffic-driving, basket-building category carried at a deliberately thin margin to make the membership renewal feel earned. Return on capital is nonetheless high, because a narrow range turns very fast against extended supplier payment terms: the wine is sold before it is paid for, so the supply chain's working capital funds the retailer. The commercial consequence for producers is severe — enormous volume against very few SKUs, a landed price dictated by the mark-up cap, and enough scale to commission own-label bottlings from suppliers who cannot afford to decline.

## Who is not making money

The counter-case proves the rule. The grower earns least: he carries the land, the capital and the vintage risk, sells into a market that publishes his price, and owns no brand. Mid-sized family estates are squeezed hardest — too small for scale economics, too large to sell out at the cellar door, carrying a winery that is idle for most of the year. Vineyard land in the most prestigious appellations returns very little against its capital value, and is bought for reasons other than yield.

## Conclusion

Money is being made by those selling inputs into a fragmented industry, by those owning protected scarcity and the distribution that monetises it, and by retailers large enough to treat the wine as a means to another end. What unites all three is that none of them is a price-taker. The businesses losing money are those that own the most capital and control the least of the final price — which is to say most of the people who actually grow grapes and make wine.

questionText: There is much talk of consolidation in the wine industry, but where is the industry fragmenting and why? Give examples of businesses that are succeeding as a result.
body:
## Consolidation and fragmentation are the same phenomenon

Both are happening at once, and for one reason: returns to scale are strongly positive in some activities of this industry and strongly negative in others. Scale wins where fixed costs are large and the product is undifferentiated — glass, closures, distribution, retail buying, high-volume brands. It loses where value comes from scarcity, place, story or proximity to the drinker, and where technology has removed the fixed costs that used to force producers to be big. So the question is not whether the industry is consolidating, but which activities have had their cost structure changed. I take four such areas, explain the mechanism in each, and name businesses winning as a result. I draw the examples from four continents deliberately: a fragmentation argument that only works in one market is an argument about that market.

## 1. Production — the capital barrier has collapsed

Making wine used to require owning a winery. Custom-crush and contract facilities, mobile bottling and mobile filtration, leased tank space and freelance winemaking now let a producer buy the whole production chain by the hour. The consequence is measurable: the number of bonded wineries in the United States has grown several-fold since the turn of the century, from roughly 2,000 to well over 10,000 on trade estimates, while the share of volume held by the largest few companies has also risen. Both tails have grown and the middle has hollowed out.

Who wins: virtual and micro-négociant businesses that carry no plant — Cameron Hughes in California built a business buying finished lots and selling them under lot numbers, with no vineyard and no winery. In Australia and New Zealand, contract crush has let a generation of small labels reach market without capital.

## 2. Route to market — the distribution moat has leaks

Distribution consolidated ferociously, and that is exactly what created the opening. In the United States the 2005 Supreme Court decision in Granholm v. Heald struck down discriminatory bans on interstate direct shipment, and direct-to-consumer sales have grown into a major channel for wineries too small for a distributor to bother with. Elsewhere, third-party logistics, bonded-warehouse fulfilment and low-cost e-commerce platforms mean a producer can reach a consumer without ever entering a distributor's portfolio.

Who wins: Naked Wines, which funds independent winemakers from subscriber deposits, was bought by Majestic in 2015 and eventually gave the merged group its name — a business that exists only because it needed neither distributor nor shelf. In Champagne, grower Champagnes bottled by récoltants-manipulants such as Egly-Ouriet and Larmandier-Bernier have taken value away from the houses they once sold fruit to, because sommeliers and specialist merchants will now buy 20,000 bottles a year direct.

## 3. Consumer taste — the discovery cost has fallen to zero

Fragmenting demand is the deepest cause. When information was expensive, the rational consumer bought the famous name; the brand was a substitute for knowledge. Search, social media and crowd-sourced reviewing have made discovery close to free, so obscurity is no longer a commercial death sentence, and a generation whose identity is expressed through the specificity of what it drinks now treats the famous name as a negative signal. Small volume becomes an asset rather than a handicap.

Who wins: Etna's producer count has grown substantially, from a handful of estates in the 1990s to well over a hundred today, and its producers sell at prices the same fruit could not have commanded as anonymous Sicilian bulk. Georgia's qvevri producers, Jura, the Canaries and England have all been recruited from obscurity by the same mechanism. Chapel Down raised significant capital through an equity crowdfunding platform, financing a new region's expansion from the enthusiasm of its own consumers rather than from a bank. Commentary and gatekeeping

The influence of a small number of critics rested on the economics of print: a handful of publications could reach everybody and nobody else could reach anybody. That fixed cost has gone, and with it the concentration. Vivino, CellarTracker and thousands of individual accounts have distributed the gatekeeping function to the point where no single voice moves a market as one once did.

Who wins: the aggregators themselves, and the producers who no longer need a critic's endorsement to be found.

## Conclusion

The industry is barbelling, not consolidating. It is fragmenting wherever technology has stripped out a fixed cost (production plant, distribution access, publishing, market research) and wherever value derives from being identifiable rather than reliable. It is consolidating wherever the opposite holds. The businesses succeeding at the fragmented end share one trait: they own a direct relationship with either the drinker or the specialist buyer, and therefore do not need the scale infrastructure that is consolidating. The businesses in real trouble are the mid-sized ones that need that infrastructure but are too small to command terms from it.

questionText: What is a "virtual winery"? Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of this business model.
body:
## What a virtual winery is

A virtual winery is a business that owns a wine brand and controls the specification of the wine, but owns neither vineyard nor winery. It buys fruit, bulk wine or finished lots, rents crush, tank, maturation and bottling capacity from third-party facilities, and puts its capital into stock, sales and marketing rather than into plant. The winemaker may be employed or contracted; what the business owns is the recipe, the label and the route to market.

The model is not new — the Bordeaux négociant houses, which for two centuries bought, blended, matured and shipped wine they had not grown, are its ancestor — but the modern version differs in being brand-led rather than region-led, and in being enabled by an infrastructure of custom-crush facilities, mobile bottling and a liquid international bulk market that the négociants never had. Its commercial context matters: it is growing precisely as consumers say they want provenance and authenticity, and that tension runs through everything below.

Working examples span the whole range of scale. Cameron Hughes built a business in California buying finished lots from wineries that needed the cash, and selling them under lot numbers with no vineyard, no winery and no fixed range. At the other extreme sits Kirkland Signature, contract-produced for a retailer in named appellations from Champagne to Napa — a virtual brand whose owner is also the customer. In between, the large contract bottlers in the United Kingdom and Germany underwrite most supermarket own-label, which is virtual winemaking by another name.

## The financial case

**Strengths.** Capital intensity is close to zero at the production end. A conventional winery is an asset used hard for six weeks and idle for forty-six, depreciating throughout; the virtual operator pays for it by the tonne and only in the years he wants it. Capital therefore goes into inventory and demand generation, which earn a return, rather than into stainless steel, which does not. Return on capital employed can be several times that of an estate of equivalent turnover. The model also flexes: in a short or expensive vintage the operator can simply buy less, or buy from another country, where an estate must harvest what it has and carry the fixed cost regardless. Start-up cost and, crucially, exit cost are both low.

**Weaknesses.** The same low barrier that let you in lets everyone else in, so margins are competed away and the model lives permanently on thin gross margin at high volume. There is no asset base to borrow against, which makes growth expensive to fund. There is no land appreciation — historically a very large share of the wealth created in wine has been capital gain on vineyard, not trading profit, and the virtual operator forgoes all of it. Input costs are exposed directly to the bulk and grape cycle with no owned supply as a hedge. And at exit, the enterprise value is brand goodwill alone, which an acquirer discounts heavily where there is no secured supply behind it.

## The brand case

**Strengths.** Freedom from place is a genuine marketing asset. The operator can build a brand around a consumer proposition, a price point or a style, and can move country or variety when demand moves — an estate is married to its appellation for a century. He can hit a retailer's price architecture to the penny, source multi-country blends, and launch and kill labels quickly. There is no cellar door, tasting room or visitor operation to subsidise, so the marketing budget goes where it converts.

**Weaknesses.** The brand has no story that a photograph can carry. Consumers, sommeliers and journalists increasingly ask who made this and where, and "we buy it in" is a weak answer in a market whose premium tier is built on provenance. The wine writer's visit, the vineyard imagery, the winemaker's name — the low-cost advocacy that estates get free — are all unavailable, so brand-building costs more in cash. Worst, the model is trivially replicable by the customer: if a contract facility can make your wine, the retailer's own-label team can commission the same thing, and your listing is your competitor's brief.

## The pragmatics

The practical constraints are where the model most often fails. Quality control is at arm's length in a compressed harvest window, and you queue for press and tank time behind the facility's owner, so you need your own winemaker physically present at vintage — an overhead the model's advocates rarely price in. Supply security is annual and unwritten: a good fruit contract can be outbid. Traceability and labelling compliance sit with the bottler of record, and appellation rules in Champagne, Rioja and Chianti Classico require bottling within the region, which closes a large part of the premium world to the model altogether. There is no protectable intellectual property in a blend, and the contract winery that makes your wine knows the specification exactly.

## Verdict

The virtual model is strong where wine behaves like a branded consumer good — high volume, defined price points, retailer-driven demand — and it is the cheapest sound way to enter a market or test a proposition. It is weak wherever value derives from place, because it structurally cannot own the thing the customer is paying for. My judgement is that it builds cash-generative businesses of low terminal value: excellent at making money, poor at accumulating worth, and increasingly exposed as the premium consumer's demand for authenticity hardens.

questionText: What are the most quantifiable signs that a wine brand is strong?
body:
## What "strong" has to mean before it can be measured

A strong brand is one that can command a price premium over the category and be repurchased without being bought — that is, without discount, without trade loading and without paying for the distribution. Everything measurable follows from that definition, and I structure the answer around it: four families of metric (price, distribution and rate of sale, consumer behaviour, and financial), then the three I would trust above all the others, then what the numbers cannot tell you. I am answering with measurements, not with a list of brands I consider strong, because a name proves nothing without the data behind it.

## 1. Price metrics

The purest evidence of strength is price achieved without support.

- **Price index against the category** — average selling price divided by the category average in the same channel. A brand consistently above 100 is capturing a premium for its name.
- **Percentage of volume sold on deal, and average depth of discount.** This is the single most revealing number on a scan-data report. Two brands can show identical rate of sale, but the one selling 60 per cent of its volume at a promotional price has bought that volume; the one selling 15 per cent on deal owns it.
- **Price achieved as a percentage of recommended retail.**
- **Price elasticity** derived from promotional response. A strong brand loses less volume to a price rise and gains less from a cut — its buyers are not shopping the price.
- **Successive annual price increases taken without share loss.** This is the hardest test a brand can pass.

## 2. Distribution and rate of sale

- **Numeric and weighted distribution** (percentage of stores, and percentage of category sales those stores represent).
- **Rate of sale per point of distribution per week** — the metric that separates a brand that is *bought* from one that is merely *stocked*. Distribution can be purchased with listing fees; rate of sale cannot.
- **Share of category value against share of shelf space.** A brand delivering more of the value than the facings is earning its place.
- **Listings retained through range review**, and the number of markets showing sustained repeat orders rather than one-off fills.

## 3. Consumer behaviour

- **Spontaneous and prompted awareness**, tracked over time — spontaneous is the meaningful one.
- **Household penetration** and **repeat purchase rate**, measured by Nielsen or IRI scan data off-trade and by Kantar Worldpanel or an equivalent household panel.
- **Share of requirements** — of the category volume a buying household purchases, how much is yours.
- **Conversion through the funnel**: awareness to trial to repeat. Wide awareness with poor conversion indicates advertising, not a brand.
- **On-premise by-the-glass listings and reorder rate**, where the brand is chosen by a professional rather than a shopper.

## 4. Financial and market metrics

- **Gross margin per case against the category**, and contribution after advertising and promotion.
- **Marketing spend as a percentage of net sales required to hold share.** A strong brand needs less; a rising ratio at flat share is an early warning that the equity is being rented.
- **Transaction value.** What an acquirer pays is the market's own quantification of brand equity: Constellation Brands paid of the order of $315 million for Meiomi in 2015 for a brand carrying essentially no vineyards or winery — the money bought consumer demand and nothing else.
- For fine wine, the secondary market is an unusually clean instrument: **secondary price against release price, Liv-ex trade volume, bid-offer spread**, auction sell-through rate, and the ratio of allocation demand to allocation offered.

## The three I would weight most heavily

Rate of sale per point of distribution; price realisation with low promotional dependency; and repeat-purchase rate. Each is chosen because it is hard to fake. A brand can buy awareness, buy distribution and load the trade to inflate depletions, but it cannot make a consumer take it off the shelf at full price and then come back. Together these three answer the only question that matters: does demand exist independently of what we are spending to create it?

## Limits of the numbers

Two caveats keep the answer honest. First, coverage is uneven — scan data is good off-trade and poor on-trade, DTC and travel retail sit outside most panels, and emerging markets have thin data, so a brand can look weak where it is simply unmeasured. Second, these metrics are lagging. They confirm strength that already exists; the leading indicators (search behaviour, sommelier advocacy, unprompted mention) are the least quantifiable of all.

## Conclusion

The most quantifiable signs of a strong wine brand are a sustained price premium taken with little promotional support, a high rate of sale per point of distribution, and a high repeat-purchase rate — corroborated by penetration, by the marketing ratio needed to hold share, and ultimately by what a buyer will pay for the name alone.

questionText: Do today's wine labels do a good job of communicating the most important information to consumers?
body:
## What the label is being asked to do, and for whom

A wine label has three jobs and they conflict. It must comply — carrying the legally mandated declarations. It must sell — winning a two-second glance on a shelf of two hundred competitors. And it must inform — telling the buyer what is in the bottle and whether it suits the occasion. "The most important information" therefore has no single answer: it depends entirely on who is holding the bottle. I take the question as asking whether the label serves the buyer's decision, and I answer it segment by segment, weighing what labels genuinely do well against what they conspicuously do not.

## Whose information? A segmented view

- **The engaged enthusiast and the trade** — a small minority of buyers. They want producer, vineyard or cru, vintage, alcohol, appellation, importer, sometimes dosage or residual sugar. They read the label as a technical document.
- **The involved but uncertain majority** — buy on grape variety, brand, country and price. They want style: is it dry, is it heavy, will it work with what I am cooking.
- **The occasion and gift buyer** — risk-averse, wants signals of appropriateness and quality at a price point: medals, brand familiarity, weight of glass, prestige cues.
- **The price-driven buyer** — needs price, volume and a familiar category name; almost nothing else on the label is read.
- **The health- and lifestyle-aware buyer**, increasingly the younger consumer — wants alcohol, calories, ingredients, additives, organic or vegan status.

## What labels do well

The mandatory content is accurate, enforced and consistent, which is not a small thing. EU and UK rules mandate net volume, actual alcoholic strength within a tolerance of 0.5 per cent, country of origin, bottler or importer, a lot number and a declaration of sulphites above 10mg per litre. Nothing else on the shelf in a supermarket carries an origin guarantee comparable to a protected designation.

Geographic indications are also, for those who hold the code, information of extraordinary density: "Chablis Premier Cru Montée de Tonnerre 2020" specifies grape, style, soil, climate, yield ceiling and ageing potential in five words. New World varietal labelling was arguably the single most successful communication reform in modern wine, and it worked because it answered the question the majority of buyers actually ask. Back labels, food-matching icons, sweetness scales such as the International Riesling Foundation's sweetness scale, and — belatedly — the EU's move to ingredient and nutrition declarations delivered off-label through a QR code all represent real progress.

## What labels do badly

The mandatory content is the information regulators wanted, not the information buyers want. "Contains sulphites" tells the consumer nothing actionable. Alcohol is stated but its meaning is not: a 250ml glass of a 14 per cent wine is three and a half UK units, and no label helps anyone work that out.

More seriously, the European system requires prior knowledge to decode. Chablis does not say Chardonnay, Sancerre does not say Sauvignon Blanc, and no classic appellation states whether the wine is dry — the one thing an uncertain buyer most wants to know. Sweetness is unstated on the great majority of still wines, and Prosecco labelled "Extra Dry" is sweeter than one labelled "Brut", which is not merely unhelpful but actively misleading. Quality-implying terms — Reserve, Vieilles Vignes, Grand Vin, Superior — are unregulated in most of the world. Château imagery attaches to brands with no château. Back-label prose is largely marketing ("hints of forest floor"), written for the enthusiast and unread by everyone else. And there is no drinking window, no serving temperature, no indication of whether the wine will improve.

## The verdict

No. Today's labels do a good job of complying and an excellent job of selling, and a poor job of communicating.

The evidence for that is behavioural: the whole apparatus the trade has built around the bottle — shelf talkers, staff recommendation, medal stickers, critic scores, aisle signage segmenting shelves by style rather than by origin, and phone apps that photograph the label to tell the consumer what it means — exists because the label itself does not answer the buyer's question. An information system that requires a second information system to interpret it has failed.

Segment the verdict and it sharpens. For the enthusiast and the trade, labels work well, and they are the people who write the rules. For the involved-but-uncertain majority, labels work only in New World varietal form. For the health-aware younger consumer — the fastest-changing segment and the one the category most needs to recruit — the label has until very recently told them almost nothing they asked for.

I would reject the counter-argument that decoding is part of wine's pleasure and that simplification cheapens it. Complexity that rewards the initiated is a barrier to recruitment dressed up as a virtue, and a category losing consumers to drinks that explain themselves cannot afford it.

questionText: What are the commercial advantages and disadvantages of packing/bottling wine in the local market of consumption? Is this trend a good thing for the wine industry?
body:
## Scope

By "packing or bottling in the local market of consumption" I mean shipping wine in bulk — flexitank or ISO tank — and packaging it at destination, whether into glass, bag-in-box, PET or can. I answer only the commercial case, as the question asks: costs, prices, margins, working capital, bargaining power and regulation. The technical arguments about oxygen ingress, stability and handling are real but are a different question, and I set them aside deliberately.

## Commercial advantages

**Freight economics, which drive everything else.** A twenty-foot container holds roughly 9,000 to 10,000 litres of wine in bottle, but around 24,000 litres in a flexitank. Shipping the liquid alone therefore moves more than twice the wine for one freight cost, and the difference is larger still when the glass, carton and pallet are also being carried across the world to no purpose. For wine selling below about £8 or $10 retail, freight is a material share of landed cost, so this saving is often the difference between a viable listing and no listing.

**Packaging bought locally.** Glass is the heaviest and usually the most expensive component. Buying it in market removes the freight on the empty bottle, lets the packer use lightweight and high-recycled-content glass to suit local deposit and packaging-tax regimes, and matches the carton and pallet configuration to the retailer's warehouse.

**Working capital and agility.** The bulk stock is a single undifferentiated asset until the moment of packaging, so it can be committed late. A packer can respond to a promotion in weeks rather than months, avoids obsolete finished stock in the wrong SKU, and carries far less write-off risk. For retailer own-label, where forecast error is punished immediately, this is decisive.

**Format flexibility and market entry.** Bag-in-box, cans, 187ml and retailer-specific pack sizes rarely justify a dedicated production run at origin. Local packing also lowers the minimum order quantity for a first listing, so entry costs less.

**Carbon as a commercial factor.** Retailers now carry published supply-chain emissions targets, and bulk shipping is one of the largest single reductions available to them. That converts an environmental argument into a listing criterion.

## Commercial disadvantages

**It forfeits provenance, and with it price.** "Bottled in the UK" is a weaker proposition than estate bottling, and the law makes the point for us: Champagne, Rioja and Chianti Classico among many others require bottling within the delimited zone. The model is therefore confined by regulation as well as by consumer perception to the commodity end of the market.

**It destroys pricing power.** Bulk is a brokered, spot-priced, specification-driven market with published indications. Once a wine is a specification rather than a bottle, the buyer can substitute origin at every renewal, and the producer becomes a price-taker in a market where he was previously at least partly a price-setter. This is the central commercial cost and it is structural.

**Value migrates out of the producing country.** The bottling margin, the packaging spend and the employment move to the consuming market, and the export value per litre falls. Spain exports more wine by volume than any other country and realises a markedly lower average price per litre than the major exporters, a difference driven substantially by the bulk share of its trade.

**Bargaining power concentrates.** Each major market has only a handful of large contract packers, so the producer swaps a diversified customer base for dependence on a small number of intermediaries who also serve his competitors.

**Brand and integrity risk.** Quality control at arm's length in another jurisdiction, with the liquid arriving unpackaged, raises the commercial exposure to blending, substitution and counterfeit — and the reputational cost of any such incident falls on the origin, not the packer.

## Is it a good thing for the industry? No

Individually rational, collectively damaging — that is my verdict, and I will defend it.

The test I apply is simple: where did the freight saving go? If local bottling made the industry better off, we would see it in producer margins. We do not. It has shown up in retail price points and in retailer margin, because the party that captured the saving is the party with the negotiating power, and bulk shipping increases that power by making origins substitutable. The trend is excellent for retailers, good for large brand owners who can arbitrage supply, and good for consumers. It is bad for producing regions, which lose value-added activity and see their average export price fall, and bad for the industry as a whole because it accelerates the commoditisation of the bottom two-thirds of the market — the two-thirds that most needs to escape it.

The exception I would concede is genuinely commodity wine. For a £5 bottle, shipping glass around the world is indefensible on cost and on carbon, and resisting bulk there is wasted effort. The industry's real task is not to fight the trend but to hold a firm line above it, and appellation bottling rules — often criticised as protectionist — are in fact the most effective commercial defence the producing regions have.

questionText: "The consumer's limited knowledge is a blessing for the wine industry." Discuss.
body:
## Scope, and the loaded word in the proposition

I read this as a question about the industry's balance sheet, not the consumer's. The claim is that a knowledge asymmetry between seller and buyer works in the seller's favour, and I test it as I would any other asymmetry: who captures the rent, at what cost, and over what horizon. Whether limited knowledge is bad for the drinker is a different question and I do not answer it.

"Blessing" is also loaded, and deliberately so. It implies not merely that the industry benefits passively but that it has an interest in the ignorance persisting — that the trade uses limited knowledge to its advantage. That reading is the one worth testing, because it is the one that makes the proposition uncomfortable. My conclusion, argued below, is that limited consumer knowledge is a short-term blessing to particular sectors and a long-term liability to the industry as a whole, and that the sectors it enriches are not the ones that carry the eventual cost.

## The blessing, sector by sector

**Producers.** Limited knowledge is what allows a wine to be sold on its label rather than its liquid. It permits generous latitude in what goes into a bottle: blending across sites and vintages, a wide tolerance on what "old vines" or "single vineyard" mean in practice, and the use of terms such as Reserve, Vieilles Vignes and Grand Vin, which carry no legal definition in most jurisdictions and which sell precisely because the buyer assumes they do. It also protects the mediocre. A consumer who cannot identify reduction, volatile acidity or premature oxidation will not return the bottle, and a producer who ships a flawed lot will hear nothing. That is a real, quantifiable saving.

**Retailers.** The asymmetry is the foundation of the modern wine aisle. Own-label works because the shopper has no benchmark against which to judge what the wine is worth, so the retailer captures a margin no branded supplier could. Deep-discount mechanics — an inflated recommended price against a permanent "half price" — function only where the consumer cannot value the wine independently. Category management by price band rather than by quality assumes, correctly, that price is being used as a proxy for judgement.

**Educators.** An entire profitable sector exists because of the gap. Wine education, from introductory courses to this examination, is a business whose addressable market is precisely the distance between what consumers know and what they wish they knew. A perfectly informed consumer base would abolish it.

**Commentators and journalists.** The same logic. Demand for a trusted proxy — a score, a recommendation, a list — exists only because buyers cannot judge for themselves. The critic's authority is a direct function of the reader's uncertainty, and the fine-wine market's dependence on scores is the purest expression of it.

**The fine-wine trade.** Scarcity narratives, en primeur, allocations and secondary-market pricing all rest on a buyer who accepts a valuation he cannot independently derive. It is not an accident that the periods of steepest price inflation coincided with the entry of large numbers of new and inexperienced buyers.

Taken together, this is a serious case. Across five sectors, limited knowledge lowers cost, widens margin, sustains pricing power and creates whole businesses. In the short term the proposition is simply true.

## The curse — what compounds over time

**It caps the category.** A consumer who does not know what he likes is a risk-averse consumer. He buys the same three brands, defaults to price as a signal, and does not trade up, because trading up requires the confidence to spend more on something unfamiliar. The industry's entire premiumisation strategy depends on a consumer who knows enough to want better — and that is the consumer the asymmetry prevents from existing. Beer and spirits have spent two decades simplifying and explaining themselves and have taken share while doing so.

**It makes fraud invisible until it is catastrophic.** Where buyers cannot detect adulteration, adulteration persists until a regulator or a journalist finds it, by which point the damage is category-wide rather than firm-specific. The 1985 Austrian diethylene glycol scandal, which cost Austria its export market for a generation, the 2008 Brunello di Montalcino investigation into unauthorised varieties, and the conviction of Rudy Kurniawan in 2013 for counterfeiting rare Burgundy and Bordeaux each punished honest producers hardest. Ignorance does not prevent the reckoning; it defers and enlarges it.

**It builds no loyalty.** A consumer whose choice rests on price and packaging can be taken by anyone with better packaging or a lower price — including, increasingly, categories that are not wine at all. The knowledge that the trade withholds is precisely what would make its customers hard to poach.

**It hands power to intermediaries.** If the consumer cannot judge, someone must judge for him, and that someone captures the value. Retailer buyers, critics and platforms have accumulated exactly the leverage that an informed consumer would have retained for himself — and producers pay for it in listing terms and margin.

**And the exploitation is a withdrawal, not an income.** Every unregulated quality term, every phantom château, every anchored discount spends a small amount of the trust the category holds. That account is finite, and the recent and rapid loss of confidence in alcohol's health claims shows how quickly a reserve of credibility can be drawn down.

## Which consumer?

The proposition is not uniform. For the novice, limited knowledge is a blessing to the seller and a barrier to entry to the category — good for the transaction, bad for recruitment. For the involved enthusiast, knowledge is what has driven the growth of every interesting margin in the trade over thirty years: grower Champagne, single-vineyard bottlings, obscure varieties, the entire specialist merchant sector. That business exists because consumers learned. For collectors and investors, limited knowledge is the ignorance the counterfeiter needs. For new buyers in fast-growing markets, it produced spectacular short-term prices for a few labels and a counterfeit problem that suppressed the same market afterwards.

## Verdict

The proposition is true for the short term and for parts of the trade, and false for the industry as a whole over any horizon that matters. Limited knowledge is a blessing to whoever is selling this bottle today and a liability to whoever needs to sell the next one at a higher price. It suppresses exactly the behaviour — curiosity, trading up, loyalty — on which the industry's stated strategy depends, and it converts every fraud into a category-wide crisis.

**What the other side gets right.** I concede the strongest counter-argument: no consumer market operates on full information, wine is genuinely and irreducibly complex, and an industry that waited for an educated consumer would sell very little. Some asymmetry is not exploitation but the ordinary condition of a specialist product, and the trade's job is to make the wine reliably good rather than to make every buyer an expert. That is fair. But there is a difference between tolerating an information gap and being organised around one — and the proposition, read honestly, describes the second.

questionText: How much should a consumer trust the words of a wine commentator?
body:
## Who is a commentator

The question collapses if the term is read narrowly. A wine commentator is anyone whose published or spoken words about a wine are intended to influence a purchase, and that is a very wide field: subscription critics and their scores; newspaper and magazine columnists; specialist publications funded by advertising; sommeliers recommending across a table; retail floor staff and buyers' shelf notes; educators; competition judges awarding medals; bloggers and social-media influencers; crowd-sourced platforms such as Vivino and CellarTracker, where the commentary is an aggregate of strangers; and the producer's own back label, which is commentary too, simply the least disinterested kind.

## And who is the consumer

Equally wide, and the answer differs for each. The complete novice, buying occasionally and mainly worried about making a mistake. The involved regular buyer with preferences but no framework. The enthusiast or collector, spending seriously and able to taste critically. The investor, buying wine he may never open. And the trade professional, who reads commentary as market intelligence rather than as advice.

"How much should a consumer trust" therefore has no single answer. It has an answer per pairing, and the interesting work is in the criteria that generate it.

## Six tests of trustworthiness

**1. Incentive and funding.** Who pays? Robert Parker built The Wine Advocate on a subscription model that took no advertising, and that independence was the source of his authority as much as his palate was. A publication funded by the advertising of the producers it reviews faces a structural conflict, however honourably its staff behave. A sommelier's list may be shaped by supplier support; a retailer's recommendation is constrained to what is in the building; an influencer paid per post is an advertisement with a first-person voice. None of these is disqualifying, but each changes the weight the words can bear.

**2. Disclosure and links to producers.** The test is not whether a commentator has relationships but whether they are declared. A critic who consults for estates, sells wine, brokers it, or accepts hosted travel is not thereby corrupt, but a reader who does not know cannot discount properly.

**3. Method.** Blind or not; tasted in one flight or over days; how many wines in a session; whether samples were solicited or supplied; whether the wine was revisited. A hundred-point distinction drawn from thirty seconds in a room of two hundred bottles is a precision the method cannot support. Competition medals deserve particular scepticism, because entry is paid and self-selected, so the population judged is not the population on the shelf.

**4. Track record and reputation.** The only real evidence. Has this person been right, in the sense that their calls survived contact with the bottle five and ten years later? Reputation built over decades of checkable predictions is the strongest signal available, and it is the one thing a new commentator cannot manufacture.

**5. Relevance and calibration.** A commentator can be honest, competent and useless to a particular reader. Trust here is a question of fit: whether the commentator's taste, price range and drinking window match the reader's. The correct procedure is to calibrate — buy several wines a critic praised, and find out whether you agree. Until then the score is a stranger's opinion expressed in decimals.

**6. Accountability.** Can the reader check anything? Published methodology, corrections, revisited notes and stable scales all raise trust. In 2008 Wine Spectator granted an Award of Excellence to Osteria L'Intrepido, a restaurant that did not exist — a submitted list and a fee were sufficient. That is what an unaccountable process looks like, and the lesson generalises well beyond that one award.

## Applying the tests

For the **novice**, the aggregate crowd is more useful than the individual expert. A Vivino average is a poor guide to quality and a good guide to whether most people enjoyed the wine, which is the novice's actual question. Retail staff are trustworthy on suitability and untrustworthy on comparison, because they can only recommend what they stock.

For the **involved regular buyer**, one well-chosen critic, calibrated against personal experience, beats twenty uncalibrated ones. This is where trust should be highest, because the cost of being wrong is a disappointing Tuesday.

For the **collector and investor**, the stakes invert the logic. Commentary moves price here, so the incentive pressure on the commentator is greatest exactly where the buyer most needs independence; and the conviction of Rudy Kurniawan showed how far provenance can be fabricated while expert palates around the table said nothing. High spending demands lower trust and more verification, not more deference.

For the **trade professional**, commentary should be treated as data about the market, not as a verdict on the wine.

## My answer

Trust the description; do not trust the verdict.

A competent commentator is genuinely reliable on matters of fact and near-fact: whether a wine is faulty, whether it is typical of its origin, whether it is sweet, oaked, tannic, ready. Those judgements are checkable, and consensus among good tasters on them is high. Trust there should be high.

The verdict — the score, the ranking, the buy recommendation — is a different object. It compresses an aesthetic judgement, a stylistic preference and an implicit price-value calculation into one number, and it is the part most exposed to incentive, to method and to the difference between the commentator's palate and yours. Trust there should be provisional and low until earned by a personal track record.

So my answer to "how much" is: considerably less than most consumers do, and in a specific way. A consumer should treat commentary as a filter that reduces two hundred choices to ten, not as an authority that selects one; should require to know who pays; and should invest the small effort of calibrating one or two voices rather than deferring to whichever score is nearest. Jancis Robinson uses a twenty-point scale, Parker a hundred-point one, and the difference is instructive — the finer scale implies a discrimination that no taster can reproducibly deliver, and consumers read the implied precision as certainty.

**The strongest case against my position** is that the alternative to trusting commentators is worse. A shelf holds hundreds of unfamiliar bottles; the consumer cannot taste before buying; and without commentary the default proxy is price, which is a far poorer guide to quality than a critic. Scepticism, pushed too far, produces paralysis or snobbery, and the crowd-sourced alternative simply substitutes an unaccountable many for an accountable few. I accept all of that. It is why my answer is not "do not trust" but "trust conditionally, and know what you are trusting them for". The commentator's proper role is to narrow the field and to describe accurately. The verdict was never theirs to give.

questionText: Which is more important in wine: tradition or innovation?
body:
## Definitions, and the difference that matters

**Tradition** is a practice transmitted across generations and valued partly *because* it is transmitted: its authority comes from having been done before. In wine it is codified more formally than in almost any other industry — appellation law is tradition with statutory force, fixing varieties, yields, training systems, minimum ageing and, in places, the shape of the bottle.

**Innovation** is the introduction into a context of a practice new to that context, adopted because it changes an outcome. Its authority comes from results, and it is context-relative: qvevri fermentation is tradition in Georgia and innovation in the Barossa.

The difference is therefore not old versus new but two different sources of legitimacy: tradition legitimises by continuity, innovation by demonstrated advantage. That matters for this question because it means they are not naturally in opposition. Most traditions are simply innovations that survived long enough to be forgotten as innovations.

**Important** needs defining too, because the answer changes with it. Important to what — the quality of what is in the glass, the survival of producers, the value the wine commands, the cultural inheritance, or the distinctiveness that makes wine different from other drinks? I take all five, and I argue the question along the chain from the land to the end user, because both forces operate at every link and an answer that examines only the cellar will mislead.

## In the vineyard

The case for tradition here is strong and often underrated. Site selection in the classic regions is the accumulated result of centuries of trial that nobody can now afford to repeat: the Mosel's steepest south-facing slate, the Côte d'Or's mid-slope, the *cru* boundaries of Barolo. Massal selection preserves genetic diversity that clonal nurseries narrowed. Bush vines, dry farming and high-density planting are traditional answers to heat, drought and poor soil that precision viticulture is now rediscovering with instruments.

The case for innovation is equally strong and, at one moment, was decisive: grafting European vines onto American rootstock after phylloxera saved European viticulture, and every "traditional" vineyard in France today rests on a nineteenth-century technological rescue. That is the single most important fact in this debate — the tradition survives only because of an innovation. The same pattern is running again: rootstock selection for drought, canopy management and later pruning for delayed ripening, precision irrigation where it is permitted, and disease-resistant varieties that cut fungicide passes.

## In the winery

Tradition's case: large old oak, concrete, ambient fermentation, basket pressing, extended lees ageing, solera systems, foot-treading in the Douro — practices retained not from sentiment but because they produce results that stainless steel and selected yeast do not. The recent movement of good producers *back* to these methods is the strongest available evidence that tradition encodes real knowledge.

Innovation's case: temperature-controlled fermentation, which from the 1960s made dry white wine possible in warm regions and effectively created the modern industries of Australia, Chile, South Africa and southern Spain, is a larger contribution to the quality of what most people drink than anything tradition has offered. Add inert-gas handling, refrigeration, hygiene, sterile filtration and cross-flow, and the plain fact is that faulty wine has become rare. Innovation raised the floor; tradition still largely defines the ceiling.

This link also shows the continuum most clearly. Amphora fermentation is a Georgian tradition adopted as an innovation in Friuli and Australia. Ripasso, once a domestic economy, is now a technique. Carbonic maceration travelled from Beaujolais as an innovation everywhere else.

## In packaging and at the point of sale

The screwcap is the clean case. It was an innovation against a five-hundred-year tradition; New Zealand producers organised a collective move to screwcap in the early 2000s, and it is now so entrenched there that it is the local tradition, while cork remains traditional and commercially necessary elsewhere. One generation converted an innovation into a tradition.

At the consumer end, tradition still does most of the selling. The consumer pays for Burgundy's *climats*, for Champagne's method, for Rioja's ageing categories — that is, for tradition made legible. Meanwhile the route to market has been reinvented: direct shipping, e-commerce, subscription, canned and kegged wine. Note which is which: innovation in how wine reaches the drinker, tradition in why the drinker wants it.

## What tradition is actually for

Before ranking, the strongest form of the case for tradition. Wine is not sold as a beverage; it is sold as a place, a history and a set of constraints voluntarily accepted. Strip those away and you have a well-made alcoholic drink competing on price against other well-made alcoholic drinks — which is the fate of every category that innovated away its identity. Tradition is what allows a hectare in Chambolle-Musigny to be worth what it is worth. It is also a genuine repository of knowledge: appellation rules are, at their best, the empirically selected answers to that place's problems, and their conservatism has repeatedly protected regions from fashions that would have cost them their distinctiveness.

## The ranking, since the question asks for one

If forced to choose — and the question does force it — I judge **innovation more important now, and tradition more important to value**.

Innovation is more important now because the binding constraints have changed. Warming, water scarcity, disease pressure, labour cost and falling consumption are problems tradition has no answer to, since tradition is by definition an answer to the conditions that produced it. Regions are already conceding this: Bordeaux approved six new varieties for its regional appellations in 2021, among them Touriga Nacional, Marselan and Alvarinho, and Champagne has admitted the fungus-resistant Voltis to trial. When the most tradition-bound appellations in the world amend their varietal lists, the argument is effectively settled on the ground.

Tradition is more important to value because it is the entire reason wine commands a premium over other agricultural products. Innovation raises the floor; tradition sets the price.

But the ranking is less interesting than the relation between them, and here is where I would rest the answer: in wine, innovation's usual purpose is to preserve a tradition, not to replace it. Grafting preserved the French vineyard. New varieties are being admitted so that Bordeaux can still taste like Bordeaux at two degrees warmer. Resistant vines are being trialled so that Champagne can keep farming Champagne. The two are not competing forces but a single mechanism with a long feedback loop: innovation earns its place by surviving into tradition, and tradition earns its keep by making the innovation worth undertaking. A region that has only tradition becomes a museum and dies of climate; a region that has only innovation becomes a factory and dies of price. The producers who will matter in twenty years are those who can tell which of their traditions carry knowledge and which merely carry habit.

questionText: To what extent is wine just another commodity?
body:
## What a commodity is

A commodity is a good defined by three conditions. It is **fungible**: one producer's output is interchangeable with another's, so the buyer is indifferent to source. It is **specified to a standard**: it can be graded, so that a contract can be written and settled without inspecting the particular lot. And its price is **set by a market rather than by the seller**, which makes every producer a price-taker. Wheat, copper and crude oil satisfy all three.

The word "just" adds a fourth test, and it is the one the question really turns on. "Just another commodity" implies not only that wine can be traded like a commodity but that there is nothing left over — no cultural, aesthetic or provenance value that resists the trade. So I ask two things of each segment: does it meet the three conditions, and if it does, is that all it is?

The answer varies so completely by segment that any single verdict on "wine" would be false. I take the four segments where the global trade actually operates.

## Grape contracts

At the fruit stage wine is unambiguously a commodity, and the evidence is that the market itself says so. Grapes are contracted by the tonne against a specification — district, variety, sugar, rot tolerance, sometimes a maximum yield — and the price is published: the California Grape Crush Report publishes average prices per ton by district and variety every year, which is precisely the price-discovery apparatus of a commodity market. Growers hedge nothing, take the posted price, and are substitutable within a district. When there is a surplus, contracts are not renewed and vines are pulled; when there is a shortage, plantings follow. This is agricultural commodity behaviour without qualification.

## Bulk wine

Finished wine traded in bulk is a commodity that has moved one step down the chain. It is quoted per litre by country, colour, variety, vintage and analysis; brokers such as Ciatti make a market in it; it ships in flexitanks, and a flexitank moves more than twice the wine of a container of packaged bottles, which is what made the trade viable at scale. Bulk wine now accounts for something approaching two fifths of the volume of world wine exports.

The commodity conditions are all met, and the consequence is exactly what commodity theory predicts: a buyer sourcing an own-label Chilean Sauvignon Blanc can switch to a South African one at renewal on a cent per litre, and the producer has no defence. Origin here is a specification, not an identity.

## High-volume brands

This is where the answer inverts, and it is the most interesting segment. The liquid inside a large commercial brand is bought as a commodity — often on the bulk market described above — but it is sold as something that is emphatically not one. The whole purpose of a brand is to defeat fungibility: to make the consumer unwilling to accept the identical wine under another label, and therefore to move price-setting from the market back to the seller.

So the same wine can be a commodity upstream and a differentiated good downstream, and the value created in that transformation is the brand owner's margin. The important implication is that commoditisation is not a state of the product but a position in the chain. It is happening most aggressively at the point where the wine is anonymous, and it is being actively resisted at the point where it meets the consumer.

## Fine wine

By any production definition, fine wine is the opposite of a commodity: non-fungible by construction, since the whole proposition is that this vineyard in this vintage from this producer cannot be substituted, and made in quantities that cannot expand.

And yet fine wine has been made to behave more like a commodity than any other segment. Liv-ex trades on a standard-in-bond specification, with settlement rules, published indices and a bid-offer spread; a case of a given château and vintage in bond is genuinely interchangeable with any other such case, which satisfies the fungibility condition exactly. Wine funds hold it as an asset class, en primeur is a forward purchase, and price is discovered on an exchange rather than set by the producer once the wine leaves the estate. The market has taken the least fungible product in the industry and engineered fungibility into it — not by changing the wine but by standardising the contract.

That is a genuine paradox and it deserves to be stated plainly: fine wine is not a commodity in production and is close to one in trade.

## Where the analogy breaks

The opposing case is strong and must be stated at full strength. Vintage variation defeats standardisation: a commodity is the same every year by definition, and wine is not, which is why no true futures market with delivery obligations has ever established itself. Supply cannot respond to price on a commodity timescale — a vine takes three years to crop and appellation rules often forbid expansion at all, so the elasticity that defines commodity markets is absent. Most wine is consumed within a year of purchase for reasons of pleasure, occasion and identity, which no commodity satisfies. And crucially, the industry's own economics depend on refusing commodity status: appellations, brands, scores, cellar doors and the entire apparatus of provenance exist to prevent substitution. An industry that spends its whole marketing budget resisting a description is evidence against that description.

## Conclusion

To a great extent at the bottom, hardly at all in the middle, and in a curious re-engineered form at the very top.

By volume, most of the world's wine is a commodity, and increasingly so: fruit and bulk are traded on specification and price, and the growth of bulk shipping has extended commodity behaviour further up the chain than it once reached. By value, most of the world's wine is not a commodity, because the value is concentrated in exactly the segments where substitution is refused.

I concede what the opposing case gets right: wine's cultural weight, its vintage variation and its inelastic supply mean it will never be *just* another commodity in the way copper is, and anyone who models it that way will misprice it. But I would not take much comfort from that. The commodity zone has been expanding, and it expands by taking wines that were sold on identity and re-describing them as a specification. The industry's central strategic problem is not whether wine is a commodity — it is which of its wines it is prepared to let become one, and whether the rest can be defended. Those defences are legal, cultural and reputational, and none of them is permanent.

questionText: Do government drinking guidelines make sense?
body:
## Scope and the two tests

A drinking guideline is non-statutory advice from a health authority on how much alcohol may be consumed at what level of risk. It is not law: the drink-drive limit, the purchase age and minimum unit pricing compel, whereas a guideline only persuades. That distinction runs through the whole answer.

"Make sense" admits two tests, and I apply both. **Internally**: is the guidance scientifically coherent, self-consistent and comprehensible? **Instrumentally**: does it achieve the purpose set for it? A guideline can pass one and fail the other, and in my judgement most of them do exactly that.

## What the guidelines actually say

The divergence between countries is the single most important fact in this question. The United Kingdom's Chief Medical Officers revised their guidance in 2016 to 14 units a week for men and women alike, spread over three or more days, and abandoned any claim of a safe level; a UK unit is 8g of ethanol, so that is roughly 112g a week. The United States Dietary Guidelines have advised no more than two drinks a day for men and one for women, on a standard drink of 14g — for a man, about double the British allowance. Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council recommended in 2020 no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than four on any one day, on a 10g standard drink. Canada's guidance moved in 2023 to a continuum of risk on which two drinks a week or fewer is described as low risk — a reduction of roughly an order of magnitude from its own previous advice. France advises a maximum of two glasses on any day and no more than ten a week, with alcohol-free days. Above all of them, the World Health Organization stated in 2023 that no level of consumption is safe.

The definition of the unit being counted also varies internationally, from 8g in the United Kingdom to around 20g in some European countries, so even the measuring stick is not common.

## What a guideline is for

Guidelines in public health generally do four things. They give a population a simple heuristic where individual risk calculation is impossible. They give clinicians and employers a threshold to work against. They anchor downstream policy — labelling, licensing, advertising codes, taxation. And they signal an official position, since a government that declines to state one has effectively said that any amount is acceptable.

Judged against those purposes rather than against biological precision, they are doing something reasonable and cheap.

## The case that they make sense

The underlying evidence supports the direction of travel. Dose-response relationships for alcohol with liver disease, several cancers and hypertension are well established, and the earlier "J-curve" showing cardio-protection at low doses has been substantially undermined by the recognition of abstainer bias — former heavy drinkers who quit through illness were counted as non-drinkers. Guidelines that moved downwards were responding to evidence, which is what one wants from them.

A heuristic is also necessary. Personalised risk is unknowable to the drinker; a number that can be remembered is worth more in practice than an accurate model nobody can use. And guidelines do real institutional work: they underpin the alcohol content and health messaging that now appears on labels, they give a doctor a language for a difficult conversation, and they legitimise not drinking, which matters socially.

## The case that they do not

**They cannot all be right.** The same global evidence base yields limits that differ several-fold between comparable countries. Either most of them are wrong, or the number is not really a scientific output at all but a policy judgement dressed as one. I think it is the second, and presenting a policy judgement as a biological threshold is where the credibility is lost.

**They are internally contradictory.** If there is no safe level, what is 14 units? A threshold implies safety below it and danger above it, and both authorities and campaigners now deny the first while continuing to publish the second.

**They are not understood or usable.** Very few drinkers know their national limit, and fewer can convert real drinking into it: a 250ml glass of 14 per cent wine is about three and a half UK units, so a quarter of the week's allowance is gone in one restaurant pour. A guidance system whose arithmetic defeats its audience has failed at the only thing it exists to do.

**They target the wrong distribution.** Alcohol-related harm is heavily concentrated in a minority of very heavy drinkers, and they are precisely the group least responsive to advisory numbers. The moderate majority who might comply were carrying modest risk anyway. So the instrument is aimed away from the harm.

**Nothing follows from breaching them.** Being non-statutory is presented as a virtue but means there is no mechanism at all beyond persuasion.

**The efficacy evidence is thin.** There is little good evidence that publishing guidelines changes consumption. The interventions with a measurable effect are price, availability and marketing restriction — Scotland introduced minimum unit pricing in 2018, and that class of measure has an evidence base that guidance alone does not.

## My verdict

Yes in principle, no as presently constructed.

Governments should state a position on alcohol; the alternative is silence that reads as endorsement, and the anchoring function for labelling and clinical practice is genuinely useful. To that extent guidelines make sense and should exist.

But most of them do not make sense as written. They express a policy judgement with a false air of biological precision; they contradict their own "no safe level" framing; they are not comprehensible to the people they address; they are aimed at the population least implicated in the harm; and there is little evidence that they work. Three changes would fix most of that: communicate absolute risk honestly — the United Kingdom's 2016 review anchored its number to a comparably small lifetime risk of death, and saying so plainly is more persuasive than any threshold — harmonise the standard drink internationally so the advice is at least commensurable, and stop pretending that advice can substitute for the pricing and availability measures that actually move consumption.

**The strongest argument against my position** is that I am demanding a precision no public health message can carry. Guidelines are not scientific statements; they are behavioural nudges, and nudges are allowed to be crude if they shift a population mean slightly in a good direction. On that reading, incoherence between countries is unimportant and my objection is a category error. I take the point seriously, and it is why my verdict is not that guidelines should be abolished. But a nudge that nobody can follow, in a direction nobody understands, backed by numbers that contradict each other across borders, is not a crude instrument — it is an ineffective one, and it spends public credibility that stricter and more honest measures will need.
