questionText: Temperature is one of the most impactful environmental variables on wine grape growing. How does temperature affect viticulture?
body:
## What makes temperature the "most impactful" variable

Impact here means two things: how much of the outcome a variable controls, and how little the grower can do about it. Temperature scores highest on both. It sets where vines can be grown at all, which varieties will ripen there, when every operation in the year happens, and how much disease pressure and how much crop the grower ends up with. Unlike nutrition, water on an irrigated site, or canopy density, it cannot be dialled in — it can only be selected for at planting and modified at the margins afterwards. Water availability is its equal in arid zones, and sunlight is bundled with it, so I would not claim primacy without qualification. But since the responses to temperature are almost all structural, it is the variable a viticulturist must get right first.

## The thresholds that matter

Vine shoot growth effectively stops below about 10C, which is why growing degree days are summed above that base and why site selection in marginal regions is really a search for accumulated heat. Green shoots are killed at roughly -1 to -2C, so a spring radiation frost after budburst removes the primary crop. Dormant vinifera buds survive to about -15C, with bud death common below -20C and trunk and root death below about -25C — the constraint that defines Ontario, the Finger Lakes, Ningxia and much of central Europe. Photosynthesis is most efficient around 25-30C and declines above that as stomata close; anthocyanin synthesis is inhibited above roughly 30C while malic acid respiration accelerates, which is why hot vintages give pale, low-acid, high-pH reds. Sunburn appears once berry surface temperature passes about 45C, well below air temperature on an exposed western face. Fruit set needs settled weather of roughly 20C: cold, wet flowering gives coulure and millerandage, an outcome Merlot in Bordeaux and Grenache across the south of France show most years.

## Cold-limited zones: protecting the crop and the plant

Where winter kill is the binding constraint the responses are structural and blunt. Growers hill soil over the graft union each autumn, or, in Ningxia and parts of Ontario, bury whole canes. They plant on slopes above the frost-draining valley floor and beside large water bodies — the Finger Lakes and Lake Erie exist as wine regions for this reason alone. They choose hardy varieties and, at the extreme, hybrids. Against spring frost the annual round is: delayed pruning to postpone budburst by a week or more, high trunks to lift buds out of the coldest layer, and then wind machines, sprinklers or bougies on the night — Chablis running water because it can also freeze the shoot in an insulating ice shell. Cover crops are mown or removed before frost season because bare, moist, compacted soil stores and re-radiates far more heat than grass.

## Marginal zones: chasing every degree

In the Mosel, Rheingau, Champagne and southern England the season's work is heat capture. Steep south-facing slopes and low training on single stakes put fruit close to warm slate; stony soils in the Médoc and Châteauneuf re-radiate at night. Leaf removal on the fruit zone after set raises berry temperature and degrades methoxypyrazines — essential for Cabernet Franc in the Loire, actively harmful in a warm year. Crop thinning brings a Pinot Noir crop to ripeness in a cool vintage. Row orientation, vine spacing and shoot number are all set against the heat summation the site can supply.

## Hot zones: shading, cooling and timing

Above the optimum the levers reverse. Growers retain the afternoon-side leaf wall and confine leaf removal to the morning face; they use sprawl or bush training so the canopy shades its own fruit, which is why goblet persists across La Mancha, Sicily and the southern Rhône. Kaolin films and shade cloth reduce berry temperature; overhead sprinklers give evaporative cooling during a spike where water permits. Site selection moves to altitude — Salta, the Uco Valley, the Sierra de Gredos — and variety to late-ripening, heat-tolerant Grenache, Mourvèdre, Assyrtiko and Touriga Nacional. Harvest is taken at night to deliver fruit cool, and picking dates are pulled forward.

## Soil temperature, humidity and a warming baseline

Soil temperature is the neglected half of the question. Dark, stony, well-drained soils warm early and advance budburst — an advantage in Germany, a frost liability in a warming spring. Wet clay stays cold and delays the whole season; mulch cools the root zone and buffers the surface. Temperature also acts through humidity: warm, humid conditions drive downy mildew and botrytis, while mild winters allow Pierce's disease and its vectors to overwinter, so a temperature change is also a spray-programme change.

Warming should be treated as a shift in these same thresholds rather than a separate topic. It advances budburst into the frost window, compresses harvest, decouples sugar from phenolic ripeness, and pushes varieties past their niche. The responses are the ones already listed — later-ripening varieties and clones, higher trunks, drought-tolerant rootstocks, altitude — which is precisely why temperature, and not weather in general, is the variable a grower plants against.

questionText: Water availability is increasingly an issue in some wine producing regions. How can a viticulturist best ensure water sustainability when establishing and managing vineyards in drought-prone regions?
body:
## Definitions and scope

Three words decide this question. **Availability** is how much water a grower can physically, legally and affordably obtain in a given season — a stock question. **Sustainability** is whether the rate of extraction can continue indefinitely without drawing an aquifer below recharge, taking a river below ecological flow, or salinising the soil — a rate question, and a different one. A vineyard can be water-available and wholly unsustainable, which is the condition of a good deal of the world's irrigated vineyard. **Drought-prone** means structurally arid: perennial rainfall well below evapotranspirative demand, not a run of dry vintages. I therefore exclude Bordeaux or Marlborough in a hot summer and confine the answer to places like inland Chile's Limarí, Mendoza, the Swartland and Klein Karoo, the Riverland and McLaren Vale, Paso Robles and the San Joaquin, La Mancha and Jumilla, Santorini and the Negev — sites under roughly 200mm of growing-season rainfall against an evapotranspirative demand several times that.

The answer has two halves because the question does: what is decided at establishment, and what remains available once the vines are in the ground.

## Establishing: where sustainability is actually decided

**Size the vineyard to the water budget, not the land.** The first act is a hydrological audit — aquifer recharge rate, licensed allocation, river flow and its trend, water quality and salinity. Mendoza's supply is Andean snowmelt with a declining trend; planting an area that only works in a full-snowpack year is the original error, and no in-season technique corrects it.

**Rootstock and scion.** Drought-tolerant, deep-rooting stocks — 110R, 140Ru, 1103P — rather than 101-14 or Riparia Gloire; Ramsey and Ruggeri where salinity accompanies aridity, as in the Riverland. Scions chosen for low water use and late ripening: Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan, Assyrtiko, Xinomavro, Touriga Nacional. This is the cheapest and most permanent lever available and it exists only at planting.

**Density, training and layout.** Low densities let each vine command more soil volume: dry-farmed bush vines at 1,600 vines per hectare across La Mancha and Jumilla are a water strategy, not a tradition. Santorini's basket-trained kouloura is the extreme case, harvesting dew and sheltering fruit where there is effectively no summer rain. Deep ripping before planting opens the profile so roots follow stored winter moisture down instead of sitting in a drip bulb.

**Irrigation design.** Drip or subsurface drip rather than the flood irrigation still widespread in Mendoza; storage dams to capture winter flow; and the decision to install monitoring — capacitance probes, dendrometers, a pressure chamber — at planting rather than retrofitting.

## Managing an established vineyard

**Scheduling, not volume.** The gains here come from knowing the vine's status. Regulated deficit irrigation holds a mild, measured stress from fruit set to veraison and relieves it before the vine shuts down; partial rootzone drying, developed in Australia, alternates wetted sides to trigger the stress signal at lower total volume. Both reduce application substantially without a quality cost; both require the sensors above.

**Reform the canopy and the training regime.** Transpiration is proportional to functional leaf area, so a large VSP wall on a dry site is a self-inflicted wound. Trimming to a lower canopy, reducing shoot number, moving to a sprawl or bush habit and shading fruit with the canopy rather than cooling it with water all cut demand.

**Change the fertilising regime.** Nitrogen drives vegetative growth and therefore water use; on a drought-prone site it should be low, split and delivered by fertigation timed to actual soil moisture rather than broadcast in spring. Compost and under-vine mulch raise organic matter, water-holding capacity and infiltration while lowering soil temperature — the single best in-vineyard improvement to the water balance. Cover crops must be terminated or restricted to alternate rows once they compete.

**Remove water-based frost protection.** Overhead sprinkler frost protection consumes more water in a few nights than the vineyard uses in a month. In a drought-prone region it should be replaced by wind machines, heaters, delayed pruning and higher trunks.

**Reduce losses and reuse.** Fix leaks and pressure-compensate the lines; recycle treated winery wastewater to the rows, as many South African and Australian wineries now do; desalinated supply underpins agriculture in parts of the Middle East and the Aegean islands.

## The legal and shared dimension

Water sustainability is rarely a decision one grower can make alone, and the better response works with the regulation. California's Sustainable Groundwater Management Act obliges basins to reach balanced extraction, which caps planting in Paso Robles regardless of a grower's own efficiency. Chile's water code allocates tradable rights that can be over-allocated relative to the river. Australia's Murray-Darling allocations are traded annually, so in a dry year irrigating a low-value block costs more than the crop is worth. Much of the EU restricts or prohibits irrigation in appellations such as Champagne and Bordeaux. A viticulturist must plant for the legal regime that will exist, not the one that exists now.

## Conclusion

Sustainability is settled at establishment — by matching planted area to a long-term water budget and by choosing rootstock, variety, density and training that need little water. In an established vineyard the grower can only improve efficiency: schedule with measurement, mulch, cut leaf area, strip out sprinkler frost protection and moderate nitrogen. Those measures are worth a great deal, but they cannot rescue a vineyard that was too large for its aquifer on the day it was planted.

questionText: Labour supply for vineyard work is decreasing in many parts of the world. If this trend continues, how will this affect viticulture, and how can vineyard managers around the world best prepare for, and handle, a shortage of workers?
body:
## Scope

This is a viticultural question, and I treat it as one: labour cost enters only where it decides which viticultural technique is viable. The real subject is which vineyard tasks can be done by machine, which cannot, and how a vineyard should be designed and staffed on the assumption that hands will be scarce.

## The global picture

The shortage is not uniform, and the responses differ with the cause. In the United States, tighter immigration enforcement and the cost and administrative load of the H-2A visa have shrunk the Latin American farmhand pool that California and Washington were built on, while an ageing existing workforce is not being replaced. In Western Europe, France, Germany and Italy depend on Central and Eastern European seasonal crews whose home economies now compete for them; the United Kingdom lost free movement of labour altogether. South Africa's vineyards have moved steadily toward mechanisation since minimum-wage reform and the 2012–13 farmworker disputes. New Zealand runs a managed Pacific-island scheme, the Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme, precisely because domestic labour will not do the work. In parts of the Middle East, growers in Lebanon have had to rely on displaced populations rather than a settled workforce. China and Japan face rural depopulation and ageing.

The common thread is that grape growing must remain profitable against these costs. Where fruit sells for a few hundred units a tonne, a task that can only be done by hand simply stops being done; where it sells for thousands, hand work survives. So the shortage does not affect all viticulture equally — it squeezes the middle hardest.

## Mechanisation through the vineyard's life

**Establishment.** Land clearing, deep ripping, levelling, laser-guided post driving and GPS-guided planting machines are all mechanised and were among the first tasks to be so. Grafting is done in the nursery. But training a young vine through its first three years — tying, desuckering, establishing the cordon — is hand work, and it comes at the point when the vineyard is earning nothing.

**Winter pruning.** The largest single labour item of the year, and the one that decides the answer. Spur-pruned cordons can be pruned mechanically, either fully or as a mechanical pre-prune followed by a light hand pass, which is standard practice across inland Australia and California. Cane pruning — Guyot in Burgundy and Bordeaux, the two-cane systems of Marlborough — resists mechanisation because cane selection and laying-down are judgement tasks. Converting a vineyard from cane to spur pruning, or to minimal pruning, is therefore a genuine viticultural response to a labour shortage, with real consequences for yield, bunch size and fruit exposure that must be accepted deliberately.

**The growing season.** Spraying, mowing, mid-row cultivation and under-vine weeding are fully mechanised, and autonomous and GPS-guided tractors are extending this. Trimming and leaf removal are mechanised, the latter by air-pulse and roller machines that now do a respectable job in the fruit zone. Shoot positioning and wire-lifting on VSP is hand work, which argues for movable foliage wires or a sprawl system. Bud rubbing, shoot thinning and green harvesting remain manual, and can partly be designed out by adjusting winter pruning load instead.

**Harvest.** Machine harvesting with on-board destemming and optical sorting now produces fruit good enough for serious wine, and it also delivers cool fruit at night, which hand picking rarely does. Grubbing up at the end of the vineyard's life is mechanical.

## What cannot be mechanised

Steep and terraced sites — the Mosel, the Douro, Côte-Rôtie, Priorat, the Wachau — cannot take a harvester, and monorails and winch tractors only partly close the gap. Untrellised bush vines and old, irregularly planted parcels defeat machines. Selective picking of botrytised berries in Sauternes and Tokaj, successive tries in the Layon, and whole-bunch delivery where the appellation demands it are irreducibly manual: Champagne requires whole bunches to be delivered intact to the press, which rules out machine harvesting there as a matter of law rather than preference.

The effect on viticulture, if the trend continues, follows directly. Plantings migrate to flat, uniform, machine-compatible sites; training systems simplify; marginal steep vineyards are abandoned, as vineyard area in the Mosel and parts of the Douro already shows; capital intensity rises and holdings consolidate; and the gap widens between fully mechanised volume production and a shrinking hand-tended premium tier that can carry the cost.

## Handling the shortage without mechanising everything

The second half of the answer is labour management. The best-placed vineyards employ a smaller permanent crew year-round rather than bidding for seasonal peaks: staggering pruning from early winter, filling gaps with trellis repair, soil work and machinery maintenance, and training each worker across pruning, tractor driving, spraying and machine operation. Cross-training converts an unskilled seasonal cost into a skilled retained one, and it is necessary anyway — mechanisation does not remove the labour problem so much as move it from unskilled hands to skilled operators, who are also scarce. Piece-rate and quality-linked pay, housing, and progression retain people once trained.

## Conclusion

Mechanisation answers most of the annual round and all of establishment and removal; it does not answer steep slopes, selective picking or the judgement tasks of pruning and canopy work. The decisive preparation is therefore made at replanting — row width, trellis, training system and site chosen for machine access — supported by a small, cross-trained, permanent crew for what machines still cannot do.

questionText: Discuss which vine varieties would be most suitable for the production of dessert wines. Explain your choice with specific reference to any climatic requirements.
body:
## What I mean by dessert wine, and how I am choosing

A dessert wine is a wine made with the assumption of sweetness, spanning perhaps 30 g/L of residual sugar in a Kabinett-weight wine through 100–150 g/L in a Sauternes to well over 400 g/L in a Tokaji Eszencia or a Pedro Ximénez. That spread matters because the concentration route dictates the climate required, and the climate then dictates the variety. So I choose varieties by four criteria: retained acidity at very high sugar, the behaviour of the skin under the relevant concentration route, aromatic compound levels strong enough to survive concentration or fortification, and compatibility with the production method the climate allows. On those criteria my choices are Semillon, Riesling, Furmint, Chenin Blanc, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, Pedro Ximénez and the Douro's Touriga Nacional-led field blend. I discuss them by route rather than one by one.

## Humid autumn mornings, dry afternoons: noble rot

Botrytis cinerea concentrates sugar and acid while adding glycerol and botrytis character, but it needs a specific and rare climate: morning mist or fog to raise humidity, followed by warm, dry, breezy afternoons to check the infection. Continuous humidity gives grey rot instead. Sauternes has this from the confluence of the cool Ciron with the warmer Garonne; Tokaj from the Bodrog and Tisza; the Layon from its tributary valleys; the Rheingau and Mosel from river fog.

The varietal requirement is not one trait but several, and this is where candidates go wrong. **Semillon** is genuinely thin-skinned and permeable, so it rots readily and evenly, but it is only moderately acidic — which is why Sauternes blends it with Sauvignon Blanc for acid and aroma. **Furmint** is thin-skinned and very high in acid, so it carries 150 g/L of sugar without cloying, and its firm skin holds shape through the aszú soak. **Riesling** and **Chenin Blanc** succeed for a different reason: exceptional natural acidity and late, uneven ripening that lets pickers work successive tries through a long autumn. Icewine requires a reliable, sharp winter freeze after a long enough autumn to leave sound fruit on the vine, and in Germany, Austria and Canada the law defines it by a minimum must weight reached only once the grapes have frozen naturally -- in practice usually at about -7C or below -- rather than by a specific legal temperature threshold. The climatic requirement is continental: Ontario, British Columbia, Germany's warmer river valleys and Austria. The varietal requirement is thick, tough skin and a resilient stalk to survive months of hanging without rotting or dropping, plus high acidity to balance the sugar. **Riesling** is the benchmark; Vidal, a hybrid, is used across Ontario precisely because its skins are tougher still. Botrytis varieties chosen for permeability are the wrong plants for this job — the same trait that makes Semillon ideal in Sauternes makes it a liability hanging until January.

## Hot and dry: raisining on the vine and on the mat

Where autumn is hot, dry and sunny, water is lost by evaporation rather than fungus. Passerillage on the vine and drying on mats or in lofts both demand varieties with thick, resistant skins that will dehydrate without splitting or rotting, and enough acidity that the concentrate is not flat. **Pedro Ximénez** in Montilla-Moriles is the clearest case of climate dictating both variety and method: a neutral, high-sugar-accumulating grape laid on esparto mats under a reliably rainless Andalusian sun, producing a wine of enormous sweetness whose interest is raisin and fig rather than varietal aroma. Italy's dried-grape tradition works the same way with **Garganega** for Recioto di Soave and **Corvina** for Recioto della Valpolicella, both chosen for loose bunches and thick skins that resist rot in the drying loft.

## Fortification: a different demand again

Ignoring fortified wine here would be a serious omission, since much of the world's sweet wine is fortified. Arresting fermentation with spirit means the wine keeps grape sugar, so the variety must supply intense flavour and, for reds, colour and tannin extracted very quickly before the spirit goes in. **Touriga Nacional**, with Touriga Franca and Tinta Roriz, gives the Douro small berries, thick skins and high anthocyanin — exactly what a two-day maceration requires — and the Douro's hot, dry summers ripen them to the necessary sugar. **Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains** is the white counterpart: its terpene concentration is high enough to survive fortification and years of oxidative ageing, which is why it appears in Rivesaltes, Beaumes-de-Venise, Samos and, as the red-berried Brown Muscat, in Rutherglen — all hot, dry places where it would rot if the autumn were damp.

## Conclusion

The relationship runs in both directions, and the best choices show it. Semillon adapted to the Sauternes niche over centuries, while in Montilla-Moriles the climate dictated a method and Pedro Ximénez was adapted to it. Judged strictly on suitability, I would name Riesling and Furmint as the most versatile — high acid, capable of botrytis, passerillage and, for Riesling, freeze concentration — Semillon as the best specialist for noble rot, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains and Pedro Ximénez for hot, dry fortified and raisined styles, and Touriga Nacional for sweet reds.

questionText: Does soil preparation affect the potential yield and quality in a vineyard?
body:
## Yes — and the answer turns on what soil preparation means

Soil preparation is everything done to the soil before planting, plus the maintenance of the root zone thereafter. It covers physical steps — deep ripping and subsoiling, levelling, mounding, drainage, stone removal or crushing, terracing, weed control — and chemical ones — liming or gypsum to correct pH and sodicity, incorporation of phosphorus, potassium and organic matter — and biological ones such as fallowing, green manure and biofumigation against nematodes and replant disease.

My position: preparation strongly determines *potential yield*, because it sets rooting depth and therefore the water and nutrients the vine can draw on; it affects *quality* mainly negatively, by removing limitations rather than creating excellence, and it can reduce quality if overdone. The reason it matters so much is timing. After planting, only the top 20–30 cm of soil is genuinely accessible; the subsoil can never be altered again for the forty or more years the vineyard stands. Robert White's work on vineyard soils and Richard Smart's on canopy and site both make this point, and Claude and Lydia Bourguignon's soil-biology surveys are routinely commissioned before replanting in Burgundy for exactly this reason.

## What the soil has to do

Three functions frame the whole answer. It **supplies water**: the plant-available water held between field capacity and wilting point, over the depth roots can actually reach. It **supplies nutrients**, with availability controlled by pH — iron and manganese lock up in alkaline soils, aluminium becomes toxic below about pH 5. And it **supports the vine physically**, anchoring roots and trellis for decades; it must also drain and admit air, since waterlogged roots die. Preparation is the one chance to improve all three at depth.

## Physical preparation

**Why:** to remove compaction and hardpans from previous land use, ensure drainage, and open a deep, uniform root zone. **How:** deep ripping or subsoiling to 60–100 cm, often crosswise; installing tile or mole drainage; mounding rows on wet sites; laser levelling on flat land; terracing on slopes. **When:** in dry conditions, so the soil shatters rather than smears, and well ahead of planting.

The yield effect is direct: roots that reach stored subsoil moisture carry a larger crop to ripeness without stress, and uniformity of rooting depth is what produces an evenly ripening block. The quality effects run both ways. Subsurface drainage is why the great gravel banks of the Médoc perform in wet years; Marlborough and Hawke's Bay growers mound rows for the same reason. Terracing in the Douro and Priorat is a soil-preparation decision that fixes density and mechanisation for a generation. But over-cultivation destroys structure and invites erosion — the reason Napa's hillside ordinances regulate it — and ripping a shallow soil can homogenise away the very drought stress that limits vigour.

## Chemical preparation

This is the half that otherwise solid papers omit. **Why:** because the immobile nutrients cannot be corrected later. Lime moves through soil only a few centimetres a year, so pH correction to depth is only possible by incorporating it pre-plant; the same is true of phosphorus and, largely, potassium. Gypsum is worked in pre-plant on the sodic soils common in inland Australia. **When:** months ahead, so reactions complete before roots arrive.

The quality link is specific and often missed. Excess potassium in the must raises pH and destabilises colour in red wine, so a potassium-rich soil should not be further enriched. Nitrogen is mobile and leaches, so it belongs in the growing season, not the pre-plant mix; too much drives vigour, shading, herbaceous flavours and botrytis, while too little gives low yeast-assimilable nitrogen, stuck ferments and reductive characters in the winery. Organic matter, by contrast, is worth adding generously: it raises water-holding capacity, cation exchange and infiltration, which is the cheapest simultaneous improvement to yield and drought resilience.

## Preparing for the wine you intend to make

The same operations serve opposite targets. For a classed-growth Médoc block the aim is a moderate, uniform, deep-rooted, low-vigour vine, so preparation concentrates on drainage and uniformity and deliberately withholds fertility. For high-volume Pinot Grigio on the Veneto plain the aim is reliable tonnage at low cost, so preparation means levelling, drainage, fertility correction and row spacing set for machinery. Neither is better preparation; they are different specifications, and a candidate who prepares the second site as though it were the first has wasted the owner's money.

## New technology and established vineyards

Modern preparation begins with measurement: soil pits, EM38 electromagnetic conductivity mapping, texture and depth mapping, full chemical analysis, and nematode and virus testing of the site. That data allows variable-rate amendment and, importantly, block boundaries drawn on soil rather than on convenience. In an established vineyard you cannot re-prepare, only maintain: compost and under-vine mulch, mid-row ripping to relieve tractor compaction, cover-crop choice, controlled traffic, and foliar or fertigated correction of what the roots cannot reach.

## Conclusion

Soil preparation does affect potential yield and quality, and asymmetrically. It sets the ceiling on yield through rooting depth and water supply, and it protects quality by removing waterlogging, compaction, pH lock-up and nutrient extremes. It cannot compensate for the wrong climate or the wrong variety, and preparation aimed at maximum fertility will reduce quality. Done to a specification derived from the wine intended, it is the highest-leverage decision a vineyard manager ever makes, because it is the only one that cannot be revisited.

questionText: What are the principal pests and diseases facing vine growers today, and how can they best be managed?
body:
## Definitions and selection

**Pests** are animals that damage the vine — arthropods, nematodes, birds and mammals. **Diseases** are caused by fungi, oomycetes, bacteria, phytoplasmas and viruses. To **manage** is not to eradicate but to hold losses below an economic threshold, using prevention, monitoring and targeted intervention within the legal and philosophical limits the grower works under. **Principal** I define by three tests: global incidence, economic severity, and the absence of a cheap cure. That last test is what makes the modern list different from the historic one — the mildews are serious but routinely controlled, whereas trunk disease and the vector-borne viruses have no cure at all.

On those criteria I take eight: powdery mildew, downy mildew, botrytis bunch rot, the trunk-disease complex, Flavescence dorée, Pierce's disease, the leafroll and red blotch viruses with their vectors, and fanleaf with its nematode. Phylloxera I dismiss briefly: resistant rootstocks have made it a manageable historical problem everywhere they are used, and it now matters only where own-rooted vines survive — Chile, parts of the Barossa under quarantine, Santorini's sand.

## Fungal diseases: the routine but unrelenting group

**Powdery mildew** (*Erysiphe necator*) is the most universal. It needs no free water and is most active around 20-27C, so it strikes in dry Mediterranean and Australian seasons where growers may be least alert. Management is preventive: an open canopy through shoot thinning and leaf removal, sulphur — which is also the organic grower's principal tool — and, conventionally, DMI and strobilurin sprays rotated by mode of action to manage resistance.

**Downy mildew** (*Plasmopara viticola*) needs warm rain, so it dominates in Bordeaux, the Loire, northern Italy and humid New World sites. Copper is the organic answer and the organic problem: it is a protectant only, it washes off, and it accumulates permanently in soil, which is why the EU caps copper at an average of around 4 kg per hectare per year. Conventional growers use systemics; both depend on drainage, canopy openness and forecasting models.

**Botrytis bunch rot** is managed almost entirely by cultural means: loose-clustered clones, fruit-zone leaf removal at set, restrained nitrogen, and avoiding any wound — insect, powdery mildew scar or split — that admits it. Botryticides are a supplement, timed at flowering and bunch closure.

**The trunk-disease complex** — Esca, Eutypa and Botryosphaeria dieback — is in my view the most serious current threat, because it is incurable, chronic and worsened by the loss of sodium arsenite. Infection is through pruning wounds, so management is entirely preventive: prune late and in dry weather, make small wounds, apply wound sealants or *Trichoderma*, adopt double pruning, use clean and hot-water-treated nursery material, and practise remedial curettage on valuable vines.

## Bacteria and phytoplasmas

**Flavescence dorée** is a phytoplasma spread by the leafhopper *Scaphoideus titanus*. It is a notifiable disease in France and Italy, with compulsory insecticide treatment and rogueing in declared zones — a real conflict for certified organic growers, who must use pyrethrum with its poor selectivity or seek derogation. Hot-water treatment of planting material at the nursery is the other control.

**Pierce's disease** is caused by the bacterium *Xylella fastidiosa*, vectored in California by the glassy-winged sharpshooter. Management is area-wide vector control, removal of riparian host plants, quarantine on nursery movement, and — the only durable answer — resistant varieties from the long-running breeding programme at UC Davis. Cold winters remain the best natural control, which is why it does not threaten northern Europe yet.

## Viruses: the incurable group

Leafroll (particularly GLRaV-3) delays ripening and strips colour; it is spread by mealybugs and soft scale. Red blotch produces a similar ripening failure and is associated with insect transmission and, above all, infected planting material. Fanleaf degeneration is transmitted by the dagger nematode *Xiphinema index*, which persists in old roots for years. Since nothing cures a virus, management is threefold: certified virus-tested planting material, roguing and replanting infected vines before spread, and vector control — mealybug mating disruption, systemic insecticide where permitted, and for fanleaf a long fallow, thorough root removal and biofumigation with brassica green manure before replanting.

## Pests: damage versus transmission

The useful distinction is between pests that cause direct physical damage and those whose importance is as vectors. Deer, kangaroos, wild boar, rabbits and birds eat buds, shoots and fruit; they are managed by fencing, guards, netting and scaring devices, and the damage is proportional and visible. Nematodes, leafhoppers, mites and mealybugs cause modest direct injury but transmit the diseases above, so they must be managed at population thresholds far below the level at which their own feeding matters. That difference — treating a vector prophylactically, a browser reactively — is the heart of a sound pest strategy.

## Conclusion

The principal threats have shifted from acute to chronic. The mildews and botrytis are managed competently every year by canopy work and a spray programme calibrated to the grower's philosophy. What is not managed is the incurable group — trunk disease, leafroll, red blotch, fanleaf, Flavescence dorée and Pierce's disease — where the only effective controls are clean planting material, vector suppression and preventive pruning hygiene. Growers should be spending less anxiety on phylloxera and more on the nursery they buy from.

questionText: "This wine has been bottled un-fined and unfiltered." Assess the implications for the winemaker.
body:
## Two different operations, confused at the candidate's peril

**Fining** is a chemical and colloidal operation: an agent is added that binds a target compound by adsorption or opposite charge and is then removed with it. Bentonite adsorbs heat-unstable grape proteins; gelatin, isinglass, casein, egg albumen and pea or potato protein bind astringent and oxidisable phenolics; PVPP removes browning precursors; activated carbon removes colour and some taints. **Filtration** is a physical separation of suspended particles by size: depth filtration through diatomaceous earth or sheets, crossflow, and membrane filtration down to a nominal 0.45 micron for a sterile filtration. Neither substitutes for the other. No filter removes soluble protein, and no fining agent removes a yeast population reliably.

Assessing the claim on the label therefore means asking what the winemaker must do instead, and I read the question as a technical one, from vineyard through bottling.

## What the winemaker is giving up

Fining and filtration between them manage two risks. The first is **instability**: protein haze in white wine, tartrate precipitation, colloidal and colour instability in reds, and microbial instability from *Brettanomyces*, lactic acid bacteria, or residual sugar refermented by *Zygosaccharomyces bailii*. The second is **clarity and palate**: turbidity, sediment in bottle, and excess astringency or bitterness. Forgoing both moves those risks earlier in the process, where they must be designed out, and later into the bottle, where they cannot be corrected.

## Yield and fruit condition

The first substitution is in the vineyard. Lower yields and fully ripe, sound fruit give lower grape protein, softer and more polymerised tannin needing no protein fining, and less nitrogen-driven vegetal character. Rot must be excluded absolutely: botrytis brings laccase and beta-glucans, and glucans blind a filter and destabilise the wine, so a winemaker who intends not to filter must sort ruthlessly. Ripe phenolics also mean the wine will not need gelatin or albumen to soften it.

## Juice and must handling

Clarification techniques that are neither fining nor filtration remain available and become central: long cold settling, flotation, and centrifugation. Pectolytic enzymes added at the crusher degrade pectin so that solids settle rather than stay in suspension. Press fractions are separated and the hard, phenolic-rich later fractions declassified rather than fined out later. Gentler whole-bunch pressing lowers the solids load in the first place.

## Fermentation choices

The wine must be taken absolutely dry, because residual sugar is the substrate for refermentation in a bottle with no sterile filter. Malolactic fermentation must be complete and confirmed analytically, since residual malic acid in bottle is a slow bomb. Yeast selection matters for flocculation and for low polysaccharide production; a strain that settles compactly leaves a cleaner wine off lees.

## Elevage does the clarifying

This is the substitution the examiners look for. Time in vat or barrel replaces the filter. Successive rackings off gross and then fine lees, each with settling time, progressively clarify the wine; a cold winter in an unheated cellar precipitates potassium bitartrate as effectively as a chilled tank; and extended ageing polymerises tannin and pigment so that colloidal material falls out rather than remaining suspended. The implications are practical: tank and barrel space occupied for far longer, capital tied up, more handling labour, greater topping and racking losses, and more cumulative oxygen exposure, which itself has to be managed with careful topping, inert gas and sound cooperage.

## The sulphur dioxide regime becomes the whole microbial defence

Without a sterile membrane, molecular SO2 is the only barrier between the wine and *Brettanomyces*. The winemaker must hold roughly 0.5 to 0.8 mg/L of molecular SO2 throughout élevage, and because the molecular fraction collapses as pH rises, this forces attention onto pH: a wine at pH 3.9 needs several times the free SO2 of one at pH 3.4. Picking earlier, acidifying where legal, and blending to a lower pH therefore become part of the unfined, unfiltered decision. Supporting tools include lysozyme against lactic bacteria, DMDC at bottling, and scrupulous hygiene — steam or ozone sanitation, closed transfers, low dissolved oxygen — because an infection can no longer be filtered out.

## What is legal where

Permitted treatments are jurisdictional. Fining agents are set by permitted lists under OIV, EU and national rules; potassium ferrocyanide is permitted under strict oenologist supervision in the EU (no residue may remain), while in the United States it is essentially unused and is being formally delisted by TTB rather than ever having had a blanket in-force prohibition. Animal-derived agents — isinglass, casein and egg albumen — trigger allergen declaration in the EU, which is one reason vegetable proteins have displaced them. Organic and biodynamic certification narrows the list further, and some appellations and traditional codes discourage or effectively prohibit heavy processing. A winemaker choosing not to fine or filter is not escaping regulation, but the regulation now bears on additives such as DMDC, lysozyme and SO2 limits instead.

## Assessment

The implication is a different risk profile, not simply an omission. Decisions are pulled forward — yield, fruit health, pH, complete dryness — and cost is added in the form of extended élevage and a stricter SO2 and hygiene regime. My judgement is that this is a sound choice for a dry, low-pH, tannic red with two years in wood, where time genuinely substitutes for intervention. For an aromatic white with residual sugar, or for any high-pH warm-climate wine facing a container crossing the tropics, I would not forgo at least a coarse polishing filtration; the risk transferred to the bottle is too large to accept for a stylistic claim.

questionText: Sauvignon Blanc appears in many styles throughout the world. Compare and contrast Sauvignon Blanc winemaking practices around the world.
body:
## The technical variables that make the styles

Sauvignon Blanc arrives at the winery with three things the winemaker can act on: a pool of odourless cysteine- and glutathione-bound thiol precursors that yeast must cleave to release 3-mercaptohexanol, its acetate and 4-methyl-4-mercaptopentan-2-one; methoxypyrazines already formed in the grape and reduced only by sunlight and time, not by winemaking; and high acid with a low tolerance of phenolic extraction. Every stylistic difference around the world comes from choices about oxygen, yeast, oak and blending applied to that raw material. I compare on those four axes, and then separately on volume, because the high-volume route is technically distinct rather than simply less good.

## Oxygen: the reductive and oxidative poles

The reductive route is the modern default in Marlborough, Chile's Casablanca and Leyda, South Africa's Elgin and Durbanville, and Touraine. Fruit is machine-harvested at night, chilled, sulphited at the crusher, pressed under inert gas at low pressure with ascorbic acid, and the juice settled cold. The purpose is to preserve glutathione and the thiol precursors, which oxidise readily; thiols themselves are lost to even small oxygen pickups later, so the wine stays under nitrogen or carbon dioxide to bottling, is closed under screwcap and often retains around 1 g/L of dissolved carbon dioxide to lift the aromatics.

The oxidative route is deliberately opposite and is practised in white Bordeaux and Pessac-Léognan, in parts of Sancerre, and in Margaret River. Juice hyperoxidation, or simply relaxed handling, allows polyphenol oxidase to oxidise the oxidisable phenolics so they polymerise and drop out before fermentation. The wine that results is less overtly aromatic and more citrus and mineral in profile, but it is far more oxygen-stable and ages for a decade rather than three years. Which pole a producer chooses is a longevity decision as much as an aroma one.

## Yeast: expression is inoculated in or fermented out

Yeast is not neutral here. Strains differ substantially in beta-lyase activity, and an expressive commercial strain releases several times more thiol from the same precursor pool than a neutral one, which is the single largest technical lever on Marlborough's passionfruit character. Fermentation conditions amplify it: cool ferments of 12-15C with generous assimilable nitrogen maximise both thiols and acetate esters, whereas barrel-fermented lots run warmer, at 18-22C, deliberately trading aromatic intensity for texture and integration.

The counter-practice is ambient fermentation on indigenous flora, used in Sancerre, in parts of Bordeaux and by a growing minority in New Zealand and South Africa. This gives slower, cooler, mixed-population ferments with more non-*Saccharomyces* activity, lower ester expression, higher glycerol and a broader, less varietal wine. Neither is old-world or new-world practice; both are in use in both.

## Oak, lees and vessel

Oak in Sauvignon Blanc is used for texture and oxygen transfer, not for aroma — new oak overwhelms the variety. The Bordeaux and Margaret River model ferments in barriques of mostly seasoned wood, ages on full lees with bâtonnage for six to twelve months and often allows partial malolactic fermentation, converting acidity into texture. Fumé Blanc in California, the term Robert Mondavi coined in the 1960s, established the same idea in the New World; the useful contrast today is with the newer Californian and Chilean lots fermented in concrete eggs, foudres or amphorae, which give oxygen exchange and lees contact without oak flavour. Loire practice generally uses no small oak at all, relying on extended lees ageing in tank. In Styria and Friuli the vessel of choice is large old wood, and in the orange-wine fringe skin contact is applied for weeks, which extracts exactly the phenolics that the reductive school works to avoid.

## Blending

Blending is a technical instrument, not an afterthought. In Bordeaux and Margaret River, Semillon adds weight, wax and ageing capacity while diluting pyrazine. In Marlborough, blending across Wairau and Awatere lots is standard, the Awatere component supplying higher acid and more herbaceous, saline character. In Rueda the appellation permits Sauvignon Blanc alongside and blended with Verdejo. Press-fraction blending is the finest-grained version: free run kept separate, the phenolic later fractions either declassified or reintroduced in measured proportion for structure.

## The high-volume model

Most Sauvignon Blanc in the world is made at scale, and the technical route is genuinely different. Machine harvest, refrigerated bulk transport, must clarification by flotation or centrifuge rather than long settling, pectolytic enzyme addition, fermentation in temperature-controlled tanks of hundreds of thousands of litres with a reliable, fast, expressive strain plus staged nitrogen, then back-blending of unfermented juice or rectified concentrate to a few grams per litre of residual sugar to fill the mid-palate and soften the acidity. Stabilisation is by bentonite for protein and by carboxymethylcellulose or potassium polyaspartate rather than energy-hungry cold stabilisation. The wine is sterile filtered, bottled under screwcap, and often shipped in flexitank and bottled in market, which adds an oxygen and SO2 management problem the estate producer never faces. Chile's Central Valley, Pays d'Oc, South African bulk and much of Marlborough work this way.

## Conclusion

Comparing across the world, the decisive variable is not latitude or tradition but oxygen management from picking to bottle, with yeast strain the second lever and oak a distant third. A producer with the knowledge and nerve to move along the reductive-oxidative axis can make wines from the same fruit that share almost nothing.

questionText: Discuss the roles of enzymes in winemaking.
body:
## What an enzyme is, and where they come from

An enzyme is a protein that catalyses a specific biochemical reaction, lowering its activation energy without being consumed. It acts on one substrate at an active site, and its rate depends on temperature, pH, substrate concentration and the presence of inhibitors. Two practical consequences follow immediately: enzymes work slowly at cellar temperatures, so timing matters, and because they are proteins they are themselves adsorbed and denatured by bentonite — which is why enzyme should be added before fining, not after.

Three sources matter in a winery. **Endogenous grape enzymes**, some useful and some destructive. **Microbial enzymes** from yeast and lactic acid bacteria, which do most of the chemistry of fermentation. And **added commercial preparations**, most of them produced from *Aspergillus niger*, sold as pectinases with defined side activities and permitted under national additive lists. I take the winemaking process in order.

## Reception and pressing: the spoilage enzymes first

The grape's own oxidative enzymes are the first thing a winemaker must control. **Tyrosinase**, a polyphenol oxidase present in healthy fruit, oxidises hydroxycinnamic acids and is largely inactivated by modest SO2 and removed with the solids. **Laccase**, produced by *Botrytis cinerea*, is the serious one: it is far more resistant to sulphur dioxide than tyrosinase, remains active at wine pH and in alcohol, and attacks a much wider substrate range including anthocyanins, so a rotten load will brown and lose colour in tank despite normal sulphiting. The management is therefore not chemical but physical — sort rot out, press quickly, hyperoxidise the juice so the substrate is consumed and precipitated before fermentation, or denature the enzyme with heat, as flash détente does by heating must to around 85C. Any candidate who discusses only added enzymes has missed the enzyme that most often costs money.

## Pre-fermentation in white and rosé: clarification

Grape pectin holds colloids in suspension and makes juice viscous. Added **pectolytic enzymes** — polygalacturonase, pectin lyase and pectin methylesterase — depolymerise it, giving faster and more complete cold settling, better free-run yield, easier pressing and a juice that will filter later. In rosé the requirement is subtly different: the winemaker wants rapid settling and a delicate colour, so the preparation must be free of anthocyanase activity, since a glycosidase that liberates aroma will also strip the little colour a rosé has.

**Aroma-release enzymes** with beta-glucosidase side activity hydrolyse the odourless glycosidic precursors of monoterpenes, freeing free terpenes in Muscat, Gewurztraminer and Riesling. They are used on skin contact or post-fermentation, and their limitation is that they release everything, including compounds better left bound.

## Red maceration: the neglected half

Enzymes are used at least as much in red winemaking. **Extraction preparations** combine pectinase with cellulase and hemicellulase side activities to degrade the skin cell walls, releasing anthocyanins and tannin faster and more completely. The practical results are a shorter maceration for the same extraction, better press yields, improved colour intensity in the first days, and the release of cell-wall polysaccharides that help stabilise colour and soften the mid-palate. The trade-off is loss of control: an over-dosed red extracts harsh seed and skin tannin along with the colour.

## Alcoholic fermentation: the yeast's own enzyme suite

Fermentation is enzymology. Yeast invertase hydrolyses sucrose — which is what actually happens when a must is chaptalised — and the glycolytic enzymes convert hexoses to pyruvate, with pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase completing the conversion to ethanol. Strain differences that winemakers describe as aromatic are enzymatic: **beta-lyase** cleaves cysteine-bound precursors to release the volatile thiols of Sauvignon Blanc, and alcohol acetyltransferases form the acetate esters, balanced against esterases that hydrolyse them back. Yeast beta-glucosidase also contributes to terpene release.

## Malolactic fermentation and lees ageing

The malolactic enzyme of *Oenococcus oeni* decarboxylates L-malic acid to L-lactic acid; the same organism's citrate pathway generates diacetyl, which its diacetyl reductase then reduces to acetoin and butanediol — which is why leaving a wine on lees after malolactic reduces the buttery character rather than increasing it.

On lees, autolysis is enzymatic: yeast proteases and glucanases break down the dead cells and release mannoproteins and polysaccharides, giving texture, protein and tartrate stabilisation and colour stabilisation. Added **beta-glucanase** preparations accelerate this, and also degrade the botrytis glucans that would otherwise blind a filter.

## Pre-bottling and the risks

Before bottling, pectinase and glucanase preparations are used to restore filterability. **Urease** is permitted in some markets to hydrolyse urea and reduce ethyl carbamate risk. **Lysozyme**, itself an enzyme, hydrolyses the cell walls of Gram-positive bacteria and is used to inhibit or delay lactic acid bacteria, allowing a lower SO2 regime.

Three risks are worth stating. Preparations are proteins and add to the protein haze load. Over-dosing pectin methylesterase liberates methanol, which is legally capped. And preparations carrying **cinnamyl esterase** side activity release free hydroxycinnamic acids, the exact substrate *Brettanomyces* converts into 4-ethylphenol — so a cinnamyl-esterase-free preparation must be specified for any red destined for long élevage.

## Conclusion

Enzymes act at every stage, but their role is consistent: they accelerate or complete reactions that would otherwise happen slowly or not at all. They save time, yield and energy, and they can rescue filterability or aroma release. What they do not do is create style — and the enzymes with the largest effect on quality are the ones the winemaker never adds, but must exclude.

questionText: Compare and contrast winemaking techniques best employed for Syrah grown in Cornas, McLaren Vale and Hawke's Bay.
body:
## What is distinct about each place

The three are not stand-ins for their countries, and the winemaking only makes sense against what makes each specific.

**Cornas** is the outlier of the northern Rhône. It permits no white grapes at all, where Côte-Rôtie allows up to 20 per cent Viognier and Hermitage and Crozes up to 15 per cent Marsanne and Roussanne — so co-fermentation, the classic northern Rhône softening and aromatic tool, is unavailable here as a matter of law. Its steep granite amphitheatre faces south and is sheltered from the north wind, making it the warmest and earliest-ripening of the northern appellations. The fruit arrives with high anthocyanin, ripe but assertive tannin and firm acidity, and there is no white grape and no appellation white to lean on.

**McLaren Vale** is not Barossa. It is Mediterranean and maritime, cooled by afternoon gulf breezes, with a mosaic of soils — the deep sands of Blewitt Springs giving perfumed, fine-boned Shiraz, the ironstone and clay of Seaview and Willunga giving darker, firmer wine. Compared with Barossa's warmer, more continental sites, the fruit is medium-bodied rather than opulent, more savoury and red-fruited, with better natural acid retention. Barossa's traditional winemaking answer was full ripeness and American oak hogsheads; McLaren Vale's contemporary one is very different.

**Hawke's Bay** is the marginal site of the three. Syrah ripens at its limit on the free-draining Gimblett Gravels, a defined area of roughly 800 hectares, and the neighbouring Bridge Pa Triangle. The risk is not excess ripeness but pyrazine, thin colour and low tannin, and the season can end wet.

## Cornas: extraction is not the problem, structure is

The traditional model still defines the appellation: whole-bunch fermentation with stems providing tannin, structure and lift; open wooden or concrete vats; long cuvaison of three to four weeks with foot treading and pigeage; and, in the most traditional cellars, a submerged cap. Ambient yeast, warm ferments and post-fermentation maceration all push extraction hard, because the wine is built to be reductive and tannic and to need a decade. Maturation is in old foudres and demi-muids rather than new barriques, because the tannin needs air and time, not oak flavour, and many wines are bottled unfined and unfiltered. The modernist strand within the appellation destems fully, controls temperature and uses a proportion of new oak, producing an earlier-drinking wine — but with no Viognier permitted, even the modernists cannot soften the wine that way. Chaptalisation is permitted; acidification is not, so picking date is the acid decision.

## McLaren Vale: managing ripeness and alcohol

Here the winemaker starts from the opposite problem. Sugar accumulates ahead of phenolic ripeness, so the defining decisions are picking earlier than the region once did, and controlling alcohol. Contemporary practice includes partial whole-bunch inclusion where stems are genuinely lignified, cold soak for a few days to build colour, fermentation in small open fermenters with hand plunging or gentle pump-overs, and cooler ferment peaks than in Barossa to preserve red fruit and perfume. Acidification with tartaric acid at the crusher is routine and legal, since natural pH runs high. Maturation has moved decisively from American oak hogsheads toward seasoned French puncheons and larger foudres, with concrete and amphora used for a proportion of the blend to keep the fruit unmarked by wood. Alcohol adjustment by reverse osmosis or spinning cone is legal in Australia and used discreetly. Blending with Grenache and Mataro is a McLaren Vale reflex that Cornas cannot use and Hawke's Bay does not need.

## Hawke's Bay: building a wine that has little to give

The techniques invert again. The winemaker must extract carefully from a must with modest anthocyanin and tannin, so cold soak of several days is used to draw water-soluble colour before alcohol arrives, and extraction thereafter is gentle — pump-over or délestage, or a genuine infusion approach, since hard plunging pulls green tannin from unripe seeds. Ferment temperatures are held moderate to retain floral and peppery rotundone character. Whole-bunch is used, but only in ripe years and only where stems are brown and lignified; in a cool vintage it would add exactly the green note the region is fighting. New Zealand has no appellation constraint, so co-fermentation with a few per cent of Viognier is available and is used. Malolactic fermentation is often completed in barrel, and maturation is in seasoned French barriques with a low new-oak proportion and a shorter élevage, because the wine's frame will not absorb more. Where Cornas fears dilution, Hawke's Bay fears rain at harvest, so selective picking and sorting matter more here than anywhere.

## The techniques set side by side

Stems: structural and traditional in Cornas, selective and vintage-dependent in the other two. Extraction: maximal in Cornas, moderate and perfume-preserving in McLaren Vale, minimal and colour-seeking in Hawke's Bay. Acid: fixed by picking date in Cornas, added in the two New World regions, where acidification with tartaric acid is routine and legal in Australia and New Zealand, while in Cornas chaptalisation is permitted and acidification is not. Oak: large and old in Cornas, moving that way in McLaren Vale, small and seasoned in Hawke's Bay. Blending: forbidden in Cornas, a Rhône-blend habit in McLaren Vale, a small Viognier option in Hawke's Bay.

## Conclusion

The common thread is that each winery is correcting what its site does not supply. Cornas has structure and needs time; McLaren Vale has ripeness and needs restraint; Hawke's Bay has perfume and needs gentleness. The best wine in each place comes from techniques chosen against that specific deficit — which is why applying Barossa's methods in McLaren Vale, or Côte-Rôtie's in Cornas, produces a lesser wine.

questionText: Temperature management is the key to modern winemaking. Discuss.
body:
## The proposition, and my position

Temperature is the only variable a winemaker manipulates at literally every stage, from the harvester in the vineyard to the container crossing the equator, and refrigeration is what made quality winemaking possible in warm climates — so in that historical sense it is indeed the defining technology of *modern* winemaking. But "the key" overstates it. Temperature is an enabling control, not a style in itself; it works alongside oxygen and microbial management, and applying the right number at the wrong stage is worthless. I therefore agree with the statement in its historical claim and qualify it in its analytical one. The way to test it is to walk the process.

## Harvest and fruit storage

A rise of 10C roughly doubles the rate of most chemical and enzymatic reactions, so fruit delivered at 32C is oxidising and fermenting spontaneously before it reaches the crusher. Night machine harvesting, refrigerated transport and short haul times deliver fruit at 12C instead. Where fruit must wait, cool rooms hold it at 4C overnight, which also firms the berries for whole-bunch pressing. Temperature is used as a positive tool here too: cryoextraction chills botrytised fruit to about -7C so that the most watery berries stay frozen in the press, and carbonic maceration requires whole berries held at 30C under carbon dioxide for the intracellular enzymes to work.

## Processing the must

Two operations are commonly confused and are not the same thing. **Must chilling** is the reduction of white juice temperature through a plate or tube-in-tube heat exchanger immediately after pressing, to slow oxidation and microbial activity and to allow cold settling of white juice at 10C for 12 to 24 hours before racking clear juice off the solids. It is protective and clarifying. Cold soak holds destemmed red must at 4-7C for up to about six days, below the threshold at which yeast will start, to extract water-soluble anthocyanins and gentle tannin before alcohol changes the extraction profile. The two share a temperature and share nothing else, and calling white must chilling a cold soak is a category error.

Heat is also a processing tool. Thermovinification and flash détente use it for extraction and to destroy laccase in rotten fruit or to strip smoke taint: flash détente takes must to 85C and then vacuum-cools it in seconds.

## Fermentation

Here the values are stylistic decisions. Aromatic whites at 14C, barrel-fermented whites at 20C, reds at 28C: the cool white ferment retains fermentation esters and volatile thiols that would be stripped by carbon dioxide at higher temperature, the warmer barrel ferment trades some aroma for texture and oak integration, and the red ferment needs the heat to extract anthocyanin and tannin and to allow a healthy, fast conversion. Control matters because fermentation is strongly exothermic: an uncooled large red tank will climb past 35C on its own, and above 35C yeast is stressed, volatile acidity rises and stuck fermentation follows. Sparkling base wines ferment cool, and the second fermentation is conducted at 12C over months precisely because a slow, cold ferment gives finer, better-integrated bubbles.

## Malolactic and post-fermentation

Malolactic bacteria work well at 20C and stall below 15C, so barrel halls are heated to secure it in a cool cellar — and cooling to below 15C with an SO2 addition is exactly how the winemaker *blocks* malolactic in an aromatic white. Extended maceration on skins after fermentation is held warm to continue tannin polymerisation, or cooled to stop it.

## Stabilisation

Cold stabilisation at -4C for one to two weeks precipitates potassium bitartrate, and it is one of the largest energy costs in the winery, which is why contact seeding, electrodialysis, carboxymethylcellulose and potassium polyaspartate have become mainstream alternatives — a genuinely modern shift away from temperature. Heat is used in the laboratory for the opposite test: heat stability trials hold a sample at 80C for two hours to force protein haze and set the bentonite dose.

## Ageing and long-term storage

A cellar held at 13C and stable is the target for maturation: warmer wine oxidises faster, evaporates more from barrel and matures on a shorter arc. Stability matters as much as the number, since cycling drives wine past the cork. But temperature is also used as a deliberate style-maker in oxidative wines: estufagem holds Madeira at up to 50C for at least three months, canteiro lofts do the same more slowly over years, and tawny Port and Rutherglen Muscat are matured warm on purpose.

## Bottling and beyond

Wine is bottled cool and still; flash pasteurisation at around 72C is available as a microbial alternative to sterile filtration for sweet or lower-alcohol wines. After bottling the winemaker's control ends but the risk does not: a container crossing the tropics can exceed 40C, so temperature-controlled shipping and warehousing are now part of the technical specification for any wine intended to arrive as it left.

## Conclusion

Temperature management is not the key to modern winemaking so much as its precondition. Nothing else is applied at every stage; nothing else so directly enabled warm-climate white wine, reliable red fermentation and stable long-distance shipping. But its value lies entirely in knowing what it is for at each step — protective at pressing, extractive in cold soak, stylistic in fermentation, transformative in estufagem. A winemaker who controls temperature and neglects oxygen or microbiology will still make poor wine.

questionText: How, and to what extent, can yeast influence the final style and quality of wines?
body:
## Stating the extent up front

Yeast creates most of the volatile compounds in a finished wine that were not in the grape, and it can destroy a wine outright. But it cannot supply what the fruit does not contain. My position is therefore a graded one: yeast's positive influence on style is greatest in neutral or precursor-driven whites and in high-volume wines, and smallest in structurally driven reds where extraction, oak and time dominate. Its influence on *quality* is asymmetric — its capacity to ruin a wine, through stuck fermentation, sulphides or spoilage, is far greater than its capacity to elevate one.

## The organisms involved

*Saccharomyces cerevisiae* completes almost every fermentation, with *Saccharomyces uvarum* and *Saccharomyces bayanus* and their interspecific hybrids used for low-temperature and high-alcohol ferments and for sparkling base wines. An uninoculated must, however, begins with a mixed population: *Hanseniaspora uvarum*, *Metschnikowia pulcherrima*, *Torulaspora delbrueckii*, *Lachancea thermotolerans* and *Starmerella bacillaris*, most of which die out between 4 and 7 per cent alcohol having already contributed acids, glycerol and aroma. The spoilage organisms are *Brettanomyces bruxellensis*, whose teleomorph is *Dekkera bruxellensis*, and the sulphur-tolerant refermenters *Zygosaccharomyces bailii* and *Saccharomycodes ludwigii*. And a distinct group defines whole categories of wine: the flor races of *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* — beticus, montuliensis and cheresiensis — that form the velo in Jerez and the voile under which Vin Jaune ages in the Jura.

## How yeast makes style

**Fermentation kinetics.** The first contribution is finishing the job. Strains differ in alcohol tolerance, temperature range, nitrogen demand and fructophilic character, and a wine that sticks at 8 g/L of sugar has a microbiological problem for life. This is the single largest quality decision in strain selection and it is rarely what candidates discuss.

**Esters and higher alcohols.** Yeast alcohol acetyltransferases form the acetate esters — isoamyl acetate, 2-phenylethyl acetate — and ethyl esters of fatty acids, and these are the aroma of most young, fruity white wine in the world. Their formation is strain-specific but heavily modulated by temperature and assimilable nitrogen, which is why a bulk Chilean or Pays d'Oc white can be aromatically engineered by yeast, nutrient and cooling alone.

**Release of bound grape aroma.** Yeast beta-lyase cleaves cysteine- and glutathione-bound precursors to liberate the volatile thiols responsible for Marlborough and Loire Sauvignon Blanc; yeast beta-glucosidase liberates monoterpenes in Muscat and Riesling. Here the yeast is not creating aroma but unlocking what the vineyard supplied — the clearest illustration of the limit on its influence.

**Texture, colour and stability.** Strains differ in glycerol and in polysaccharide and mannoprotein release; mannoproteins soften the palate, help protein and tartrate stability and stabilise colour. Extended lees ageing, as in Champagne and Muscadet sur lie, is yeast influence continuing long after fermentation. Some strains adsorb anthocyanins onto their cell walls and lighten a red; others produce more pyruvate and acetaldehyde and so form more of the stable pyranoanthocyanins that hold colour for decades.

**Modulating alcohol and acid.** This is where current research sits. *Lachancea thermotolerans* produces lactic acid during fermentation, lowering pH in warm-climate musts in Spain and Australia where acidification is otherwise the only tool; *Starmerella bacillaris* diverts carbon to glycerol and can shave a modest amount of ethanol; *Torulaspora delbrueckii* is used in sequential inoculation for aromatic complexity with low volatile acidity. Sequential and co-inoculation of these with *Saccharomyces* is a genuinely modern technique.

## Where yeast destroys or defines quality

Sulphide production is strain-dependent and nitrogen-dependent: a high-demand strain in a low-nitrogen must generates hydrogen sulphide and mercaptans, and low-sulphide strains exist precisely because of this. Some strains produce enough SO2 to inhibit the malolactic bacteria the winemaker was counting on.

*Brettanomyces bruxellensis* decarboxylates hydroxycinnamic acids and reduces the vinylphenols to 4-ethylphenol and 4-ethylguaiacol, which at threshold gives spice and beyond it gives a wine that tastes of nothing else. *Zygosaccharomyces bailii* and *Saccharomycodes ludwigii* are notably resistant to sulphur dioxide and to sorbate, which is why a sweet wine bottled without sterile filtration is at risk of refermenting.

Yet the flor yeasts show that "spoilage" is a matter of context, not organism. Under the velo in Jerez, yeast metabolises alcohol and glycerol aerobically, produces acetaldehyde and consumes oxygen, and creates the entire character of Fino and of Vin Jaune. To say that spoilage yeast expresses terroir is loose thinking, but to say that a film yeast can be the defining quality driver is simply true.

## Inoculated, ambient, and what the choice actually buys

Inoculation buys reliability, reproducibility and a predictable aromatic outcome; ambient fermentation buys a mixed-population contribution, more textural breadth, more vintage variation and more risk. This is not an old-world and new-world divide — most of Burgundy inoculates, much of New Zealand and California does not — and treating it as one is exactly the kind of generalisation that shows a candidate has not looked. Nor is it true that selected yeasts make only short-lived wines; longevity is set by pH, phenolics, SO2 and oxygen management, not by the strain.

## Conclusion

Yeast influences style profoundly and quality decisively, but not independently. It determines which of the grape's precursors are expressed, adds a layer of fermentation aroma, contributes texture and colour stability, and can modestly shift alcohol and acid. What it cannot do is add ripeness, structure or concentration. So: a large influence on style, a larger one on the risk of failure, and a small one on the ceiling of quality, which the vineyard sets.

questionText: Outline the most important quality control checks during bottling and why each is necessary.
body:
## Scope: what bottling quality control is, and why it is the last chance

Quality control is the testing and inspection that verifies a batch conforms to specification; quality assurance is the system that makes conformity repeatable. At bottling the two converge, because bottling is the last point at which anything can be changed. Once the closure is in, a defect is no longer a correction but a recall, unsaleable stock, a disappointed consumer and lasting brand damage. That is the logic behind every check below: each is justified by the cost of the failure it prevents. Wine is a foodstuff, so the frame is a HACCP plan sitting inside a quality assurance system — ISO 9001 or ISO 22000 for most commercial producers — and inside EU wine and food law. I cover the wine, the dry goods, the packaging operation, compliance with specification, and staff safety.

## Checks on the wine

**Microbiological status.** Plating or membrane counts for yeast, *Brettanomyces* and lactic acid bacteria, with residual sugar and malic acid measured alongside. Necessary because fermentable sugar plus a viable population means refermentation in bottle — gas, haze, pushed corks — and residual malic acid means a possible bottle malolactic. The result sets the filtration specification: a 0.45 micron membrane retains yeast and most spoilage bacteria, with a 0.65 micron prefilter to protect it, and integrity is confirmed by a bubble-point test before and after the run. Without that test a torn cartridge is invisible until the market finds it.

**Free and total sulphur dioxide, read against pH.** Necessary because protection depends on molecular SO2, not on the free figure alone: a target of roughly 0.5 to 0.6 mg/L molecular for a dry red and 0.8 mg/L where sugar is present requires about 25 to 30 mg/L free at pH 3.5, and considerably more at pH 3.8. Total SO2 is checked at the same time against the legal ceiling — 150 mg/L for dry red and 200 mg/L for dry white and rose in the EU, rising to 400 mg/L for the sweetest categories — because the addition that protects the wine must not make it unsaleable.

**Dissolved and total package oxygen.** Measured in tank, at the filler and on filled bottles off the line. Necessary because line pick-up is the largest single determinant of early shelf life; a reading above about 1 mg/L total package oxygen in an aromatic white stops the line and sends the operator to the filler-bowl inerting and the vacuum-jetting step.

**Physical stability.** Protein by heat test, tartrates by conductivity or cold test, turbidity, and iron and copper for casse risk. Necessary because a haze or a crystal in a bright wine reads to the consumer as a fault even where it is harmless — and because every remedy has a lead time. This is why the analysis is booked days before the fill, not on the morning of it.

**Sensory.** A trained panel tastes the tank before filling and a bottle off the line. Necessary because no instrument detects a fault nobody thought to assay for.

## Checks on dry goods

Bottles are inspected dimensionally, for internal cleanliness and for glass defects. Closures are checked for oxygen transmission rate, extraction or torque force and, for cork, releasable TCA on a soak test — necessary because cork taint is perceptible at only a few nanograms per litre, so one bad lot compromises an entire run. Labels, capsules and cartons are verified against approved artwork, barcode and the destination market's mandatory text. Necessary because a wrong barcode blocks a retailer's delivery as effectively as a faulty wine does.

## Checks on the packaging operation

Fill height, closure torque or insertion depth, headspace volume and headspace oxygen, seal integrity, label placement, batch coding and traceability marks, sampled at a defined frequency and recorded. Necessary because these are continuous processes that drift: fill height governs legal net content and headspace oxygen, and low torque leaks. Alcohol must sit within the EU label tolerance - 0.5% abv for most still wines, but 0.8% abv for sparkling, liqueur and overripe-grape wines - or the label is wrong. Volatile acidity is checked against the legal ceiling, of the order of 1.2 g/L as acetic acid, and against the buyer's tighter internal limit. Sulphites must be declared once total SO2 exceeds 10 mg/L; egg, milk and fish fining residues are verified so the allergen declaration is accurate; ochratoxin A is screened against the EU limit of 2 micrograms per kilogram. Retail customers impose their own analytical specification, and a delivery outside it is rejected at the depot at the supplier's cost.

## HACCP, and the safety of the people running the line

HACCP identifies the critical control points — the final filter, the filler, the closure — each with a limit, a monitoring method, a corrective action and a record; everything else sits in prerequisite programmes such as CIP verification and glass-breakage policy. Finally, the operators. Bottling is the winery's most hazardous operation: glass breakage causes cuts and eye injuries, line noise requires hearing protection, palletising causes lifting injuries, CIP chemicals and SO2 are burn and respiratory hazards, and tank entry kills through carbon dioxide asphyxiation. A manager who signs off the wine but not the line has passed the cheaper check and failed the more important one.
