questionText: Does great wine need a great story?
body:
## Definitions

Most answers to this question fail because they will not say what a great wine is, and an undefined subject cannot be tested against a requirement. So I will commit.

By great wine I mean a wine that satisfies four intrinsic criteria and one external one. Intrinsically it must have complexity that rewards attention rather than merely pleasing; balance that holds at every stage of its life; length and persistence; and the capacity to develop, so that it is a different and better thing in fifteen years than at release. The external criterion is that greatness must be recognised and sustained over time by informed judges who are not the producer — because "great" is a comparative and a claim on posterity, and no individual can make that claim unilaterally.

This definition deliberately excludes two things. It excludes the merely excellent: a first-rate Muscadet, faultless and delicious, is a very good wine and not a great one, and an essay that lets any well-made wine be great cannot answer the question. And it excludes the purely commercial reading in which a globally successful brand is "great". That is a legitimate alternative definition, and I address it separately at the end, because the answer under it is different — and that difference is the most interesting thing in the question.

By great story I mean a compelling non-sensory narrative attached to the wine: origin myth, founder, heroic vintage, historic vindication, dynasty, terroir romance, or scarcity legend.

The question then divides into two, and conflating them is what produces muddle. Does a wine need a story to *be* great — to possess the qualities above? Or does it need one to *become* great — to be recognised, priced and remembered as such? My answer is no to the first and yes to the second.

## Greatness is a property of the liquid, and stories cannot manufacture it

The strongest evidence that greatness does not require narrative is that it survives the removal of narrative. The 1976 Paris tasting, where Californian wines beat classed-growth Bordeaux and white Burgundy judged blind by a French panel, is decisive here precisely because the stories were not in the room. Stag's Leap and Montelena had no history, no dynasty and no myth; Mouton and Haut-Brion had all three. The wines were assessed as liquid and the story-less ones won. Whatever else that tasting proves, it proves that story is not a necessary input to quality.

The reverse test is equally telling. Wines with magnificent stories and inadequate quality do not become great; they become cautionary tales. Estates with four centuries of history and famous names have declined into mediocrity within living memory in every classic region, and the story did not save them — buyers left, prices fell, and the narrative sat there doing nothing. If story were sufficient, or necessary in the constitutive sense, that could not happen. Greatness is made by site, plant material, farming, vintage and judgement in the cellar, and a story is downstream of all of them.

A third test is temporal, and it follows directly from my definition. Greatness has to be demonstrable in the glass fifteen or thirty years on, and the wines that deliver at maturity are not reliably the ones that carried the best stories at release. Every serious cellar contains celebrated bottles that never developed and unheralded ones that did. A mature bottle is wholly indifferent to what was said about it when it was young.

There is also a plain practical argument. There exist, at any moment, wines of genuinely great quality made by growers nobody has written about — in the Jura, in the Canaries, in Georgia, in the Wachau, in the high Andes. Their greatness is a fact about them before anyone narrates it. Recognition lags; quality does not wait for it.

## But no wine becomes great without one

Now the other half, and I think it is the more important one. Greatness, on my definition, requires sustained external recognition — and recognition is a social process that runs on narrative.

Consider how new entrants actually achieved great status. Sassicaia was first sold commercially at the end of the 1960s and won a blind Decanter tasting of Cabernet-based wines in the 1970s; the wine's quality was real, but what converted that into greatness was a transmissible story — the aristocratic experiment, Bordeaux varieties on Tuscan coastal scrub, the defiance of the DOC system. Penfolds Grange was made semi-clandestinely by Max Schubert in the 1950s and initially rejected by his own management before being vindicated: that narrative of persecution and vindication is now inseparable from the wine, and it is the reason Grange occupies the position it does rather than merely being an excellent Shiraz. In both cases the story did not create the quality. It created the attention that allowed the quality to be assessed at all.

The economics reinforce this. Fine wine is an experience good sold years before it can be assessed, at prices far above its production cost, to buyers who mostly will not drink it. In that market, narrative is the mechanism by which trust is transferred. Burgundy's climat system is a story about place, codified; Champagne's houses sell a story about occasion; classification itself — 1855, the Grands Crus, the appellation hierarchy — is institutionalised narrative. Remove the story and the price collapses long before the quality does, which tells you exactly what work it is doing.

The risk in this, and the reason the question is a contemporary issue rather than a philosophical one, is that story is now cheap to manufacture and quality is not. A great deal of contemporary wine marketing consists of narrative applied to unremarkable liquid — the invented heritage, the borrowed grandfather, the sustainability claim with nothing behind it. If consumers learn that the story is unreliable, they discount all stories, including the true ones, and the producers with genuine narratives are the ones who lose most.

## The alternative definition

If "great" is instead read commercially — the globally successful brand — the answer inverts. Under that definition story is not merely helpful but essential, because a brand is a story with a product attached, and its greatness consists precisely in the strength of that association rather than in complexity, ageing capacity or development. The largest Champagne and Prosecco brands and the great New World labels are great in this sense, and their narratives are their principal asset. I note this to show the definition is doing real work, not to hedge: on my chosen definition the answer is different, and that is why the definition had to come first.

## Conclusion

No, great wine does not need a great story to be great. Greatness is a property of the liquid, produced in the vineyard and the cellar, demonstrable blind and independent of anything written on the label — and the Paris tasting settles that. But yes, great wine needs a great story to be *acknowledged* as great, to command the price that funds the farming that sustains the quality, and to be remembered. My position is therefore that story is not a condition of greatness but a condition of its recognition — and that the industry's real problem today is not that great wines have stories, but that so many ordinary wines have borrowed them.

questionText: Many wine regions can produce wines at a wide range of price points. Referencing at least two of such regions, compare and contrast methods of managing vineyards for high priced wines and low priced wines.
body:
## Scope and the test applied

I compare **Bordeaux** and the **Barossa Valley**, both of which sell wine from a few euros to several hundred, and I apply one test throughout: a vineyard's revenue per hectare is yield multiplied by price per tonne, so a low-priced wine must reach its revenue through volume and a high-priced wine can reach it through price. Every decision below is therefore judged not on whether it improves the wine but on whether the improvement is recoverable at that wine's price. Six issues follow.

## 1. Site and planting density

At the top, site is bought rather than managed. In the Médoc the deep gravel croupes with free drainage and a high water table beneath are worth many multiples of the Entre-Deux-Mers clays, and the classed growths plant tight — planting densities of 8,000 to 10,000 vines per hectare in the Médoc — to force root competition and hold yield per vine low while keeping yield per hectare workable. Generic Bordeaux plants at a fraction of that density on flatter, more fertile ground, because wide rows admit larger machinery and cut the per-hectare cost of every subsequent pass.

The Barossa shows the same split geographically: Eden Valley's elevated, cooler, poorer sites and the Barossa floor's old dry-grown blocks carry the premium wines, while irrigated high-vigour plantings on the valley's deeper alluvial soils carry the volume. The contrast is the same one: the premium site is chosen for constraint, the commercial site for capacity.

## 2. Yield and crop load

This is the central decision. The generic Bordeaux yield ceiling sits in the region of 55 to 60 hectolitres per hectare and growers aim at it, because at commodity grape prices the only route to a viable return is the full crop. A classed growth in the Médoc will commonly work at 35 to 45, achieved by conservative bud load at winter pruning, shoot thinning and, in a generous year, a green harvest. Cutting a third of the crop is only rational when the bottle price rises by more than a third — which at first-growth prices it does, and at generic prices it never does.

Barossa contract growers are frequently paid by the tonne against a quality grade, which makes the same arithmetic explicit: a grower on a premium contract restricts crop because the price band pays for it, and a grower on a commercial contract carries maximum crop because it does not.

## 3. Water

Irrigation is prohibited in Bordeaux's appellations other than by derogation, so water management there is soil management — cover crops sown or ploughed out to regulate vine water status, which is a premium tool because it costs tractor passes. In the Barossa the contrast is sharper than anywhere. Premium fruit comes from dry-grown or minimally irrigated old blocks where deficit stress concentrates the crop; commercial fruit is irrigated to sustain yield, and water is a purchased input whose cost is set against the tonnage it buys. Irrigating a premium block to yield would destroy more value than the water costs.

## 4. Canopy management and labour

Leaf removal, shoot positioning, lateral trimming and bunch thinning are labour, and labour is the largest controllable cost in viticulture. A premium estate does them by hand, selectively, fruit zone by fruit zone and often side by side to manage sun exposure. A commercial block does them once, mechanically, or not at all — accepting more shading and a less even ripeness because the wine's style does not require the precision and the price will not fund it.

## 5. Plant material and vine age

Premium blocks favour massal selection or low-yielding clones on devigorating rootstock, and old vines are retained despite falling productivity: the Barossa Old Vine Charter, which recognises vines from 35 years upward, exists precisely to convert that low yield into a price premium. Commercial blocks favour certified high-yielding clones on vigorous rootstock and replant on economic rather than sentimental grounds, because a block that has fallen below its target tonnage no longer pays its costs.

## 6. Harvesting

The clearest divergence of all. Commercial fruit in both regions is machine-harvested, at night for temperature, in a single pass, with the date set by sugar and by winery logistics — one pass over many hectares, at a small fraction of the cost per hectare of hand picking. Premium fruit is picked by hand into small boxes, parcel by parcel, sometimes over several tries as blocks reach phenolic rather than sugar ripeness, and then sorted at the winery. Hand picking costs several times what machine harvesting costs per hectare and requires a large, skilled, briefly-employed crew, which is now the binding constraint in both regions.

## Conclusion

The methods are not different in kind; they are the same decisions taken with opposite answers, because the two price points face opposite economics. High-priced viticulture spends labour and forgoes yield to buy precision, and can do so only because the bottle price recovers it. Low-priced viticulture protects yield and mechanises everything, because at commodity prices cost per tonne is the only variable that decides whether the block survives.

questionText: Referencing at least three wine regions, discuss how climate change is influencing grape growers' viticultural practices.
body:
## Scope

Climate change is not simply warming: growers face a rising mean and, more damagingly, rising variability around it. The question asks what growers now *do* differently, so I take three regions — cool, moderate and warm — and set out the changed practice in each. I organise by region rather than by practice, because the same warming demands opposite responses in Chablis and the Barossa, and that contrast is the answer.

## Chablis: a cool region whose problem is volatility, not heat

Warming has advanced budburst by days to weeks, which lengthens the window in which a spring frost can destroy a crop. Chablis growers have therefore changed the pruning calendar: winter pruning is pushed later, and double pruning — a rough mechanical pre-prune followed by a late hand finish — delays budburst on the retained buds. Where the site allows, the fruiting wire has been raised, since cold air pools at ground level. Above that sit capital defences: aspersion, which sprinkles water so that latent heat of fusion holds the bud at zero as ice forms; candles and straw burners; and wind machines to break the inversion layer. Hail has become the second recurring loss, answered by netting where permitted and, more often, by insurance.

Warmer summers have brought their own reversal. Chaptalisation, once routine in Chablis, is now needed rarely, and acidity retention has become the priority — so harvest dates are pulled earlier and picking runs on acid and pH as much as on sugar. Canopy work has changed with it: growers now leave more leaf on the afternoon side and trim later, where the region's inherited practice was to open the fruit zone as widely as possible. Wetter, warmer springs have raised downy mildew pressure, so spray programmes start earlier and are timed on infection models rather than on the calendar.

The economics are brutal: frost protection is a capital cost carried every year against a loss that arrives in some years, and the insurance premium rises with each event. That is why the practice change here is defensive and capital-intensive.

## Bordeaux: a moderate region where the constraint is legal

Bordeaux's problem is drought and heat spikes on top of earlier ripening. Because irrigation is prohibited in the appellations other than by derogation, water management is soil and plant management: cover crops sown to compete with vine vigour in wet years and ploughed out in dry ones, mulching to hold soil moisture, and — the more durable change — rootstock choice, with deeper-rooting, drought-tolerant stocks replacing shallower ones at replanting. Canopy practice has undergone the same reversal as Chablis for a different reason: systematic leaf removal on the west side is now avoided because sunburn, not under-ripeness, is the risk, and trellises are being raised to increase leaf area per unit of fruit so that sugar accumulation does not outrun phenolic ripeness.

The distinctive change is legal. Faced with alcohols that its style cannot carry, Bordeaux moved to admit a short list of additional varieties, including Touriga Nacional, Marselan and Alvarinho. This is the point most answers miss: in appellation Europe the binding constraint on adaptation is often the rulebook, and the practice that has to change first is the regulation governing plant material, yields, irrigation and picking dates.

Harvest logistics have changed too — picking earlier in the day or at night, and picking parcel by parcel over a longer window, which raises the labour bill in a region already short of pickers.

## Barossa Valley: a warm region managing water and heat

Here the constraint is physical rather than legal, since Australia does not restrict variety by region. Water is the first practice: drip irrigation scheduled against soil moisture probes and vine water potential rather than a fixed programme, regulated deficit irrigation to stress the vine at a chosen phenological stage, under-vine mulch, and the removal of mid-row cover crops where they compete for scarce water. Water itself is now traded and priced, so an irrigation decision is a cash decision.

Canopy management has been reoriented from exposure to shading: fruit is deliberately kept in dappled shade, leaf removal is minimal and done on the eastern side only, and sprawl or vertical shoot positioning is chosen for the shade it casts rather than for airflow. Sunburn and berry shrivel, not botrytis, are the losses being managed. Pest and disease pressure has shifted with the drier, hotter season — less downy and powdery mildew, more mealybug and mite pressure — so spray programmes have been rebuilt around different targets and shorter windows.

The strategic change is plant material: Mediterranean varieties planted alongside Shiraz and Grenache, and the deliberate retention of dry-grown old bush vines whose deep root systems ride out drought — the reason the Barossa Old Vine Charter has commercial as well as heritage value.

## Comparison

The three regions face the same trend and change opposite practices. Chablis spends capital to protect against volatility at the start of the season; the Barossa spends operating cost on water and shade to protect fruit at the end of it; Bordeaux must first change its law before it can change its vineyard. The common thread is that every one of these is a reversal of received practice — pruning later, shading rather than exposing, watering less rather than more — which is why growers cannot simply do what they have always done more carefully.

questionText: Identify the most important trunk diseases in vineyards around the world. How can they be best controlled and managed?
body:
## Scoping the question

Grapevine trunk diseases are **fungal** colonisations of the permanent wood — trunk, cordon and spur — that enter almost exclusively through pruning wounds, occlude the vascular system and cause progressive dieback, yield loss and vine death. They are not viral, and they are not phylloxera or flavescence dorée, which attack the root and the phloem respectively and fall outside the question. They are now the single largest cause of unplanned vine replacement worldwide.

## Part 1: the most important trunk diseases

**Esca.** A complex rather than a single pathogen, involving *Phaeomoniella chlamydospora*, *Phaeoacremonium* species and, in the mature form, the white-rot basidiomycete *Fomitiporia mediterranea*. It presents as tiger-stripe leaf chlorosis and, in the apoplectic form, sudden collapse of a whole vine in high summer. It is the dominant trunk disease of Mediterranean Europe — Italy, Spain and southern France — and became far more damaging after the loss of arsenite.

**Eutypa dieback.** *Eutypa lata*. Stunted, cupped, chlorotic spring shoots and a wedge of dead wood in section. Spores are released by winter rainfall, so it is worst in regions with wet, cool winters: coastal California, cooler and wetter southern Australian regions, and Cognac, where Ugni Blanc is notoriously susceptible. Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc are also documented as susceptible.

**Botryosphaeria dieback.** The Botryosphaeriaceae, including *Diplodia* and *Neofusicoccum* species. Cordon and spur dieback with internal necrosis, and the one that dominates in warm and arid regions — inland Australia, South Africa, the Californian interior, Spain — where vines are already under heat and water stress.

**Phomopsis dieback.** *Phomopsis viticola* and related *Diaporthe* species. Basal shoot lesions and cane bleaching, favoured by wet, cool springs; it matters most in northern Europe, Oregon and New Zealand.

**Young-vine diseases.** Petri disease, caused by the same *Phaeomoniella* and *Phaeoacremonium* fungi as Esca, and black foot, caused by *Ilyonectria* and related soil fungi, kill or stunt vines in their first few years and are largely nursery-borne. A vine of five to seven years is a young vine, not a middle-aged one, and the fact that decline appears this early is diagnostic of a nursery rather than a vineyard infection.

## Part 2: control and management

There is no curative chemistry: sodium arsenite, the one genuinely effective curative treatment, was withdrawn in the European Union in the early 2000s, and nothing has replaced it. Management is therefore a matter of preventing infection, protecting wounds, and removing infected wood.

**Prevent infection at the wound.** Prune as late in dormancy as the region permits, so wounds are exposed for less time and heal faster as sap rises; prune in dry weather, since spore release is rain-driven; and prune in two passes, mechanically pre-pruning then finishing by hand, which also reduces cost.

**Reduce wound size and respect the vine's architecture.** Large cuts into old wood are the highest-risk entry points. The Simonit and Sirch approach to respecting sap flow — small cuts, on the same side, leaving a desiccation cone away from the sap path — is now widely adopted precisely because it is a training decision that costs nothing but skill.

**Protect the wound.** Physical sealants and paints, wound-protectant fungicides, and Trichoderma-based wound biocontrol products applied immediately after cutting. Timing is everything: a wound is most susceptible in the first days.

**Sanitation and remediation.** Remove and burn infected prunings and dead vines rather than mulching them back into the row, which recycles inoculum. On individual vines, remedial surgery works: trunk renewal by cutting back below the necrosis and re-training a watershoot or sucker, and curettage to excise decayed wood, both of which can return a vine to production far more cheaply than replanting.

**Clean planting material.** For Petri and black foot the leverage is at the nursery: hot-water treatment of dormant cuttings, typically around 50 degrees Celsius for about thirty minutes, hygiene in hydration tanks and grafting, and avoiding planting stress in the young vineyard.

## Control compared by climate

The right programme differs by where the vineyard is. In **winter-rainfall Mediterranean regions** — southern France, Spain, coastal California — spore release is tied to winter rain, so pruning *timing* is the primary lever: pruning late, and never immediately before rain, delivers more than any product. In **warm arid irrigated regions** — the Barossa, South Africa's interior, the Californian Central Valley — Botryosphaeria dominates and infection periods are less predictable, so routine wound protection and, critically, the relief of water and heat stress that predisposes vines to dieback matter more than calendar timing. In **cold continental regions** the pruning window is short and the wood frozen, so late and double pruning are hard to schedule; the emphasis shifts to sanitation, clean nursery stock and remedial surgery.

Varietal susceptibility should shape the programme too: a susceptible variety on a high-value site justifies hand wound-painting that would be uneconomic elsewhere.

## Conclusion

The four diseases that matter globally are Esca, Eutypa, Botryosphaeria and Phomopsis dieback, with Petri disease and black foot the young-vine equivalents. Since none can be cured, management is a discipline rather than a treatment: prune late and small, protect every wound, sanitise ruthlessly, buy clean plants, and operate surgically on individual vines — with the balance between those levers set by the region's rainfall pattern and heat load.

questionText: Is the use of cover crops worthwhile in viticulture?
body:
## The test I am applying

A cover crop is a sward — sown or permitted to volunteer, permanent or seasonal, in every row or alternate rows — grown between vine rows or under the vine. It does four things: it takes up water and nitrogen, it binds and structures soil, it changes the surface's physical and thermal behaviour, and it provides habitat.

The question is not what cover crops do but whether they are worthwhile, and worthwhile is a comparative judgement: worth the seed, the tractor passes, the water and nitrogen forgone, against the alternatives of cultivated bare soil or a herbicide strip. My position is that **a cover crop is worthwhile wherever a grower can name the specific problem it is solving and has matched the species and management to that problem — and is actively harmful where water is the limiting factor and the sward is permanent and unmanaged.** The practice is not good in itself; it is good against a purpose. I test five purposes.

## Erosion and trafficability

On slope this is the strongest case in viticulture. In the Douro, where soils are thin, schistose and exposed to violent autumn rain on steep terraced ground, a cover crop between rows holds the soil that a grower otherwise pays to carry back up the hill. The same logic applies to the Mosel and to Priorat. Verdict: unambiguously worthwhile, and worthwhile even where water is short, because losing soil is a permanent loss and losing a little crop is an annual one.

The related benefit is trafficability. A sward carries a tractor across wet ground in a rainy harvest and prevents the compaction that a bare, worked mid-row suffers under repeated passes — a decisive argument in Bordeaux, Champagne and Oregon, and irrelevant in a dry-harvest region.

## Vigour and nitrogen

Here climate and water availability split the answer completely. On fertile, deep, well-watered soils — Marlborough's alluvial fans, much of Bordeaux's cooler clay, New World sites on old orchard ground — excessive vigour causes shading, poor fruit set, herbaceous character and botrytis. A grass sward that competes for water and nitrogen is the cheapest devigorating tool available, cheaper and more durable than shoot thinning or trimming. Sown legumes reverse the polarity, fixing nitrogen for a block that is under-vigorous or where juice YAN runs too low for a clean ferment.

On dry sites the same competition is a straight loss. In an unirrigated Barossa old-vine block, La Mancha or inland Spain, a permanent sward in the growing season takes water the vine needs at flowering and veraison. The answer is not "no cover crop" but a winter-growing sward mown or ploughed in before budburst, capturing the soil benefits in the wet season and removing the competition in the dry one. Verdict: worthwhile with different species and different management, not the same practice applied everywhere.

## Soil biology and structure

Root channels, organic matter, mycorrhizal association and improved water infiltration are real and cumulative, and in compacted or crusted soils they can increase the water reaching the vine rather than reduce it — the Douro case again, where the sward helps rain penetrate rather than run off. The honest qualification is that these benefits are slow, hard to measure in one season, and easy to claim without evidence.

## Frost

The counter-case that most answers miss. A tall sward insulates the soil and prevents it radiating stored heat on a still, clear spring night, so cover crops measurably increase radiative frost risk. In Chablis or the Loire the correct practice is to mow tight, or to cultivate the mid-row bare, ahead of the frost window. Verdict: on a frost-prone site an unmanaged sward is worse than bare soil, which is exactly why the judgement has to be site-specific.

## Biodiversity, predators and certification

Flowering swards support predatory mites and parasitoid wasps and reduce insecticide need, and for a certified organic grower a cover crop is close to compulsory, since herbicide is unavailable and permanent mechanical cultivation is expensive and erosive. Where certification carries a price premium, this alone can settle the economics.

## The economics

This is where the judgement is finally made. A cover crop costs seed, sowing, and repeated mowing or rolling passes — diesel, machinery hours and labour recurring several times a season — and it costs yield wherever it competes. Set against that, it may replace herbicide, reduce fertiliser, reduce erosion repair, and permit certification. At premium price points, where a small quality gain or a certification is recoverable in the bottle price, the calculation is easy. At commodity price points in a dry region, a permanent sward that costs tonnage and water is difficult to justify, and a herbicide strip under the vine with a mown mid-row is often the rational compromise.

## Conclusion

Cover crops are worthwhile — but as a targeted intervention, not as a default. On slopes, on fertile over-vigorous sites, in wet-harvest regions and under organic certification they earn their cost several times over. In dry, low-vigour, frost-prone or commodity-priced situations, a permanent unmanaged sward costs water, crop and money. The grower who can state what the sward is for, and has chosen the species, the row pattern and the mowing regime accordingly, is nearly always right to have one.

questionText: What is the role of pruning when managing an established vineyard?
body:
## Defining pruning in an established vineyard

In an established, functioning vineyard the vine's permanent architecture already exists. Pruning here is not training: it is the annual removal of the great majority of the previous season's wood, and the retention of a chosen number of buds on a chosen configuration of one-year-old wood. It is the single decision that most determines next season's crop, and — because it dictates where the fruit will sit and how the canopy will fill — it also determines the vineyard's disease exposure, its harvestability, its frost risk and its labour bill.

Its role is therefore economic as much as agronomic. I take four roles in turn: setting yield, shaping the season through the winter cut, maintaining the vine's longevity, and controlling cost.

## Role 1: setting yield, to a style

The primary purpose is to establish the crop level, because retained bud number is the grower's most direct control over yield. Bud load is set against the vine's capacity and against the target wine.

The contrast is best made concretely. In Gevrey-Chambertin, densely planted Pinot Noir is short cane pruned, retaining few buds per vine so that each vine carries a small crop; the density recovers yield per hectare while keeping yield per vine low, which is the arithmetic behind Burgundian quality. In the Central Valley of California, a high-trained quadrilateral cordon at low planting density retains a very large bud number per vine, because the wine is a high-volume commodity and the vineyard's job is tonnes per hectare at the lowest possible cost per tonne. Both are correct; they are answers to different questions.

Variety constrains the choice before style does. Varieties whose basal buds are unfruitful, Nebbiolo and Sultana among them, must be cane pruned to bring fruitful buds into the retained wood, whereas Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz and Chardonnay tolerate spur pruning on a cordon and therefore permit mechanisation. Style then fine-tunes it: a Mosel Riesling grower and a sparkling base grower want different crop levels and different ripeness curves from the same vine.

## Role 2: what the winter cut decides beyond yield

Too much discussion of these effects is displaced onto summer canopy work. They are decided in winter.

**Ventilation and disease.** Spur or cane number and spacing set how many shoots will occupy a metre of fruiting wire. Retain too many and the canopy closes, humidity in the fruit zone rises, spray penetration falls and botrytis and powdery mildew follow. A well-spaced winter cut is the cheapest disease control there is, because it costs nothing extra.

**Ease of harvest and mechanisation.** Pruning to a tidy, uniform cordon at a consistent height puts the fruit in a defined zone that a harvester can shake and a picker can find quickly. An untidy winter cut raises harvest cost every year afterwards, and can make machine harvesting impossible.

**Frost alleviation.** Pruning late delays budburst, moving the vulnerable phase past the worst of the frost window; double pruning — a rough pre-prune followed by a late final cut — achieves this at scale. Leaving extra buds as insurance, then removing surplus shoots after the frost risk passes, is the other winter-decided response. Raising the fruiting wire above the coldest air is a third.

## Role 3: vine longevity and the pruning wound

Every cut is an entry point for the trunk disease fungi that now cause most premature vine death. The role of pruning therefore includes protecting the vine's own permanent structure: cut late and in dry weather, keep wounds small, avoid large cuts into old wood, respect the sap flow so the desiccation cone forms away from the vascular path, and apply a wound protectant or biological treatment promptly. A vineyard pruned carelessly for ten years is a vineyard that has to be replanted early, which is the largest single cost a grower can incur.

## Role 4: the rest of the calendar, and the cost

Pruning continues through the season. Spring desuckering and shoot thinning correct the winter bud count against actual budburst; summer hedging and trimming stop lateral growth competing with ripening and keep the row trafficable; and green pruning — dropping under-ripe, raisined or rotten clusters before harvest — evens out maturation where a premium wine requires it.

Finally, pruning is the largest single labour operation in the vineyard year. Hand pruning is skilled, slow and increasingly hard to staff, and it is justified where precision of bud count and wound care buys a quality or longevity return. Mechanical and minimal pruning cost a fraction of that; minimal and mechanical pruning trials in Australia showed vines self-regulating to acceptable crop levels, which suits warm-region commodity fruit and is unsuitable where crop level must be exact.

## Conclusion

The role of pruning in an established vineyard is to set the coming crop and, in the same operation, to determine the canopy's ventilation, the vineyard's harvestability, its frost exposure and the working life of every vine — and to do all of this at the largest labour cost of the year. It is the point at which a grower converts a vine's capacity into a chosen wine style at a chosen cost, which is why it is a question of economic value and not only of technique.

questionText: Old vines have a mystique to them. What are the practical challenges and solutions to maintaining vineyards of old vines?
body:
## Defining old vines, and setting the mystique aside

There is no legal definition, so the definition has to be argued from context. Since the average commercial vine is replanted somewhere in its twenties or thirties — the economic rather than the biological lifespan — a vineyard that has passed that point is old, because it has survived the moment at which its replacement was financially rational. Codified schemes agree: the Barossa Old Vine Charter, which begins at 35 years and rises through Survivor, Centenarian and Ancestor tiers, and South Africa's Old Vine Project, which certifies vines of 35 years and over with a seal stating the planting date. In a region whose viticulture is a century old, forty years is old; in Santorini, whose ungrafted, basket-trained kouloura vines are continually renewed from an ancient root system, age is measured in the rootstock's centuries rather than the canopy's decades. I use 35 years and upward throughout.

Whether old-vine wine is better is not the question and I set it aside. The question is why these vineyards are hard to keep alive and how it is done.

## The challenges

**1. Declining and erratic productivity.** Yield falls with age and, more awkwardly, becomes variable and uneven between vines, so a block cannot be managed to a target tonnage. Bud fruitfulness declines, and vines that have lost cordon arms carry irregular crops that ripen at different rates.

**2. Trunk disease and the accumulated wound burden.** This is the central agronomic problem. Every winter cut is an infection point, so an old vine carries decades of accumulated Esca, Eutypa and Botryosphaeria colonisation in its permanent wood. Dead arms, dieback and apoplectic collapse are the visible result, and there is no curative treatment.

**3. Missing vines and mixed ages.** Gaps accumulate. Interplanting young vines creates a block of two ages with different vigour, ripening and water demand, harvested and pruned as one — which is a management problem, not just an aesthetic one.

**4. Mechanisation is largely impossible.** This is the challenge most often understated. Old vineyards are typically bush-trained or on obsolete trellis, irregularly spaced with rows too narrow for modern machinery, often on slopes, and frequently with trunks too fragile and gappy for a harvester to straddle and shake. Pruning, harvesting and often spraying must be done by hand, and hand work has to be skilled: pruning an irregular old vine to preserve its remaining structure cannot be given to an inexperienced crew.

**5. Labour supply.** That skilled seasonal labour is scarce and rising in cost everywhere old vineyards exist.

**6. Virus load and, sometimes, own-rooted fragility.** Decades of accumulated virus depress vigour further, and ungrafted survivors in phylloxera-free sands carry their own risks.

It is worth correcting one common error. Old vines are generally **less** susceptible to drought and water stress, not more: their deep, established root systems reach reserves young vines cannot, which is precisely why the world's surviving old vineyards are concentrated in dry regions — South Africa, Australia and Santorini — where they have outlasted everything planted around them.

## The solutions

**Remedial surgery rather than replanting.** Trunk renewal is the key maintenance operation: cut back below the necrosis and re-train a watershoot or sucker from the base to rebuild a trunk from the vine's own established root system. Curettage removes decayed wood from a standing trunk. Both restore a productive vine at a fraction of replanting cost and, importantly, without losing the root system that makes the vine valuable.

**Pruning as preservation.** Prune late and in dry weather, keep cuts small, avoid opening old wood, respect the sap flow, and protect wounds promptly. On an old vine this is not optimisation; it is the difference between another decade and none.

**Fill gaps by layering, not interplanting.** Where the training system permits, layering a cane from a neighbouring vine into the gap fills it with wood of the same age and genetic material rather than introducing a young vine of different vigour.

**Nutrition and soil.** The temptation is to feed a declining vine back to health. This has to be weighed against the soil's own fertility and the rootstock's vigour: on a naturally vigorous soil or a vigorous stock, added nitrogen produces canopy the old vine's compromised vascular system cannot support, stressing it further and worsening disease expression. The correct approach is usually restrained, diagnosed feeding — leaf and soil analysis first — with organic matter and careful water management to sustain root function rather than force growth.

**Canopy and harvest.** Accept unevenness and manage it: selective hand harvest in two passes, and shoot thinning to even the crop between strong and weak vines.

## The economics

This is what actually decides whether an old vineyard survives. A modern trellised block can be mechanically pruned and harvested, and its cost per tonne keeps falling as machinery improves. An old block cannot follow, so its costs rise with labour while its yield declines — a widening gap, in the wrong direction, on both terms of the equation.

The only durable solution is commercial. The value of the fruit must be raised until it covers the hand labour: single-block bottlings, old-vine designations on the label, and long-term grower contracts at premium prices. This is exactly what the Barossa Charter and the Old Vine Project are for — they are not romance, they are the mechanism that converts age into a price high enough to pay the pruners.

questionText: Examine the advantages and disadvantages of deliberate stem inclusion, or additions, during the winemaking process.
body:
## Where stems enter the process

Stems reach a wine at three points, and the argument differs at each. At the press, as whole uncrushed bunches so the rachis stays with the fruit. At the fermenter, as intact clusters under the cap or as a measured proportion of destemmed rachis returned to a crushed must. And after fermentation, as stems left with the skins during extended maceration or in a qvevri. I take the question across all three points and across white, rosé, red, sparkling and fortified production. The starting position matters: the mechanical destemmer made destemming the default, so the burden of proof sits with inclusion, not against it.

## The press house: whites, rosé and sparkling

Here the stem is a pressing aid, not a flavour. A lattice of rachis — roughly 2-5% of bunch weight but a much larger share of its volume — opens drainage channels through the cake, so juice runs at lower pressure over a shorter cycle. The advantage is cleaner, lower-solids juice with less phenolic pickup, less bitterness and less oxidative browning. That is why whole-bunch pressing is the norm for traditional-method base wine, where the fractionated cycle separates a low-phenolic cuvée from a firmer, more oxidisable taille: in Champagne, 4,000 kg of whole bunches yields 2,550 litres of legally usable juice, of which the first 2,050 litres are the cuvée. The same logic governs direct-press Provençal rosé, where pale colour and no grip are the entire brief.

The disadvantage is economic and non-negotiable. Whole-bunch pressing demands hand-harvesting into shallow crates, cuts throughput per press cycle, and requires press capacity sized for uncrushed fruit. Machine-harvested fruit arrives destemmed by definition. Below the mid price tiers that cost cannot be recovered.

## The fermenter: red wine

In red ferments stems do four things, each double-edged.

They buffer temperature and hold the cap open, improving drainage and making the pomace press out faster — worth having in a warm vintage or a deep vat, immaterial in a small one.

Intact berries within a whole cluster ferment intracellularly, generating carbonic-derived esters that read as aromatic lift, perfume and spice. Pushed too far, the same chemistry gives banana and confection that flattens varietal identity.

The rachis contributes tannin unlike seed or skin tannin: fine-grained, drying at the finish, and consistently read by tasters as heightened acidity and tension. Where fruit is soft and structurally light this is a real gain, which is why the advantage concentrates in Grenache, Syrah and Pinot Noir. It is a poor fit for Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot, which already carry firm tannin and, in Cabernet's case, a pyrazine profile that stems reinforce rather than balance.

And stems absorb. They take up water and alcohol, so a whole-bunch ferment finishes marginally lower in alcohol, and they adsorb anthocyanins, so it finishes paler.

## The case against, which is why most wine is destemmed

Ripeness is the first argument. Stems lignify later than fruit, and a green rachis delivers herbaceous, bitter, stalky character and an aggressive finish. Only a fully brown, woody stem is usable, and in a cool or interrupted season that condition simply is not met — so the technique carries vintage risk that destemming does not.

Second, chemistry works against the sensory impression. Stems leach potassium, raising pH and lowering titratable acidity, which weakens colour, reduces the efficacy of a given free SO2 and increases microbial vulnerability — the opposite of the freshness the taster reports.

Third, capacity and yield. Stems occupy tank volume, absorb wine that is then lost to press, and lower the effective throughput of a fermenter that has been paid for by the litre.

Fourth, hygiene. Stems arrive with vineyard debris, spoilage yeasts and residues, and cannot be sorted as reliably as berries.

Fifth, control. Whole-bunch fermentation is slower to start, harder to homogenise and harder to reproduce vintage to vintage — a serious objection for any brand selling on consistency.

## Skin-contact whites, qvevri and fortified

Whites are routinely and wrongly left out of this discussion. In qvevri and modern skin-contact winemaking, stems are included deliberately to supply tannin that acts as an oxidative buffer during long unsulphured maceration, and to give the drying grip that defines the style. The disadvantage is severe bitterness where stems are unripe, and a wine whose texture excludes most of the market.

In fortified production the case is weakest. Port's maceration is cut short by fortification, so stem tannin is extracted harshly and incompletely; near-universal destemming there is a considered decision, not a default.

## Conclusion

Stem inclusion is justified in two narrow places: as a mechanical pressing aid for premium white, rosé and sparkling base wine, and as a structural and aromatic tool for soft, low-tannin red varieties in ripe vintages, where the rachis is lignified. Everywhere else the balance of pH, colour, ripeness risk, hygiene, capacity and cost explains why the industry destems. It is a technique whose upside is real but conditional, and the conditions are demanding.

questionText: Compare and contrast winemaking techniques for "high end" and "entry level" Chardonnay in at least two regions.
body:
## Defining the tiers

By "entry level" I mean Chardonnay retailing under about £8 a bottle at UK retail, where duty, VAT, freight and margin leave roughly £1 or less per bottle for the wine itself — a figure that fixes every technical decision that follows. By "high end" I mean wine retailing above about £40, where the winemaking cost per bottle is immaterial against the price and the constraint is quality of raw material, not budget. The two are not points on one scale but different production models: the first optimises consistency and cost per litre at volume, the second optimises expression of a specific parcel and accepts variability.

I compare Burgundy and South Eastern Australia because both produce at each tier, which lets the comparison run across price and across region at once. I follow the process in sequence, since that is where the tangible differences sit.

## Intake and pressing

Entry level: machine-harvested at scale, destemmed and crushed, pressed hard in a large pneumatic press to maximise recovery — 700 litres or more per tonne — with press fractions blended back. Juice arrives warm and oxidised; some producers hyperoxidise deliberately, letting polyphenol oxidase strip oxidisable phenolics that are then settled out, which buys stability later.

High end: hand-picked in crates, whole-bunch pressed without destemming, long slow cycle at low pressure, and only 500 to 650 litres of free-run per tonne taken forward, with the hard press cut away entirely. Protective handling under an inert atmosphere in Burgundy's more reductive houses; deliberate juice oxidation in others. The tangible difference is not the equipment but the yield taken and the fractions rejected.

## Juice preparation and fermentation

Entry level: cold settle or, more commonly at volume, flotation with gelatine or pea protein for speed; bentonite added to juice to remove heat-unstable protein before ferment; juice clarified hard to low solids. Fermentation in stainless steel of 50,000 litres or more, cooled to 14-16°C, with a selected aromatic yeast strain and DAP to guarantee a clean, fast, reproducible finish. Aroma is engineered in — thiol- and ester-driven, fresh, fruit-forward.

High end: settled overnight only, kept deliberately turbid because the solids carry lipids and nitrogen that a barrel ferment needs; indigenous or partly indigenous yeast, accepting a slower and warmer ferment at 18-22°C in a 228-litre piece or a small foudre. Warmth and barrel volume create the reductive, struck-match character and the fatty acid profile that defines the style. Higher risk, and the answer to why: complexity comes from a slower, less controlled ferment.

## Malolactic and lees

Entry level: malolactic is usually blocked in Australia to keep malic acidity and crisp fruit, and acidification with tartaric is routine; where it is used, it is inoculated and fast. Lees handling is minimal — the wine is racked clean quickly to free the tank. Texture is bought in, using inactivated yeast preparations or mannoprotein additions at bottling rather than time.

High end: full spontaneous malolactic through the following spring, lees kept for 11 to 18 months with periodic bâtonnage or, increasingly, none at all — the choice between the two being a deliberate style decision about mannoprotein release versus reductive protection. The mechanism is the same in both tiers; the difference is that one buys it with time and one buys it in a bag.

## Oak and maturation

Entry level: oak flavour from staves, chips or powder in tank, dosed to a target and often combined with micro-oxygenation to soften phenolics over weeks. It is a flavour addition, not a maturation vessel, and it delivers vanillin and coconut without the slow oxygen ingress that changes structure.

High end: barrel maturation with 20-50% new French oak, tight-grained, over 12-18 months, where the wine is simultaneously receiving oxygen at a low, steady rate through the stave and evaporating in a cold cellar. A new barrel costs of the order of €800 and is used over three or four vintages, adding well over €1 a bottle — which is precisely why the technique does not migrate down.

## Stabilisation to bottle

Entry level: cold stabilisation or, more cheaply, CMC or potassium polyaspartate for tartrate stability; bentonite to protein stability; sterile membrane filtration and screwcap, because a wine shipped worldwide and drunk within two years must be absolutely stable in a warm warehouse.

High end: light or no fining, coarse filtration or none, bottling at the estate, more tolerance of tartrate crystals because the market accepts them. The wine is protected by lower pH, higher extract and a slower supply chain instead of by intervention.

## Where the regions diverge

The tier gap is wider in Australia than in Burgundy. Australia's entry level is built for scale — multi-region blending across a large geographical indication, large-format oak alternatives, engineered aroma — while its high end, in Margaret River or the Yarra Valley, has largely converged on the Burgundian toolkit of whole-bunch pressing, wild ferment and barrel maturation. Burgundy's entry level, by contrast, is made in the same cellars and often in the same way as its top wines, differing mainly in fruit source, yield and the proportion of new oak. In Burgundy the tier is set principally by the vineyard; in Australia it is set by the winemaking. That is the sharpest contrast the question offers, and it is a difference of production model, not of skill.

questionText:
Write concise notes on four of the following:

- Lysozyme
- Mannoprotein
- CMC - Carboxymethyl cellulose
- Copper sulphate
- Ascorbic acid
- YAN – Yeast assimilable nitrogen
body:
## Lysozyme

**What it is.** An enzyme extracted from hen egg white that hydrolyses the peptidoglycan of Gram-positive bacterial cell walls, lysing the cell.

**What it does.** It is antibacterial only, and specific: it kills lactic acid bacteria — *Oenococcus*, *Lactobacillus*, *Pediococcus* — and has no effect on yeast, including *Brettanomyces*, or on acetic acid bacteria, which are Gram-negative. Its two working uses are to delay or suppress malolactic fermentation, for instance in an aromatic white where malic acidity is wanted, and to control lactic bacteria in a high-pH must or a stuck ferment where SO2 is ineffective because so little of it is in the molecular form.

**Dose and limits.** Permitted in the EU and by the OIV to a maximum of 500 mg/L in must and wine combined. Working rates are 100-500 mg/L against a developing bacterial population, lower for prophylaxis.

**Effects and limitations.** It remains active as pH rises, which is its advantage over SO2. But it is a protein: it can precipitate with tannin, stripping colour and clarity in reds, and it can leave the wine protein-unstable, requiring bentonite afterwards. It is an allergen requiring declaration on the label, is neither vegan nor acceptable under some organic schemes, and is expensive.

## CMC — carboxymethyl cellulose

**What it is.** A cellulose derivative, a soluble anionic polysaccharide, used as a tartrate stabiliser. E466.

**What it does.** It does not remove potassium or tartaric acid. It is a crystallisation inhibitor: the polymer adsorbs onto the surface of nucleating potassium bitartrate crystals and blocks their growth, so a supersaturated wine stays clear. The commercial argument for it is energy — it substitutes for cold stabilisation at around -4°C for several days, which is one of the largest electricity costs in a winery.

**Dose and limits.** E466, permitted in the EU to a maximum of 100 mg/L. Typical dose is up to 100 mg/L, added in-line at least two to five days before bottling and always after fining but before final filtration, since it raises filterability index.

**Effects and limitations.** Effective and sensorially neutral in whites, rosés and sparkling wines. It is not suitable for reds: it destabilises colloidal colour and can throw a pigment deposit. The wine must already be protein-stable and filtered, or CMC will blind the filters. It does not prevent calcium tartrate instability.

## Copper sulphate

**What it is.** CuSO4, added as a solution to remove reductive sulphur compounds.

**What it does.** Cu2+ reacts with hydrogen sulphide and with free thiols such as ethanethiol to form insoluble copper sulphides, which are then removed by settling or filtration. It treats rotten-egg and struck-flint reduction; it does not remove disulphides, which must first be reduced back to thiols, and it does not fix mercaptan-derived heaviness permanently.

**Dose and limits.** The OIV and EU cap treatment at 1 g/hL of copper sulphate, with residual copper in the finished wine not to exceed 1 mg/L. Effective doses are small, of the order of 0.1-0.6 mg/L of copper, and should always be established by bench trial on graded additions.

**Effects and limitations.** It is a blunt tool. Copper also binds desirable volatile thiols, so overdosing a Sauvignon Blanc strips passionfruit and box aromas along with the fault. Residual copper above roughly 0.5 mg/L is a pro-oxidant in bottle and can throw a copper casse haze, so the wine must be filtered off the precipitate and the residue verified analytically before bottling.

## YAN — yeast assimilable nitrogen

**What it is.** The fraction of must nitrogen that *Saccharomyces* can actually use: ammonium ions plus free alpha-amino nitrogen, excluding proline, which yeast cannot assimilate anaerobically. Reported as mg N/L.

**What it does.** It determines yeast biomass and fermentation rate. A must fermenting to 12-13% abv needs of the order of 150 mg N/L, and the requirement scales with sugar — roughly 25-30 mg N/L for every 1% of potential alcohol, so a high-Brix must needs proportionally more.

**Dose and limits.** Deficiency is corrected with diammonium phosphate or with a complex organic nutrient, added in split doses at inoculation and around one third of sugar depletion, when uptake is most efficient. DAP addition is capped at 100 g/hL in the EU, and thiamine at 0.6 mg/L.

**Effects and limitations.** Below about 150 mg N/L, ferments run sluggish or stick and yeast produce hydrogen sulphide as a stress response. Above roughly 250-300 mg N/L, nitrogen is left in the finished wine as a microbial substrate, increasing spoilage risk, and urea from excess DAP is a precursor to ethyl carbamate. Organic nutrients also supply sterols and vitamins that DAP does not, which matters in a clarified white juice with low solids.

questionText: What are the critical winemaking considerations for a producer of inexpensive off-dry still white wines?
body:
## Definitions and the commercial frame

By "inexpensive" I mean a shelf price under about £7 in the UK or US$8 in the United States, which after duty, VAT, packaging, freight and retail margin leaves of the order of 50p a litre for the wine — a figure that decides everything below. "Off-dry" I take in the EU and OIV sense of medium dry: sugar above 4 g/L and up to 12 g/L, or up to 18 g/L where total acidity is within 10 g/L of the sugar figure. In perception terms sweetness is detectable from around 5-6 g/L in a high-acid wine and much higher in a soft one, but the legal band is what governs labelling.

This is a technically demanding category, not a lesser one. The producer is making a microbiologically fragile wine, at very large volume, on a margin that permits no reworking, for a consumer who will notice inconsistency between bottles. The critical considerations follow from that.

## Fruit ripeness and intake

The style needs moderate ripeness, not high ripeness. Fruit picked at 11-12% potential alcohol gives a finished wine of 10.5-11.5% abv where residual sugar reads as balance rather than as weight, keeps duty low in banded markets, and retains the natural acidity the sugar has to be hung on. Aromatic varieties suit the style because sweetness carries aroma. Fruit health matters more than at any other price: machine harvesting at volume permits no sorting, and botrytis brings laccase, glucans that blind filters, and an oxidation risk the winery cannot afford to chase.

## Juice preparation and fermentation

Clarify fast — flotation rather than static settling, because tank turnaround is a real cost — with bentonite in juice to fix protein stability early. Ferment cool, at 13-16°C, on a selected aromatic yeast with adequate nitrogen, to protect thiols and esters and, critically, to give a predictable and reproducible ferment. Blend across parcels to a specification, since consistency of the finished sugar and acid is what the customer is buying.

## Concentrating sugar in the winery

Where more sugar is wanted than the fruit supplies, the options are reverse osmosis or vacuum evaporation of a portion of the juice, or cryoconcentration; all remove water and raise sugar, acid and any fault character together, and all carry a volume loss that at this price is hard to justify. Enrichment with rectified concentrated grape must raises alcohol, not residual sugar, and is a different decision. In practice the economics favour buying sweetness in as a separate stream rather than concentrating the whole batch.

## Stopping the ferment short

Arresting fermentation at the target sugar is the most direct route and the most demanding. The options are chilling the tank to 2-4°C to drop the yeast out, followed immediately by racking and centrifugation; sterile membrane filtration at 0.45 microns to remove the population; fermenting under pressure so accumulating CO2 inhibits the yeast, which is how low-alcohol lightly sweet styles are made; or a heavy SO2 addition, which works but leaves a bound-SO2 burden the wine will carry to the shelf. The risk is that arrest is never complete: viable cells and residual nutrient in the same tank is the definition of an unstable wine.

## Adding sweetness back

The lower-risk and more common route is to ferment to dryness — a clean, stable, low-nutrient base — and sweeten before bottling. The options are unfermented grape juice held sterile under refrigeration and SO2, in the German Süssreserve tradition; rectified concentrated grape must, which is neutral, storable and dosable to a specification; or blending in a separate sweet wine component. In the EU sweetening may only be done with grape-derived products; sucrose is not permitted for this purpose, and chaptalisation is a permitted alcohol adjustment, not a sweetening one. This route lets one dry base wine be split into several sugar specifications for different markets, which is a decisive commercial advantage at scale.

## Hygiene, which is not negotiable

A wine with fermentable sugar, modest alcohol and a warm supply chain will referment if a single viable cell reaches it. That demands full CIP on every tank, line and valve — caustic wash, rinse, acid, sanitiser such as peracetic acid — sanitary fittings with no dead legs, replacement of perished gaskets, and swab or ATP verification rather than assumption. The filler, the filler bowl and the capper are the highest-risk points in the plant because they sit downstream of the last filter. Hygiene here is a bottling-line discipline as much as a cellar one.

## Preventing refermentation in bottle

Belt and braces, and all three levers are used together. Sorbic acid inhibits yeast but not bacteria and is capped at 200 mg/L and used at 150-200 mg/L; it must be accompanied by SO2, or lactic bacteria metabolise it to the geranium taint. SO2 is dosed to a molecular SO2 target of 0.8 mg/L, which at pH 3.2 needs roughly 25-30 mg/L free — higher than a dry wine of the same pH would need. Dimethyl dicarbonate, capped at 200 mg/L in the EU, kills yeast on contact at the filler and leaves no residue, but has no persistence, so it only secures a wine that is already close to sterile. Sterile filtration into an aseptic filler is the most reliable of all and increasingly the industry standard.

Finish with a low-oxygen-transmission screwcap and a warehouse specification, because the last critical consideration is that this wine must survive a shipping container, not a cellar.

questionText: Which winemaking decisions affect the ageing potential of a finished wine?
body:
## Definitions and scope

By "ageing potential" I mean the period over which a wine will hold or improve in bottle before its fruit falls away and its structure hollows out — a capacity for beneficial development, not merely survival. By "finished wine" I mean the wine as it leaves the winery, packaged and sealed, which puts everything up to and including the closure inside the scope of the question and everything after it outside.

The vineyard sets the ceiling: phenolic ripeness, berry size, acidity and freedom from rot determine what the cellar has to work with, and no winemaking decision recovers what was not picked. But the ceiling is rarely the binding constraint, and the question is about winemaking, so I confine the answer to vinification and maturation. Four mechanisms do the work — the antioxidant reservoir, pH, oxygen exposure, and colloidal structure — and every decision below acts through one of them.

## Building the antioxidant and structural reservoir

Ageing is, chemically, slow oxidation. A wine lasts in proportion to what it has to spend on that oxidation before the fruit is consumed.

In reds that reservoir is phenolic. The decisions are maceration length and temperature, cap management, whether to press early or hold on skins after dryness, and which press fractions to keep. Extended post-fermentation maceration matters because it allows tannin to polymerise and to bind anthocyanin into polymeric pigment, which is both colour-stable and slower to oxidise than free anthocyanin. A wine extracted hard and pressed at dryness has tannin but no polymerisation; it will be tough young and hollow at ten years.

In whites the reservoir is lees and glutathione rather than tannin. Ageing on gross lees supplies mannoproteins and a reducing environment; the decision to leave a wine on lees for a year rather than rack it clean in spring buys years in bottle. Sulphur dioxide is the reservoir of last resort, which is why free SO2 at bottling is an ageing decision.

## pH, and the malolactic decision

pH governs everything downstream. Below about pH 3.4 a given free SO2 delivers far more molecular SO2 - at pH 3.2 some 20 mg/L free SO2 gives the 0.8 mg/L molecular target, where at pH 3.8 it takes nearer 80 mg/L. Low pH also shifts anthocyanin towards the coloured flavylium form and slows oxidative reaction rates. So acidification, and the choice of when to acidify, is one of the highest-leverage ageing decisions available.

Malolactic fermentation is the sharpest trade-off in the paper. Completing it removes malic acid as a microbial substrate and makes the wine biologically stable — essential for a red destined for a decade in bottle. Blocking it, as in an age-worthy Riesling, keeps a higher acidity and lower pH, which preserves aroma and freshness for longer, but leaves a wine that must be sterile-bottled and never rewarmed. Both routes can produce long-lived wine; what fails is choosing neither cleanly.

## Oxygen: how much, and how fast

The distinction that matters is between oxygen given slowly during maturation, which polymerises tannin and stabilises colour, and oxygen given at bottling, which is simply consumed and lost. A new 225-litre barrel admits of the order of 20-30 mg/L of oxygen a year, spread over the whole élevage; that is why barrel-matured reds soften and gain longevity while the same wine held anaerobically stays angular. Micro-oxygenation in tank is the industrial substitute for the same mechanism.

Against that, total package oxygen at bottling, which for a wine intended to age should be held under about 1 mg/L, is pure debit: it is spent on the first months in bottle and takes free SO2 with it. Sparging, inerting the filler bowl, jetting the headspace and minimising the drop into the bottle are therefore ageing decisions, not merely handling ones. So is the closure, since oxygen ingress rate sets the whole trajectory: a tin-lined screwcap admits very little, an engineered technical cork a specified amount, and a synthetic closure a great deal more.

## The entry-level case, which runs the other way

For a wine designed to be drunk within eighteen months, "ageing potential" means shelf life, and the decisions invert. Protective, reductive handling from press to bottle; no malolactic, to keep acidity and primary fruit; no phenolic extraction, because phenolics brown; ascorbic acid at bottling with adequate SO2 behind it; CMC rather than cold stabilisation; a very low-ingress screwcap. The aim is to hold the wine still, not to develop it, and a bag-in-box or PET package with a high oxygen transmission rate is a deliberate decision to shorten life in exchange for cost.

## Sparkling and fortified wine

In traditional-method sparkling, ageing potential is bought at tirage. The base wine's acidity, the length of time on lees before disgorgement, the dosage level and the closure under which lees ageing occurs all count; long autolysis supplies mannoproteins and reductive capacity, dissolved CO2 and low pH suppress spoilage, and a crown cap seals more tightly than a natural cork during that period.

In fortified wine the decisive choices are the timing and strength of the spirit addition and the maturation regime. Fortifying mid-ferment leaves both high alcohol and high residual sugar, two preservatives at once, which is why vintage Port ages for decades. Oxidative maturation goes further: a Madeira heated and held in cask, or an oloroso passed through a solera, has already undergone the oxidation that would spoil a table wine, and so is effectively indestructible in bottle.

## Conclusion

The decisions that matter most are those setting pH, the antioxidant reservoir, and the rate of oxygen supply — and among them the malolactic decision, the élevage regime and the total package oxygen at bottling carry the greatest weight, because each acts on the wine's entire life rather than on one stage of it.

questionText: How and to what extent can a winemaker influence the textural profile of a wine?
body:
## What textural profile is, and what that makes relevant

Textural profile is the set of tactile and trigeminal sensations a wine produces in the mouth, as distinct from its aroma and its taste: viscosity and weight, the grain and drying force of astringency, the sharpness acid imparts, the warmth of alcohol, the prickle of dissolved carbon dioxide, and the mouth-coating fullness given by colloids. Defining it that way sets the scope, because it identifies exactly six physical variables the winemaker can move — phenolics, polysaccharides, alcohol, acidity, sugar, and dissolved CO2 — plus the colloidal state that determines how the first two are perceived. Everything below acts on one of those.

Viticulture sets the phenolic and sugar raw material and I take that as given. The question is what the cellar does with it, so I work through vinification and maturation in process order, then judge how far the influence actually extends.

## Extraction: putting phenolics in, and choosing which ones

Astringency is the precipitation of salivary proteins by tannin, and its perceived grain depends on tannin size and origin. Skin tannin is softer and better polymerised than seed tannin, so decisions that limit seed extraction — gentle crushing, early pressing, avoiding aggressive pump-overs late in ferment when alcohol is high and seed tannin most soluble — reduce coarseness directly. Warmer ferments and longer maceration extract more; extended maceration after dryness extracts less new tannin but allows what is present to polymerise into longer, softer chains. Press fraction selection is the bluntest textural instrument in a red cellar.

In whites the same chemistry works at a much lower threshold. Skin contact of a few hours before pressing adds a phenolic grip that gives an otherwise thin white a spine; pushed to days or weeks, as in qvevri and skin-contact styles, it produces genuine tannic structure and a drying finish. Rosé sits between the two, and pale direct-press styles are defined by the deliberate avoidance of that grip.

## Fermentation and lees: adding polysaccharides

Polysaccharides coat the palate and, more usefully, bind tannin so that it precipitates less salivary protein — they make a wine feel rounder and simultaneously less astringent. This is why the lees decision is the strongest single textural lever in white winemaking. Yeast strain matters because strains differ in glycerol and polysaccharide production; ageing on gross lees releases mannoproteins during autolysis; bâtonnage accelerates that release and adds a reductive dimension; and the same effect can be bought directly with mannoprotein or inactivated-yeast preparations where time is not available.

Malolactic fermentation softens texture by converting a dicarboxylic acid to a monocarboxylic one, lowering titratable acidity and raising pH, which reduces perceived sharpness. It is available in every still style and is often the difference between a taut white and a broad one.

## Maturation: oak, oxygen and time

Barrel maturation acts on texture in two ways that are frequently conflated. Ellagitannin from the wood is itself astringent and adds grip, but it also acts as an oxygen intermediary, and it is the slow oxygen ingress that polymerises tannin and softens the wine. Micro-oxygenation in tank isolates that second mechanism and is used precisely to convert green, aggressive tannin into rounder tannin without adding oak flavour. Time in any vessel does some of this on its own.

## Subtracting texture before the bottle

Fining and filtration take texture away, and the decisions are as consequential as the ones that add it. Gelatine, egg white and PVPP remove astringent and bitter phenolics selectively; bentonite strips protein and, over-used, leaves a white noticeably thinner; tight membrane or pad filtration removes the colloids that carried mouthfeel. Conversely, texture can be added at the last moment: oenological tannins are added at 5-20 g/hL to restore grip, gum arabic at 100-250 mg/L to smooth a hard finish, and dissolved CO2 is the cheapest lever of all: 500-700 mg/L reads as freshness in a young white, under 400 mg/L reads as flat. Residual sugar and alcohol level complete the set, sweetness adding weight and alcohol adding both viscosity and warmth, so a partial dealcoholisation thins a wine as surely as a hard filtration does.

## Sparkling wine

Here texture is largely pressure and lees. Pressure sets the intensity of the trigeminal prickle — roughly 5-6 bar in a traditional-method sparkling wine against 1-2.5 bar in a frizzante — and long lees ageing after the second fermentation releases mannoproteins that integrate the bubble into a finer, creamier mousse. Dosage is the final adjustment: a brut nature at under 3 g/L reads leaner and more angular than a demi-sec of the same base wine.

## Fortified wine

Spirit timing is the master decision. Fortifying to about 19-20% abv while some 90-100 g/L of sugar remains, as in vintage Port, delivers weight from sugar and warmth from alcohol at once, and cuts maceration short so tannin is extracted incompletely and firmly. Biological ageing under flor consumes glycerol and leaves a fino thin, saline and cutting; oxidative ageing in a solera concentrates the wine by evaporation and leaves an oloroso viscous and broad. Two textures, from the same base wine, decided entirely in the cellar.

## To what extent

Extensively, but asymmetrically. The winemaker has near-complete control over the perception of texture — CO2, sugar, mannoprotein additions, fining and filtration are all fast, cheap and reversible in blending, and can make almost any wine feel rounder or leaner. What cannot be manufactured is the quality of tannin: fine-grained, sustained astringency comes from ripe skin phenolics, and the cellar can only choose how much of it to extract, how far to polymerise it, and how much to strip. Texture can be adjusted by anyone; it can only be built where the fruit allows.
