questionText: Is there an ideal terroir for the production of sparkling wines?
body:
## Defining terroir, and stating my position

Terroir is the whole natural environment of a delimited site — geology and soil, topography of slope, aspect and altitude, mesoclimate, and soil biology — as it expresses itself through a particular plant material. The modern working definition is broader than the physical one: the OIV's 2010 definition treats terroir as the interaction between a physical environment and applied viticultural and oenological practices. That inclusion of human practice is what makes the question answerable at all for a category the trade rightly calls manufactured.

My position is that there is no single ideal terroir for sparkling wine, because the category contains styles with incompatible site requirements; but there is an ideal terroir for each style, and there is one generalisation that holds across all of them. The ideal site for sparkling wine is a marginal one — a site too cool to ripen fruit reliably for still wine — because the style's requirements turn that viticultural deficiency into an asset. For the autolytic traditional-method style specifically, the Champagne combination is the closest thing to an ideal that exists, though a large part of what makes it so is human and legal rather than physical.

## The physical brief, and why it differs by style

**Autolytic traditional method.** The base wine must be high in acid, low in potential alcohol, restrained in primary aroma so that autolysis has room to speak, and clean enough for whole-bunch pressing. That brief points to a cool climate at the edge of ripening — Champagne's northern latitude, Tasmania, the English chalk downs, and altitude as a substitute for latitude in Trentodoc, Limoux and the higher Penedes sites for Cava. It points to free-draining soils with a reserve of water: Champagne's chalk drains and yet stores moisture and reflects light, the Kimmeridgian marls of the Aube and Chablis do similar work, and limestone recurs from Franciacorta to Robertson. Lake or maritime moderation lengthens the ripening period without raising peak heat, which is the mechanism behind Franciacorta, Marlborough, Anderson Valley and the cooler South African wards used for Cap Classique. Sites within a region are not equivalent either: the Cote des Blancs, the Montagne de Reims and the Aube each contribute something different, which is an argument that no single terroir suffices even inside the ideal region.

**Aromatic tank method.** Prosecco reverses the brief. Glera is a relatively neutral, moderate-acid variety whose value lies in delicate floral and pear aromatics that a long autolytic ageing would destroy, so the site must deliver ripeness and aromatic retention rather than searing acidity. The steep hills of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene give the aromatic definition; the flat Treviso plain gives the volume. Asti has the same logic in stronger form: Moscato Bianco on the Piedmont hills, picked to preserve terpenes, fermented once and arrested. A site ideal for Champagne would produce poor Asti.

**Ancestral method.** Pet-Nat requires healthy fruit and a reliable residual-sugar and yeast population at bottling, and comparatively little else; its character is dominated by process decisions. It is the hardest style for which to argue an ideal terroir, and the honest observation is that it is made successfully almost everywhere.

## The manufactured element

Even within the traditional method, the largest determinants of the finished wine are human. Blending is the central technology, and it exists specifically to override site: multi-village, multi-variety assemblage smooths parcel differences, and the reserve-wine system is designed to erase vintage variation altogether — a deliberate suppression of what terroir would otherwise express. Press fractionation discards the phenolic later pressings; the decision on malolactic conversion determines the acid profile as decisively as the site does; time on lees creates the autolytic character that most consumers identify as the style; and dosage adjusts the final balance after everything else. A house style is engineered, and reproduced from fruit that varies enormously year to year.

The delimitations are human too. Champagne's boundary was fixed by a legal settlement in the 1920s after the grower riots, and Prosecco was reorganised in 2009, when the grape was renamed Glera and the denomination extended across a large area of the Veneto and Friuli — an explicit demonstration that the boundary of an "ideal" terroir can be redrawn by administrative decision. Conversely, the human element also creates terroir claims: the hills of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019 on the strength of their cultural landscape, and the grower movement and single-parcel cuvees in Champagne are an attempt to reassert site against the blending house.

## Weighing it

The physical case for a single ideal is genuinely strong for one style. Chalk, marginal cool climate, gentle slopes and a long, unforced ripening period do produce base wine of a quality that is very hard to match, and new regions consciously seek chalk or limestone at cool latitudes. But three objections defeat the claim of a universal ideal. Different sparkling styles want opposite things from a site. The processing decisions contribute more of the finished character than the site does, which is precisely what "manufactured" means. And the leading regions' boundaries are legal artefacts as much as geological ones.

## Conclusion

There is no ideal terroir for sparkling wine as a category. There is an ideal site brief for each style, and one principle common to all: choose a site whose climate is marginal for still wine, because low sugar and high acid are the style's assets rather than its faults. For traditional-method wine, Champagne remains the benchmark — but I would attribute that as much to three centuries of accumulated human technique and to the legal boundary drawn around it as to the chalk, which is exactly why Tasmania, England and Trentodoc can now approach it.

questionText: What options are available to control final sugar levels in wine?
body:
## Defining the target

Final sugar means residual sugar: the fermentable and unfermentable sugars left in the finished wine. Even a bone-dry wine holds roughly 1-2 g/L of unfermentable pentoses, so zero is not on the table. EU labelling defines dry as up to 4 g/L, or up to 9 g/L where total acidity is no more than 2 g/L below the sugar; then medium dry to 12 g/L, medium to 45 g/L and sweet above 45 g/L. Sparkling wine has its own ladder: brut nature under 3 g/L, extra brut under 6, brut under 12, extra dry 12-17, sec 17-32, demi-sec 32-50 and doux above 50. Those numbers matter because they are what the winemaker is actually aiming at, and because perceived sweetness is not the same thing — a 9 g/L Riesling at pH 2.9 tastes drier than a 4 g/L Pinot Grigio.

This is a winery question. Vineyard sugar accumulation — late harvest, botrytis, passerillage, cane-cutting — sets the raw material, and I treat it only as the starting condition. I work through the cellar chronologically: what arrives, what the ferment does, how it can be stopped, and what can be blended in afterwards.

## Setting the starting sugar

Enrichment raises must sugar: sucrose where chaptalisation is allowed, rectified concentrated grape must (RCGM) where it is not, or water removal by vacuum evaporation, reverse osmosis or cryoextraction. Sugar can equally be reduced before fermentation — glucose oxidase, membrane systems coupling reverse osmosis to a sugar-stripping resin, or water addition where permitted, as in Australia for high-Baumé fruit. These fix the potential alcohol, and so determine how much sugar there is room to leave.

## Fermenting to dryness — the ordinary case

Most wine is dry because the yeast was allowed to finish, and that is an active achievement, not a default. It needs a strain with sufficient alcohol tolerance, correct rehydration, YAN of the order of 200 mg/L for a normal must and considerably more for a high-sugar one, staged nutrient additions, temperature held in range, and oxygen during the growth phase to build yeast sterols. Where any of these fail, the wine ends with sugar nobody chose, and restarting a stuck ferment with an acclimatised culture is far harder than avoiding one. High-sugar musts — Amarone, a Barossa red at 16% potential alcohol — are the difficult case, because osmotic stress and ethanol toxicity make dryness the accomplishment. Running the logic backwards is a crude sweetening tool: pick a slow, low-tolerance strain and sugar remains, but the endpoint is unpredictable.

## Stopping the fermentation

Every precise method here removes or immobilises yeast at a chosen sugar level.

- **Chilling** to around 0-4C settles the yeast and halts activity — Mosel Kabinett, Loire demi-sec. It is reversible on warming, so it must be locked in by something else.
- **Sulphur dioxide** at mutage dose is the traditional sweet-wine tool. In Sauternes the ferment usually stalls unaided once alcohol and botrytis metabolites overwhelm the yeast; SO2 then fixes the result rather than causing it.
- **Physical removal** — centrifugation, cross-flow, then sterile filtration. Asti is the clearest case: one tank fermentation under pressure, chilled and filtered at around 7% abv with the sugar still in place. Prosecco DOC labelled Extra Dry sits at 12-17 g/L by the same route.
- **Fortification.** Spirit to about 15% abv upwards kills the yeast, and the timing sets the sugar. Port fortified at roughly 6-8% abv retains something like 100 g/L; a Vin Doux Naturel such as Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is arrested earlier and sweeter; Pineau des Charentes fortifies juice that never fermented at all.
- **Pressure.** Accumulated CO2 inhibits yeast, which contributes in tank-method sweet sparkling alongside the chilling.

## Adding sugar back

Blending after fermentation is the most controllable option, because the base wine is finished and the addition is dosed against an analysis rather than guessed at mid-ferment. Süssreserve — sterile unfermented juice — is used in Germany and increasingly in England, and brings acidity and grape aroma with it. RCGM does the same arithmetic without flavour, which is why it dominates at commercial scale. In sparkling wine the liqueur d'expédition at disgorgement sets the whole style, and is the reason one base wine can be sold as brut and as demi-sec. Sherry is the instructive fortified case: it ferments bone dry without exception, so every sweet sherry is a blend, sweetened with Pedro Ximénez or Moscatel wine, or with RCGM for commercial cream styles.

## Holding the sugar where you put it

Above roughly 4 g/L the wine is refermentable, so sugar control is only as good as the stabilisation behind it. Sterile filtration at 0.45 micron, molecular SO2 held on target, sorbic acid, capped at 200 mg/L in the EU and useless without SO2 because lactic bacteria turn it into geranium taint, or DMDC at 200 mg/L. Dealcoholised wine is the extreme: stripping the alcohol leaves a sweet liquid with no defence at all, hence back-sweetening followed by aseptic bottling.

## Conclusion

The options divide by how precisely they hit a number. Fermenting dry and blending back are the two accurate methods, and between them account for most of the world's wine; arresting a live fermentation is the imprecise one, tolerated where the arrest itself creates the style, as in Port and Asti. Choosing between them is a choice about how much control the style can afford to give up.

questionText: Compare and contrast winemaking techniques for an early-drinking and an age-worthy Pinot Noir still red wine in a premium region.
body:
## Region, and what the two targets mean

I take the Côte de Nuits as my premium region: land values, the cru hierarchy and a market that pays three-figure sums for single-vineyard bottlings define premium far better than any statement about quality alone. It is also a region that genuinely makes both wines — a village Gevrey-Chambertin from young vines against a premier cru off the same commune — so the comparison is not smuggling in a difference of fruit quality dressed up as winemaking. Where I need a New World counterpoint I use Central Otago, premium on the same test.

**Early-drinking** means built to show best between roughly one and four years from vintage: primary red fruit, supple tannin, no requirement for reductive reserve. **Age-worthy** means built to improve for a decade or more: enough phenolic structure and acid, and enough oxygen-buffering capacity, that the wine gains complexity rather than merely surviving. Pinot Noir makes this hard, because its anthocyanins are largely non-acylated and therefore intrinsically unstable, and its tannin is modest. Age-worthiness in Pinot cannot be extracted by force; it has to be assembled.

## Picking

Both wines want whole, unbroken fruit, but the decisions diverge. For the early-drinking wine machine harvesting is defensible: it is fast, cheap and lets the winery pick at optimum ripeness across a wide window, and the berry damage it causes releases juice and colour that suits a wine wanted fruity and forward. For the age-worthy wine that damage is disqualifying — oxidation and premature extraction start in the bin — so hand-picking into small crates, cool, with sorting at the winery, is the only route, and it is also the only route that permits whole-bunch work later. The contrast is not quality of fruit but optionality: machine harvest closes doors that hand harvest keeps open.

## Must adjustments

Both may need chaptalisation in a cool Burgundian vintage and acidification in a warm Otago one. The difference is intent. In the early-drinking wine adjustment is used to hit a commercial target — a little sucrose for mid-palate weight, a little tartaric for freshness — and enological tannin at crush is genuinely useful, since a skin-derived proanthocyanidic tannin binds anthocyanin into polymeric pigment and holds the colour of a thinly extracted wine. Tannin is far more widely used across styles than candidates usually credit. In the age-worthy wine adjustments are minimised, not for ideology but because the wine must age on its own phenolic architecture; an added gallotannin gives immediate grip but does not build the long chains that soften over ten years.

## Destemming, whole berry and cold soak

These are three different things and get conflated. Cold soak works because anthocyanins are water-soluble and extract at 5-10C before alcohol appears to dissolve seed tannin: it gives colour and primary aroma with little grip, which is exactly the early-drinking profile, so a three-day soak there is a colour tool. In the age-worthy wine a cold soak is used more sparingly, because the aim is not maximum early colour but colour that has tannin to bind to. Whole-bunch inclusion is a different mechanism again: intact berries ferment intracellularly, generating carbonic aromatics, while the stems contribute their own tannin, absorb some alcohol and heat, and open the cap for gentler extraction. It also has a cost — the stems raise potassium and so nudge pH upwards, and unlignified stems give green pyrazine-like notes. So whole bunch is a structural and aromatic investment for the age-worthy wine, and largely 100% destemming for the early-drinking one, where cleanliness of fruit is the whole point.

## Fermentation and cap management

The early-drinking wine ferments warm-ish and fast on a cultured strain chosen for fruit expression, with pump-overs: efficient, oxygenating, and extracting quickly to a modest total. The age-worthy wine ferments longer and often on ambient yeast, with punch-downs by hand or foot — slower, gentler, more selective for skin than seed phenolics — and often a cold start to stretch the ferment. Pump-over versus punch-down is the clearest contrast in the answer: one maximises extraction per unit time, the other maximises control over which phenolics come out.

## Post-fermentation maceration and pressing

The early-drinking wine is pressed at or just before dryness, and the press fraction goes straight back in for colour and volume. The age-worthy wine sits on skins for a further one to three weeks: colour intensity actually falls as pigment adsorbs onto skins and lees, but polymeric pigment and softer tannin build — a deliberate trade of present appearance for future stability. It is then pressed gently, in fractions, and each fraction assessed before blending.

## Élevage

Eight to ten months in older barrels or larger foudre for the early-drinking wine, an early first racking, fining and filtration to bottle bright and stable. Sixteen to eighteen months, with perhaps 30-50% new oak, extended lees contact, minimal racking and no fining or filtration for the age-worthy wine. Oak here is not flavour but slow oxygen ingress plus ellagitannin as a polymerisation co-factor.

## Conclusion

Every divergence follows one principle: the early-drinking wine is made by extracting quickly and stabilising what you got, the age-worthy wine by extracting slowly and letting oxygen assemble it. Both are interventions; they simply pay off on different timescales.

questionText:
Write concise notes on each of the following:

a) Smoke taint in grapes and wine
b) Volatile acidity
c) Metatartaric acid
d) Spinning cone technology
body:
Four notes of roughly equal length, deliberately: this question rewards even coverage, and the marks lost are lost by writing three good notes and one thin one.

## a) Smoke taint in grapes and wine

Smoke taint is the ashy, burnt, medicinal character taken up by vines exposed to bushfire smoke. The active compounds are volatile phenols from lignin pyrolysis — guaiacol, 4-methylguaiacol, syringol and the o-, m- and p-cresols — with detection thresholds in the low micrograms per litre. The mechanism that catches people out is that the vine glycosylates them: most of the taint sits in grapes as non-volatile glycosides, so juice analysis for free phenols badly understates the risk. Acid hydrolysis and yeast and oak glycosidases release them during fermentation and, critically, for years in bottle, which is why a wine passed at bottling can be undrinkable at three years.

Degree of taint depends on smoke density and duration, proximity to the fire, and phenological stage — exposure from véraison onwards is far worse than at flowering. Handling: hand-pick to exclude leaf matter, press whole bunches, take free run only, minimise skin contact, ferment cool, avoid glycosidase-active enzymes, then remediate with activated carbon, PVPP or casein fining, or reverse osmosis coupled to a phenolic-adsorbent resin. All of these strip fruit as well as taint. The honest judgement, and the one few candidates make, is that at high taint levels the correct decision is not to make wine at all — declassify, sell the fruit, or claim on crop insurance — because remediation cost plus reputational risk exceeds the value of a mid-priced wine, and the taint returns in bottle.

## b) Volatile acidity

VA is the fraction of a wine's acidity that is steam-distillable, dominated by acetic acid with ethyl acetate as the second compound of consequence — the two are usually discussed together because acetic acid smells of vinegar and its ester of nail varnish. EU caps total VA at 20 milliequivalents per litre for red, 1.2 g/L as acetic acid, and 18 for white and rosé, with derogations upwards for botrytised and long-aged styles; the US TTB limit is 1.4 g/L for red and 1.2 g/L for white. Acetic acid is generally detectable from around 0.6-0.9 g/L depending on the wine's weight, and ethyl acetate turns solventy above roughly 150-200 mg/L.

Acetobacter and Gluconobacter are the usual suspects but not the only ones. Saccharomyces itself produces acetic acid, more so under osmotic stress or nitrogen deficiency — hence high VA in high-sugar musts; lactic acid bacteria produce it from sugars in a sluggish MLF and from citric acid at the end of one; Brettanomyces produces it aerobically. Hygiene, full vessels, inert gas, adequate molecular SO2 and prompt completion of MLF are the controls. VA is not automatically a fault: at low levels it lifts aromatics, and it is part of the accepted character of traditional Amarone and of some classed-growth Bordeaux — the test is integration, not the number.

## c) Metatartaric acid

Metatartaric acid is a polyester of tartaric acid, made by heating tartaric acid under vacuum so the molecules esterify into chains. Added to wine it acts as a protective colloid: the chains adsorb onto the surface of nascent potassium bitartrate crystals and block their growth, so crystals never reach visible size. It does not remove tartrate — it prevents it precipitating.

It is capped at 100 mg/L in the EU and typically dosed at that rate. The advantages are real: it is very cheap, works instantly, needs no energy or capital equipment, and unlike cold stabilisation costs no volume, colour or aroma. The disadvantage is that the ester bonds hydrolyse back to tartaric acid, and the rate is temperature-dependent, so protection lasts perhaps 12-18 months in a cool cellar but only weeks at 25-30C — and once it fails, the wine is less stable than if it had never been treated. Against the alternatives: cold stabilisation is slow and energy-hungry but permanent; electrodialysis is permanent and gentle but capital-intensive; carboxymethylcellulose is a colloid like metatartaric but does not hydrolyse, which makes it the better modern choice for whites. Metatartaric therefore suits inexpensive, high-turnover wine bottled and drunk within a year, and is the wrong tool for a wine that will be aged or shipped through the tropics.

## d) Spinning cone technology

A spinning cone column is a counter-current stripping column: wine flows down over alternating fixed and rotating cones as a thin film, meeting nitrogen or steam rising through a vacuum, which pulls out volatiles at low temperature and so avoids the cooked character of ordinary distillation. It is run in two passes. The first, cooler pass removes a small aroma fraction which is set aside; the second, warmer pass strips ethanol. Recombining the aroma fraction with the dealcoholised base, then blending that back into untreated wine, is what allows a precise alcohol reduction with much of the aroma retained — this separation of the flavour fraction from the alcohol is the point of the technology.

Uses beyond alcohol reduction include desulphiting stored grape juice and concentrate, and partial removal of smoke taint or excess ethyl acetate. Regulation constrains it: the EU permits a reduction of no more than 20% of the alcohol for the product still to be sold as wine, with separate categories now for dealcoholised and partially dealcoholised wine. It is not reverse osmosis, which is a membrane separation at ambient temperature and pressure, and it is nothing like centrifugation, which separates solids by density and removes no volatiles at all.

questionText: When, how and why should sulphur dioxide be used in winemaking? Are winemakers playing it too safe with sulphur dioxide additions?
body:
## Why: three jobs, one molecule

SO2 does three distinct things, and the dose is set by whichever job dominates. It is **antioxidant**, though indirectly: it scavenges hydrogen peroxide produced as phenolics oxidise, so it intercepts the oxidation cascade rather than reacting with oxygen quickly itself. It is **antioxidasic**, denaturing polyphenol oxidase and, more importantly, botrytis laccase. And it is **antimicrobial** against wild yeast, lactic acid bacteria, acetic acid bacteria and Brettanomyces. It also binds acetaldehyde, which both removes a stale aroma and permanently ties up that portion of the SO2.

Which is why the only figure that matters is molecular SO2, not total or even free. Molecular SO2 is the antimicrobial form, and the target is around 0.5-0.8 mg/L, but the proportion of free SO2 in that form is governed by pH: at pH 3.0 roughly 6% of free SO2 is molecular, at pH 3.5 about 2% and at pH 4.0 under 1%. A high-pH Grenache therefore needs several times the free SO2 of a low-pH Riesling for the same protection — and may not be able to reach it inside EU totals of 150 mg/L for dry red and 200 mg/L for dry white, with 400 mg/L for some botrytised sweet wines. That single calculation should drive every addition, and in practice it often does not.

## When, and at what rate

**Receival and crush:** 20-30 mg/L on clean, cool, hand-picked fruit and 50 mg/L or more where fruit is split, rotten or machine-harvested warm, principally to knock down laccase and spoilage flora. Omitted entirely for carbonic maceration or an intended ambient ferment.

**Cold soak:** the stage most people forget. A red held at 8-12C for three or four days is an ideal medium for acetic acid bacteria and Kloeckera, so 30-50 mg/L, or the deliberate decision to run with none and accept the microbial risk for aromatic complexity.

**Juice settling in whites:** 30-50 mg/L after settling, which also suppresses indigenous yeast and buys clean juice for a chosen inoculum.

**Fermentation:** none. It would inhibit the yeast and drive H2S formation.

**Post-MLF:** the critical addition, because the wine is at its most vulnerable — no sugar, no competitive flora, warm. An addition of 30-60 mg/L to reach 25-35 mg/L free, made immediately malic acid tests clear.

**Barrel ageing:** the other forgotten stage. Oxygen ingress and evaporation erode free SO2 continuously, so check and adjust at every racking, topping up to hold 25-35 mg/L free, and sterilise empty barrels with a burnt sulphur disc.

**Bottling:** adjust to 30-40 mg/L free for a dry white and 25-35 mg/L for a dry red; sweet wines need considerably more, at 0.8 mg/L molecular or above, to hold the sugar.

## How: forms, dosing and measurement

Potassium metabisulphite is about 57% available SO2, and is the small-winery default — but it must be dissolved in water or wine first and added during a pump-over or racking, because dumped dry into a tank it stratifies and locally over-sulphurs. A 5-10% aqueous PMS solution dosed volumetrically is more accurate. Larger wineries use liquid SO2 from a cylinder, metered by an inline dosing pump, and a sulphitometer on the crush pad to dose incoming fruit proportionally to flow. Barrels take sulphur discs or effervescent tablets. Measurement is by aeration-oxidation for free and total SO2 — the reliable method — with Ripper titration acceptable for whites but distorted in reds by phenolics; molecular SO2 is then calculated from free SO2 and pH.

Safety is the part almost nobody writes about. SO2 gas is acutely toxic, corrosive to eyes and airways, denser than air, and pools in tank pits, sumps and empty vessels — it is immediately dangerous to life at around 100 ppm, and occupational limits are in the low parts per million. Sulphuring a barrel room, or entering a recently sulphured or CO2-purged tank without atmosphere testing, forced ventilation and a confined-space permit, kills people. PMS powder is itself a respiratory irritant. And SO2 is not an inert gas: blanketing fruit or headspace is a job for CO2, nitrogen or argon, never for SO2.

## Are winemakers playing it too safe?

My view is that the profession is not over-dosing so much as dosing badly. Total SO2 usage has fallen substantially, and the real fault is imprecision: additions made to a habitual number rather than calculated from measured pH and free SO2, which simultaneously over-sulphurs low-pH whites and leaves high-pH reds unprotected. Timing is the second fault — small early additions are far more efficient than a large corrective one, which mostly binds.

Where I do think caution is excessive is at bottling, where fear of a stray refermentation produces sulphurous young whites that would show better fruit at 25 mg/L free. But the alternatives are partial, not substitutes. Rigorous hygiene, inert gas handling, temperature control and sterile filtration are the genuine ones. Ascorbic acid is antioxidant only and pro-oxidant without SO2 present; lysozyme acts on lactic bacteria alone; chitosan targets Brettanomyces; DMDC sterilises at bottling but has no residual effect; bioprotective non-Saccharomyces yeasts at receival occupy the niche without protecting the finished wine. None combines all three functions at a few cents per bottle. The low-sulphur category proves the point — its best wines are exhilarating and its failure rate, in VA and mousiness, is uncomfortably high.

questionText: To what extent are winemaking interventions desirable in a small-scale winery producing high-quality, dry red wine?
body:
## Terms, and how I read the question

By **small-scale** I mean a winery under about 10,000 cases a year: one where lots are handled individually and by hand, where the winemaker tastes every vessel weekly, and where capital equipment — optical sorters, reverse osmosis, rotofermenters — cannot be amortised. Scale says nothing about quality: plenty of small wineries make ordinary wine and several of the world's benchmark reds come from estates producing far more than this. **High quality** I define as a wine that is balanced and concentrated without heaviness, complex, capable of improving in bottle, and legible as coming from its place — provenance is part of the definition, not a marketing add-on, and price is a consequence of quality rather than evidence of it.

Two readings I reject. This is not a question about whether to minimise intervention: every choice in a cellar is an intervention, and deciding not to destem is as active a decision as adding tannin. Nor is it about hygiene and fault-fixing; I take the wine as healthy and the question as being about which choices optimise quality. So the answer is not *how much* to intervene but *which* interventions the quality objective justifies. My position, argued below, is that interventions which preserve optionality and work with the fruit are strongly desirable, while those that overwrite site character are not — because at this quality level site difference is the thing being sold.

## Fruit selection and sorting

The most desirable intervention of all, and the one small scale makes uniquely available. Hand-sorting on a table at 3,000 cases costs a few hours; at three million it is impossible, which is why large producers buy optical sorters instead. Removing raisined and mouldy berries lifts quality more than any subsequent decision, because no cellar technique removes laccase-oxidised or dehydrated character afterwards. I would spend money here before anywhere else.

## Pre-fermentation choices

Cold soak, whole-bunch inclusion and saignée pull in different directions and cannot all be right. Cold soak extracts anthocyanin and primary aroma before alcohol appears, which suits a variety short of colour; whole bunch adds stem tannin, aromatic lift and cooler, slower fermentation but raises pH and risks greenness from unlignified stems. Compare the traditionalist Barolo school of long submerged-cap macerations in large Slavonian botti against the modernist school of short rotofermenter macerations and French barriques: both make serious wine, and the difference is not one of competence but of what each is willing to trade — perfume and tension against approachability and colour. Whole bunch is well-founded in Côte-Rôtie, where whole-bunch inclusion and co-fermentation with a little Viognier are long-standing, but transplanted to a warm site with short vegetative cycles it produces stalky wine. Saignée I regard as the least desirable of the three: it concentrates everything indiscriminately, including alcohol and any unripe phenolics, and is usually a correction for a viticultural failure.

## Yeast

Ambient fermentation is not a virtue in itself, and the argument that it expresses site is weaker than usually claimed — a resident cellar population is a winery signature at least as much as a vineyard one. Its real benefit is a slower, more complex fermentation from sequential non-Saccharomyces activity; its real cost is risk of sluggishness and VA. A cultured strain gives reliability and a predictable profile but narrows the aromatic range. At small scale I would ferment ambient on sound fruit, with a cultured strain held ready — the intervention being the contingency, not the default.

## Fermentation and cap management

This is where extraction is decided, and gentleness is worth more than power. Punch-downs are more selective for skin than seed phenolics; pump-overs mix and oxygenate efficiently; rack-and-return and rotofermenters extract hard and fast and, in my view, belong to a volume model rather than this one. Temperature is the greater lever: a peak in the high twenties builds structure, cooler preserves aroma, and small vessels allow the winemaker to run several regimes and blend. Extended post-fermentation maceration trades present colour for polymeric pigment and softer tannin, which is desirable for a wine intended to age and pointless for one that is not.

## Additions — tannin and acid

Acidification is desirable when it restores balance in a warm vintage and undesirable when it becomes a routine substitute for picking earlier, because the wine then tastes of two separate things. Enological tannin at crush is useful and under-used in the sense that it stabilises pigment; added late for grip, it is cosmetic and shows as a hard finish. The test I apply is whether the addition assists what the fruit already contains or supplies what it lacks.

## Oak and élevage

The intervention most often overdone. New oak supplies slow oxygen ingress and ellagitannins that help polymerise pigment — genuinely useful — but at high percentages it substitutes a purchased flavour for a grown one, and it is expensive at small scale. I would rather buy larger-format and older barrels and spend the difference on sorting. Fining and filtration protect the buyer against haze and refermentation; for a high-quality red bottled with reasonable free SO2 and sound hygiene, I would generally forgo both, accepting sediment as the cost.

## Conclusion

Interventions are desirable in direct proportion to how far they serve the fruit rather than replace it. Sorting, thoughtful extraction, temperature control and oxygen management are close to obligatory at this level. Saignée, heavy new oak, late tannin and habitual acidification are not, because each one narrows the very distinctiveness the wine is priced on.

questionText:
What handling procedures could a winemaker implement to make mid-priced still wine from each of the following:

a) English Chardonnay: potential alcohol 8%; pH 2.8; total acidity 14.5; and
b) Barossa Valley Grenache Noir: potential alcohol 16.5%; pH 4.2; total acidity 3.9.
body:
## Mid-priced, and the four levers the question hands you

By mid-priced I mean a wine retailing at roughly £10-20 in the UK: it must carry real processing costs and a recognisable varietal identity, but cannot support hand-sorting, barrel fermentation or long ageing, and it will be drunk within a year or two. That rules some remedies out on cost alone. The question's parameters then set the structure: alcohol, pH and titratable acidity, and so the four tools of chaptalisation, water addition, acidification and deacidification.

## a) English Chardonnay — the problems in this juice

At 8% potential alcohol the juice carries roughly 135 g/L of sugar, short of the 12% a consumer expects and below the minimum strength at which the product can be sold as wine. TA of 14.5 g/L is around double a palatable level. pH 2.8 is the more interesting number: it is a microbiological gift, since at pH 2.8 some 9% of free SO2 is in the molecular form, so tiny sulphur additions protect the wine — but it also puts the juice below the threshold at which malolactic bacteria will function. Fruit this underripe will be malic-dominant and green, and in a cool wet English season on the Kent, Sussex and Hampshire chalk, botrytis and sour rot are likely, bringing laccase with them.

## a) Handling: alcohol, then acidity and pH

Enrichment is compulsory. Zone A, where England sits, permits enrichment of up to 3% vol, taking this juice to 11% — the ceiling, not a choice. Sucrose is the right vehicle at about 17 g/L of sucrose per 1% of alcohol, so roughly 50 g/L, added in stages during fermentation; RCGM works but costs more. Must concentration is exactly wrong here, because removing water concentrates the acid too.

Deacidification then does most of the work, and one method will not be enough. Calcium carbonate is the powerful option: 1 g/L of calcium carbonate removes about 1.5 g/L of tartaric acid as insoluble calcium tartrate and raises pH sharply — but it removes only tartaric, this juice's excess is largely malic, and it leaves residual calcium that can throw crystals slowly and unpredictably in bottle. Potassium bicarbonate is gentler in practice only because it is limited to small corrections, removing roughly 1.1-1.5 g/L of acidity per gram added - similar potency per gram to calcium carbonate - but it forms bitartrate that must then be cold-stabilised out and is impractical beyond about 2 g/L. The right tool for malic-dominant acid is double-salt deacidification: treat a fraction of the must with excess calcium carbonate seeded with calcium tartrate-malate so both acids precipitate together, then blend back to target.

Malolactic fermentation is then essential, and for a specific reason: it converts diprotic malic acid to monoprotic lactic acid, so converting 1 g/L of malic acid drops titratable acidity by roughly 0.5 g/L, softens the sharp malic edge to a rounder lactic one, and adds diacetyl weight that flatters lean fruit. But *Oenococcus oeni* struggles below about pH 3.1, so the sequence matters: chemically deacidify first to lift pH into the low threes, keep SO2 minimal, warm the wine to 18-20C, inoculate a proven acid-tolerant strain with bacterial nutrient, and only sulphur once malic tests clear.

## a) Palatability and stability

The wine will still taste taut, so I would leave 6-10 g/L of residual sugar — the cheapest effective palate correction at this price — plus lees ageing and oak staves rather than barrels. The stability risks are calcium tartrate thrown slowly by the deacidification, which argues for treating must rather than wine; refermentation of that residual sugar, requiring sterile filtration and molecular SO2, which the low pH makes easy; and protein haze, handled with bentonite.

## b) Barossa Grenache Noir — the problems in this juice

The mirror image. At 16.5% potential alcohol this is hot, unbalanced, expensive in duty and at real risk of sticking; TA of 3.9 g/L is flabby. pH 4.2 is the serious problem: at pH 4.2 the figure is around 0.4%, so SO2 is almost useless and the wine is open to lactic bacteria, acetic bacteria and Brettanomyces, while colour is poor because anthocyanins are largely in colourless forms at that pH — and Grenache is anthocyanin-poor and oxidation-prone anyway. Raisined fruit also implies low YAN.

## b) Handling: alcohol, acidity and stability

Water addition is the cheap first move — Australian rules permit watering back high-sugar must to a floor of about 13.5 Baumé — but it dilutes acid and colour further, so it must be paired with acidification. Reverse osmosis or spinning cone give precise alcohol reduction on toll at this volume, though they may cost more than the margin allows.

Acidify pre-fermentation with tartaric: 1 g/L of tartaric acid moves pH by roughly 0.1, so reaching pH 3.5 needs a large addition, best split either side of fermentation and followed by cold stabilisation, since much will precipitate as bitartrate and let pH drift back. Cation exchange on a portion of the wine complements it, lowering pH without adding acid mass.

Ferment with an alcohol-tolerant strain, staged nutrients and temperature capped near 28C — a stuck ferment at pH 4.2 with sugar present would be a spoilage disaster. Press early rather than macerating long, because extended skin contact leaches potassium and pushes pH higher still. Add oenological tannin at crush to bind what pigment there is, blend with Shiraz or Mataro in the Barossa manner for colour and structure, and use oak chips with micro-oxygenation. Stability then demands sterile filtration, screwcap and prompt sale.

## Conclusion

The English wine's problems are chemical and correctable within the law; the Barossa wine's are microbiological and only partly correctable. At mid price I would back the Grenache to reach the shelf in balance, and treat the English fruit as what its numbers say it is — a sparkling base being asked to do the wrong job.

questionText: Compare and contrast the options available as preservatives for addition to still wine.
body:
## What counts as a preservative

A preservative is a substance added to wine to prevent decomposition, whether by microbial growth or by undesirable chemical change, oxidation above all. That definition fixes the scope narrowly. Fining, protein and cold stabilisation, filtration and must treatments all protect a wine, but they are physical or clarifying operations rather than preservative additions, and I set them aside; so too inert gases, which exclude oxygen rather than react with it. What remains is a short list: sulphur dioxide, ascorbic acid, sorbic acid, dimethyl dicarbonate (DMDC), lysozyme, chitosan and, most recently, fumaric acid. I compare them on five axes — what they act against, whether they work unaided, dose and legal ceiling, sensory and cost penalty, and consequence for the label.

## What each acts against

SO2 alone is both antimicrobial and antioxidant, and that is the most important contrast in the question. Its molecular fraction inhibits yeast and bacteria; its free fraction binds acetaldehyde, scavenges quinones and mops up hydrogen peroxide, slowing browning. Every other option is a specialist.

Ascorbic acid is purely antioxidant, and only as a fast oxygen scavenger; it does nothing to microbes. Sorbic acid, DMDC, lysozyme and chitosan are purely antimicrobial, with sharply different spectra. Sorbic acid inhibits yeast but not bacteria. Lysozyme lyses gram-positive lactic acid bacteria and leaves yeast and acetic acid bacteria untouched. DMDC kills yeast on contact and is markedly weaker against bacteria. Chitosan is used chiefly against *Brettanomyces*, and fumaric acid to inhibit malolactic bacteria. The choice therefore starts from the named threat: a wine with residual sugar faces a yeast problem, a high-pH red a bacterial one, and a fragile aromatic white bottled with oxygen pickup a purely chemical one.

## Whether they work unaided

The second contrast is dependency, and it is decisive. SO2 works alone; nothing else reliably does.

Ascorbic acid is the clearest case. It consumes oxygen quickly but yields hydrogen peroxide, so without a working minimum of about 30 mg/L free SO2 beside it, it accelerates the browning it was added to prevent. Sorbic acid fails differently: lactic acid bacteria metabolise it to the geranium taint, so it also requires SO2 cover. DMDC has no residual activity whatever — it hydrolyses within hours to methanol and carbon dioxide, so it only works on wine already filtered to a low cell count, and only if the filler is aseptic. Lysozyme allows early SO2 to be reduced or delayed, but it is a partial substitute, never a replacement. The honest conclusion of the comparison is that the alternatives are complements to SO2, not options instead of it.

## Dose, pH and legal ceiling

SO2 is dosed to a molecular target of roughly 0.5-0.8 mg/L, which requires around 30 mg/L free at pH 3.4 and nearer 75 mg/L at pH 3.8. That pH dependence is itself a contrast: sorbic acid likewise weakens as pH rises, whereas DMDC and lysozyme are largely indifferent to it. EU organic ceilings sit 50 mg/L below the conventional ones for dry wines - 100 mg/L red and 150 mg/L white and rose below 2 g/L residual sugar - and at least 30 mg/L below for all sweeter categories.

Against that, sorbic acid is capped at 200 mg/L in the EU and used close to it, 150-200 mg/L. Ascorbic acid is capped at 250 mg/L and is added in-line immediately before the filler. DMDC is capped at 200 mg/L and dosed at the cap. Lysozyme is capped at 500 mg/L and used at 250-500 mg/L. Fumaric acid is permitted at low tens of grams per hectolitre to block malolactic fermentation, and is the newest of the group.

Cost tracks that spread. SO2 as potassium metabisulphite is trivially cheap; sorbate and ascorbic acid are cheap; lysozyme and DMDC are expensive, and DMDC additionally demands dedicated metering equipment and careful handling because it is acutely toxic before it hydrolyses.

## Sensory and cost penalty

Excess SO2 is pungent, mutes fruit and bleaches young red colour, and it is the option with the greatest capacity to spoil the wine it protects. Sorbate at legal dose can read as a slightly confected note even before any geranium fault appears, which is why it is used almost exclusively in off-dry commercial wines rather than fine wine. Lysozyme can strip colour from reds and leave a protein instability in whites that then needs bentonite. Chitosan can flatten aroma if overdosed. DMDC's advantage is precisely that at legal dose it is sensorially silent — you buy microbiological security without touching the wine.

## Label and market consequence

SO2 above 10 mg/L total requires an allergen declaration in the EU and US, a real constraint for producers courting sulphite-averse consumers. Lysozyme is egg-derived: it is an allergen requiring declaration and it is neither vegan nor acceptable to many organic schemes. Chitosan from crustacean shell is not vegan, though the fungal-sourced form is. DMDC requires no declaration at all but is indefensible in natural-wine positioning. Organic and low-intervention certifications narrow the whole list at once.

## Conclusion

No option matches SO2's combination of dual action, independence, low cost and legal headroom, and the comparison shows why no single alternative has displaced it. The others are best understood as targeted risk reducers that let total SO2 fall: ascorbic acid buys oxygen protection at bottling, sorbic acid guards residual sugar, lysozyme and fumaric acid control bacteria, and DMDC delivers sterility without sensory cost. The skill is in matching the specific instability to the specific agent rather than reaching for more sulphur.

body:
## Scope and the shape of the decision

Pre-bottling treatment means everything done to the wine in bulk after maturation and before it is packaged: fining, protein and tartrate stabilisation, filtration, preservative adjustment, gas management and the choice of package itself, since the package sets the oxygen budget the wine must survive. In each of the four cases below the same question is asked — what instability must be removed, what is the minimum intervention that removes it, and what constraint (certification, style, cost) forbids the obvious route. Packaging is treated as part of the answer throughout, not just glass.

## a) A vegan wine

The governing constraint is that no product of animal origin may be used, including as a processing aid that is filtered out and does not appear in the finished wine. That rules out isinglass, gelatine, casein and potassium caseinate, egg albumen, and — a point often missed — lysozyme, which is egg-derived, and chitosan sourced from crustacean shell rather than from *Aspergillus niger*.

The practical decisions are therefore substitutions. Protein stability is unaffected, since bentonite is a clay: dose to the heat-test minimum, often 20-60 g/hL, determined by bench trial rather than habit. For clarification and tannin softening in reds, pea or potato protein at roughly 10-30 g/hL replaces gelatine, though it is a gentler agent and may need a longer settling time or a crossflow pass behind it. For browning and phenolic pinking in whites, PVPP - trialled anywhere from 10 to 80 g/hL, within the OIV ceiling of 80 g/hL - is synthetic and compliant. Where fining is only about clarity, filtration can substitute entirely.

Beyond the wine, the QA burden is documentary: written declarations from suppliers for every aid, filter media and fining agent, plus checks on adhesives, capsules and any beeswax closure treatment, since certification bodies audit the whole package.

## b) An orange wine

Here the constraints are stylistic rather than legal, and the answer is largely about what not to do. Extended skin contact leaves a white wine with red-wine phenolic structure, so protein instability is usually already resolved by tannin-protein binding — run a heat test and expect to skip bentonite, which would strip texture. The wine is oxidatively robust for the same reason, so oxygen tolerance during transfer is high.

Two real risks replace those. First, skin contact extracts potassium and pushes pH up, so a molecular SO2 of 0.5-0.8 mg/L that needs only 25-40 mg/L free at pH 3.5 needs 50-80 mg/L at pH 3.8 - an uncomfortable figure for a category whose buyers expect low sulphur. Second, these wines commonly go through spontaneous fermentation and long unsulphured elevage, so *Brettanomyces*, acetic acid bacteria and residual sugar with viable yeast are live threats.

The decision is where on the intervention scale to sit. If the wine is to be sold unfined and unfiltered, as most are, that must be earned by clean racking, low viable counts confirmed by plating, cold storage and controlled shipping, not assumed. If filtration is used, a coarse 1.0 micrometre pass preserves texture where a 0.45 micrometre membrane would flatten it. Tartrate stabilisation is usually declined outright, the category tolerating crystals and sediment. Packaging follows: dark glass and a closure with modest oxygen transmission.

## c) An organic wine

Organic wine is regulated, and the regulations differ by market — the first consideration is which market's rules apply. In the EU, the reference is a positive list of permitted oenological practices with lower SO2 ceilings: EU organic caps total SO2 at 100 mg/L for dry red and 150 mg/L for dry white and rose, roughly 50 below conventional. Several stabilisation routes are excluded, notably electrodialysis and cation exchange for tartrate stability, dealcoholisation, physical SO2 removal, filtration below about 0.2 micrometres and heat treatment above 75 degrees C. Cold stabilisation by traditional chilling, gum arabic or metatartaric acid remains available.

The US is not equivalent. The US National Organic Program allows no added sulphites in wine labelled organic, with total below 10 mg/L; the workable export category is "made with organic grapes", which permits up to 100 mg/L. A single bottling cannot easily satisfy both, so the label claim must be fixed before the treatment plan is written.

Practically, the lower SO2 ceiling forces cleaner microbiology: complete malolactic fermentation, malic below 0.2 g/L, tight filtration within the permitted pore size, and organic-certified fining agents.

## d) A mass-market, inexpensive wine

The temptation is to say such a wine should be heavily fined and heavily treated. That is wrong, and it is expensive. Balanced winemaking with modest, trial-determined additions produces a better entry-level wine than blanket dosing, and every gram of bentonite costs money, occupies tank time and generates lees loss.

What genuinely differs is the risk profile. The wine will sit warm on a supermarket shelf for a year with no owner, so it must be absolutely stable: heat-stable to the bench minimum, cold-stable via CMC at 5-10 g/hL or metatartaric acid at around 10 g/hL for fast-turn stock rather than energy-hungry chilling, sterile-filtered through a 0.45 micrometre membrane where there is residual sugar, and carrying free SO2 at bottling nearer 35-40 mg/L than the fine-wine norm.

Package choice is a pre-bottling decision, not an afterthought: bag-in-box, PET and can all admit more oxygen than glass, so each demands a higher dissolved-oxygen discipline at fill and a shorter declared shelf life. Consistency across very large blends, and throughput on the line, complete the picture.

questionText:
You are responsible for quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC) for an importer of bulk wine. Explain the QA and QC procedures that you will need:

a) between the completion of winemaking and the start of the bulk transport process; and
b) following receipt of the bulk wine at its destination.
body:
## Definitions and my standpoint

Quality assurance is the system that prevents defects — written specifications, approved supplier lists, audits, HACCP plans, procedures, training and records. Quality control is the measurement that detects them — the analyses, the microbiology and the sensory assessment on a defined sampling plan. QA asks whether the process is capable; QC asks whether this particular parcel conforms. Conflating them is what makes bulk programmes fail, because measurement without a system produces numbers nobody acts on.

My standpoint matters as much as the definitions. As the importer's QA/QC manager I own neither the cellar that made the wine nor the plant that will bottle it. My levers are the contractual specification, the audit, the approval sample and the right to reject. Every control below is one I can either execute myself or impose on a third party.

## a) Between completion of winemaking and the start of bulk transport

**QA.** I issue a written product specification for the parcel: analytical ranges, a sensory profile with agreed reference standards, and full legal compliance for the destination market — permitted additives, allergen declaration, residue and contaminant limits, and the import documentation the market requires. I maintain an approved supplier list covering the winery, the bulk logistics operator and the flexitank or ISO tank provider, and I audit each on a schedule, with the winery's HACCP plan and traceability system as audit scope. I require a nominated lot with one-up, one-down traceability. The controlling procedure is the pre-shipment approval sample: nothing loads until my laboratory and my tasting panel have released that sample against the specification in writing.

**QC before loading.** On the approval sample I run alcohol, pH, TA, volatile acidity, residual sugar, malic acid, free and total SO2, dissolved oxygen, dissolved CO2, turbidity, copper and iron, plus microbiology by plating and PCR for *Brettanomyces*, lactic and acetic acid bacteria and viable yeast. Stability is tested, not assumed: a heat test at 80°C for protein, a cold test at minus 4°C for 72 hours or a conductivity mini-contact test for tartrates, and a filterability index. The targets I write into the specification are a molecular SO2 of 0.5-0.8 mg/L, typically 20-40 mg/L free at pH 3.2-3.5 and more above that;

**Treatments I specify.** Bentonite to the heat-test minimum for whites and rosés; tartrate stability by chilling, electrodialysis or an inhibitor as the wine's certification allows; filtration to crossflow or a 0.65 micrometre membrane to drop viable counts; SO2 corrected upward at fill because the voyage will consume it; nitrogen sparging to hit the oxygen target. I also specify the vessel — a flexitank of the order of 24,000 litres is filled effectively brim-full and cannot be inerted or sampled in transit, whereas an ISO tank can be blanketed and sampled — and I require a temperature logger in the container, with loading temperature at or below 15°C.

## b) Following receipt at destination

**QC on discharge.** I draw a representative sample before the wine leaves the container, or immediately as it enters my holding tank, and I compare it directly with the retained loading sample and its certificate of analysis. ...dissolved oxygen above roughly 1 mg/L - the level AWRI associates with less-than-ideal handling - as an oxidation risk;

**Treatments and bulk storage.** SO2 is corrected back to the molecular target before anything else. Reduction is treated by racking or splash-transfer and, if needed, a trace copper addition, remembering that copper is limited to 1 mg/L residual in the EU and under OIV limits - and to 0.5 mg/L in the United States. Elevated dissolved oxygen is stripped by nitrogen sparging. Any haze or microbiological positive triggers re-filtration, and tartrate stability is re-tested because the wine has seen both heat and cold. The holding tank must be pre-cleaned and swab-verified, nitrogen-blanketed, ullage-free and held at 12-15°C, with free SO2 and dissolved oxygen re-checked fortnightly until bottling.

**QA.** The wine sits in quarantine status until I release it, and non-conformances follow a documented decision tree: accept, accept after treatment, or reject and claim on the shipping insurance — which is only possible because paired samples exist. I audit the contract bottler, issue the bottling specification, and verify it afterwards on total package oxygen at bottling below about 1.5 mg/L, fill height, closure and label compliance. Retained samples are kept at each stage, an accelerated shelf-life trial is run, and the supplier scorecard is updated so the next shipment's specification is tighter than the last.

## Conclusion

The importer's authority is not in the cellar; it is in the specification, the audit and the paired sample. QA makes conformity likely, QC proves it, and the two together are what let me tell a bottler, with evidence, whether the wine that arrived is the wine I bought.

And this was really key - the question said "You are responsible for QA and QC for an importer of bulk wine. Explain the QA and QC procedures that you will need". Very few candidates did this.

questionText: A winery has received a customer complaint for a piece of glass found in a bottle. Describe the QA and QC procedures best employed by the winery to investigate the issue.
body:
## Definitions and scope

Quality assurance is the system built to prevent a defect: the HACCP plan, the written procedures, the supplier approval and audit regime, the training and the records that prove all of it happened. Quality control is the measurement that detects a defect: inspection, analysis and the sampling plan that governs them. An investigation of this kind uses both, and in a specific order — QC establishes the facts about this bottle and this batch, QA establishes whether the system that should have prevented it was working and where it failed.

The question asks only about investigating the complaint. I therefore do not write a recall plan; whether to withdraw or recall product is a decision that this investigation informs and that follows it. Nor is this the place to catalogue how glass gets into bottles: the sources of contamination matter only once the investigation points at one. Physical contamination by glass is a food safety hazard, not a quality preference, so the investigation is also a legal obligation — traceability and the ability to act on unsafe food are required of every food business, in the EU under Regulation (EC) 178/2002 and equivalently elsewhere — and there is a reputational exposure alongside it.

## Stage 1 — secure and verify the evidence (QC)

The first duty is to establish that there is in fact a glass shard in the bottle, because complaints are frequently tartrate crystals, closure fragments or capsule material.

I log the complaint immediately in the complaints register: date received, complainant, place and date of purchase, the lot code and best-before printed on the bottle and any code on the closure, and a description in the customer's own words. I ask for photographs before anything moves. I then retrieve the physical evidence — the bottle, its contents, the closure and, ideally, the packaging — by courier with a documented chain of custody and a signed receipt, rather than allowing it to be posted loose or discarded. The complainant is handled courteously and without admission of liability, and asked to retain any other bottles from the same purchase.

In the laboratory the object is examined and photographed under magnification, weighed and measured. Two questions decide the direction of the whole investigation. Is it glass at all, or crystal, closure or plastic? And if it is glass, is it from this bottle or foreign to it? The bottle is inspected for a corresponding fracture at the base, heel, shoulder or internal neck surface; the fill level, closure seating and any evidence of prior opening are recorded. Where the answer is not obvious, the shard's composition and colour are compared against the bottle by the glass supplier's own laboratory, which can usually determine whether the two are the same melt.

## Stage 2 — trace the batch (QA)

The lot code is the key to everything. It resolves to a bottling record, and from there I pull the complete file for that run: date, time, line, shift and operator; the glass supplier, delivery and pallet lot with its certificate of conformity; the depalletiser, rinser and bottle-inverter settings; in-line inspection or camera records; and the line clearance checks at the start and end of the run.

The critical documents are the HACCP records. Foreign body contamination by glass is a recognised hazard, so the plan should carry a control point covering it, with monitoring records, defined critical limits and a documented glass breakage procedure — typically requiring that any breakage on the line is logged and that a defined number of bottles either side is isolated and destroyed. I check whether that procedure was followed on the day, and whether any breakage was recorded near the time this bottle was filled. Complementing this, I check the glass register for damage to lighting, guards and instruments in the filling hall.

## Stage 3 — is it systemic? (QC and QA together)

I next establish scale, because a single random event and a batch defect demand different responses. I retrieve and inspect the library samples of the same lot, then arrange inspection of a meaningful sample of remaining stock in the winery's own warehouse and, if justified, at the distributor. I interrogate the complaints register for other reports against the same lot, supplier delivery or line, and I review the glass supplier's audit status and certification.

This is where practical logic matters. If the run finished months ago and the wine is in consumers' hands, stopping the bottling line achieves nothing; the useful actions are stock inspection and traceability. If the same glass delivery or the same line is still in use today, then quarantining that glass and halting the run are proportionate and urgent.

## Stage 4 — root cause, corrective action and closing out (QA)

The investigation ends in a documented report: the evidence, the findings, a formal root cause analysis using five-whys or a cause-and-effect diagram, and a conclusion on whether the failure lay with the glass supplier, the line, the procedure or the customer's account of events. From that follow corrective actions, a revision of the HACCP plan if the hazard analysis or its control limits proved inadequate, re-training or equipment change where indicated, and a verification step confirming the action worked. The complainant receives a substantive reply.

The report is also what the winery's management, its retail customers and, if necessary, the regulator will use to decide whether any wider action on product in trade is required — the decision this investigation exists to inform.

coversCore.section: Opening section 'Definitions and scope', which states the investigation boundary explicitly, and the four investigative stages that follow; recall is named once, in the closing section, only as the decision the investigation feeds and is deliberately not described
coversCore.examinerQuote: The question only asks about investigation, not product recall.

claims.claim: Regulation (EC) 178/2002
claims.matchText: Regulation (EC) 178/2002

source.publisher: EUR-Lex - Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 (General Food Law), Articles 18-19
source.quote: The traceability of food, feed, food-producing animals, and any other substance intended to be... incorporated into a food or feed shall be established at all stages of production, processing and distribution... [operators] shall immediately initiate procedures to withdraw the food in question from the market

claims.note: Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 (the General Food Law) is correctly cited: Article 18 imposes traceability at all stages, Article 19 requires immediate withdrawal and notification of the competent authority where food may be unsafe. Both obligations are exactly what a glass-in-bottle complaint triggers.

questionText: How has the market transparency facilitated by the internet and social media influenced the supply, demand and pricing of wine? Who benefits?
body:
## Scope: transparency means price discovery, not publicity

I take market transparency to mean the near-zero cost at which any participant can now discover three things: what a given wine sells for anywhere in the world, what it is judged to be worth, and who holds stock of it. Wine-Searcher and Liv-ex do this for price, Vivino and CellarTracker for crowd judgement, the critics' sites for expert judgement, and social media acts as the distribution layer that pushes all of it in front of consumers who were not looking for it.

That distinction matters, because a producer's Instagram account is publicity, not transparency. I therefore say very little about social-media activation and concentrate on what price discovery has done to supply, to demand and above all to pricing — and then take a position on who has captured the value.

## Supply

Transparency has shortened the chain and made it policeable. A producer can now see the shelf price of its own wine in every market it sells to, which means it can see exactly what each intermediary is taking, and can see parallel trade the moment it appears. The response has been tighter allocation control and, in the United States especially, a decisive move into direct-to-consumer selling. Producers no longer need a distributor to be findable.

It has also brought new supply into the market. A decade ago, reaching a global audience required a distributor in each market. Etna, the Swartland, the Jura and the revived Georgian qvevri producers went from obscure to allocated largely through sommeliers, critics and social media rather than through conventional distribution. The same is true at the other end: bulk-market price reporting has made bulk wine values visible to growers who previously only knew what one broker told them.

## Demand

The effect on demand is two-sided, and I think this is where most analysis stops too early.

Search-driven discovery is winner-takes-most. A high aggregate rating compounds, because it raises the wine in the search results that generate the next tranche of ratings. That mechanism built Whispering Angel's dominance of premium rosé and it explains why a handful of names absorb a disproportionate share of demand in every newly opened market.

Simultaneously, demand has fragmented at the tail. A consumer in Melbourne can find, price and buy Trousseau from the Jura. The middle is what has hollowed out: the competent, unremarkable, unrated regional wine that used to sell because it was the only thing on the shelf.

## Pricing

This is the heart of it. A consumer standing in a shop or sitting at a restaurant table can check a wine's price against every other listing in the world in seconds, and that single fact has changed pricing behaviour at every level.

**Retailers** have lost pricing power on known-value items. National price bands have converged, and the margin on any wine a consumer can name has compressed. The most important commercial response is own label and exclusivity — supermarket tiers such as Tesco Finest, the private-label ranges that carry Aldi and Lidl, merchant-exclusive cuvées, and Naked Wines' model of funding winemakers to make labels that exist nowhere else. All of these do one job: they remove the comparator.

Restaurants have lost the ability to defend the convention of pricing a bottle at a multiple of its retail value -- often cited at around three times -- because the guest can see the retail value. The better operators have moved to cash-margin pricing, to growers' wines bought direct that appear on no other list, and to by-the-glass programmes where the comparison is harder to make.

**Producers** now set release prices in public. Bordeaux en primeur is the clearest case: a release priced above the visible back-vintage market on Liv-ex simply does not sell, and the campaign is now negotiated in front of the customer. Producers must also manage price coherence across markets, because with duty and tax differentials visible, the cheapest market sets the reference price everywhere.

The important counter-case is that transparency is not uniformly deflationary. Where supply is genuinely scarce, transparency revealed how far below the clearing price releases had been set, and producers in Burgundy, Napa and Champagne have raised prices to capture margin that was previously going to the secondary market.

## Who benefits

My view is that transparency has redistributed margin to the two ends of the chain and to the platforms in the middle, and that the traditional intermediary is the loser.

The **consumer** is the clear winner below roughly £15 a bottle, where wines are comparable, substitutable and priced against each other in public.

The **producer** is the winner at the scarce end, because it now knows its wine's clearing price and can either take that margin at release or sell direct and take all of it.

The **intermediary** — distributor, importer, traditional merchant — is squeezed from both sides, and survives only by owning something that cannot be price-compared: an exclusive label, a locked allocation, guaranteed provenance and storage, or genuine advice.

The uncomfortable conclusion is that the largest single beneficiary may be neither party but the platforms themselves. Wine-Searcher, Liv-ex and Vivino -- which has claimed a very large user base, in the tens of millions -- monetise the very transparency that erodes their customers' margins.

coversCore.requirement: Analyse who benefits from market transparency (consumer, producer, or intermediaries), not just describe social media activity
coversCore.section: Final section 'Who benefits', which allocates the gain across the three parties, and the framing line in 'Scope' that rules out cataloguing social-media activity
coversCore.examinerQuote: Often the question about who benefits was not addressed at all.

coversCore.requirement: Give an opinion on who benefits, backed by argument, rather than only description

questionText: With reference to Bordeaux and other regions, discuss the commercial viability of the en primeur model. Outline the pros and cons for all parties, from producer through to consumer.
body:
## What viability means here

The mechanics are quickly stated and I will not dwell on them: a wine is sold as a future in the spring following the harvest, moves château to courtier to négociant to merchant to consumer, and is delivered two years later. The question is not how that works but whether it still pays.

I test viability on three conditions. The model is commercially viable only if it delivers cash and price realisation to the producer, a margin proportionate to the risk borne by each intermediary, and a reason for the consumer to prepay. Fail any one for long enough and the system unwinds. My argument is that Bordeaux currently satisfies the first, is straining the second and has, for most vintages, stopped satisfying the third.

## The financial case for the château

The financial logic for the producer is strong and unchanged. Selling the crop eighteen months to two years before bottling converts an eighteen-month working-capital drag into positive cash flow, and it transfers the cost of financing and storing the stock onto the chain. That is a real balance-sheet benefit, and for estates carrying replanting or building programmes it is the difference between borrowing and not.

The logistical case is equally real. A first growth making perhaps 15,000 to 20,000 cases has no wish to build a global credit-control, allocation and shipping operation. The Place does that for a fee, and reaches perhaps a hundred markets.

The cost is option value. In a great vintage the château sells at a price the market promptly exceeds, and it never recovers that margin. Château Latour left the system after the 2011 vintage precisely to capture it, releasing only when the wine is ready — which requires the balance sheet to hold a decade of stock, and is why almost nobody has followed.

## The financial case down the chain

The margins are thin and the risk is not. The courtier takes a small commission, commonly cited at around 2%, for matching allocations, and bears almost no risk in doing so. The négociant's position is the opposite: it finances the purchase, carries the price risk for two years, and accepts allocations conditional on also taking the weak vintages — which is the real cost of the system to them, and the reason the Place tolerates release prices it privately considers too high. The merchant then holds customer money against undelivered wine, so its margin is compensation for counterparty and storage risk as much as for selling.

For the consumer the bargain has narrowed to two things: access to wines that will be allocated out later, and the chance of buying below the eventual market price. The first is real at the very top and largely illusory below it. The second is an investment proposition dressed as a purchase, and it depends entirely on release pricing being disciplined.

## Release pricing, and what happens afterwards

The pricing record is the evidence. The 2019 campaign, run in the first summer of the pandemic, worked because the chateaux moved: the 2019s were released meaningfully below the 2018 opening prices and sold through quickly. The 2020 campaign showed the reflex return, as the 2020s came out meaningfully above the 2019 releases into a small crop.

Set against that is the 2010 and 2011 vintages, much of which still trades at or below its release price a decade on. Liv-ex's recurring finding — that physical back vintages are frequently available below the price of the new release — is the single most damaging fact for the consumer proposition, and it is now visible to every buyer. The market has voted with its feet, Bordeaux's share of secondary-market trade by value having fallen sharply from a large majority in 2010 to a minority now. The Rhône offers en primeur with far weaker justification, since most wines are still obtainable on physical release. Vintage Port's declaration in the second year is a related device, again driven by cash flow rather than by consumer benefit.

The most interesting comparator is what the Place de Bordeaux now does with Masseto, Opus One, Almaviva and Penfolds: distribute them globally as physical wine on annual release. Merchant/importer counterparty risk is real, as demonstrated by the 2016 collapse of Premier Cru, which owed customers a substantial sum reported in the tens of millions of pounds. It is not viable as a general system: the layers each take a margin the consumer can now see, for a service the internet has largely replicated. I expect it to survive at the top fifty estates as a cash-flow and marketing ritual, with the Place surviving far more robustly as a distribution channel than as a futures market.
