questionText: As export director of a 100,000-case winery in the New World, you have been asked to increase exports from 10% to 25% of total production volume. What are the factors that would be most relevant to your strategy?
body:
## The winery I am representing

I will answer as a real case, because the right strategy is unrecognisable in the abstract. My winery is a family-owned Paso Robles estate making 100,000 cases: Cabernet Sauvignon and Rhône-variety blends, a little Chardonnay, sold at roughly US$20 to $28 on the domestic shelf, with a strong tasting room and wine club. Ninety per cent goes into the United States, split between our own direct-to-consumer channel and two state distributors. Ten thousand cases currently go abroad, to a Canadian agent and a UK importer.

## The number decides the strategy

The first and most important factor is arithmetic. Moving from 10% to 25% of 100,000 cases means finding a home for 15,000 additional cases, since a standard 20-foot container carries just over a thousand cases.

That is a small number, and recognising it dictates everything that follows. It cannot justify chasing mass-market distribution across many markets: a single national listing with a British or German multiple would be several times this volume, at a price that would sit below our cost of production and would visibly undercut our US shelf price. Equally, it is far too much to place with a scattering of small agents in fifteen countries, each of which would cost me two visits a year for two hundred cases.

The realistic shape is therefore three markets, each taking 4,000 to 6,000 cases, sold through the premium independent and on-trade channels where our price point belongs. This is a depth strategy, not a breadth strategy, and I would rather deepen the two markets I already have than add five new ones.

## Price architecture: the constraint that decides everything

The second factor, and where most export plans fail, is whether the wine can reach the foreign shelf at a price that is coherent with its domestic price. Working backwards: our FOB is roughly $110 a case. Add freight and insurance, import duty, an importer margin of about 30%, a wholesale margin, retail markup and sales tax, and a $24 California wine lands on a UK shelf well above £20 — because UK excise duty on still wine is over £2 a bottle before VAT is added.

At that price we are competing with classed-growth Bordeaux and Barossa Shiraz of real reputation, not with the $24 domestic competition we beat comfortably. So my strategy has to accept either a lower FOB, which is margin-dilutive against a tasting-room sale where we keep the whole retail dollar, or a genuinely premium positioning. I would choose the second, and I would tell the board plainly that this project reduces our average margin per case. Canada is the obvious deepening opportunity, and the challenge is structural: the provincial monopolies control listings, and the LCBO is widely regarded as one of the largest single purchasers of wine in the world. I would build private-order and licensee business rather than pursue a general listing.
- **The United Kingdom** is the best market for our style but the hardest on price, and its post-Brexit import certification requirements are still unsettled. I would work the independent merchant and restaurant trade, not the multiples.
- **Sweden** I would decline. Systembolaget buys by blind tender against a published specification; it is a superb volume opportunity at a price we cannot meet, and winning it once tells you nothing about next year.
- **Japan** I would add as the third market: importer-led, on-trade weighted, appreciative of Californian wine, and willing to pay for provenance.

The concentration risk deserves a word. The punitive duties China imposed on Australian wine from late 2020 removed that country's largest export market almost overnight, and that is the argument for spreading 15,000 cases across three markets rather than betting it on one.

## Budget and resourcing

The incremental 15,000 cases generate a gross profit measured in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars, so the export budget must be a fraction of that. I would plan on an all-in annual spend of the order of $150,000: my own salary contribution, samples and sample freight, four market visits, two trade fairs, label and compliance work, and a modest depletion allowance for each importer. That is what is affordable. Plans built on brand-marketing budgets, national advertising or a dedicated in-market team are not.

## Measurement and timing

Finally, I would set the plan over three years rather than one, and measure depletions rather than shipments. Shipping 15,000 cases into a warehouse is easy and is how export businesses are destroyed; selling them through to consumers, at a price that holds, is the thing being asked for.

questionText: Outline key changes in consumer taste preferences over the past decade. Which wine-producing regions have evolved their offer successfully to match these changes?
body:
## Scope

I read this as a question about taste — what wine consumers now want in the glass — and not about the values they attach to a purchase. Sustainability, organic certification and provenance claims have grown enormously in the same decade, but they change what a consumer will forgive, not what they want to drink, so I leave them aside. I also treat "taste preference" as market-specific rather than global, which is the second half of my argument.

## The changes worth naming

Four shifts have mattered commercially.

**Lighter, fresher, less oaked.** The high-alcohol, heavily extracted, new-oak red that defined the 2000s has lost its consumer. Alcohol is being managed down and oak used as seasoning rather than as flavour.

**Dry rosé became a category rather than a season.** Pale, dry, savoury pink wine turned into a year-round, premium-capable style, which is a genuinely new consumer behaviour rather than a variation on an existing one.

**Sparkling wine became an everyday drink.** The occasion decoupled from celebration, and simultaneously the top of the category moved drier, with brut nature and extra brut now normal in Champagne.

**Texture and freshness at the fashionable end** — skin contact, lees, salinity, low sulphur — which is small in volume but sets the on-trade agenda that mainstream buyers follow three years later.

Two counter-currents keep this honest. Mainstream American taste moved towards *sweeter* reds, not drier ones, and the fastest-growing branded segment there is off-dry. And in China the preferred style remains full-bodied dry red with visible oak. Anyone who describes the decade as a single move towards lightness has only looked at one market.

## Regions that changed their offer, and what it bought them

**Provence** is the clearest case of a region deliberately narrowing its style to own a category. It standardised on pale, dry, fresh rosé, invested in presentation, and pushed the price ceiling upwards. That did not simply sell more rosé; it created a premium rosé occasion that had not existed and that other regions — Languedoc, Navarra, Marlborough — now supply beneath it.

**Prosecco** is the sharpest recent example. The DOC already sold vast volume, which is not the same as adapting. Prosecco DOC Rosé was approved in 2020 and reached shelves that winter, and it did two things at once: it captured the rosé consumer inside an already trusted brand, and it carried a higher price than white Prosecco, so it premiumised the category rather than merely extending it. That is what a successful evolution looks like — new consumers and better margin from the same vineyard.

**Australia** rebuilt an entire varietal offer. Chardonnay was remade over the decade in the Yarra, Adelaide Hills and Margaret River from broad and oaky to tight and mineral, and the same producers moved Shiraz towards a medium-bodied, whole-bunch style and rehabilitated Grenache from the Barossa's old vines. This restored Australia's credibility in exactly the premium on-trade that had abandoned it.

**Rioja and Vinho Verde** show Old World adaptation. Rioja's 2017 rule change, which created Viñedo Singular and village wines, legitimised the fresher, less oak-driven, site-expressive style its younger producers were already making. Vinho Verde moved from cheap spritzy semi-sweet to serious single-varietal Alvarinho and opened a price bracket it had never reached.

## The fortified regions: the hardest adaptation

Fortified wine faced the decade's taste shift head-on — high alcohol, sweetness, an association with an older consumer — and the responses are instructive.

**Port** attacked the occasion rather than the wine. White Port and tonic gave the category a summer, low-strength, mixed serve, and rosé Port aimed at the same consumer. Simultaneously the trade moved out of basic ruby and into aged tawny and single quinta, where the price and the margin are, and the Douro's growers built a genuine dry red table wine business on the back of the same vineyards.

**Jerez** repositioned rather than reformulated. En rama bottlings, single-vintage and single-vineyard releases, and the VOS and VORS age categories reframed Fino and Manzanilla as gastronomic wines sold by the glass at the table. Jerez has been reforming its own rules to give more recognition to vineyard names, ageing zones and unfortified wine styles, an explicit attempt to let style follow demand.

**Madeira** did something similar with single-varietal Colheitas. **Marsala** is the counter-case: little repositioning, and continued decline.

## Where the rules got in the way

Appellation law is the brake on Old World adaptation, and its effect is visible. A Barossa producer changed its Shiraz style in three vintages; a Chianti or Rioja producer needed a consorzio vote. That Bordeaux approved six new varieties for its regional appellations in 2021 is a landmark precisely because it took so long.

## Conclusion

The regions that succeeded did not follow taste — they picked one change and built an offer around it. Provence and Prosecco did that best, because each created a new occasion at a higher price rather than defending an old one; Australia executed the most difficult reversal; and among the fortified regions Port adapted the occasion most successfully while Jerez adapted the audience.

questionText: Identify and assess the financial considerations when planning an investment in planting a vineyard and building a winery.
body:
## What I am assessing, and on what axes

The question is a capital-allocation problem, not a horticultural one, so I assess it as an investor would: total capital required, the shape of the cash-flow curve, the payback period, and the sensitivities that decide whether the project returns anything at all.

Almost every number depends on two variables — the **size** of the operation and the **price level** of the finished wine — so I define three scenarios and quote costs against them.

## Three scenarios

**A. Volume.** 400 hectares in Chile's Central Valley or the Riverina, fully mechanised, selling bulk and entry-level bottled wine at a few euros a litre.

**B. Premium estate.** 20 hectares in an established premium region — Barossa, Stellenbosch, Marlborough or a Languedoc cru — selling at €10 ex-cellars.

**C. Trophy.** 5 hectares in Napa or on the Côte d'Or, selling above €50 a bottle.

## Land

Land is the largest and most variable line. Grand cru Burgundy changes hands in the millions of euros per hectare.

The financial significance is that in Scenario C the land price cannot be recovered from wine sales at any plausible yield and price, so the investment case must rest on capital appreciation and brand equity. In Scenario A land is a minor line and the case rests entirely on operating efficiency. Vine material, rootstock, trellis, irrigation, land preparation and the years of husbandry before a commercial crop come to a figure in the tens of thousands of euros a hectare, more at high density, less where mechanisation and irrigation are simple.

Two financial features matter more than the number. First, there is no revenue at all until year three, and no full yield until year five or six, so this is a capitalised cost carrying interest through a dead period. Second, in the European Union the right to plant is itself an asset: EU planting authorisations are rationed to a small annual percentage of the existing area, which means the alternative — buying a planted, permitted, producing estate — may be both faster and cheaper than building one.

## The winery, and whether to build one at all

The winery is the second large lump and the worst asset in the business by utilisation: it is used intensively for perhaps eight weeks a year. A new French oak barrel typically costs several hundred euros, and a first barrel park is therefore a significant capital item on its own. Add tanks, press, destemmer, refrigeration, the building itself and a cellar, and I would not budget under €2 to €3 million for a functional 20-hectare estate winery; an architect-designed gravity-fed cellar is a multiple of that and returns nothing except a visitor experience.

The serious financial question is therefore whether to build at all. Custom crush or contract winemaking removes the single largest capital item and converts it into a variable cost, at the price of losing control and any cellar-door asset. For Scenario A that is usually wrong, for Scenario C it is often right for the first five vintages.

## Working capital, the cost nobody budgets

The most underestimated number is stock. Wine held eighteen months before release, or four years for a Barolo or a Rioja Reserva, is cash on a shelf. For Scenario B, two vintages in stock at cost is comfortably another €1.5 million, and it never comes back — it recurs every year.

## Payback: a worked case

For Scenario B: land at €150,000 a hectare gives €3.0 million, planting €0.7 million, winery and barrels €2.5 million, working capital €1.5 million — call it €7.7 million before financing.

At 50 hl/ha across 20 hectares the estate makes about 133,000 bottles. At €10 ex-cellars that is €1.33 million of revenue, and at a 60% all-in operating cost ratio roughly €530,000 of EBITDA. Against €7.7 million that is a payback of some fourteen years, with the first five cash-negative and interest accruing throughout. That is the realistic answer, and it explains why estates are usually bought rather than built and why the buyers are frequently not wine businesses.

## Sensitivity: price does the work

Yield is capped by appellation and by quality ambition, so price is the dominant lever. Doubling ex-cellars price to €20 roughly triples EBITDA and halves the payback; halving it to €5 means the project never returns its capital. Every other decision — density, oak regime, closure, packaging — is second order beside the question of what the wine will sell for and whether a route to market exists to sell it.

## Conclusion

The financial considerations rank clearly: the price level the wine can achieve, the cost of land in the region that supports it, the working capital to carry stock, and only then the capex of vineyard and winery. On any honest model a new premium estate pays back over ten to fifteen years at best. The investment is defensible where land appreciation or an existing brand shortens that; it is not defensible on wine trading alone.

questionText: How important is it for wine producers to develop new products?
body:
## What counts as a new product, and how I will judge importance

By new product development I mean anything that puts a genuinely new proposition in front of a consumer: a new brand, a new style within an existing brand, a new format or pack, or entry into an adjacent category. I exclude repackaging and vintage-to-vintage change, which are maintenance.

My answer is that importance varies enormously, and it varies on one axis: whether a producer's demand depends on being chosen from a shelf, or on being scarce. Where the consumer chooses between substitutable options, new product development is close to existential. Where demand exceeds supply, it ranges from unnecessary to actively harmful. I will take three tiers of producer in turn, then the motivations, then the failures.

## Why producers do it

The motivations are worth separating, because the wrong motivation is the usual cause of failure.

The strongest is **distribution**. Retailers ration shelf space and review ranges annually, and newness is the currency in which listings are won and defended. A brand that brings nothing to a range review is a brand that gets cut.

The second is **consumer recruitment**. Wine is losing occasions to spirits, beer, cocktails and hard seltzer, particularly among drinkers under thirty-five, and the category cannot recruit them with the same product it sold their parents.

Third is **margin**: a new tier or a new pack is the least resistant way to raise a realised price without repricing the existing range.

Fourth is **occasion**: single-serve, outdoor and lower-strength formats reach moments a 75cl cork-finished bottle cannot.

Fifth, and least respectable, is **surplus** — developing a product to absorb volume the existing range cannot sell. That motivation is where most failures come from.

## Mainstream branded producers: very important indeed

For a producer selling several million cases into grocery, new product development is not a choice. Volumes in mature markets are flat or declining, so growth has to be bought with newness.

The most instructive recent example is Treasury's 19 Crimes brand running a Snoop Dogg 'Cali Red' collaboration around 2020: the wine itself is unremarkable, but the collaboration recruited consumers who were not buying wine at all. That Prosecco DOC approved a rosé category in 2020 is a category-level version of the same move — it captured the rosé consumer inside a trusted name and did so at a higher price than white Prosecco. Canned formats, no- and low-alcohol ranges and wine-based ready-to-drink lines all belong to the same logic: defending share against adjacent categories on their own terms.

## Regional producers and co-operatives: important, but as adaptation

For a co-operative or a regional body facing structural decline, new product development is survival rather than growth. The Douro built a serious dry red table wine business out of vineyards planted for Port; Jerez and Port developed mixed serves and lighter styles to reach a consumer who will not drink a fortified wine after dinner; Vinho Verde replaced a cheap semi-sweet spritz with single-varietal Alvarinho at three times the price. In each case the existing product had a shrinking audience, and the alternative to development was managed decline.

## Fine wine: mostly unnecessary

At the top, new product development is largely irrelevant, because the product is scarcity and consistency. The great domaines of the Côte d'Or have introduced essentially nothing in living memory, and their demand has never been stronger. A line extension here does not add a consumer; it borrows credibility from the grand vin and repays it slowly.

The genuine exception is the second wine, which is the most successful new product development fine wine has produced. Second labels monetise fruit that would otherwise be sold in bulk, recruit consumers at a reachable price, and do not touch the grand vin. But they only work where the parent brand is strong, and third wines and distant branded ranges show where the elastic runs out.

## Where it has not worked

Three failure patterns are visible.

**Proliferation.** SKU counts expand faster than shelf space, complexity costs are real, and retailers eventually delist both the extension and the original.

**Dilution.** Extending a premium name downwards is easy and almost impossible to reverse; the price the consumer will pay is set by the cheapest bottle carrying the label.

**Novelty without repeat purchase.** Blue wine, heavily flavoured wines and most of the first decade of no-alcohol products generated publicity and no second purchase, because the motivation was surplus or noise rather than an identified consumer need.

The cautionary case is Beaujolais Nouveau: a spectacularly successful piece of product development that then defined the region in the consumer's mind for thirty years and took a generation to escape. A new product changes what a producer is understood to be, and that is not always recoverable.

## Conclusion

How important is it? Very, for the great majority of wine by volume, where the alternative to development is delisting. Barely at all for the small fraction whose demand exceeds supply, where it is at best a distraction. The producers who get it wrong are rarely those who do too much or too little; they are those who extend a brand when they needed a new one, or invent a product when what they needed was a better version of the one they had.

questionText: Who do you consider to be the real pioneers in today's wine industry, and why?
body:
## Two definitions, and the test I will apply

A pioneer is not simply someone doing something unusual. I define a pioneer as a person or institution that does something materially new **and** whose example is then taken up by others, changing the default practice of a significant part of the trade. Three tests follow — novelty, adoption, and consequence — and consequence has to show up in something countable: hectares planted, cases shipped, rules rewritten, costs removed. Someone who is first and whom nobody follows is an eccentric. Someone who is followed but was not first is a populariser. Both are routinely mislabelled.

By "wine industry" I mean the whole chain: plant breeding and nurseries, growing, production, packaging, logistics, regulation, route to market and communication. Most answers to this question name winemakers only, which is where the romance sits and very little of the leverage.

My argument is that today's real pioneers are mostly institutional and technical rather than charismatic, that they cluster at the two ends of the chain — plant material and route to market — and that several figures the trade calls pioneers fail the adoption test outright.

## Plant material: the breeders

The most consequential new thing being done in wine is the reconstruction of what a vine is. INRAE's ResDur programme released fungus-resistant varieties such as Floreal, Voltis, Artaban and Vidoc; the German and Swiss institutes had been breeding PIWI varieties for decades before that; and Andrew Walker's Pierce's disease-resistant selections at UC Davis address a threat no spray programme can manage.

Why they qualify: adoption is measurable in regulation, which is the hardest thing in wine to move. Champagne admitted Voltis on a trial basis, and Bordeaux admitted a short list of new varieties for the same reason. A variety that reduces fungicide passes cuts cost, diesel, soil compaction and operator exposure simultaneously — one intervention, four benefits, and it works at commodity scale rather than only at the top of the market.

The honest qualification is that the planted area remains small. But regulation moving in advance of demand is exactly the signal that distinguishes pioneering from novelty.

## Closures and packaging: the clearest case in living memory

The Clare Valley Riesling producers who bottled their 2000 vintage under screwcap, and the New Zealand Screwcap Initiative that followed in 2001, meet all three tests better than anyone else I can name. Within a decade the closure of choice for an entire hemisphere had changed, and random oxidation and cork taint were removed from a whole category of wine. Standing behind them is the Australian Wine Research Institute, whose long-running closure trial from the late 1990s supplied the evidence that made the decision defensible rather than merely brave — a reminder that research institutes are pioneers too, and are almost never named as such.

The live frontier is now the container rather than the closure: lightweight glass, bag-in-box, cans, kegs and flat or paper bottles. The pioneers here are largely retailers and logistics buyers, not producers. A supermarket that sets a maximum bottle weight for its own-label supply shifts more glass in one buying round than any single winery will in its existence, because it changes a specification rather than a preference. The same is true of bulk shipping in flexitanks with bottling at destination, which took a substantial share of long-haul trade in under twenty years and removed more carbon and freight cost from the industry than every winery sustainability programme combined. Nobody's name is attached to it, which is my point about where pioneering actually happens.

## Systems: certification as a national instrument

Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand now certifies the overwhelming majority of the country's vineyard area, and export customers treat it as a condition of listing. The pioneering move was not the agronomy; it was changing the unit of action from the estate to the country, so that sustainability became a market-access asset rather than a marketing claim. California's sustainability programmes and the various regional carbon calculators follow the same logic.

At the far end of the same spectrum, Tablas Creek in Paso Robles was certified under the Regenerative Organic scheme in 2020, which is standard-setting rather than commercially significant — a useful contrast, because it shows the difference between a pioneer of practice and a pioneer of scale.

## Route to market: where the economics actually changed

Naked Wines, whose customers pre-fund production, moved working capital risk off small producers and onto consumers who wanted the wine anyway. Whatever one thinks of the wines, the financing structure was genuinely new and it has been imitated. More broadly, direct-to-consumer selling and low-cost digital reach mean a producer of a few thousand cases can now find a global niche audience without a distributor's permission. That is the single largest change in how wine gets sold in my working lifetime, and it has no famous author.

## The critical part: who is not a pioneer

Natural wine is the clearest case. Almost every practice under the banner — ambient ferments, whole bunches, minimal sulphur, skin contact on whites, amphorae — is a revival of pre-industrial technique, not an invention. Its influence on mainstream cellar practice is real and its commercial footprint is trivial next to the attention it receives. Josko Gravner earns the title on style creation; the movement as a whole fails the consequence test.

English sparkling wine transplants an existing model to a new place. That is skilled, commercially interesting and climatically significant, but the varieties, the method, the equipment and the market positioning are all borrowed intact from Champagne. Doing an established thing well in a new latitude is achievement, not pioneering, and the distinction matters because the industry hands out the word for geography rather than for novelty.

Two further categories fail the test for the opposite reason. Celebrity-fronted brands and the newer generation of drinks-industry entrants are exercising existing marketing technique on an existing product; and the many producers now described as pioneers of regenerative or low-intervention farming are, with a handful of exceptions, adopting agronomy developed outside wine altogether. Adopting well is valuable. It is not the same claim.

The inversion is more interesting. Sacha Lichine bought Château d'Esclans in 2006 and built Whispering Angel into a brand of several million bottles a year, in the process establishing pale dry rosé as a year-round premium category rather than a summer afterthought. The trade is sniffy about it. On novelty of proposition, breadth of imitation and measurable commercial consequence, it outscores almost every cult producer of the same period.

And some of today's most consequential pioneers are not in wine at all: the ready-to-drink, no-and-low and premium spirits operators who have taken wine's occasions while the industry argued about oak.

## Conclusion

The real pioneers in today's wine industry are the breeders at INRAE, Geisenheim and Davis; the Clare Valley and New Zealand screwcap groups with the AWRI behind them; the architects of national certification in New Zealand; the retail buyers rewriting packaging specifications; and the builders of customer-funded and direct routes to market. What they share is that their work is adopted by people who never met them. That is the only definition of pioneering that survives contact with an industry this large.

questionText: Wine is celebrated for its diversity of styles. Is this diversity under threat?
body:
## What is a style, and what would count as a threat

By **style** I mean the recognisable sensory identity of a wine — the product of variety, site, climate, viticulture, winemaking and maturation, expressed as a package a taster could name blind. I will also argue that price and quality tier are part of style, because a €6 and a €60 wine from the same appellation are different products, not the same product at two prices.

By **threat** I mean something narrower than change. A threat is a force that reduces the number of distinguishable styles *reaching consumers*, on a timescale that matters. That distinction is the crux: styles that exist but cannot be bought are, commercially, extinct, and styles that vanish from one place while appearing in another have moved rather than died.

My position is this. **Diversity of sensory style is not under threat; it is being redistributed, and on balance it is increasing.** What is genuinely under threat is diversity of *price and quality tier* — the mid-priced, regionally specific wine that carries most of the information — and because that is where most stylistic difference is actually purchased, the loss matters more than the headline picture suggests.

## The forces of convergence

**Consolidation** is the strongest case for the prosecution. Production, distribution and retail have all concentrated, and the narrow point of the funnel is the retailer: a large UK supermarket lists a few hundred wines at a time, out of hundreds of thousands in production. Listings are won on specification — a price point, an ABV, a flavour brief — and specification buying manufactures sameness far more efficiently than any winemaker can.

**Cellar technology** makes the specification achievable. Cultured yeast selected for a flavour outcome, enzymes, tannin and oak additions, micro-oxygenation, reverse osmosis and spinning-cone alcohol adjustment, acidification and deacidification: the toolkit lets a producer hit a target profile from a wide range of raw material. Technology is style-neutral in principle and convergent in practice, because it is deployed to meet a brief.

**Viticulture** is where convergence is least discussed and most real, and it goes well beyond variety. A handful of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir clones account for a very large share of new plantings worldwide, narrowing the genetic base within a variety. Rootstock choice is made for phylloxera, nematodes and vigour, and a small number of rootstocks dominate. Vertical shoot positioning has replaced local training systems across most of the world because it suits machinery, and machine harvesting in turn requires uniform row spacing, canopy height and fruit-zone geometry — so the machine specifies the vineyard. Higher cropping levels dilute site character; herbicide and fertiliser regimes flatten differences in soil biology. Every one of those decisions is defensible individually, and their sum is a global vineyard that looks and yields more alike than it did.

## The forces of divergence

Against that, the last two decades have produced more new styles than any comparable period I can point to. Skin-contact whites, pét-nat, low-sulphur reds, seriously made rosé, dealcoholised wine, canned and kegged formats, and traditional-method sparkling from a dozen countries that had none. Old varieties have been recovered and commercialised across Iberia, Italy, Greece and Eastern Europe, and disease-resistant crossings are creating genuinely new sensory territory.

The distribution channel is the reason these survive. **E-commerce and social media** cut the cost of reaching a scattered audience to near zero, which is precisely the condition a niche style needs. A producer of two thousand cases can now build a viable global customer base without a distributor's permission — an impossibility in the supermarket-dominated world of the 1990s. **Premiumisation** funds the same effect, because difference is what a consumer paying above commodity prices is buying.

## Climate change: which way does it cut?

Most answers assume it destroys diversity. I think the net effect is closer to neutral, with an important asymmetry.

Against: it collapses styles defined by marginality. Light, low-alcohol Mosel Kabinett, the taut base wines of Champagne, brisk Muscadet, delicate Loire Cabernet Franc and Sherry's flor ecology in a hotter Jerez are all defined by conditions that are moving away from them. Worse, appellation law fixes them geographically — a style whose defining balance has migrated 300 kilometres north cannot follow it.

For: warming has created viable production in England, Denmark, Belgium, Tasmania and at altitudes in Argentina and Chile that were previously too cold, and it has made late-ripening varieties workable in places that could never finish them. Every one of those is net-new style.

My verdict: climate change produces net *change* rather than net loss, but a real transition-period deficit, because established styles disappear in a decade while new ones need a generation to acquire an identity anyone recognises.

## Regulation, health and the demand side

Political and regulatory forces cut both ways. Appellation rules preserve styles and simultaneously prevent adaptation — Bordeaux's admission of a short list of new varieties, capped at a small share of plantings and of the blend, is preservation and obstruction in one act. Conversely the UK's 2023 duty reform, which taxes wine by alcoholic strength, is a rare instance of regulation actively *creating* stylistic diversity by making lower-alcohol wines cheaper to sell.

Health and anti-alcohol pressure, from warning labels to lowered consumption guidelines, principally shrink volume rather than variety — though they push producers towards the no-and-low category, which adds styles.

The generational argument needs care. The claim that younger cohorts have abandoned wine rests largely on national market-tracking surveys and self-reported consumption panels; those are useful for direction but weak on magnitude, they rarely follow the same people over time, and they cannot separate a cohort effect from a life-stage one. What the data support is that younger drinkers spread spending across more categories — spirits, RTDs, craft beer, no-alcohol — not that wine's stylistic range is contracting. Competition takes occasions, not styles.

## The part that is genuinely under threat

Diversity of quality and price is the weak point, and it is the element of style least often examined. Costs of glass, freight, labour and energy have risen fastest at the bottom, retail margin has not moved, and the entry tier is being squeezed towards a smaller number of very large brands. Premiumisation protects the top. The casualty is the middle: the €10–20 wine of specific origin, made in commercially meaningful quantity, which is where most consumers ever encounter a regional style at all. Lose that and stylistic diversity survives as a connoisseur's museum while the mass market gets a shorter menu — a hollowing that Prosecco overtook Champagne in global volume in the last decade already illustrates at category level.

## Conclusion

No, the diversity of wine styles is not under threat; it is greater now than a generation ago and the digital route to market is what has secured it. But that answer is only true of the styles that exist. The diversity a consumer can actually reach is narrowing, because the mid-priced tier that carried it is being squeezed out between commodity brands and luxury. The threat is not to the range of wine. It is to the range of wine anyone can buy.

questionText: To what extent is France's wine classification system a model for the rest of the world?
body:
## Scope: is, not should

The question asks whether France's system *is* a model for the rest of the world, which is a descriptive question about observed adoption, not a normative one about merit. I therefore judge it by what other countries have actually built, and treat the merits of the French system only where they explain why it was or was not copied.

My answer is that the extent is large but uneven, and the unevenness is the whole point. France has exported its **architecture** — the place-based, rule-bound, three-tier appellation framework — almost universally. It has exported its **hierarchies** — the ranking of vineyards and estates within a region — almost not at all. And the architecture's grip is loosening as climate and market change expose what it cannot do.

## France does not have one classification system

Weaker discussion of this topic treats "the French system" as a single thing. It is two, and they work quite differently.

The **national framework** is a pyramid of three tiers: Appellation d'Origine Protégée, Indication Géographique Protégée and Vin de France. The INAO was created in the 1930s and the AOC system codified from 1935, and AOC became AOP under the EU's PDO framework following the reforms of the late 2000s. What makes it distinctive is that it regulates far more than origin: an AOP cahier des charges fixes the delimited area, permitted varieties, maximum yields, minimum ripeness, pruning and training, ageing requirements, and submits the wine to a tasting for approval. IGP relaxes most of that and permits varietal labelling; Vin de France removes it entirely.

The **regional hierarchies** sit inside that framework and are mutually inconsistent. Burgundy ranks *land*: Grand Cru and Premier Cru are legal appellations attached to parcels, with the Grands Crus standing as appellations in their own right. The 1855 Médoc classification ranked merchants' brands by their trading prices and has been altered only once, so it ranks *names*, is unrevisable in practice, and floats free of the vineyard. Saint-Émilion revises its classification roughly every ten years, ranking *estates* and admitting the possibility of demotion — which is why it is periodically litigated. Alsace has just over fifty Grands Crus, ranking land but added piecemeal over decades. Champagne's échelle des crus ranked *villages* for grape pricing and has lapsed as a commercial mechanism.

That heterogeneity matters for the question. A country wanting to copy France must first decide which France it is copying, and the four options contradict each other on what is being ranked and whether the ranking can change.

## Where the architecture has been copied — extensively

Inside the EU, adoption is near-total, partly by law. Italy's DOCG/DOC/IGT, Spain's DOCa/DO/VdlT with the estate-level Vino de Pago, Portugal's DOC/Vinho Regional and Greece's OPAP-derived tiers are all recognisably the same shape: a top tier with binding production rules, a permissive regional tier, and a table-wine floor. Germany's 2021 wine law reform introduced a new origin-based pyramid running alongside - not in place of - the ripeness-based Prädikat logic that had been Germany's model since 1971, a significant shift in emphasis even though the old Prädikat labels survive.

Outside the EU the shape recurs without the rules. The United States has American Viticultural Areas, Australia has Geographical Indications under the Label Integrity Programme, South Africa has the Wine of Origin scheme, New Zealand only legislated for geographical indications in the 2010s, Argentina has DOs with Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael as its controlled appellations, and Chile, Japan and China have all built GI systems in the last thirty years. The EU's trade agreements and the TRIPS framework have pushed the same template further still, since protecting a GI abroad requires having one at home.

So on architecture the answer to "to what extent" is: to a very great extent, and increasingly.

## Where the hierarchy has not been copied — almost anywhere

The New World schemes are delimitation-only. An American Viticultural Area requires 85% of the grapes to come from the named area and imposes no rule on yield, variety, ripeness or method; Australian and South African GIs are similar. They copied the map and left the code behind — which means they adopted the least French part of the French system.

The ranked-vineyard idea has essentially two serious imitators. Germany's VDP built a Burgundian pyramid of Grosse Lage and Erste Lage, but as a private members' association, not a state instrument. Barolo and Barbaresco's MGA scheme delimits named vineyards without ranking them — a conscious decision to take Burgundy's geography and refuse its hierarchy. Beyond those, Hungary's historic Tokaj vineyard classification and the Douro's vineyard scoring system, which grades sites by points for the allocation of Port production rights, both predate or parallel the French models rather than imitating them.

## Why the hierarchy did not travel

The architecture is administrable: draw a boundary, write rules, audit compliance. Any competent ministry can do it in a decade.

A hierarchy is not administrable in the same way, because it requires an agreed history. Burgundy's crus encode centuries of observed differences between adjacent parcels under near-identical management and a single variety — conditions no young region can synthesise. Rank vineyards in a region planted forty years ago and you are ranking the winemakers, which is contestable, litigable and immediately obsolete. Saint-Émilion's periodic disputes show that even in France ranking estates is barely sustainable, and the 1855 classification's immunity to revision shows the alternative is a hierarchy that has stopped tracking reality.

## The disadvantages, and the counter-model

The French system's costs are real. It guarantees origin and process, not quality, so a poorly made Grand Cru outranks an excellent IGP on the label. It is rigid against change: varieties, yields and methods are fixed by rules that take years to amend, precisely when a warming climate requires flexibility. It drives its most inventive producers out of the system — the Vin de France declassification route, and Italy's Super Tuscan precedent, are both innovation escaping classification. And it is illegible: several hundred AOPs, named after places most consumers cannot locate.

Meanwhile the genuinely dominant global model is a different one. Most wine is sold on variety and brand, and where a hierarchy exists it is usually the producer's own — a bin- or tier-ladder within a single brand, offering the consumer a legible quality ranking that requires no knowledge of geography. On volumes sold, that model has been imitated far more widely than anything France has produced.

## Conclusion

To a considerable extent, and decreasingly. France's national three-tier appellation architecture is the template for the classification systems of most wine-producing countries and remains the default answer to the question "how should origin be regulated". Its internal hierarchies — the part the trade actually reveres — have almost no imitators outside the private sphere, because they cannot be manufactured. And in the market rather than the statute book, the brand-and-variety ladder has out-competed both.

questionText: Can one wine ever be objectively better than another?
body:
## Three senses of "objective"

The question turns on a word that is doing three different jobs, and separating them settles most of the argument.

**Objective as mind-independent.** A property the wine has whether or not anyone tastes it, like its alcohol or its pH. In this sense "better" cannot be objective, and no amount of analysis will make it so. "Better" is a value predicate; no measurable constituent of wine entails it. Anyone claiming objectivity in this sense loses.

**Objective as intersubjective.** A judgement is objective when it is not arbitrary — when it is answerable to reasons, made on stated criteria, and reliably converged upon by people qualified to make it. This is the sense in which we call a medical diagnosis or a chess annotation objective. Wine judgement can be objective in this sense.

**Objective as fault-freedom.** A wine can be defective on criteria the whole trade agrees on: cork taint, oxidation, volatile acidity above threshold, reduction, refermentation. This is the narrowest and firmest ground.

## "Better" at what

"Better" needs a second definition, because it hides three claims.

**Preference** — I like this more. Personal, incorrigible, and not what the question asks about.
**Quality** — this wine is better made, more complete, more rewarding of attention. A claim that invites agreement and can be defended with reasons.
**Value** — better for the money, or better for this purpose. Objective once the purpose is fixed, and trivially so.

Only the second is interesting, and it carries an implicit clause: better *within a shared purpose*. A vin jaune and a Napa Cabernet are not competing at anything. "Better" is comparative within a style, a use, or an intention, and the question is ill-formed without one.

My position: **yes, one wine can be objectively better than another, in the fault-based and intersubjective senses, and no in the mind-independent sense.** Further, the claim is strong when the gap is wide and collapses when the gap is narrow — which is the opposite of where the trade spends its confidence.

## Hume, and why the standard sits in the judge

David Hume's "Of The Standard Of Taste" of 1757 remains the central treatment. Hume starts from the sceptical position — sentiment is not representation, so no sentiment can be false — and then observes that in practice we do not behave as though all verdicts are equal: nobody, he says, would rank Ogilby with Milton. Something must explain that.

His answer is that the standard lies not in the object but in the properly qualified subject. A true judge has delicacy of taste (detects components others miss), practice, comparison across the range, freedom from prejudice, and good sense. The joint verdict of such judges is the standard of taste. Hume then concedes what makes him honest: even among true judges, irreducible variation persists from temperament and from the culture of the age.

Transpose that and you have the wine trade exactly. We do not claim that quality is in the liquid. We claim that trained, practised, comparison-rich tasters converge, and we institutionalise the claim — through examinations, panels, appellation approval tastings and blind competitions.

## BLIC, and the analogy with fine art

The trade's working criteria are balance, length, intensity and complexity, with typicity and ageing potential as riders. Their status is instructive: each is a *descriptive* property, checkable by anyone trained. Whether a finish persists for three seconds or thirty is a matter of fact. Whether the alcohol protrudes from the acid and fruit is a matter of fact. Complexity is roughly countable. What is conventional is the *link* between those properties and the verdict "better".

The fine-art parallel is exact and worth making. Nobody thinks a Rembrandt is better than a hotel-lobby print in the sense that "better" is a pigment. But no one treats the comparison as mere preference either, because there are criteria — draughtsmanship, control of light, compositional invention, difficulty overcome — that trained viewers apply with substantial agreement. The criteria are conventional and not arbitrary: they track what repays sustained attention. BLIC does the same work, and inherits the same status.

## What can actually be measured

Chemistry measures composition and faults: alcohol, titratable acidity, pH, residual sugar, volatile acidity, TCA, Brettanomyces markers. It identifies defects reliably and quality not at all. There is no analyte that scales with quality, and there will not be one, because quality is not a substance.

Sensory science measures something more useful — reliability. Trained panels discriminate and rank reproducibly on defined attributes. That is the empirical basis for the intersubjective claim, and it is real. Its limits are equally real, which brings me to the objections.

## The four strongest objections

**Unreliability.** Published studies of a large American state-fair competition found that individual judges frequently scored replicate pours of the same wine differently within a single flight, and inter-critic agreement on the same wine is often weak. This is the most damaging objection and it must be conceded: it refutes the objectivity of any individual verdict. It does not refute the aggregate claim, because noisy individual measurements can still yield a stable mean — which is precisely why competitions use panels and why a single critic's score should never be treated as a fact.

**Context effects.** Experiments in which the same wine is presented at different stated prices have found that the higher price raises both reported enjoyment and measured activity in reward-related regions of the brain. Judgement is contaminated by information. The trade's answer is blind tasting, which is not a philosophical solution but is a working one, and its existence shows the profession already accepts the objection.

**Cultural relativity.** Criteria are formed inside a tradition. A Jerez taster's standard for a fino and a Burgundian's for a village Chambolle are not commensurable, and the global adoption of one set of criteria reflects commercial power as much as insight.

**Circularity.** True judges are identified by their agreement with the standard they themselves set. Hume saw this. My answer is that the circle is real but not vicious: it is the same circle in every skilled practice, and it is broken pragmatically, because training demonstrably changes what a taster can detect, and that change is testable independently of any verdict.

## Where the claim holds and where it breaks

**Faults.** Near-total agreement. A corked bottle is worse than a sound one, and no preference rescues it. Objectively better, in the plainest sense.

**Wide gaps within a shared style.** An industrial supermarket Chardonnay against a fine Chablis: trained tasters would be close to unanimous, the reasons would be statable in BLIC terms, and disagreement would signal inexperience rather than a different valid view. Objectively better, in the intersubjective sense.

**Close comparisons within a peer group.** Latour against Margaux in the same vintage. Here the claim fails. Rankings shuffle between tastings — the 1976 Paris tasting demonstrated it once and every re-run has confirmed it — because there is no fact left to discover. What remains is preference wearing the clothes of judgement.

**Across purposes.** Ill-formed until a purpose is supplied.

## Conclusion

Yes — but only within limits worth stating precisely. One wine can be objectively better than another where a defect is present, and where the quality gap is wide enough that qualified judges converge on stated criteria. That is objectivity in Hume's sense, not the physicist's, and it is enough to teach on, examine on and price on. It is not enough to settle the top of any peer group, and the trade's habit of asserting it there is the least defensible thing we do.

questionText: How relevant is tradition to 21st century wine consumers?
body:
## Tradition, defined three ways

Tradition is a practice transmitted across generations and valued partly *because* it is inherited — the inheritance is doing work that the practice's own merits would not do alone. That definition matters here, because it means tradition is a claim about provenance, not about quality, and consumers treat it accordingly.

For a consumer, tradition arrives in three quite different forms.

**As practice**: foot-treading, basket presses, chestnut and old oak, the solera, méthode traditionnelle, hand harvesting, appellation rules on yield and ageing. Consumers meet this only indirectly — when it changes the taste in the glass or the price on the shelf.

**As narrative signal**: "family-owned since 1720", monastic origins, heraldic labels, the château, the word "traditional" itself. This is the form most consumers actually encounter, and it is a marketing asset independent of whether any traditional practice survives behind it.

**As ritual**: Champagne at celebrations, Port at Christmas, fino with tapas, Beaujolais Nouveau in November. Here tradition belongs to the consumer rather than the producer, and it is the most durable form of all.

My answer works through those three, because the honest verdict differs for each.

## Five consumers, not one

The question cannot be answered for a single consumer, and the most common failure is to assume the enthusiast is representative. Five segments, with a judgement on each:

The **involved enthusiast** is small in number, large in spend, and highly tradition-sensitive as a source of information — provenance, vintage, estate history are how they navigate. Yet their taste is increasingly counter-traditional: skin contact, low sulphur, pét-nat, forgotten varieties. Tradition is their vocabulary, not their preference.

The **mainstream everyday buyer** accounts for most volume and buys on brand, grape, price, shelf position and a remembered taste. Tradition is close to irrelevant except as background reassurance that the wine is a real thing from a real place.

The **gift and occasion buyer** is where tradition is worth most. Buying a bottle as a signal to someone else makes heritage cues directly useful, because the recipient must be able to read them without tasting. This single segment sustains a large part of the premium market.

The **new-market entrant** — in China, Brazil, India, West Africa — uses European tradition as a status proxy, imported wholesale and often without its content. Simultaneously, local traditions are being constructed at speed.

The **moderation-first younger drinker** treats tradition as a liability where it reads as formality, complexity or exclusion. Not hostility to heritage; hostility to being made to feel ignorant.

Relevance, then, is not high or low. It is highest where the wine is a message to someone else, and lowest where it is a Tuesday.

## Where tradition demonstrably works

Consumers pay for place, and appellation names still command premiums that identical liquid without them does not. They pay for continuity of ownership: Primum Familiae Vini, whose entire proposition is continuity of family ownership, exists because that story converts. They pay for ritual: the traditional-method sparkling category owns celebration in a way no substitute has dislodged, which is a consumer tradition, not a producer one. And cellar-door and wine-tourism revenue is almost entirely a trade in tradition — the visitor is buying the cellar, the family, the age of the vines, and taking a bottle home as evidence.

Note what these have in common. In each case tradition is functioning as a *shortcut*: a low-effort proxy for quality, authenticity or social meaning in a category with punishing information costs. Consumers are not valuing the past. They are using it.

## Where consumers have already abandoned it

The counter-evidence is decisive where tradition costs the consumer anything.

Closures: screwcaps took over the New Zealand and Australian bottling of white wine within roughly a decade, and consumers did not defend the cork. Formats: bag-in-box, cans and kegs grow while the "traditional" 75cl glass bottle attracts criticism on carbon grounds.

Categories: Prosecco outsells Champagne several times over by volume, on a tank-method process, a young brand history and an informal proposition — precisely the opposite of the traditional pitch, and it won. Meanwhile the categories with the most tradition per bottle have suffered most: Sherry shipments have fallen by a very large margin from their 1970s peak, and traditional German Riesling lost the UK market almost entirely. Both are, technically and historically, among the most traditional wines made. Tradition did not save either.

Labelling: consumers navigate by grape variety, a New World convention, rather than by appellation, and every European region that has added a varietal or a plain-English descriptor to its label has done so because consumers asked for it by not buying.

## When innovation becomes tradition, and back

This is where the question becomes interesting, and it also explains the pattern above.

Almost everything the consumer now reads as traditional began as disruptive technology. The Champagne bottle, remuage and dosage were 18th and 19th century innovations — a technological solution to an unstable product, now the definition of "traditional method". Rioja's long American-oak ageing was a 19th century import from Bordeaux, codified into law only in the 20th, and is now the thing modernists were accused of betraying. Barrique ageing in Barolo was heresy in the 1980s and is unremarkable now. Screwcap in Clare Valley will be a tradition within a generation, and Prosecco's tank method is already defended in traditional terms by the people who make it.

It runs the other way too. Practices lose traditional standing when the market retires them: Beaujolais Nouveau went from ritual to punchline, sweet German Riesling from mainstream to museum, and the solera has shrunk with the category that housed it.

The consequence for the consumer is the important part. Tradition is not a fixed set of practices but a status conferred retrospectively on whatever survived long enough to look inevitable. That is exactly why it works as a signal — it feels like a guarantee — and exactly why it is not one.

## What follows for the trade

Sell the benefit and let tradition carry it, rather than the reverse. Use heritage where it does real work: gifting, occasion, provenance reassurance, tourism, and the top of the range. Drop it where it obstructs: closure, format, label complexity, tone of voice, and anything that requires the consumer to already know something. And treat a producer's own conviction that consumers care about tradition with suspicion, because the trade is itself the most tradition-loving segment of the market and consistently projects its own preferences onto people who do not share them.

## Conclusion

Tradition is highly relevant to 21st-century wine consumers, but almost never as tradition. It is relevant as a proxy — for quality, authenticity, provenance and social meaning — and consumers keep it exactly as long as it is cheap to hold and abandon it the moment it costs them convenience, clarity or money. Its power is real at the premium and occasion end of the market and has already gone from the everyday purchase. The direction of travel is that the proxy keeps working while the practices behind it quietly change, which suits the trade rather well and is not something we should mistake for consumer loyalty to the past.

questionText: Which diseases of the vine are the greatest threat to vineyards around the world today, and why?
body:
## What makes a disease a threat

A disease's threat is not its notoriety but the product of four things: the annual economic cost it imposes, how fast and how far it spreads, whether it can be cured or only suppressed, and whether it attacks the crop or the vineyard asset. That last distinction organises my answer. The mildews cost growers more money every year than anything else, but they are contained within the season. The incurable diseases — trunk disease, and the vector-borne bacteria and viruses — destroy the planted capital itself and shorten the productive life of the vineyard. Those, I argue, are the greatest threat today.

## Trunk disease: the greatest threat

Esca, Eutypa dieback and Botryosphaeria dieback are the most serious global threat because they are incurable, cumulative and universal. Wood-colonising fungi enter through pruning wounds, spores released after rain, and progressively occlude the vascular system. The vine does not die in a season; it declines over years, losing spurs, then arms, then the trunk.

Why that is worse than an annual disease is economic. A vineyard's business case assumes twenty-five to forty productive years to amortise establishment; trunk disease can put a block into decline by year twelve to fifteen, and replanting a mature premium block costs both the planting and the lost income of the establishment years. It bites hardest exactly where value is highest: old-vine blocks in the Barossa, Rioja and the southern Rhone, and the mature vineyards of Bordeaux, Cognac and Tuscany. There is no curative chemistry since sodium arsenite, withdrawn in the EU in the early 2000s, so growers are left with wound protection, late pruning, sanitation and remedial surgery — all labour-intensive at a time when skilled vineyard labour is the scarcest input in most regions.

## Vector-borne bacteria and viruses: incurable and spreading

**Pierce's disease** (*Xylella fastidiosa*, spread by sharpshooters) kills the vine within a few seasons, has no cure, and its range is set by winter cold — which climate warming is moving poleward. The same bacterium has been established in Puglia since the 2010s on olives, which demonstrates both the regulatory response an outbreak triggers and the cost of eradication zones.

**Flavescence doree**, a phytoplasma vectored by the leafhopper *Scaphoideus titanus*, is a threat less through vine death than through the regulatory regime it forces: it is a notifiable quarantine organism in the EU, which makes insecticide treatment and the uprooting of infected vines compulsory across Burgundy, Beaujolais, the Languedoc and northern Italy. That obligation directly conflicts with organic and biodynamic certification, so it threatens growers' commercial positioning as well as their vines.

**Grapevine red blotch virus** is the most insidious, because it kills nothing. It impairs ripening — sugar accumulation stalls and anthocyanin synthesis is suppressed — so the fruit is downgraded while the vine looks healthy. It moved through North American vineyards inside apparently clean nursery material before it was even described, and the only remedy is to rogue and replant. **Grapevine leafroll**, spread by mealybugs and scale, does the same more slowly and is the defining vineyard-longevity problem of South Africa. Both are threats because the disease is in the planting material and in the global nursery trade, which means the grower can buy a fifteen-year problem on day one.

## The mildews and rots: the greatest cost, not the greatest threat

Downy and powdery mildew, and Botrytis bunch rot, remain the largest recurrent expense in the vineyard and can take an entire crop in a wet season, as northern Europe found in 2021. But they are curable, and the real threat they now pose is a regulatory and resistance one: fungicide resistance is well documented, actives are being withdrawn faster than they are replaced, and copper — the organic grower's only reliable downy mildew tool — is under EU restriction. A wet-climate organic vineyard may soon have no adequate control, which converts a manageable disease into a structural one.

## Why the threat is growing

Four forces compound. Climate change is extending vector ranges and lengthening the infection window: warmer winters raise overwintering survival of leafhoppers and mealybugs, and wetter, warmer springs extend the mildew infection period in regions that previously escaped it. The global trade in propagation material moves latent viruses faster than testing catches them, which is how red blotch crossed a continent unnoticed. The vineyard's narrow clonal genetic base means a pathogen that defeats one defence defeats it everywhere, and there is no equivalent of the annual varietal turnover that arable agriculture uses to stay ahead of disease. And the loss of active ingredients, combined with scarce and costly skilled labour, is removing the tools with which growers previously bought their way out.

## Conclusion

The greatest threats are trunk disease and the vector-borne viral and bacterial diseases, because they are incurable, they are carried in planting material or by mobile vectors that regulation cannot fully contain, and they destroy the vineyard rather than the vintage. The mildews are the greatest cost, but a cost is not a threat while it can still be paid; the danger there is the shrinking chemical toolbox. A grower planning today should treat clean, tested plant material and pruning-wound discipline as the two highest-return investments available.

questionText: What effects do vineyard pests have on grape quality, and how do grape growers control them?
body:
## Grape quality, and the three ways pests damage it

By grape quality I mean the condition of the fruit at the weighbridge: sugar, acid and pH balance, phenolic and aromatic ripeness, evenness of ripening across the block, and the physical and microbial integrity of the berry. That is a different thing from wine quality, and pests act on it by three distinct routes: they damage the berry directly and open it to spoilage organisms; they vector disease that alters ripening physiology; or they reduce the vine's capacity to ripen a crop at all. I organise the answer by pathway, because the control logic follows the pathway rather than the species.

## Pathway one: loss of vine capacity through root and canopy feeding

**Phylloxera** and **nematodes** attack the root system, so their effect on grape quality is indirect but severe: a debilitated vine has less leaf area per unit of crop, and stalls at low sugar with unripe seed tannin and uneven veraison. Phylloxera thrives on clay soils and is checked by sand, which is why Chile, and pockets of Colares and South Australia, remain ungrafted while Victoria's Yarra and King Valleys sit inside declared phylloxera zones. Root-knot and dagger nematodes are the reverse — a sandy-soil problem in the Australian Riverland and California's Central Valley — and *Xiphinema index* additionally vectors fanleaf virus, so it damages quality twice.

Control here is genetic and pre-plant, and it is decided once. Grafting to *V. berlandieri* and *rupestris* hybrids solves phylloxera; nematode tolerance requires specific choices such as Ramsey, Freedom or Harmony. Beyond that, control is quarantine and hygiene: footwear and machinery disinfestation, restricted vine movement, and area-wide zoning. Chemical nematicides are largely withdrawn, so biofumigant cover crops such as mustard and long fallows are what remain.

## Pathway two: sap-feeders as disease vectors

**Mealybugs and soft scale** spread grapevine leafroll virus, and the quality effect is precisely measurable in the fruit: delayed and incomplete veraison, suppressed anthocyanin, retained malic acid and lower sugar, with the added problem that infected vines look normal. South Africa's Western Cape has made this its defining vineyard-health programme. **Leafhoppers** vector phytoplasmas — *Scaphoideus titanus* carrying flavescence doree through Burgundy, Beaujolais and northern Italy — while sharpshooters carry *Xylella* in California and Texas, killing the vine outright.

Control is a package, not a spray. Roguing and replanting with certified virus-tested material removes the reservoir; monitoring with pheromone and yellow sticky traps sets treatment thresholds; biological control using parasitoid wasps and predatory beetles suppresses mealybug where ant populations are also managed, since ants farm mealybug and must be baited out. Insecticide is targeted at the vulnerable crawler stage, and in the flavescence doree zones it is legally compulsory — a control decision taken away from the grower entirely.

## Pathway three: direct berry damage and taint

This is where the quality loss is most immediate. **European grapevine moth** larvae bore into berries; the wound itself is minor, but it is the entry point for *Botrytis*, *Aspergillus* and sour rot, and for vinegar flies that carry acetic bacteria into the bunch. The result is rotten fruit, volatile acidity and ochratoxin risk in warm regions — a Mediterranean and southern Italian problem, and the reason *Lobesia botrana* is a declared quarantine pest in Chile. **Wasps, birds and mammals** remove or split fruit: starlings and silvereyes in New Zealand, kangaroos and foxes in Australia, wild boar and deer in Europe. **Mites** bronze and defoliate leaves in dusty, hot conditions, cutting ripening capacity. And some pests taint the fruit without damaging it — the multicoloured Asian lady beetle, whose alkaloids taint juice at very low incidence, is a real harvest problem in Ontario and the US Midwest.

Controls differ sharply by pathway. Mating disruption with pheromone dispensers is now the standard *Lobesia* tool in European vineyards, works area-wide rather than vine-by-vine, and is compatible with organic certification; *Bacillus thuringiensis* and spinosad cover the larval stage. Canopy management that opens bunches reduces both moth shelter and the rot that follows. Birds need netting, which is expensive but the only reliable answer on premium blocks; scaring devices habituate. Vertebrates need fencing. Mites are controlled by suppressing dust on tracks and conserving predatory mites — which means avoiding the broad-spectrum insecticides used against something else.

## What I would prioritise

Almost every effective control is either decided before planting or is an area-wide programme, and almost every one interacts with the others: an insecticide applied for leafhopper removes the predators holding mites in check, and a cover crop sown for soil health shelters snails and rodents. The single greatest quality risk in most regions is the berry-damaging insect that opens the door to rot, because it converts a small compositional loss into an unsellable parcel within days of a warm, wet spell. The greatest long-term risk is the vectored virus, because it degrades ripening invisibly for a decade and the fruit never reaches the sugar, colour and tannin ripeness the site is capable of. Monitoring and thresholds rather than calendar spraying, and certified planting material rather than remedial treatment, are what let a grower spend on the right one.

questionText: To what extent does the geology of a vineyard affect the way it is managed?
body:
## Geology is not soil, and the difference decides the answer

By **geology** I mean the parent material beneath the vineyard — its lithology, mineralogy, hardness, fissuring and depth: limestone, granite, schist, basalt, sandstone, or a deposit of alluvial gravel. By **soil texture** I mean the sand, silt and clay proportions of the weathered horizon the roots actually occupy. These are not the same thing and they are not reliably correlated, because much of the world's vineyard soil was transported there — alluvium, colluvium, loess, aeolian sand — and sits over unrelated bedrock. Granite weathers to sand in the Northern Rhone and Beaujolais; limestone weathers to heavy clay as terra rossa in Coonawarra. So the same rock can demand opposite management.

The chain runs geology to soil to management: parent rock sets soil depth, stoniness, chemistry and, above all, how water behaves in the profile; those properties set vigour, rootability and trafficability; and those set what the manager does. My position is that geology exerts a large but largely **indirect and front-loaded** influence: it dominates the establishment decisions and it dominates management on extreme sites, but on deep, uniform soils the day-to-day decisions are driven by climate, water availability and the commercial target, with the rock too far below the roots to matter.

## Water: drainage and irrigation

This is geology's strongest direct effect. Fissured limestone and deep gravel drain freely, so roots descend and the vine is drought-buffered from a fractured aquifer — the schists of the Douro and the Priorat llicorella both allow dry farming at low rainfall that the same climate on shallow clay would not. Impermeable marl or clay perches water, causing waterlogging, anoxic roots and delayed spring warming, so the manager installs tile drains and open ditches, as generations did in the Medoc, and chooses a rootstock tolerant of wet feet such as SO4 or Riparia rather than 110R. Where irrigation is legal, geology sets the schedule: a shallow soil over hard rock has almost no reservoir and demands frequent, small applications, while a deep gravel over clay can be irrigated rarely and heavily.

## Chemistry: CEC, nutrition and fertiliser policy

Parent rock determines base saturation and cation exchange capacity. High active limestone raises pH and induces iron chlorosis, which is a rootstock decision above all — 41B and Fercal in Champagne and Cognac — and then a foliar-iron and organic-matter decision. Acid granite and sandstone soils are low in bases and need liming and magnesium. Low-CEC sands and gravels hold neither water nor nutrients, so nitrogen and potassium must be split into small fertigated doses or they leach; a clay-rich soil over marl holds them and needs far less. Volcanic soils are typically potassium-rich, which raises must pH, and the management answer is competition — a cover crop drawing down potassium — rather than fertiliser.

## Vigour, spacing and trellising

Vigour is the variable that connects everything. Shallow, stony, low-water-holding soils over rock produce naturally low-vigour vines, so the manager plants densely to use the ground, and trains low and small — the single stakes of the Mosel slate, the goblet bush vines of the southern Rhone galets and inland Spain. Deep alluvium produces excess vigour, so the answer is a devigorating rootstock, wider spacing, a divided or high-wire trellis to carry the canopy, and a competitive sward. The same variety, a hundred kilometres apart, is managed as two different crops.

## Physical operations: equipment, tilling, weed control and erosion

Geology decides what machinery can do. Rock at shallow depth requires deep ripping or blasting before planting, forbids under-vine cultivation, and destroys implements — so weed control shifts to mowing, mulch or herbicide because tillage is not an option. Slope and rock structure decide access: the schist terraces of the Douro and the Mosel's fractured slate cannot take a tractor, so the vineyard is worked by winch, monorail or hand at several times the cost per hectare, and that single geological fact drives the labour budget, the pruning schedule and the harvest date. Friable weathered schist and decomposed granite erode readily on slope, so permanent cover crops, straw mulch and terracing become obligatory; on the stony low-vigour sites the same cover crop competes for scarce water and must be restricted to alternate rows or terminated at bud burst.

## Where geology matters least

On the deep alluvial and aeolian plains that grow most of the world's wine — the Riverland, the San Joaquin Valley, much of Mendoza's east — the roots never reach bedrock, and the profile is uniform enough that the parent material tells the manager nothing he cannot read more accurately from a soil pit and a moisture probe. There, management is set by water allocation, heat and the tonnage contract, and two blocks over quite different underlying rock will be farmed identically. This is the honest limit on the question: geology's influence is real where the rock is close, hard, steep or chemically extreme, and close to nil where it is buried under three metres of transported sediment.

## Conclusion

Geology affects vineyard management substantially, but mostly at one remove and mostly once: it sets the constraints within which rootstock, spacing, trellising, drainage and mechanisation are chosen at planting, and those choices then govern the following thirty years. Its ongoing influence is decisive on steep, shallow or chemically extreme sites and modest elsewhere.
