questionText: How has the global coronavirus pandemic impacted consumer wine purchasing behaviours? Use examples from at least three significant markets to illustrate your answer.
body:
## Scope: which behaviours count as pandemic effects

I take this narrowly and deliberately. A great deal has changed in wine since March 2020, but much of it — the drift towards lower alcohol, the long premiumisation trend, the rise of organic claims — was already in motion and would have happened anyway. I confine myself to purchasing behaviours the pandemic either triggered outright or measurably accelerated. I also confine myself to consumers: the container shortages, dry-goods inflation and freight disruption of the last two years have been severe, but they are a supply-side story and not what is asked. My three markets are the United States, the United Kingdom and China, chosen because they behaved very differently and the differences are the argument.

## The channel shift, and how far it went

The first and largest effect was compulsory: on-trade closure moved a large block of consumption home. The striking global finding is how little drinking was lost — the OIV put the 2020 decline in world consumption at around 3% — so the volume did not disappear, it changed channel.

In the UK the off-trade absorbed it. Off-trade wine volumes rose by roughly a fifth in 2020 on Nielsen data reported by the WSTA, while hospitality lost most of its trading year. Supermarket wine became the default purchase, and the online specialists — Naked Wines, Laithwaites, the grocers' own delivery slots — took a step change in customer numbers that no marketing budget could have bought.

In the US the shift went further, because the pandemic forced a regulatory change consumers immediately used: a large majority of states temporarily permitted to-go and delivered alcohol. Direct-to-consumer winery shipments, already the fastest-growing route to market, grew of the order of a quarter by value in 2020 on the Sovos ShipCompliant and Wines Vines Analytics report. Uber's acquisition of the delivery platform Drizly in 2021 is the clearest signal that the trade read this as structural rather than temporary.

## What consumers bought once they were buying at home

Three behaviours here are specifically pandemic-shaped rather than pre-existing.

First, occasion substitution lifted the off-trade price point. A consumer who could not spend £40 in a restaurant spent £15 in a supermarket instead of their usual £8. This resembles premiumisation and I want to separate it from that trend: it is not consumers becoming steadily wealthier and more curious, it is a fixed budget displaced from one channel into another, and it should be expected to unwind as restaurants reopen.

Second, stockpiling and format. Early lockdown produced pantry-loading, a shift to larger pack sizes, and a real if temporary rehabilitation of bag-in-box in markets that had written it off.

Third, occasion loss at the top. Champagne is the cleanest evidence: CIVC shipments fell to around 245 million bottles in 2020, then rebounded above 320 million in 2021. Celebration wine depends on gatherings, and the rebound shows that demand was deferred rather than destroyed.

## China: the counter-case

China matters because it shows the channel shift was not universal. Chinese wine consumption is heavily on-trade, banqueting and gifting-led; there is no established habit of everyday domestic wine drinking to absorb displaced volume. When restaurants and banquets closed, the volume was simply lost. Bottled wine imports, already in decline, fell by roughly a quarter by volume in 2020 on China Customs figures. What did accelerate was e-commerce and livestream selling through Tmall, JD and Douyin, now a serious route to the Chinese wine consumer rather than a curiosity. And China is not past this: the Shanghai lockdown this spring has repeated the 2020 shock in the country's single most important wine city.

## What has survived reopening

This is where the answer has to commit.

- Durable: online and direct-to-consumer purchasing. Once a consumer has completed the first transaction, surrendered a card and had wine arrive, the habit holds; US DtC has kept growing after reopening.
- Durable: the premium at-home occasion. "Restaurant at home" has proved to be a genuine new occasion rather than a substitute one.
- Not durable: stockpiling, large formats and the extreme off-trade skew. These tracked closure and have unwound with it.
- Uncertain: the traded-up off-trade price point. It survived 2021, but inflation is now the stronger force acting on it, and I expect trading down through the mainstream with the premium tier holding.

## Conclusion

The pandemic did not change what consumers want from wine; it changed where and how they buy it, and it did so in two years rather than the decade it would otherwise have taken. The lasting consequences are a materially larger digital and direct channel in the US and UK, a rebuilt commercial relationship between producer and drinker wherever DtC took hold, and — in a market like China, where wine consumption is social and public rather than domestic — a cohort of consumers that reopening alone has not brought back.

questionText: What measures determine the strength of a wine brand? How can brand managers most effectively influence their brand's long-term performance?
body:
## What a wine brand is

A brand is a promise held in the consumer's mind that reduces their risk in choosing. In wine that promise can be owned by a company (Yellow Tail, Kim Crawford), by a place acting as a collective brand (Sancerre, Barolo, Prosecco), or by a retailer (own-label tiers). The distinction matters for this question, because only the first has a manager with the authority to change it. I answer part one across all three types and part two for the company brand, since that is where brand management is actually exercised.

## Measures of strength

There is no single measure, and the first sign of a competent answer is knowing that the right measures depend on what the brand is for. I use three families and then a test.

**Market measures.** Penetration (what proportion of category buyers bought the brand at least once), market share by value and volume, weighted distribution, rate of sale per point of distribution, and average selling price. Penetration is the one I would put first: growth in consumer goods comes overwhelmingly from recruiting light buyers, not from deepening loyalty among heavy ones.

**Consumer measures.** Spontaneous and prompted awareness, consideration, conversion from consideration to purchase, and repeat rate. Awareness without conversion diagnoses a brand that is famous and unwanted — a real and expensive condition.

**Financial measures.** Price premium against the category average, gross margin per case, and price elasticity: how much volume the brand loses when it takes a price rise. That last is the sharpest single test of strength, because it measures whether the consumer is buying the brand or the price. For fine wine the equivalents are secondary-market value and liquidity on Liv-ex, allocation demand and the length of the waiting list.

**The test that ties them together.** The measures must match the brand's purpose and its life-cycle stage. Yellow Tail - launched in the US market in 2001 and now selling on the order of thirteen to fourteen million cases a year worldwide - is properly judged on share, penetration, distribution points and average selling price. A first-growth château or a Napa cult wine judged on distribution points would look like a failing brand; its correct measures are secondary-market price, allocation and critical standing. Applying mass-market KPIs to a luxury brand is the commonest analytical error in this area, and it drives genuinely value-destroying decisions.

## What a brand manager actually controls

Part two is the harder part, and the honest answer is that a brand manager influences long-term performance through four levers, of which marketing communication is the least important.

**Price architecture and promotional discipline.** This is the first lever because it does the most long-term damage when mishandled. A large majority of branded wine volume in the UK grocery multiples sells on promotion, and the mechanism is a ratchet: each deeper deal resets the consumer's reference price, so the next promotion must be deeper to move the same volume, and the brand's everyday price becomes fictional. The manager's long-term job is to hold the shelf price and control the depth and frequency of deal even when it costs a quarter's volume — which is precisely the decision an annual bonus discourages.

**Range architecture.** Extensions either recruit new buyers or cannibalise existing ones, and the difference is whether they reach an occasion the core range does not. Yellow Tail's extensions into rosé, sparkling and reserve tiers used the equity to widen occasions while holding one visual identity. 19 Crimes went further, using celebrity association and augmented-reality labels to recruit consumers who were not buying wine at all — an expensive strategy that works for recruitment and is dangerous for longevity, because a brand built on a device must keep finding new devices.

**Supply security.** At any serious scale this is where wine brands actually die. A million-case brand needs contracted fruit at a known cost across multiple vintages and, ideally, more than one region or hemisphere to absorb a short crop. Casella's model of long-term grower contracts is the reason Yellow Tail could grow without the vintage variation that would have broken the consistency promise. Brand managers who cannot influence sourcing are managing a label, not a brand.

**Consistency and renewal.** The liquid must not drift, and the packaging must. Consistency protects the promise; periodic pack and communication refreshes protect relevance. Investment continuity matters more than investment level: advertising and promotion held at a stable percentage of net sales through downturns compounds, while brands cut to protect a bad year rarely recover the awareness cheaply.

## Conclusion

Strength is not one number. It is the set of measures that corresponds to the brand's purpose — penetration, share and price elasticity for a mainstream brand, allocation, secondary-market value and critical standing for a luxury one. Long-term performance is influenced far less by campaigns than by three unglamorous disciplines: refusing the promotional ratchet, extending the range only where it recruits, and securing fruit on contracts longer than the manager's own tenure.

questionText: Who or what are the most important influencers of consumer behaviour in today's world of wine?
body:
## Defining the term

"Influencer" has been narrowed by usage to mean someone with a following on social media. The question deliberately resists that: it says "who or what", and it says influencers in the plural. I therefore treat an influencer as any person, institution or force that changes what a consumer buys, and that includes things with no voice at all — a shelf price, a monopoly's range decision, an appellation name, a piece of health legislation. Some of the most powerful influences on wine purchasing are structural rather than personal.

## How I rank them

I rank by three tests: **reach** (how many purchase decisions the influence touches), **trust** (whether the consumer acts on it), and **proximity** (how close it sits to the moment of purchase). An influence that scores on all three beats one that scores heavily on a single test. This is why a critic with global authority can matter less to total wine sales than a supermarket buyer nobody has heard of.

## The gatekeepers: the most important, and the least visible

The retail buyer is my first-ranked influencer. In markets dominated by a few grocers, a range review decides what several million consumers can physically buy; no amount of consumer demand survives delisting. The state monopolies make this explicit — Systembolaget in Sweden, Alko in Finland, the LCBO and the SAQ in Canada each publish tenders, and winning one is worth more than any campaign. Sommeliers perform the same function in the on-trade at lower volume but with higher influence per bottle, because they choose on the customer's behalf.

## Price and promotion

The second-ranked influence is a "what": the shelf price and the deal attached to it. In every mainstream market, promotional mechanics move more volume than any other single lever, and they sit at maximum proximity to purchase. Regulation belongs in this category too, because it acts on price directly — Scotland's minimum unit pricing, in force since 2018 at 50p per unit, changed the cheap end of the Scottish market by statute rather than persuasion. Duty regimes, health warning labelling and campaigns such as Dry January influence purchasing at a scale no individual commentator approaches.

## Region and brand as shorthand

The third is the appellation or category name doing the work of a recommendation. A consumer who reaches for Prosecco, Sancerre or Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is being influenced by a collective brand built over decades. This influence is strong on reach and trust, weak on nothing, and it is the reason regional bodies spend generic promotional money at all.

## Critics and the specialist press

Fourth, and important to place accurately. Robert Parker's Wine Advocate, Jancis Robinson MW, Antonio Galloni's Vinous, James Suckling and Tim Atkin MW still move prices decisively at the fine end — Bordeaux en primeur pricing is still set in dialogue with published scores, and a high score on a shelf-talker demonstrably lifts rate of sale in US retail. But their reach into everyday purchasing is small and shrinking, and authority has fragmented from one dominant palate to many.

## Digital, social and peer

Fifth, and rising fastest. The important distinction is that digital influence mostly functions as validation at the point of purchase rather than as authority. Vivino, with of the order of sixty million registered users, is consulted in the aisle with the bottle already in hand. Livestream selling on Douyin and Tmall has become a genuine sales channel in China rather than a marketing one. Celebrity ownership — Kylie Minogue's wine range, Brad Pitt's involvement at Miraval, Snoop Dogg's association with 19 Crimes, Cameron Diaz's Avaline — recruits consumers who were not shopping the wine category at all, which is a different and valuable job.

Underneath all of it sits the influence consumer research keeps finding to be the strongest of any single source: friends, family and the host who poured it. Word of mouth wins on trust and proximity even though it has no reach of its own.

## The ranking changes by market and by drinker

This is where a general answer fails. In Sweden the monopoly's range decision is close to absolute. In China the gift context, the giver's status and now the livestream host outweigh critics entirely. In the US, the distributor's book and the retail chain's set determine availability before any consumer influence operates. In the UK the supermarket promotion is decisive at the mainstream and the specialist merchant's recommendation at the top. By age, older drinkers still index to critics and to region; drinkers in their twenties index to peers, to apps and to whatever is visible on social platforms, and to price.

## Conclusion

The most important influencers of wine purchasing today are not the ones the word now implies. Ranked by reach, trust and proximity together, they are the trade gatekeepers who decide availability, the price and promotion attached to the bottle, and the region or brand name acting as shorthand. Critics retain decisive influence over a small and valuable slice; social and celebrity influence is the fastest-growing force and mostly does the work of recruitment and validation rather than authority; and the single most trusted influencer remains the person who last poured the consumer a glass.

questionText: Which emerging wine-producing countries or regions have the best chance of establishing themselves as a significant force on the international wine market, and why?
body:
## Definitions and the test I apply

Three words need pinning down. **Emerging** means showing growth in sales or in reputation from a low base — not merely being old and obscure. **Significant force** can be quantitative (volume that moves a category) or qualitative (a benchmark others are measured against), and I will argue that most candidates can only be one. **International market** means the growth must reach beyond the domestic market; a country drinking its own production is not a force.

Because this is a business paper I judge candidates on four commercial tests, not on style: production capacity and the ability to grow it; cost of production against the price it can command; access to capital and know-how; and route to market — breadth of distribution across a number of countries. The third and fourth are where nearly all promising regions fail, and a region that reaches only specialist merchants in two markets is niche, not significant. My three cases are Ningxia, Romania and England.

## Ningxia, China — the best quantitative chance

Ningxia is the strongest case on capacity and capital. It has of the order of 35,000 to 40,000 hectares under vine, an explicit provincial and national policy of expansion, a state-run classification scheme to build reputation, and land available at a scale no European region can offer. Capital and know-how have arrived from outside: Moët Hennessy built Ao Yun in Yunnan and a Chandon sparkling operation in Ningxia, and Pernod Ricard has held Helan Mountain for years. Those investments matter commercially because they import viticultural and winemaking competence faster than domestic training can.

The obstacles are real and I would not underplay them. Winter vine burial adds a large recurring labour cost that pushes the cost base above what the quality reputation currently supports; production has been directed almost entirely at the domestic market; and export success depends on a political relationship that has recently worsened rather than improved. But the counter-argument is precisely that geopolitics, not capability, is the binding constraint — and constraints of that kind change quickly. If the trading relationship normalises, China is the only emerging producer with the volume, capital and state backing to become a force on both measures at once.

## Romania — the best value proposition

Romania is the case most people miss. It has of the order of 180,000 hectares of vineyard, placing it among the largest producers in the EU, a low cost base, EU membership giving tariff-free access to the largest premium wine bloc in the world, and EU restructuring funds that have already paid for replanting and modern cellar equipment. Quality has risen sharply without any corresponding critical attention, which is the definition of an underexploited asset.

Its failure is commercial rather than agricultural: almost all of the crop is consumed domestically, ownership is fragmented, there is no recognised umbrella brand, and no meaningful generic export body. That is a solvable problem — it is the problem Chile solved in the 1990s — and it is solvable with money rather than with time, which is what makes Romania the best risk-adjusted bet on this list. Broad international exposure is achievable because the cost base fits the price points where multiple markets buy volume.

## England — high reputation, capped scale

England has already achieved the harder half. Traditional-method sparkling wine has critical acclaim, and Champagne money has voted with its feet: Taittinger's Domaine Evremond in Kent and Pommery's English venture are commercial validations, not curiosities. Climate change is a structural tailwind here in a way it is a threat almost everywhere else.

But on my tests England fails on scale and on breadth. England and Wales have under 4,000 hectares planted, the cost of production is high, and the price point restricts distribution to specialist and prestige listings in a handful of markets. England will be a qualitative force and a real competitor to entry-level Champagne. It will not be a quantitative one this decade, and a candidate who claims otherwise has not done the arithmetic on hectares.

## What I am not choosing

South Africa and New Zealand are sometimes offered here and neither qualifies: both have decades of established international distribution, recognised generic bodies and settled critical reputations. They face commercial challenges, but a mature region in difficulty is not an emerging one. India I would also set aside — its wine growth is genuine but almost wholly domestic, and it is emerging as a market rather than as a producer. The northern-European climate beneficiaries, including Germany's expanding possibilities for red wine, are interesting but represent style change within established industries rather than new entrants.

## Conclusion

Ningxia has the best chance of becoming a significant force in both senses, because it is the only candidate with the capacity, capital and policy support to scale — conditional on a political relationship it does not control. Romania has the best chance of becoming a significant volume force, because its only missing ingredient is a route to market. England will become a significant qualitative force and is structurally incapable of becoming a quantitative one.

questionText: Which are the most attractive markets for premium Italian wines, and why?
body:
## Two definitions before any market can be judged

**Premium.** There is no agreed threshold, so I set one and use it consistently: for this answer, wine retailing above roughly US$25 a bottle, which in Italian terms means classic-appellation reds — Barolo, Barbaresco, Brunello di Montalcino, Chianti Classico Gran Selezione, Amarone, the Bolgheri and Tuscan international blends — plus a thin premium white and Franciacorta tier. This deliberately excludes the volume engine: Prosecco, Pinot Grigio delle Venezie, everyday Chianti and Montepulciano d'Abruzzo.

**Attractive.** This can mean three different things and they point to different countries: growth, absolute size (which favours mature markets), or profitability per bottle. I weight profitability and absolute size for premium wine, because a premium producer with limited volume needs margin and depth, not growth rate on a small base.

That distinction does most of the work here, because Italy's biggest export markets by volume are not the same as its best premium markets. Italy vies with France for the title of largest producer by volume and is second to France by export value; the largest markets for Italian wine by volume are Germany, the USA and the UK. Only one of those three is a premium market.

## The United States — the most attractive, decisively

The US is my first choice on every measure that matters. Italy supplies of the order of a third of US wine imports by volume and is the leading imported origin, but the point is the mix rather than the volume: the US is where premium Italian wine actually sells at premium prices, and the reason is distributional history rather than fashion. Italian-American restaurant culture built a national on-trade base for Italian wine over generations, so Barolo, Brunello and Super Tuscans have by-the-glass and by-the-bottle placement in cities across the country, not only in the coastal metropolitan markets. Fine-wine retail and the auction market support the same names.

The structural qualifications matter. Three-tier distribution means the producer's margin is shared, importer selection is the single most consequential commercial decision an Italian estate makes, and consolidation among distributors has made access harder for small estates. Section 301 tariff exposure was a live threat in 2019–2021 and Italian wine escaped where French wine did not — a reminder that the position is politically contingent. Even so, no other market combines this depth of premium listings with this scale.

## Italy itself — the market most people overlook

I would rank Italy second, and I would defend it. Roughly half of Italian production is consumed in Italy, and the Italian on-trade sells premium domestic wine with no import duty, no importer margin, no freight, no label compliance and no need to explain the appellations. Margin per bottle to the producer is higher than in any export market. Add the cellar-door and enoteca channel: wine tourism in Piedmont, Tuscany and the Veneto delivers direct sales at full retail, with the customer paying to visit. For an estate of a hundred thousand bottles, the domestic on-trade plus cellar door can be more profitable than a US importer relationship, and it carries far less brand risk. The obvious counter is that the Italian market is mature, price-sensitive at the mainstream and offers little volume growth — which is why it is second rather than first.

## Switzerland and Canada — the margin markets

Switzerland is small but records among the highest average price per litre of any Italian export market: a wealthy, wine-literate, culturally adjacent consumer base that buys Piedmont and Tuscany at real prices. Volume is limited, so it complements rather than replaces the US.

Canada is attractive for a different reason. The provincial monopolies — the LCBO in Ontario, the SAQ in Quebec — offer a single negotiation, predictable payment and large listings, and Quebec in particular is a strong premium Italian market. The cost is total dependence on a listing decision and constrained brand-building.

## Germany and the UK — large, but not premium

Germany is the largest Italian market by volume and among the least attractive for premium wine. Its channel structure is discount-led, average prices are low, and it buys Italian wine as value. The UK is a genuinely important premium market in London's on-trade and its fine-wine merchant trade, and it remains a global pricing centre for fine wine — but the headline Italian volume is overwhelmingly Prosecco and Pinot Grigio, and post-Brexit administration, duty and a weaker pound have all worked against premium imports. Both are markets to be present in, not markets to build a premium strategy on.

## Conclusion

The most attractive market for premium Italian wine is the United States, because it alone combines scale, established premium listings and a distribution history that has already done the educational work. The most underrated is Italy itself, where the margin per bottle is unmatched. Switzerland and Quebec are the high-value satellites. Germany and the UK are large by volume and structurally hostile to premium pricing, and treating their volume rankings as a guide to premium opportunity is the error this question is designed to expose.

questionText: You are the production director of a one million-case winery which aspires to become carbon neutral by the end of the decade. What steps would you take to achieve this objective?
body:
## Scope: carbon neutrality is not sustainability

Carbon neutral means net zero carbon dioxide equivalent across a defined boundary, achieved by reducing emissions as far as practicable and neutralising the remainder. It is a narrower objective than sustainability: water use, biodiversity, soil health and social conditions are all legitimate goals and none of them is what I have been asked to deliver. Some of them trade against carbon — a lightweight bottle is better for carbon and worse for perceived quality; organic conversion may raise tractor passes and therefore diesel. I will say where those tensions arise, but I will not write a sustainability plan.

I also define the boundary at the outset, using the GHG Protocol scopes. Scope 1 is what we burn and emit directly: tractor and truck diesel, boilers, refrigerant leakage, fermentation CO2. Scope 2 is purchased electricity. Scope 3 is everything upstream and downstream: glass, closures, cartons, bought-in grapes and bulk wine, freight, employee travel, and end-of-life packaging. A carbon-neutral claim that covers only Scopes 1 and 2 is not credible in wine, because most of our footprint is Scope 3.

## Step 1: measure before acting

Nothing can be planned until the baseline exists. I would commission a full inventory to the GHG Protocol using the international wine industry greenhouse gas accounting tool developed jointly by the Californian, Australian, New Zealand and South African industry bodies, so the result is comparable with peers rather than bespoke. I would have it verified by a third party — membership of International Wineries for Climate Action requires independently verified inventories, and that external discipline is what stops the exercise becoming marketing.

The output must be expressed per unit as well as in total: kilograms of CO2e per 75cl bottle shipped, and per case. Total emissions fall when you sell less wine, which is not an achievement; the intensity metric is what management should be held to, with the absolute figure reported alongside it.

## Step 2: where the emissions actually are, and therefore what to attack first

At one million cases — twelve million bottles a year — the ranking is fairly predictable and it should drive everything. Across published winery inventories, packaging dominates, and within packaging glass is typically the single largest line, of the order of a third to a half of the total, because glass furnaces run at high temperature on gas. Distribution is generally second, electricity for refrigeration third, and the vineyard, despite being where most of the visible activity happens, is usually a modest share.

That ordering is the analysis the question wants. If glass and freight are more than half the footprint, then a programme that starts with cover crops and solar panels is well-intentioned and arithmetically incapable of reaching the target.

## Step 3: the plan, in production chronology

**Vineyard.** Reduce tractor passes by combining operations and moving to lighter machinery; trial electric or hybrid tractors as they become commercially viable. Cut synthetic nitrogen to the measured requirement — nitrous oxide is a greenhouse gas of the order of 265 times more potent than carbon dioxide over a century, so fertiliser discipline outperforms most other vineyard measures. Cover cropping, compost and reduced tillage sequester carbon in soil, and I would claim that conservatively: the gains are real but slow, hard to measure and reversible.

**Winery.** Refrigeration is the dominant electrical load. Insulate tanks and the barrel hall, recover heat, fit variable-speed drives, and cool at night. Replace chilled cold stabilisation with electrodialysis or with CMC or potassium polyaspartate additions, which removes a very large refrigeration load outright. Fix refrigerant leakage and move to ammonia or CO2 systems, since F-gas leaks are a Scope 1 line most wineries never count. Install on-site solar to cover the daytime load and contract a certified renewable supply for the remainder.

**Packaging — the biggest single lever.** Lightweight the standard bottle. Moving a standard bottle from around 550g to around 400g across twelve million bottles removes of the order of 1,800 tonnes of glass a year, with a proportionate cut in furnace emissions and in freight weight. Require higher recycled cullet content from suppliers and engage them on their own furnace decarbonisation. Move a defined share of volume out of glass altogether: bag-in-box and cans for everyday tiers, kegs for on-trade accounts.

**Distribution.** Ship in bulk and bottle in market wherever the brand allows: a flexitank moves around 24,000 litres in a container against roughly 9,000 litres shipped in bottle. Sea freight always, never air. Optimise pallet configurations and consolidate loads.

## Step 4: sequencing and governance

I would rank every intervention on tonnes of CO2e abated per pound of capital, build a phased plan against it, and re-measure annually with third-party verification. Supplier contracts get carbon clauses, since Scope 3 is delivered by other people's factories.

## Step 5: offsetting the residual

Offsetting comes last, deliberately. Some emissions — freight, glass melting, harvest diesel — cannot be eliminated this decade, and the residual must be neutralised to claim neutrality. I would buy only verified removals rather than avoidance credits, under Gold Standard or Verra, with demonstrable additionality and permanence, and prefer insetting: sequestration in our own vineyards and land, which is auditable and on our balance sheet. The offset line should shrink every year. An offset budget that stays flat is evidence the reduction programme has failed.

questionText: 'Natural wine does not need a legal definition.' Discuss.
body:
## What the term denotes, and where it fractures

By "natural wine" I mean wine from grapes farmed without synthetic herbicides, pesticides or fertilisers — in practice usually certified organic or biodynamic — hand-harvested, fermented with indigenous yeasts, and bottled with as little added and as little removed as the producer judges possible: no acidification, no enzymes, no concentrate, no cultured yeast, usually no fining, often no filtration, and either no sulphur dioxide or a small addition at bottling.

That definition is a description of intent, not a threshold, and I want to be honest that the category genuinely does not agree with itself. Two producers can both claim the term while disagreeing over temperature-controlled fermentation, cross-flow filtration, a cultured yeast used to restart a stuck ferment, or 25 mg/L of SO2 before shipping. Sulphur is the fault line. For one wing any addition is a breach of faith; for another, a modest dose is the difference between a wine that survives a container crossing the equator and one that arrives refermenting and mousy. Any legal text would have to pick a side of that argument, and the movement itself has not.

**My position:** I agree with the statement. The category does not need a legal definition, and a serious attempt to write one would harm the producers it is meant to protect. What the market does need is verification of the claims producers already make, and enforcement against those who make them falsely — a different instrument, already half-built.

## What already governs the category

The claim that natural wine is ungoverned is simply wrong, and the evidence sits in three layers.

The first is the one quasi-official definition that exists. The Vin Méthode Nature charter, drawn up by a French producers' syndicate and accepted by the French authorities in 2020, requires certified organic fruit, hand harvesting, indigenous yeasts, no additives, and no severe physical intervention — no flash pasteurisation, reverse osmosis, cross-flow filtration or heavy fining. Crucially it issues two logos: one for wines with no added sulphites at all, one permitting up to 30 mg/L total sulphur dioxide added after fermentation. Membership is annual and revocable. It is opt-in, it names the disagreement rather than resolving it, and it was written by practitioners.

The second layer is private association. Vini Veri and VinNatur in Italy, the latter with a protocol capping total sulphur dioxide at around 50 mg/L and a programme that lab-tests members' wines for pesticide residues — a harder audit than most appellations impose on themselves. RAW Wine requires exhibitors to declare total sulphur dioxide and sets a ceiling of around 70 mg/L. The Natural Wine Association in the UK publishes its own guidelines. They disagree with one another, which is the point: three ceilings, 30, 50 and 70 mg/L, describing three defensible readings of the same idea.

The third layer already has the force of law. Almost every natural producer is certified organic or biodynamic, and EU organic wine rules cap total sulphur dioxide at roughly 100 mg/L for dry reds and 150 mg/L for dry whites and rosés, against conventional ceilings of 150 and 200 mg/L, alongside a restricted additive list. Demeter goes further. The farming half of the natural claim is therefore already legally certified and audited; the winemaking half is covered by charters that go beyond what any regulator would dare impose.

## How strict, and could it be enforced?

This is where the case for legislation collapses, and it is a trilemma. Write the definition strictly enough to mean what the movement means, and it excludes a large share of self-declared natural producers — including many whose wines are the reason anyone cares about the category. Write it loosely enough to be politically passable, and it captures a great volume of ordinary organic low-intervention wine and hands the term to precisely the industrial players it was coined against. Write it at any level and you face the enforcement problem: no laboratory can tell you from the glass whether the yeast was indigenous, whether a cross-flow filter was used, or whether the tank was chilled. Sulphur is measurable; almost nothing else in the charter is. Enforcement would therefore rest on documentary audit of the cellar — which is exactly what Vin Méthode Nature and VinNatur already do, at their own cost.

There is a further cost that is rarely stated. To define "natural wine" in law is to declare, by statute, that the other ninety-nine per cent of the world's wine is unnatural. No regulator should be asked to codify that, and the wider industry should not want them to.

## Who would actually gain, and who would lose

**Producers.** Mostly small, undercapitalised, frequently farming under ten hectares. A further certification is a real cost in fees and paperwork against a tiny production. Against that, established natural producers do suffer free-riding — and it is their complaint, not the consumer's, that drives most calls for a definition.

**Distributors, retailers and the on-trade.** The strongest commercial argument for definition: a monopoly buyer or a supermarket category manager cannot build a listing around a term they cannot specify. But specialist importers already buy this category on relationship and charter membership, and no legal text will make natural wine a supermarket category, because unfiltered, low-sulphur wine cannot survive that supply chain.

**Regulatory bodies.** The EU took years to produce organic wine rules that amount to an additive list and two SO2 numbers. A "natural" category would require labelling law, control bodies and third-country equivalence for a fraction of one per cent of volume. It is a poor use of scarce regulatory capacity.

**Quality-assurance professionals.** The one place I concede real force. Unfiltered wines bottled with little or no SO2 are microbiologically live: refermentation, Brettanomyces, mousiness, volatile acidity. But a definition does not make an unstable wine stable. That is a technical and commercial problem, solved by cold chain, competent cellar hygiene and honest trade expectations, not by a statute.

**Consumers.** The real grievance is deception, and deception is already illegal. If a wine made with commercial yeast, nutrients and 120 mg/L of SO2 is sold as natural, that is a misleading-claim matter under existing consumer-protection law in the EU, UK and US. The gap is enforcement, not definition.

**Society.** The one genuine risk is health-halo drift — "natural" implying "healthier". That too is existing labelling law, and it would be made worse, not better, by the state putting its name to the word.

## The strongest counter-argument

The best case against me is that unprotected terms get captured: "sustainable", "artisan" and "old vine" all demonstrate it, and Vin Méthode Nature proves a workable definition can be written.

I accept the first point and it is why I do not argue for doing nothing. But Vin Méthode Nature is my model, not my refutation. It is an opt-in charter given official recognition — a protected claim, not a statutory category. It works precisely because practitioners wrote it, it can be revised annually, and producers who dislike it can simply not join. That is the opposite of a legal definition of natural wine, and it is enough.

## Conclusion

Natural wine does not need a legal definition. It needs three things: enforcement of existing misleading-claim law against those who borrow the term; official recognition of opt-in producer charters that already audit and already verify; and mandatory declaration of total sulphur dioxide, the one variable that is both measurable and genuinely contested. Definition without verification protects nobody. Verification without definition protects everyone who actually needs protecting.

questionText: Assess the main challenges and opportunities for the wine education industry around the globe in the next ten years.
body:
## What the wine education industry is

By "the wine education industry" I mean the organised, fee-earning supply of structured wine learning to two distinct audiences: the **trade** — people who earn a living from wine and need a credential or a skill — and **consumers**, who buy learning as leisure or self-improvement. It is global and unevenly institutionalised, and it has four tiers.

First, product-focused certification: the international awarding bodies and their national counterparts — Italy's AIS, Japan's sommelier system, the various national sommelier associations, the specialist regional schools. Second, professional-skills education in viticulture and oenology at degree level: UC Davis, Geisenheim, Adelaide, Montpellier, Bordeaux. Third, wine business education — the wine MBAs and specialist masters at Bordeaux, Adelaide and Sonoma State. Fourth, the informal channel: producer- and retailer-led tastings, free digital content, social media. I treat the first three as the industry proper, because they have revenue, staff, premises and a business model to defend; the fourth matters chiefly as competition for attention and as a recruitment funnel into the paid tiers. The largest awarding bodies operate at a scale of the order of 100,000 candidates a year across more than 70 countries, which is what makes this an industry rather than a cottage activity.

## Where I come out

My view, stated before the evidence: the main challenge over the next decade is **demand-side and financial — the collapsing return on investment for the individual self-funding student, compounded by a loss of social legitimacy for alcohol education**. The main opportunity is **the shift of the payer from the student to the employer and the producer, coupled with genuine localisation outside the anglophone core**. The fashionable answers — digital delivery, competition from influencers — are neither.

## Challenges

**1. The student's economics, not the provider's.** Most trade study is self-funded by people in hospitality and retail earning low wages. The post-pandemic flight of staff from hospitality in the UK, the US and Australia removed a large slice of the natural student base and it has not fully returned. Entry-level enrolment is resilient because employers push it; the profitable upper levels depend on individuals betting two or three thousand pounds on a career return, and that bet has got worse. This is the single most serious structural risk and it is rarely discussed because it is invisible in headline candidate numbers.

**2. Regulatory and geopolitical concentration.** Growth over the last decade came from a small number of markets, China above all. The reported suspension of WSET course delivery in mainland China during 2021, following a regulatory review of foreign-linked private education, showed how quickly a market can close for reasons nothing to do with wine. Russia closed in 2022 for different reasons again. India constrains alcohol promotion state by state; the Gulf constrains it absolutely. Market variation has become a governance problem rather than a marketing one, and a provider dependent on two or three geographies is fragile.

**3. Health policy and the legitimacy of teaching alcohol.** The World Health Organization's European action plan treats reducing alcohol consumption as a policy target, and Ireland legislated to require health warnings on alcohol labels. Over ten years this determines whether universities are comfortable hosting wine programmes, whether non-wine employers will fund staff study, and how consumer courses may be advertised. No major curriculum yet teaches alcohol risk honestly, and the first that does will be better protected than those that do not.

**4. Linguistic and cultural parochialism.** The dominant curricula are written in English around a tasting lexicon of gooseberry, blackcurrant and damson — references that are inert for a student in Chengdu, Lagos or Lima. Translation is not localisation, and a translated syllabus taught by a local school is exactly the product a well-funded domestic competitor can beat. This is the most under-priced challenge on my list.

**5. Disintermediation of the classroom.** Remote invigilation, normalised by Covid, decouples the awarding body from the local approved provider. The awarding body gains reach; the local school loses its geographic monopoly and its margin, and it is the local schools that employ most of the industry's people. Expect consolidation and a squeeze on small providers, particularly in mature markets.

**6. Assessment that does not scale.** Blind tasting is the credential's differentiator and its logistical bottleneck: sample sourcing, alcohol importation, invigilation. Every push into a new or restrictive market runs into it.

## Opportunities

**1. Recurring learning rather than one-off qualification.** A certificate is a poor business; maintained, updateable professional learning is a good one. Sustainability accounting, packaging regulation, no- and low-alcohol production and DTC e-commerce all change faster than a syllabus revision cycle, which is precisely why they suit a subscription model.

**2. Subject matter the incumbents do not yet own.** The technical schools — Geisenheim and UC Davis in particular — are strongly placed on climate adaptation and disease-resistant varieties. The commercial gap is larger and more valuable: carbon accounting, sustainability certification literacy and e-commerce data are barely taught outside the wine MBAs.

**3. Real localisation.** Curricula authored in Mandarin, Portuguese, Spanish and Japanese around local flavours, foods and drinking occasions. Japan's sommelier system and Italy's AIS demonstrate that a strong domestic body out-recruits an international one on home ground; Brazil and Mexico are the obvious next tests.

**4. Reframing consumer education as a commercial instrument.** WSET's own study, Consumer Wine Education: should the wine trade care?, argues that educated consumers trade up and buy across a wider repertoire. If that link is evidenced from retailers' own transaction data, consumer education becomes a marketing line funded by producers and retailers instead of a hobby cost paid by enthusiasts. That is the largest single revenue opportunity available to this industry.

**5. Reach into markets that never had a provider** — sub-Saharan Africa, South-East Asia, Latin America — at a marginal cost that finally makes small markets viable.

## Which of these are the main ones

Digital delivery is usually offered as the great opportunity. I disagree: it has already happened, it is now table stakes, and its net effect on the industry's existing businesses is deflationary. Competition from influencers and free content is likewise overstated — they compete for attention, not for fee revenue, and they are the most efficient recruitment funnel the paid tiers have ever had.

Rank instead by what can materially change revenue by 2032. Student ROI decides the size of the market. The payer shift decides who funds it. Localisation decides who captures the growth. Health policy decides the environment all three operate in. Geopolitical concentration is the tail risk that can remove a quarter of the business in a single regulatory decision.

## Conclusion

Over ten years the wine education industry will grow in headcount but change in shape: fewer, larger providers; more employer-funded and less self-funded study; more non-English curricula authored locally rather than translated; and a syllabus that has to teach sustainability and alcohol risk as competently as it teaches Burgundy. The industry's main challenge is that its historic customer — the self-funding hospitality professional — is getting poorer; its main opportunity is that its historic non-customer, the producer and the retailer, has the strongest commercial reason to start paying.

questionText: How is artificial intelligence being used within the wine industry and what might its impact be in the coming decades?
body:
## What I mean by artificial intelligence

I use "artificial intelligence" to mean systems that perform tasks we would normally expect to require human intelligence: learning patterns from data rather than following written rules, interpreting complex or ambiguous inputs, integrating several sources into a decision, and adapting to conditions they were not explicitly programmed for.

That excludes a great deal of technology the industry loosely calls smart. A tank temperature probe is a sensor; a mechanical harvester with a driver is automation; a spreadsheet with a formula is neither. Sensing measures, automation executes, AI decides. Exactly where the line falls is genuinely contested and I do not propose to adjudicate it; the commercially useful test is simply whether the system has taken over a judgement a person used to make.

## In the vineyard

This is where adoption is furthest ahead, because the vineyard generates the data and carries the cost.

**Interpretation of remote sensing.** Multispectral and thermal imagery from satellites and drones is now routinely interpreted by trained models to map vigour and estimate vine water status, driving variable-rate irrigation and selective picking. The value is greatest where water is scarce and metered — California's Central Valley, Mendoza, inland Australia, increasingly the Douro.

**Disease prediction.** Models combining local weather, canopy imagery and historical incidence forecast downy and powdery mildew and botrytis pressure, moving spraying from a calendar to a risk basis. Camera-equipped robots patrolling rows to detect disease and vine mortality are the field version of the same idea.

**Yield estimation.** Machine vision counting inflorescences and bunches replaces manual sampling and extrapolation. For a cooperative or a large brand, an accurate early yield number is worth more than most cellar improvements.

**Autonomous machinery.** Naio Technologies' autonomous weeding machines working in French vineyards, and driver-optional electric tractors of the type Monarch has trialled with California growers, are already commercial. Robotic pruning remains the hard problem, because pruning requires reading an individual vine's architecture and making a judgement — an AI task rather than an automation one — and it is also the largest remaining skilled labour cost in the vineyard.

## In the winery

**Fermentation management.** Systems that read density, temperature and nitrogen streams and predict stuck fermentations or volatile acidity risk are moving from reporting to deciding — setting pumpover frequency and cooling regimes within limits the winemaker sets.

**Sorting.** Optical sorters classifying berries and MOG by image are the most mature machine-vision application in wine and are now unremarkable in large wineries.

**Analysis.** Chemometric models interpret spectra to predict phenolic ripeness or flag taint. Smoke-taint prediction has become the pressing case in Australia and the US West Coast, where the commercial question — pick, declassify or abandon — has to be answered within days.

**Blending.** Optimising many lots against a target specification and a cost ceiling is a combinatorial problem at which machines genuinely outperform people, and it is the first place the judgement itself, not the information, gets handed over.

## Through logistics and the market

Demand forecasting, dynamic pricing, allocation and route optimisation are standard in any consumer-goods business and are arriving in wine through the large retailers first. Container monitoring with anomaly detection catches temperature excursions in transit. In the fine-wine market, price modelling and image-based authentication of labels, capsules and glass offer a real answer to counterfeiting, which manual expertise has never scaled to.

On the consumer side the application is already dominant. Vivino, whose label-recognition app has assembled probably the largest consumer wine dataset in existence, recommends by inferred taste rather than by score. Virtual sommeliers and chatbots handle first-line advice for retailers. Firms such as Tastry in California model a wine's measured chemistry against consumer preference panels and sell the output to producers and buyers — which means AI is already influencing what gets blended and what gets listed.

## Impacts

**Financial.** AI needs data density and capital, so it is scale-biased. A 500-hectare operation amortises an autonomous machine; a four-hectare Mosel grower cannot. The likely consequence is further consolidation, mitigated — importantly — by contractors and cooperatives becoming the delivery mechanism for small growers, as they already are for harvesting. The second financial issue is ownership: the agronomic data generated on a grower's land is captured by the platform or equipment vendor, and whoever holds the multi-year dataset holds the pricing power. Broadacre agriculture is fighting that battle now and wine will inherit it.

**Social and labour.** Labour is the honest motivation behind most vineyard robotics. Border closures in 2020 and 2021 left the UK, New Zealand and Australia short of pickers and cellar hands; rural populations across southern Europe are ageing; California competes for the same workers as construction. Unlike earlier mechanisation, AI-driven machines can in principle work where a machine harvester cannot — selective picking, steep sites, bush vines — so this is substitution, not merely assistance. The cost is that vineyard employment is the economic base of many rural communities, and the regions whose reputation rests on landscape and human craft are precisely those that lose most if the people leave. There is an unresolved tension between what the industry sells and what it is automating.

**Ethical.** Three concern me. Homogenisation: if many producers optimise blends against similar preference models trained on similar panels, stylistic diversity narrows, and this risk arrives with commercial success rather than with failure. Disclosure: there is no convention requiring a producer marketing a wine as handcrafted to say that its blend was machine-selected. Discovery bias: recommendation engines reward what already sells, which disadvantages the small and unknown producers the digital channel is assumed to help.

**Environmental.** This is the least-discussed motivation and possibly the strongest. Precision irrigation cuts water use where water is the binding constraint on viticulture's future. Risk-based spraying reduces passes, and fewer passes mean less diesel, less compaction, less copper and less synthetic fungicide. Electric driver-optional machines take diesel out of the row. Supply-chain optimisation reduces empty running and refrigeration load. Suitability modelling supports variety and site decisions decades ahead, and early frost and heat warnings allow action rather than post-mortem. Against this, training and running models consumes energy and the machines themselves have an embodied footprint — but in water and agrochemical terms the net effect is clearly positive.

## The coming decades

Within this decade, sensing and decision support become normal on large estates, and fermentation modelling and optical sorting standard in large wineries. Next, autonomous machinery reaches economic parity through contractors; robotic pruning is the milestone to watch, because it is the point at which the vineyard's skilled labour bill collapses. Later, preference modelling begins to influence what is planted, not only what is blended.

There are limits worth stating. Appellation law constrains adoption directly — irrigation is restricted or banned in much of Europe, so the flagship application is unavailable there. Fine wine's value rests on human authorship and scarcity, which no producer will willingly dilute. And steep-slope viticulture will stay manual longer than the technologists predict.

## Conclusion

AI's greatest impact will be felt in the vineyard and in demand-side matching, not in the cellar, and its most valuable contribution will be environmental. But it is a consolidating technology: it rewards scale, capital and whoever owns the data. The industry's task over the coming decades is not to adopt it, which will happen regardless, but to decide who owns the vineyard's data, what happens to the rural employment it displaces, and how much stylistic diversity it is willing to trade for predicted consumer approval.

questionText: Are biodynamic practices the key to more sustainable wine production?
body:
## Definitions

**Sustainable**, for this answer, means the capacity of a wine business — and of the industry it belongs to — to continue operating indefinitely on three axes. *Environmental*: soil, water, biodiversity, agrochemical load and greenhouse-gas emissions. *Economic*: profitability, access to capital, succession, the ability to reinvest. *Social*: fair pay and conditions, safe work, and the survival of the rural communities that supply labour. The boundary runs from the nursery to the consumer's recycling bin, not from the vineyard gate to the bottling line. An estate that farms beautifully and loses money every year is not sustainable; nor is one whose environmental footprint is dominated by a package it never examines.

**Key** can mean the most crucial factor, or the one that unlocks the others. I test both.

**Biodynamic practices** are, in outline: certified-organic farming as a base; composting and the field and compost preparations, principally horn manure and horn silica; a whole-farm approach treating the estate as a single organism, with land set aside for biodiversity; and timing of operations by a lunar and planetary calendar. Certification is by Demeter or Biodyvin.

**My answer is no** — biodynamics is not the key on either reading. It is a strong contributor on one axis, silent on most of the others, and its best practices are separable from the belief system that carries them.

## What biodynamics actually delivers

The environmental case is real and I do not want to understate it. Eliminating herbicides, synthetic fertilisers and synthetic pesticides is the largest single vineyard-level gain available, and biodynamic estates achieve it by construction. Composting and permanent cover crops raise soil organic matter, which improves water-holding capacity, resists erosion and sequesters carbon. Demeter certification requires whole-estate conversion, a three-year transition and the setting aside of a share of the farm for biodiversity, so habitat returns at farm scale rather than in token corners.

There is a second, less tangible effect that I think matters more than the preparations. Biodynamics compels attention: a grower making compost, walking rows on a calendar and observing individual vines makes better decisions than one following a spray diary. Château Pontet-Canet has farmed biodynamically in Pauillac since the mid-2000s, gaining formal organic and biodynamic certification in 2010, and the quality trajectory is not disputed -- but the honest reading is that meticulous, well-capitalised farming explains it at least as well as the horn silica.

That distinction is where the evidence sits. Controlled comparisons have generally struggled to isolate any effect attributable to the preparations as distinct from the organic farming underneath them. For an evidence-based answer this has to be said plainly: the anthroposophical apparatus is unproven. It does not make the farming worse, and if the calendar is what gets a grower into the vineyard at dawn, it has an instrumental value. But it cannot be the basis of an industry-wide claim.

## Where biodynamics is neutral or negative

**Copper.** Organic and biodynamic growers depend on copper against downy mildew. EU rules have progressively restricted copper to an average of around 4 kg per hectare per year precisely because it accumulates permanently in soil and is toxic to earthworms and soil microbiota. This is the strongest evidence-based critique of organic and biodynamic viticulture and it goes to the heart of the soil-health claim.

**Fuel and compaction.** Under-vine mechanical weeding and rain-washed contact sprays mean more tractor passes than a conventional programme, particularly in wet vintages: more diesel, more emissions, more soil compaction.

**Yield arithmetic.** The unit that matters commercially and environmentally is the bottle, not the hectare. Lower yields spread the same fixed footprint over fewer bottles, so a biodynamic estate can carry a higher carbon intensity per bottle than a conventional neighbour despite using fewer inputs. This is uncomfortable and it is arithmetic.

**Cost, labour and price point.** Biodynamics is labour-intensive and expensive, and it therefore concentrates where the price point absorbs it. That is a financial and a social objection at once: a model available only above a certain bottle price cannot be the industry's answer, and the industry's volume — and most of its employment — sits below it.

Scale is not an absolute barrier: Emiliana in Chile farms its roughly 1,000-hectare estate organically, with a substantial biodynamic-certified component, showing the model can operate well beyond boutique scale. But it does so in dry summers with low disease pressure. The same programme in the Loire, Alsace or England in a wet year is a different proposition entirely, and any claim that biodynamics is the key must survive the wet vintage, not the easy one.

## The comparison the question demands

**Conventional** farming has genuine sustainability advantages that are usually skipped. Systemic fungicides give effective control with fewer passes, so less fuel; they prevent the crop losses that make a bad year financially unsustainable; higher yields dilute fixed footprint per bottle; and herbicide use, whatever its effect on soil biology, avoids tillage — which on a slope protects soil carbon and prevents erosion. That is a real trade-off, not a debating point.

**Organic** delivers most of biodynamics' environmental gains, at lower cost, against a legally defined and internationally recognised standard. On a cost-adjusted basis it is the better-value certification for most producers.

**Other approaches entirely** may matter more than any of them. Integrated pest management with weather-driven spray decisions, pheromone confusion for moth control and precision application cuts agrochemical load without ideological commitment. Disease-resistant varieties are the single largest available lever, removing most fungicide passes rather than substituting one product for another, and their progressive authorisation in German and Swiss quality categories is the development to watch. Biodynamics has no equivalent.

## What sustainability requires that biodynamics never touches

This is the decisive part of my argument. Glass is typically the single largest component of a bottled wine's carbon footprint, so lightweighting, bulk shipment and alternative formats outweigh almost any vineyard decision — and packaging sits entirely outside biodynamics' compass. So do winery energy and refrigeration, and renewable generation. So does water: wineries typically consume of the order of three to six litres of water for every litre of wine (with efficient operations closer to three and the industry average nearer six), and wastewater treatment is a serious cost and a serious pollution risk. So do waste streams — pomace, lees, cardboard. So does logistics: modal shift and filling in market. So do the social questions — seasonal worker pay and housing, safety, equity, succession. And so does profitability, without which none of it continues.

Whole-business schemes address exactly these gaps. Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand, which covers the overwhelming majority of that country's vineyard area, together with Certified California Sustainable Winegrowing, South Africa's IPW and Sustainable Winegrowing Australia, are weaker than biodynamics inside the vineyard and far stronger everywhere else. They are also auditable at national scale, which biodynamics is not.

## Conclusion

On the first reading of "key" — the most crucial factor — the answer is clearly no. Packaging, energy, logistics and profitability dominate a wine business's sustainability, and biodynamics is silent on all four.

On the second reading — the thing that unlocks the rest — it is more arguable, because biodynamic converts often go on to tackle energy and packaging. But that reflects the kind of producer who converts, not a property of the practices themselves.

The defensible position is selective adoption. Composting, permanent cover crops, no herbicide, real biodiversity and the discipline of daily observation are the biodynamic practices that survive scrutiny, and they can be taken up inside a certified whole-business sustainability programme by any producer at any price point. Full Demeter certification is a legitimate choice for estates whose climate and pricing support it, and a poor prescription for the industry as a whole.

questionText: Does anyone still need wine writers?
body:
## Definitions

By **wine writer** I mean anyone whose work about wine is, at root, written words intended for publication: critics who assign scores, journalists writing news and features, technical and trade writers, authors of reference works and textbooks, public-relations and press-release writers, retail and e-commerce copywriters and the authors of back labels, newsletter and blog writers, and the scripted text behind most video and social content. I include press releases and commercial copy deliberately. Excluding them would exclude the great majority of words about wine that a consumer actually reads, and would make the question unanswerable in any honest way.

By **need** I mean a dependency rather than a preference: what would break if these people stopped writing. That has to be assessed population by population, and the useful segmentation is not demographic but by engagement and expertise — producers, trade intermediaries, engaged consumers, casual consumers, educators, and the industry's own governance.

## Where the need came from

Wine writing began as a commercial instrument. The merchant's list was the first wine writing, and its descendants — the retailer's website, the importer's tech sheet — still are. Cyrus Redding and later André Simon turned it into a subject with a literature. The decisive shift was Hugh Johnson's World Atlas of Wine, first published in 1971, which created a mass consumer readership and established that wine could be learned rather than merely bought, and Jancis Robinson's Oxford Companion to Wine, first published in 1994, which gave the trade a shared reference layer it still runs on.

Robert Parker's Wine Advocate, founded in 1978, and its hundred-point scale did something different again: it converted judgement into a number that could travel, be quoted in an advertisement and be lent against. That moved purchasing authority from the merchant, who had held it for two centuries, to the independent critic, and made en primeur a market in scores.

None of this is anglophone-specific, and it is a mistake to treat it that way. La Revue du vin de France, Gambero Rosso's Vini d'Italia, Guía Peñín in Spain and Falstaff in Austria and Germany all built domestic markets on the same mechanism. The most striking demonstration of a writer's market power anywhere is not a critic at all: the manga Kami no Shizuku, serialised from 2004, moved demand for named wines across Japan, Korea and Taiwan on a scale no Western publication has matched. Writers made markets, in several languages, and that is the baseline against which "still" has to be measured.

## What the last fifteen years changed

Three things, and they are separable.

The **economic base** collapsed. Print advertising fell away, wine columns were cut, and freelance rates have barely moved in twenty years. The writer's employer is disappearing, which is not at all the same thing as the reader disappearing, and the two are constantly confused.

**Crowd data** replaced two of the critic's functions outright. Vivino supplies a popularity signal from millions of users and Wine-Searcher supplies the price check. Both do those jobs better than any individual ever could. What crowd data cannot supply is a considered judgement of quality, which is a different thing from an average of preferences.

**Social and online channels** moved discovery to visual, personality-led content distributed by algorithm — Instagram and TikTok in the West, WeChat and Xiaohongshu in China. Reach is now decoupled from institutional authority, which is the genuine opportunity as well as the genuine threat: a writer no longer needs a masthead, but neither does anyone else. The counterpart is that independence has become the scarce asset, because a great deal of platform content is paid and undisclosed. The clearest opportunity created by the same shift is direct payment: the subscription models at JancisRobinson.com, Vinous and the Wine Advocate show that willingness to pay survived the collapse of advertising, and simply changed hands.

## Who still needs them, and for what

**The trade — the strongest dependency, and it has grown.** A buyer listing several hundred wines cannot taste them all; a monopoly tender or a multiple's range review is decided partly on documented independent assessment. The trade's need is twofold: informational — what is this, is it sound, what should it cost — and narrative, because a salesperson needs something to say. The much-derided press release is where most of that narrative originates, which is precisely why it belongs inside the definition.

**New and rebuilding regions.** Ningxia, Georgia, Uruguay, Greece, England, the Portuguese interior. A distant buyer will not find these through an algorithm optimised for what already sells, and these regions have no advertising budget. Writers remain the mechanism by which reputation crosses a border, and for them this is a dependency, not a convenience.

**The engaged consumer.** A minority, but the one that trades up and buys widely. The need is orientation and a filter against a repertoire no individual can navigate, and it is increasingly paid for directly.

**Educators and students.** The reference layer — companions, ampelographies, regional monographs, textbooks — is written by wine writers and is the substrate for every qualification, every sommelier list and, increasingly, every machine-learning wine tool. It is the least visible dependency and the hardest to reconstruct if it lapses.

**The industry's own accountability.** The Rudy Kurniawan counterfeiting case, the recurring counterfeit-Bordeaux prosecutions, labour conditions in several producing countries, and the 2020 New York Times investigation into harassment in the Court of Master Sommeliers: none of that came from creators whose model depends on access and goodwill. An industry trading on trust needs reporters, not only reviewers.

## Who does not

The majority of consumers, who buy on price, brand, occasion and shelf position, and who never read wine writing in the first place — the honest historical point is that the mass market never needed writers, it needed retailers. Large branded producers, for whom a review changes nothing at a supermarket price point. Fine-wine buyers who once needed a single number, now that scores have multiplied and the currency has inflated. And younger consumers in most markets, whose discovery is visual and social first; they may still need the underlying work, but not in that form and not from that byline.

## What happens next

The payer changes: from advertisers to subscribers and to institutional and trade clients, producing fewer, better-paid specialists and a hollowed-out middle. The surviving functions are those that cannot be crowdsourced or automated — access, verification, reporting, judgement and accountability — while the descriptive tasting note, the commodity layer, passes to crowds and to machines, and I do not think its loss should be mourned. And the growth is not in English: the expansion of wine writing over the next two decades will be in Mandarin, Portuguese, Spanish and Japanese, authored locally rather than translated.

## Conclusion

Yes — but fewer of them, for a narrower set of purposes, paid by different people. The trade needs wine writers more than ever and will increasingly pay them directly; new regions and engaged consumers need them for discovery and orientation; educators depend on them silently and completely. The casual consumer does not need them and never did.

The nuance that matters is which kind is at risk. The reviewer is being replaced from three directions at once and will survive only in specialist, subscription form. The reporter — the person who checks, verifies and publishes what the industry would rather not read — has the weakest business model and is the one the wine world can least afford to lose.

questionText: Extreme heat and drought threaten many wine regions. What steps can a vineyard manager take to mitigate their effects?
body:
## Defining the two threats

Heat and drought co-occur but act through different mechanisms and demand different responses; conflating them is the first error. By **heat** I mean canopy and berry temperature above the vine's physiological optimum. Photosynthesis is most efficient at moderate leaf temperatures and falls away above roughly 30-35C, and in the same range anthocyanin synthesis is inhibited while malic acid respiration accelerates. I separate chronic warming — a rise in seasonal means — from acute heat spikes of two or three days, because the first is a site and plant-material problem and the second is a tactical, in-season one. By **drought** I mean soil water supply below the vine's evapotranspirative demand over a sustained period: a water-balance concept, not a rainfall total, since the same rainfall is ample on deep clay and a severe deficit on shallow sand over granite.

The mitigations only make sense against the physiology. Water deficit closes stomata, which halts carbon assimilation, so sugar accumulation stalls at the moment malic acid is being respired and pH and potassium climb. Berries shrivel; exposed skins burn. Thiols and terpenes degrade, rotundone does not accumulate, and green seed tannin is locked in behind high sugar. Severe stress defoliates the vine, empties reserves and reduces bud fruitfulness for the next season, so the damage is to two crops.

## Establishment decisions, which do most of the work

The cheapest effective mitigation is made before planting. Site: higher altitude, cooler aspects, proximity to water bodies, and soils with real water-holding capacity. Plant material: late-ripening, drought-adapted varieties with thick skins and good acid retention — Grenache, Carignan, Mourvèdre, Touriga Nacional, Assyrtiko, Agiorgitiko, Xinomavro — and later-ripening clones. Rootstock is the single most underused lever: 110R, 140Ru and 1103P confer drought tolerance and deeper rooting where Riparia Gloire and 101-14 do not, and Ramsey adds salinity tolerance under irrigation. Training system: bush vines and higher trunks with a sprawling canopy shade their own fruit, which is why goblet persists across La Mancha, Sicily and the southern Rhône. Row orientation matters more as climate warms: north-south rows expose the western face to the hottest afternoon hours, so a modest rotation, or east-west rows, moves exposure to the cooler morning.

## Canopy and soil in the season

Retain leaves on the afternoon side; do late-season leaf removal only on the morning face, and never strip unacclimated fruit into a forecast heat spike, which is the classic cause of sunburn. Delay winter pruning, or double-prune, to push flowering and ripening into cooler autumn conditions — established in Spain and Australia. Raise soil organic matter with compost and under-vine mulch to increase water-holding and lower soil temperature; use straw or bark mulch where cover crops would compete. Cover crops must be managed both ways: valuable for soil structure and trafficability, but mown, terminated or restricted to alternate rows in a dry season. Kaolin and other particle films reduce berry temperature and sunburn cheaply. Shade cloth and overhead netting work but are capital-intensive.

## Water: availability, cost and law

Where irrigation exists, the gains come from scheduling, not volume: soil moisture probes and a water budget, regulated deficit irrigation to hold a mild stress from set to veraison, then relief before the vine shuts down. Overhead sprinklers give evaporative cooling during a spike where water allocation permits. But three constraints are real. Water may not exist — Chile's Maipo and South Africa's Western Cape have had allocations cut in drought. It may be legally restricted: irrigation remains restricted or banned in appellations such as Champagne and much of Bordeaux without derogation. And it is priced — Australian Murray-Darling water is traded, so in a dry year irrigating a low-value block can cost more than the crop.

## Cost realism across the wine business

Advice that suits a premium estate is often absurd for the bulk sector, which is where most of the world's vineyard area sits. A block in inland irrigated Australia or California's Central Valley returning a few hundred dollars a tonne cannot amortise shade cloth, drip retrofits or hand canopy work that a Napa or Barossa block returning thousands can. For those growers the viable mitigations are the near-free ones: rootstock and variety at replanting, mulch, irrigation scheduling, machine and night harvesting, and accepting an earlier pick. Conversely, for premium fruit the binding constraint is quality, not cost, so shading and cooling justify themselves.

## Conclusion

The effective steps are overwhelmingly structural — site, rootstock, variety, training and soil organic matter — and they must be taken years ahead. In-season measures are palliative: they buy a few degrees and a few days. A vineyard manager should therefore treat each replant as the main mitigation decision, and select in-season tools against the value of the fruit and the legal water regime, not against best practice in a fine wine region.
