questionText: To what extent is excessive precipitation during the growing season a threat in the vineyard? How can it be managed?
body:
## Scope: an event, not a climate

Excessive precipitation is rainfall that exceeds what the soil can drain and the vine can use, judged against the phenological stage it falls in. Defined that way it is not a property of wet regions at all. Mendoza can lose a crop to summer hail and downpour; Marlborough's threat is a tropical depression in March; the Douro's is a wet flowering. A dry region that takes a quarter of its annual rainfall in the week of flowering has an excess; a wet region taking the same total spread through winter does not. My position is that the threat is severe but sharply asymmetric: the damage is determined almost entirely by timing and by soil drainage, not by seasonal total, and the manageable share is smaller than growers assume because the two decisive levers — drainage and canopy architecture — are set years before the rain falls.

## Structure and soil

Heavy rain on slopes moves soil. Erosion is the permanent form of the damage: Douro terraces, Mosel and Priorat slopes and the Northern Rhône's granite lose topsoil and, in extreme events, whole walls and rows. On flat sites the equivalent is waterlogging. Saturated soil is anaerobic, root respiration stops, fine roots die, and the vine shows water stress symptoms in a wet season — a diagnosis growers routinely get wrong. Compaction is the insidious one: tractor passes on wet soil destroy structure, reduce infiltration, and make the next wet season worse.

Almost all of this is answered before planting rather than during the season. Subsurface tile drainage, deep ripping and planting on raised mounds are standard in Oregon and across New Zealand for exactly this reason. On slopes, contour planting, terracing, grassed alleys and permanent cover hold the soil in place. Rootstock choice matters too: Riparia Gloire and SO4 tolerate a moist profile far better than the drought-adapted 110R or 140Ru, which are the wrong choice on a site that floods.

## Leaching

Free-draining soils under heavy rain lose mobile nutrients. Nitrate is the most mobile and the first to go, which is why a wet spring on Marlborough's stony Wairau soils or Médoc gravel produces low yeast assimilable nitrogen and sluggish fermentations months later. Sulphur, boron, magnesium and potassium follow on sandy soils, and sustained leaching of calcium and magnesium acidifies the soil over years, reducing availability of other nutrients. Management is straightforward once anticipated: split nitrogen into smaller applications timed to demand, use cover crops to capture nitrate over winter, build organic matter to raise exchange capacity, lime to correct drift in pH, and use foliar applications when the root zone is not delivering.

## Operations — the compounding failure

The gravest risk is not the rain but the fact that it arrives exactly when work is needed. Disease pressure peaks and the sprayer cannot enter the block; spray intervals stretch past protection and a preventive programme becomes a curative one. Mowing, shoot positioning and leaf removal are delayed while vigour is at its highest. Hand harvesting stops, machines rut the rows, and fruit sits. Any management plan must therefore be built around access: grassed alleys or permanent sward for trafficability, narrow or over-row tractors, and, in wet regions, aerial or high-clearance spraying capacity.

## Timing decides the severity

**Dormancy to budburst.** Largely benign and often beneficial — it recharges the profile. Risks are erosion, waterlogging and pruning access.

**Budburst to flowering.** The most damaging window. Free water on green tissue is required for downy mildew primary infection, and repeated wetting drives secondary cycles; black rot and phomopsis follow. Rain and cool weather at flowering cause poor fruit set, coulure and millerandage, and that yield loss is irreversible. Management: preventive spray timing keyed to a disease model rather than the calendar, systemic and translaminar products with resistance rotation, open canopies, shoot thinning early.

**Set to veraison.** Abundant water drives vigour: long shoots, laterals, a dense shaded canopy. The consequences are shaded fruit with high pyrazine and low anthocyanin, poor bud fruitfulness for next year, a humid microclimate favouring botrytis, and delayed ripening. Management: shoot thinning, leaf removal in the fruit zone, trimming, devigorating cover crops sown mid-row to compete for water and nitrogen, and, at replanting, devigorating rootstocks.

**Veraison to harvest.** Dilution of sugar, acid and flavour; berry splitting when a dry spell is broken by heavy rain; botrytis and sour rot with vinegar fly. Management: fruit-zone leaf removal and loose-clustered clones before the fact, botryticide timing at bunch closure, sorting at picking, and the willingness to pick early and accept lower ripeness rather than lose the crop.

## Conclusion

Excessive precipitation is a first-order threat in any climate, but its severity is set by two weeks of the season rather than by the season. It is manageable only in part. Drainage, site, rootstock, spacing, trellis and clone determine most of the outcome and are fixed at planting; within the season the grower has spray timing, canopy work and harvest decisions, and each of those depends on being able to get into the vineyard — which is precisely what the rain removes.

questionText: A viticulturist has observed a decline in vineyard yield over the last five years. Discuss the possible causes and how the issue might be addressed.
body:
## Scope: a trend, not a run of bad vintages

Five consecutive years of decline is a different object from five poor harvests. Frost, hail, a heat spike at flowering or a wet set explain a small vintage; they do not explain a trend, and if the grower's records show a step down after one event with no recovery, that is a chronic consequence of an acute event, not a recurring one. So I look only for causes that are cumulative, progressive or self-reinforcing.

The diagnostic frame that makes this tractable is the yield equation: **vines per hectare, multiplied by bunches per vine (a function of bud fruitfulness and node number retained), multiplied by berries per bunch (fruit set), multiplied by berry weight.** Any real decline shows up in one or two of those terms, and each term points at a different family of causes. The first thing I would ask the viticulturist for is not an agronomy report but five years of that arithmetic, block by block. The second is the same figures for neighbouring growers and the regional average, because a decline shared across the district is a climate or seasonal trend and a decline confined to one estate is a management or biological one — and the two lead to entirely different responses.

## Falling vine numbers — usually the largest and least noticed term

Yield per hectare falls quietly when vines die and are not replaced, or are replaced with young vines that carry little. The dominant cause worldwide is the grapevine trunk disease complex — esca, Eutypa and Botryosphaeria dieback — which kills vines slowly and cumulatively, and whose incidence has risen since effective chemical control was withdrawn. Nursery-borne Petri disease loads young plantings from the start. Alongside it sit phylloxera on own-rooted vines, crown gall after winter freeze events in continental regions, and vertebrate or machinery damage. Layered on top, replant blocks in an old vineyard suffer replant disease from nematodes and depleted soil, so the gaps stay unproductive.

## Falling fruitfulness — the multi-year feedback loops

Bud fruitfulness is set in the season before harvest, which is why its causes compound. Viruses are the classic case: leafroll spread by mealybug moves vine to vine, so incidence rises annually and yield falls annually with it; fanleaf, vectored by dagger nematode, does the same in patches. Progressive shading of the renewal zone as vigour or canopy density creeps up suppresses primordia initiation. Repeated water or heat stress during the previous summer, when the primordia are differentiating, depresses fruitfulness the following spring, which is the real mechanism by which a warming, drying trend shows as declining yield. Pruning drift matters too and is embarrassingly common: spur positions walking away from the cordon year on year, or a slow reduction in retained node number as the pruner reacts to weak vines, mechanically reduces the crop.

## Set and berry weight — nutrition, soil and water

Poor set and small berries point at nutrition, soil condition and water. Nitrogen depletion under a permanent grass sward that was installed for devigoration and never adjusted; boron and zinc deficiency directly reducing set; potassium and magnesium decline. Soil health: falling organic matter, compaction from repeated passes, acidification, and under irrigation the slow accumulation of salinity and sodicity where the leaching fraction is inadequate — a genuine multi-year decline mechanism in irrigated Australia, inland California and parts of Argentina. Water supply: reduced allocation, a falling aquifer, or the mundane and very common failure of blocked or unevenly performing drip emitters. Cover crop competition, rootstock too devigorating for the site, and simply old vines, which yield less as trunk vasculature declines, complete the list.

## Addressing it

Diagnosis first, and in a sequence set by cost. Map missing and weak vines by counting or by imagery; that immediately separates a stand problem from a per-vine problem. Then petiole and soil analysis, an irrigation distribution-uniformity test, virus testing of the weak patches, and a check of pruning records and retained node counts against the block's history. Only then intervene.

Remedies follow the cause: remedial trunk surgery and sanitation pruning — pruning later, making small wounds, sealing or protecting them — plus systematic replanting and field grafting to restore stand density; mealybug control, roguing and replanting with certified virus-tested material where leafroll is spreading; organic matter, deep ripping and controlled traffic for compaction; recalibrated fertiliser split to demand, lime for pH, a leaching irrigation to move salt; repaired and re-uniform irrigation; adjusted node numbers and canopy work to restore light on the renewal zone. Finally, confirm the decline is not intentional — a change in pruning policy, an appellation yield cut, or a deliberate move to a higher-priced specification.

## Conclusion

A five-year decline is almost never one cause. Typically it is an uncounted loss of living vines plus a progressive biological agent plus a slow drift in soil or pruning, each individually small. The insight the situation demands is that the remedies are largely mutually exclusive uses of the same capital, so identifying which term of the yield equation is falling matters more than knowing the remedies themselves.

questionText: What are the causes and effects of nitrogen deficiency in a vineyard? How can it be remedied?
body:
## What is actually in short supply

Nitrogen deficiency is a shortfall of *plant-available* nitrogen — nitrate and ammonium in the root zone, taken up when the vine needs it — not a shortage of total soil nitrogen. The great majority of soil nitrogen is locked in organic matter and becomes available only as microbes mineralise it. That distinction drives everything below: most deficiency is a failure of release, placement or uptake rather than of stock.

## Causes

**Low organic matter.** Since mineralisation is the main supply, soils with little organic matter are structurally deficient: sandy, long-cultivated or eroded soils, and hot climates where organic matter oxidises rapidly. Australia's Riverland and California's Central Valley illustrate the type; so do the eroded slate soils of the Mosel, where topsoil has to be carried back up the slope.

**Mineralisation conditions.** Microbial release requires warmth, moisture and aeration together. A cold, wet spring in Champagne or the Rheingau suppresses mineralisation exactly when the vine's demand peaks at flowering, producing a transient deficiency on soils that test well. The mirror case is a Mediterranean summer: dry soil stops both mineralisation and mass-flow transport, so a Priorat or Douro block can be nitrogen-starved in the presence of adequate reserves. That is a water problem presenting as a nutrition problem, and treating it with fertiliser wastes money.

**Soil pH.** Strongly acidic soils suppress nitrifying bacteria and slow mineralisation, and are common under long-term ammonium fertiliser use and high-rainfall leaching. Highly calcareous, alkaline soils promote volatilisation of surface-applied ammonium and interact with induced deficiencies of other elements.

**Leaching.** Nitrate is anionic, mobile and poorly retained; free-draining soils under heavy rain or excessive irrigation lose it below the root zone. Marlborough's stony Wairau soils and the Médoc's gravels are the standard cases, as is any drip block over-irrigated on sand.

**Competition and immobilisation.** Permanent grass sward is a strong competitor for nitrogen — which is precisely why it is planted in Bordeaux and Coonawarra to devigorate — and where it was installed years earlier and never reassessed, deliberate devigoration slides into deficiency. Weeds, adjacent trees, and high carbon-to-nitrogen mulches such as straw or woodchip immobilise nitrogen as they decompose.

**Vine factors.** Rootstock alters uptake capacity: low-vigour Riparia Gloire, 101-14 and 420A extract less than 1103P, 140Ru or Ramsey on the same soil. High crop load partitions nitrogen to fruit at the expense of reserves, so an over-cropped vine becomes deficient the following season. Varieties with high demand, notably Sauvignon Blanc, show it soonest.

## Effects

**Vine growth.** Reduced shoot growth, short internodes, thin canes, and small pale leaves — chlorosis appearing on older leaves first, since nitrogen is mobile and remobilised to the growing tips — with early leaf fall. Leaf area falls, so photosynthetic capacity falls, and the vine cannot fill both the crop and its reserves. Low reserves in the permanent wood mean weak budburst and reduced fruitfulness next spring, so the deficiency compounds.

**Quantity.** Poorer set, fewer and smaller bunches, smaller berries, and over successive seasons a declining yield trend.

**Quality — and it is not simply negative.** Mild deficiency is a quality tool: less vigour, an open canopy, better light in the fruit zone, smaller berries with a higher skin-to-pulp ratio, better colour and phenolic ripeness, lower pyrazine and lower botrytis risk. Severe deficiency reverses all of it. Limited leaf area delays and truncates ripening, so sugar stalls, seed tannin stays green, herbaceous character persists in reds, and aroma precursors — thiol precursors in Sauvignon Blanc above all — are reduced.

**Through to fermentation.** Low vineyard nitrogen produces low yeast assimilable nitrogen in the juice. Below a commonly cited threshold, a yeast assimilable nitrogen figure of the order of 140 mg per litre, fermentations turn sluggish or stick; stressed yeast produce hydrogen sulphide and mercaptans, volatile acidity rises, and desirable ester formation falls. The vineyard decision therefore reaches the finished wine.

## Remedies

Diagnose before acting: petiole or blade analysis at flowering and veraison, soil analysis including pH and organic matter, and juice YAN at harvest, read together to separate true deficiency from an uptake failure caused by dry soil.

Then correct the specific cause. Build the stock with compost and manure and reduce cultivation. Change the competition: legume cover crops — vetch, clover, faba bean — mown and dropped or incorporated, or a cleared under-vine strip. Correct pH by liming so that mineralisation can proceed. Time fertiliser to demand in split applications post-flowering and post-harvest rather than one large pre-budburst dose, and fertigate to place nitrogen in the wetted zone on sandy soils where leaching is the cause. Where dry soil is blocking uptake, irrigate. Foliar urea before harvest is the targeted tool for lifting juice YAN without adding vigour. At replanting, choose a more extractive rootstock; in the meantime, moderate crop load. Winery addition of DAP is a legitimate backstop but corrects the symptom only, and is constrained under organic rules.

## Conclusion

Nitrogen deficiency is rarely an absence of nitrogen. It is a failure of mineralisation, of retention, or of uptake, and each has a different and non-interchangeable remedy. The grower's task is to establish which, because the wrong correction is both expensive and ineffective.

questionText: Evaluate the potential risks and rewards of choosing to plant ungrafted vines.
body:
## The decision being evaluated

The question is a planting decision taken now: whether to establish a new block on its own roots rather than on American or hybrid rootstock. That framing excludes the romance of surviving pre-phylloxera vineyards, which tell us that ungrafted vines *can* live, not that planting them today is sound. I evaluate the decision on five axes — pest exposure, everything else a rootstock does, propagation, commercial exposure, and law and marketing — and my position is that it is defensible only in a narrow set of conditions, because the rewards are modest and reversible while the principal risk is catastrophic and permanent.

## Rewards

**Lower and simpler establishment.** Own-rooted planting material is cheaper than a bench graft and can be produced on site from cuttings of proven vines. There is no graft union, so no incompatibility between scion and stock, no union failure years later, and one fewer entry point for trunk pathogens and, in cold regions, crown gall.

**Propagation and stand maintenance.** Layering lets a grower fill a gap with a cane from a neighbouring vine, restoring stand density without planting a young vine into a mature block or field-grafting. Over decades this holds vine age and uniformity in a way grafted blocks cannot, and it allows a self-perpetuating massal selection independent of nursery supply — no small advantage given documented trunk-disease contamination and virus status problems in commercial nursery stock.

**Recovery after winter kill.** In continental regions where trunks are periodically killed by extreme cold, an own-rooted vine can be re-established from a sucker and comes back true to variety, whereas a grafted vine that dies below the union regrows as rootstock and must be replanted or field-grafted. Against that, vinifera roots are themselves less cold-hardy than the American species used for stocks, so the advantage only holds where the soil does not freeze deeply.

**Site match without an imposed intermediary.** The rootstock dictates vigour, phenology and rooting depth. On a low-vigour granitic sand or a poor volcanic soil, a rootstock chosen from a short commercial list may devigorate a vine that is already balanced, or push vigour where none is wanted. Own roots remove that mismatch.

**Marketing.** Franc de pied, pie franco and *ungrafted* carry a genuine premium in a market that rewards scarcity and narrative — Chile, Santorini, Colares, sand blocks in South Australia and Washington. This is a real and monetisable reward, and I would rate it above the quality argument.

## Risks

**Phylloxera, which is the asset-destroying one.** The root-feeding form attacks vinifera roots directly, and there is no cure once established. Sand-dominant soils genuinely suppress it, which is why the exceptions are sandy or volcanic, but "phylloxera-free region" is a status, not a property: the insect travels on machinery, boots, water and planting material, and the collapse of AXR-1 plantings in California from the 1980s is the standing lesson in relying on a resistance assumption. A block lost at year twelve is a loss of the establishment capital, the intervening cash flow, and three further years of fallow and replanting.

**Nematodes, and the mistake of thinking only about phylloxera.** Root-knot and citrus nematodes reduce vigour and yield, and dagger nematode transmits fanleaf virus. Nematode-resistant rootstocks — Ramsey, Freedom, Harmony and the newer Californian selections — exist precisely because vinifera roots have no resistance. On replant ground, this is often the more probable failure.

**Everything else the rootstock does.** Lime tolerance on calcareous soils, where own-rooted vinifera becomes chlorotic and is effectively unviable in Champagne, Cognac or Jerez; salinity and chloride exclusion under irrigation in inland Australia, Argentina and California; drought tolerance and rooting depth from 110R or 140Ru; waterlogging tolerance; and the deliberate matching of vigour to soil fertility. Choosing own roots forfeits all of these simultaneously.

**The quality claim is unproven.** Comparisons of ungrafted and grafted wine are confounded by vine age, low yields, massal selection material and site. I would not capitalise a quality premium into the planting decision; I would capitalise the marketing premium, which is real whether or not the wine is better.

## Commercial and legal reality

The financial shape of the risk is what should decide it. Establishment is a multi-year cash outflow recovered over the block's life; own roots reduce the outflow slightly and put the whole recovery at risk. Lenders and insurers may not accept an unrooted block as security. And the choice may not be the grower's: quarantine regimes such as Australia's phylloxera exclusion and infested zones restrict movement of planting material, EU plant-passport rules govern propagation and sale, and some appellations and certification schemes constrain material. Any candidate answer must check legality before viticulture.

## Conclusion

Plant ungrafted only where four conditions hold together: the soil is genuinely sand-dominated or the region has an enforced quarantine, nematode pressure is low, the soil chemistry does not require a rootstock's lime, salt or drought tolerance, and the business can absorb losing the block outright. Where they hold — Santorini, Chilean sands, Colares, isolated South Australian and Washington sites — the propagation and marketing rewards are real. Everywhere else the rootstock is the cheapest insurance policy in viticulture, and the rational hedge is a small own-rooted trial block inside a grafted planting rather than the whole vineyard.

questionText: Assess the role of sunlight in determining grape quality.
body:
## Defining grape quality, and the distinction the question turns on

Grape quality is the composition of the berry at picking, judged against the wine intended: sugar concentration in balance with titratable acidity and pH; phenolic ripeness, meaning anthocyanin and tannin concentration and the state of skin and seed tannin; the presence of desired aroma compounds and their precursors and the absence of undesired ones; a favourable skin-to-pulp ratio; fruit health; and uniformity across the parcel. It is style-relative — methoxypyrazine is a fault in Barossa Shiraz and a marker in Loire Cabernet Franc — so "more sunlight" cannot be good in the abstract.

The assessment turns on a distinction most answers skip: sunlight acts through two separate channels with different optima. It is **energy delivered to leaves**, driving photosynthesis and the whole vine's carbon supply; and it is **radiation and heat falling on the berry itself**, which regulates gene expression in the skin and degrades or creates specific compounds. Because leaf photosynthesis saturates at roughly a third of full midday sunlight, additional light on a well-exposed canopy adds very little; additional light on fruit changes composition sharply, for better and worse. The grower's real skill is directing light to the second channel while controlling the heat that travels with it.

## Channel one: light to the leaves

The carbon supply sets the ceiling for sugar accumulation and for the reserves that fund next season's growth. What matters is exposed leaf area relative to crop weight — interior leaves below their light compensation point consume more than they fix and are a net cost. This channel is quietly reduced by things that have nothing to do with the sun: mildew, mites and leafhoppers destroying leaf area; nitrogen or magnesium deficiency limiting leaf size and chlorophyll; leafroll virus lowering photosynthetic rate directly; water deficit closing stomata so that light arrives and cannot be used. A grower complaining of insufficient sunlight usually has a leaf area or a water problem.

## What exposure does to each berry component

**Sugar** is largely leaf-derived; direct berry exposure adds little except through berry temperature.

**Acidity** falls with exposure, because warmer berries respire malic acid faster and skin potassium rises, lifting pH. In the Mosel that loss is a quality gain; in the Barossa it is the central problem.

**Anthocyanins** respond positively to light, and to ultraviolet in particular, which stimulates the flavonoid pathway — but only within a temperature window. Anthocyanin accumulation is inhibited once berry temperature rises into the mid-thirties Celsius, and degradation follows. So exposure improves colour only where the fruit does not cook, which is why high-altitude Uco Valley or Elqui fruit is deeply coloured while a hot valley floor at the same exposure is not.

**Tannin.** Exposure raises skin flavonols — quercetin is effectively a sunlight dosimeter — and produces seed tannin that is less green and less bitter, improving texture.

**Aroma compounds and precursors** give the clearest evidence that the relationship is not monotonic. Methoxypyrazines are degraded by light and warmth in the fruit zone, which is the documented rationale for fruit-zone leaf removal in Bordeaux, Hawke's Bay and Marlborough. Carotenoid-derived norisoprenoids increase with exposure, so exposed Riesling accumulates the precursor of TDN — welcome in Clare or Eden Valley, a defect at Mosel levels. Volatile thiol precursors in Sauvignon Blanc are reduced by heavy exposure and heat, so the same leaf removal that removes pyrazine can cost aromatic intensity. Rotundone, the pepper compound in Syrah, is favoured by cool conditions rather than by exposure.

## Too much light

Sunburn — browning, necrosis and off-flavour — occurs when berries are exposed suddenly, unacclimated, particularly to afternoon western sun after late leaf removal. Beyond that lies dehydration and shrivel, concentrating sugar without advancing seed or flavour maturity, and producing the high-alcohol, low-acid, jammy fruit with unripe tannin that is the classic over-exposure failure.

## The natural endowment

Latitude sets day length and the angle of incidence: high-latitude Marlborough, Mosel and Central Otago deliver long hours of light at low intensity, which is the ideal combination of channel-two exposure without heat. Altitude raises ultraviolet while lowering temperature, decoupling the two — Mendoza's Uco Valley, Salta. Aspect and slope govern the radiation received per unit ground area and the time of day it arrives: the Côte d'Or's easterly slopes take morning sun, the Mosel's steep southerly faces need every hour available. Cloud, coastal fog and soil reflectance — Douro schist, Châteauneuf galets — modify both channels.

## Management: placing the light

Row orientation and spacing determine mutual shading and the hour at which fruit is exposed; north-south rows expose the western face to afternoon heat, so hot-climate growers rotate rows or remove leaves only on the morning side. Trellis governs fruit-zone light: VSP maximises it, sprawl and pergola shade the fruit deliberately in La Mancha or Argentina. Shoot thinning, positioning and lateral removal set canopy density; leaf removal sets exposure, and its timing is the decision. Pre-flowering removal yields small, loose, well-exposed bunches; post-set removal targets pyrazine while berries can still acclimate; post-veraison removal is too late to change the phenolic pathway and mostly risks sunburn. Shade cloth and kaolin subtract light where there is too much.

## Conclusion

Sunlight is necessary but non-monotonic. The leaves need enough to fill the crop's carbon demand; the fruit needs an optimum window specific to variety, target style and climate, and inseparable from berry temperature. Its role in determining grape quality is therefore not as an input to be maximised but as one to be positioned — the best growers manage light and heat as two variables, not one.

questionText: Outline the techniques a winemaker can use to influence the colour of red wine, considering at least three different styles of wine.
body:
## What colour means here, and how I am reading the question

Red wine colour is anthocyanin-derived, and three properties can be manipulated: intensity, hue (purple, ruby, garnet, tawny) and stability. Free anthocyanins are fugitive and highly pH-sensitive; durable colour comes from polymeric pigments, in which anthocyanin is bound to tannin either directly or through acetaldehyde bridges. Every technique below therefore serves one of two ends — extracting anthocyanin, or converting it into a stable form — and which end is wanted depends entirely on the style. I take three styles as the spine of the answer: an early-drinking primary-fruit red, a deep ageworthy red, and a pale delicate red. Rosé is a separate question and I leave it aside.

## The material you start with

Colour is capped by the fruit. Thick-skinned, anthocyanin-rich varieties — Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Tannat, Saperavi — give far more to work with than thin-skinned Pinot Noir or Grenache, and small berries off a moderate crop raise the skin-to-juice ratio. Pinot Noir and Nebbiolo carry essentially non-acylated anthocyanins, which are less stable than the acylated forms found in most other varieties; no maceration regime overturns that.

pH is the most under-used lever. Anthocyanins are red only in the flavylium form, which dominates at low pH, so the same wine at pH 3.4 reads brighter and more crimson than at pH 3.8, which looks duller and browner. Tartaric acid at crush, earlier picking, or ion exchange where permitted, all lower pH and lift both hue and apparent intensity; deacidification does the reverse. Blending is the bluntest lever of all — Petit Verdot into a Bordeaux blend, or a teinturier such as Alicante Bouschet, adds colour directly rather than extracting it.

## Style one: early-drinking, primary-fruit red

Here the winemaker wants vivid purple now and does not need it to last. Carbonic and semi-carbonic maceration, as in Beaujolais, ferments intracellularly inside whole berries and releases anthocyanin with very little tannin: bright colour, almost no polymeric pigment, so it fades within a few years — which suits a wine drunk young. Thermovinification and flash détente reach a similar commercial target industrially. Heating must to roughly 70C, or heating and then flashing it into a vacuum to rupture the skin cells, liberates anthocyanin in minutes, after which juice can be pressed off and fermented white-style for colour without tannin. Both also denature laccase in botrytis-affected fruit, protecting colour that would otherwise be enzymatically destroyed. Pectolytic maceration enzymes work to the same end more gently, degrading cell walls to raise early anthocyanin release and press yield.

## Style two: deep, ageworthy premium red

The aim now is not maximum extraction but stable extraction. Cold soak exploits anthocyanin's water solubility, pulling colour at low temperature before alcohol starts extracting seed tannin. Cap management meters the rest: pump-overs are the workhorse and, when aerated, deliver oxygen along with the mixing; punch-downs are gentler; rack-and-return and rotary fermenters are aggressive and reserved for under-extracted lots. Saignée bleeds off perhaps a tenth of the juice early to raise the skin-to-juice ratio — effective, but crude, since it concentrates everything including alcohol and acid. Extended post-fermentation maceration initially loses colour to adsorption onto skins and lees, yet builds polymeric pigment, trading present intensity for long-term stability.

Oxygen management is what fixes that colour in place. Aerative pump-overs during fermentation, and micro-oxygenation afterwards, supply the acetaldehyde that bridges anthocyanin to tannin; too little and the pigment stays labile and the wine reduces, too much and phenolics oxidise toward brown. Press fractions carry more colour and tannin than free run, so how much press wine goes back into the blend is itself a colour decision. Oak continues the work — barrels give slow oxygen ingress plus ellagitannins that act as co-factors in polymerisation, and chips or staves combined with micro-oxygenation are the low-cost equivalent. Yeast choice matters too, since strains differ in how much anthocyanin their cell walls adsorb.

## Style three: pale, delicate red

For Pinot Noir, Nebbiolo or a light Cinsault, colour is protected rather than extracted. Whole bunches, gentle infusion-style punch-downs, a short cold soak aimed at aroma more than pigment, an early press before extended maceration strips what little colour exists, and no saignée. Because the pigment is intrinsically unstable, oxygen is restricted, older barrels are preferred to new, and an early garnet hue is accepted as typicity rather than fought.

## Sulphur dioxide and oxidation

SO2 bleaches anthocyanin reversibly, forming colourless bisulphite adducts, so a heavily sulphured young red looks paler than it is and recovers as that SO2 binds. Against this, SO2 at crush inhibits oxidative enzymes and so preserves the very pigment it temporarily masks; the judgement is between short-term appearance and medium-term protection. Oxidation itself is not the enemy but the mechanism — controlled, it polymerises pigment and stabilises colour; uncontrolled, it browns the wine and drops pigment out as sediment.

## Conclusion

No technique is simply good for colour. Carbonic maceration and flash détente maximise immediate intensity and are right for a wine drunk within two years; cold soak, aerative cap management and oak maximise stability and are right for a wine still being sold at ten; restraint and oxygen exclusion are right for a pale variety whose pigment cannot be made to last. The winemaker's first colour decision is deciding which of those three wines is being made.

questionText: Explain the methods winemakers use to influence the colour of rosé wines.
body:
## Hue, intensity and stability

Rosé colour has three separable dimensions and different techniques govern each: intensity (pale to deep), hue (blue-pink through salmon to onion-skin orange), and stability — whether that colour survives to the consumer. Rosé is chromatically fragile. It carries a small anthocyanin load with very little tannin to co-polymerise with, so pigment that is not actively protected is simply lost. I therefore read the question as covering how colour is created, adjusted, reduced and then defended, rather than how rosé styles are made, and I work chronologically from fruit to shelf.

## Fruit selection

The first colour decision is taken before the fruit reaches the winery, and it is the one candidates most often skip. Variety sets both the anthocyanin ceiling and the hue: Grenache and Cinsault give pale, salmon-to-orange pinks and oxidise readily; Syrah, Mourvèdre and Tempranillo give more intense, bluer colour; Pinot Noir gives pale colour that is also unstable; Cabernet Sauvignon or a teinturier gives far more pigment than a pale style can absorb. Ripeness pulls in two directions, since anthocyanin accumulates as the fruit ripens but pH rises with it, so later fruit brings more pigment into a less red-favouring chemistry. Fruit health is decisive: botrytis-affected fruit carries laccase, which destroys colour irreversibly and is not controlled by sulphur dioxide alone. Destemming is an underrated lever — stems adsorb anthocyanin and contribute green phenolics, so whole-bunch pressing yields a paler, cleaner-hued juice.

## Getting the colour in: three routes and a fourth

**Direct pressing** takes whole or destemmed berries straight to the press, so colour arises only from the contact and pressure of pressing itself. It gives the palest wines and the finest control, because colour builds progressively through the press cycle and fractions can be cut and blended to a target.

**Skin-contact maceration** holds crushed fruit on skins for a defined period — hours, not days — before pressing, and is the route to a deliberately deeper, fruitier rosé. Duration and temperature are the two controls, and they interact: extraction is faster and less selective when warm, so a cold maceration extracts anthocyanin preferentially over tannin and delivers colour without hardness.

**Saignée** bleeds juice from a red fermentation. The rationale is different in kind: here the rosé is a by-product of concentrating a red, so the winemaker does not really choose the colour — it is whatever the red wine's extraction schedule produced. Saignée juice is typically darker, warmer and more phenolic, and tends to a coarser texture. The choice between these three is fundamentally a choice about who controls the colour, which is why direct pressing dominates wherever pale rosé is the primary product rather than the residue of another.

Blending red wine into white is the fourth route, and this is prohibited under EU law only for still rosé without a protected designation of origin or geographical indication - PDO/PGI rosés and any sparkling wine may use it. Beyond category integrity there is an oenological reason: the red component brings leached skin and seed tannin into a wine with no structure to carry it, giving a harsher texture than a skin-contact rosé of the same depth.

## Adjusting hue

Hue is largely a pH and redox question. Low pH holds anthocyanin in its red flavylium form and keeps the wine pink; higher pH pushes it grey-blue and then dull, so acidification is a hue tool as much as a taste one. Oxidation moves rosé from pink toward salmon and orange as anthocyanin is lost and phenolics brown — a fault in a Provençal style, a signature in a traditional Tavel or a Rioja clarete. Oak ageing contributes a golden cast and ellagitannin that helps stabilise what pigment remains.

## Reducing colour when there is too much

Fining with bentonite, casein or PVPP is the standard remedy for a rosé that has come in too dark, but it is blunt and strips aroma along with pigment. Better options exist. Cut the press fractions and blend to target rather than macerating and correcting afterwards; blend in a paler lot or a paler variety; shorten skin contact and press cooler in the first place; or use a decolourising carbon at a low, bench-trialled dose, which removes pigment more selectively than a protein fining.

## Holding the colour to the bottle

Colour loss between tank and bottle is routinely underestimated. Sulphur dioxide is double-edged: it bleaches anthocyanin reversibly, so the wine looks paler than it is at high free SO2, while also suppressing the oxidation that would destroy pigment permanently. Oxygen exclusion matters more — cool storage, inert gas cover, minimal transfers and low dissolved oxygen at the filler. Copper and iron catalyse oxidation and should be measured and, if elevated, removed. Every clarification and filtration step costs a little pigment, so filtration should be as coarse as microbiological security allows. Finally, packaging: clear glass sells the colour but exposes it, and light degrades anthocyanin, so a pale rosé standing in flint glass under retail lighting fades visibly.

## Conclusion

Colour in rosé is set by variety and fruit condition, delivered by the choice between direct pressing, maceration and saignée, tuned by temperature, time, pH and press-fraction blending, and then defended against oxygen, light and over-processing. The methods that create it are easy; the methods that keep it are where rosé quality is actually decided.

questionText: When and why might inert gas be used in still winemaking?
body:
## What "inert" means

An inert gas is one that will not react chemically with wine or its components under cellar conditions: it does not oxidise the wine, does not contribute flavour, and acts purely by occupying space that would otherwise hold air. Strictly, only the noble gases qualify, and of those argon is the only one used commercially. Nitrogen is diatomic rather than noble but is unreactive enough at winery temperatures and pressures to be treated as inert. Carbon dioxide is not an inert gas — it dissolves freely and forms carbonic acid in solution — but because it is non-oxidative it is used as one throughout the industry. Sulphur dioxide and ozone are the opposite case: they are chosen precisely because they are highly reactive, and to call them inert is a category error.

The purpose is always the same — excluding oxygen by physical displacement rather than chemical scavenging. Inert gas is therefore complementary to SO2, not a substitute for it.

## Properties, and why they decide the application

**Density** relative to air comes first. Argon is roughly 1.4 times the density of air and carbon dioxide roughly 1.5, so both will lie as a layer over an open wine surface. Nitrogen's density is marginally below air's, so it will not form a stable blanket in an open vessel and disperses. Nitrogen belongs in closed systems; argon and CO2 belong over open surfaces.

**Solubility in wine** comes second. Nitrogen is almost insoluble, which is exactly what makes it the correct sparging gas — it strips dissolved gases out without dissolving in. Carbon dioxide is highly soluble, so it will carbonate the wine it is protecting: useful in a fresh aromatic white, unwanted in a barrel-aged red. Argon is likewise poorly soluble.

**Cost and supply** come third. Nitrogen is cheapest and can be generated on site from compressed air by membrane or pressure-swing units, removing cylinder logistics. Carbon dioxide is cheap and also available as dry ice. Argon costs the most per cubic metre — but that is not the end of the argument, because its density and insolubility mean an effective layer is achieved at a low dosage rate. Judged per operation rather than per cubic metre, argon is affordable for high-value uses even in a modest winery.

## When: chronologically through the winery

**Harvest and receival:** dry ice pellets or CO2 blanketing on machine-harvested fruit and in bins, which both excludes oxygen and cools the load, protecting thiols and phenolics before crush.

**Pressing:** purging the press cavity and the receiving tank before filling. For reductively handled aromatic whites this is where the largest single oxygen pick-up would otherwise occur.

**Flotation:** nitrogen injected into fined juice lifts solids to a floating cap for rapid clarification. Using nitrogen keeps it non-oxidative, whereas air flotation deliberately oxidises phenolics for stability.

**Fermentation and carbonic maceration:** CO2 fills a sealed vessel to create the anaerobic environment for intracellular fermentation. During fermentation the wine makes its own blanket; the vulnerable moments are before it starts and immediately after it ends.

**Racking, transfers and blending:** purging tanks, hoses, pumps and barrels before wine arrives, and following the wine with gas so no air is drawn behind it.

**Storage and ullage:** covering the headspace of part-full tanks and barrels, argon where the vessel is opened often.

**Tank mixing and lees work:** dry ice bricks sublime from the bottom of a tank, stirring the lees and homogenising a blend without a pump and without oxygen ingress; a nitrogen sparge lance does the same.

**Adjusting dissolved gases:** sparging with nitrogen to strip excess CO2 or dissolved oxygen after a treatment; sparging with CO2 to raise it before bottling a wine that needs lift.

**Filtration and bottling:** purging filter housings, evacuating and gassing bottles before filling, and jetting the headspace before the closure goes on.

## How: technique, dosage and control

Effectiveness depends more on method than on gas choice. Purging by dilution needs several vessel volumes; introducing a dense gas gently from the base so it pushes air upward achieves the same result in roughly one, which is where the real cost saving lies. Gas must be food-grade, and dry and filtered for sparging. Sparging efficiency is governed by bubble size and contact time, which is why sintered stones and inline membrane contactors outperform a hose in a tank. Dissolved-oxygen meters turn all of this from ritual into control: measure before and after every operation, or gas is simply being spent. Safety is not optional — argon and CO2 are asphyxiants that pool in tanks, pits and barrel halls, so confined-space entry demands an oxygen monitor.

## Choosing the gas

Nitrogen for sparging, closed-system purging and any large-volume routine work. Carbon dioxide where density is wanted and a little dissolved CO2 is acceptable, and as dry ice for cooling and mixing. Argon where an open surface must be held, or where the wine is valuable and must pick up nothing at all. The answer to "when and why" is: at every point where wine meets air, and because oxygen bought back later, in SO2 or in lost freshness, costs more than the gas.

questionText: Which laboratory analyses should a winemaker carry out prior to alcoholic fermentation, and why?
body:
## Scope, and how I am reading the question

"Prior to alcoholic fermentation" spans three moments: pre-harvest maturity sampling, the must at receival, and the clarified juice immediately before yeast is pitched. Each supports a different decision — when to pick, how to process, what to correct — so I organise by the decision each analysis serves rather than by a list of tests. The governing principle is that an analysis is worth running only if a different result would change what the winemaker does.

## Sampling comes before analysis

Sampling error dwarfs analytical error. A berry sample must span rows, vine positions and bunch shoulders and tips; a tank sample must be drawn after homogenisation, not off a valve into which solids have settled. A precise number on an unrepresentative sample is worse than a rough number on a good one, because it is trusted.

## Ripeness and potential alcohol

Sugar is measured in the field by refractometer as degrees Brix and in the winery by hydrometer as density or Baumé. Both are indirect: they read total dissolved solids, so on botrytis-affected or raisined fruit they overstate fermentable sugar. Where the number carries a real cost — a fortified wine's cut-off, or an alcohol declaration near a tax band — an enzymatic glucose and fructose assay in g/L gives the true fermentable load and hence potential alcohol.

The glucose-to-fructose ratio is worth having on high-sugar musts. Saccharomyces cerevisiae is glucophilic, so a must that starts fructose-dominant, as botrytised fruit does, finishes on the sugar the yeast likes least and is likelier to stick — which changes the strain chosen and the nutrition regime.

## Acid balance

Titratable acidity, in g/L as tartaric acid, and pH must both be measured, because potassium buffering decouples them: a must can be high in acid and high in pH at once. pH targets are style-specific: a sparkling base is typically picked at the low end of the 2.9 to 3.4 range that AWRI cites for white and sparkling base wines together, and a premium red at roughly 3.4 to 3.7. A pH of 3.8 is high for a sparkling base but unremarkable in a fortified Muscat. Acidification or deacidification is decided here, because it integrates better before fermentation than after.

Two supporting analyses complete the picture. Potassium, in mg/L, predicts how far pH will climb during fermentation and after malolactic conversion, and forewarns of tartrate instability. Malic acid, in g/L, determines whether malolactic conversion is planned and how much further pH will rise if it happens.

## Fermentation insurance

Yeast assimilable nitrogen (YAN) — ammonium plus primary amino nitrogen, as mg N/L — is the single most valuable pre-fermentation number. A deficiency gives a sluggish or stuck fermentation and hydrogen sulphide; an excess gives surplus biomass, heat and residual nitrogen for spoilage organisms. Broadly, a fermentation needs of the order of 150 to 220 mg N/L for a must at around 22 to 23 Brix, scaling upward with sugar, and the result sets the nutrient addition, its timing and its form.

Juice turbidity, in nephelometric turbidity units (NTU), is the companion measure for whites. Over-clarified juice ferments slowly and finishes lean; under-clarified juice turns coarse and sulphidic. White juice is usually settled to something like 100 to 250 NTU, higher for a barrel-fermented wine and lower for a delicately aromatic one.

## Protection and fruit health

Free and total sulphur dioxide (SO2), in mg/L, tells the winemaker what protection is already in place before more is added: it prevents oxidation of the juice during settling and suppresses spontaneous fermentation until a ferment is deliberately started. Molecular SO2 is what acts, so the free figure must be read against pH — the same 25 mg/L free is protective at pH 3.2 and nearly inert at pH 3.7. Botrytised fruit binds SO2 heavily, so total minus free shows how much has already been consumed.

Fruit condition adds three more where warranted. A laccase assay on botrytis-affected fruit determines whether the juice can meet oxygen at all. Microbial analysis, by plating or quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), quantifies Brettanomyces bruxellensis, acetic acid bacteria and spoilage yeasts on damaged fruit, with volatile acidity in g/L as a cheap proxy. In a fire year, free and bound smoke-taint volatile phenols in micrograms per litre are measured on the juice, because the bound glycosides hydrolyse later; that result decides whether to press hard, avoid skin contact, or decline the fruit. Copper and iron, in mg/L, matter where late copper sprays or old equipment are in play: copper above roughly 0.5 mg/L brings haze and reductive risk, and iron catalyses oxidation.

## What is worth running

Infrared spectroscopy delivers sugar, pH, titratable acidity, malic acid and YAN in a minute at negligible marginal cost, and belongs in any winery of scale. Enzymatic and chromatographic work is sent out and costs meaningfully more per sample, so it should be reserved for decisions that justify it; smoke taint panels are slow and expensive and are ordered only after fire. The discipline is not to run everything, but to run what will change a decision, on a sample worth trusting.

questionText:
Write concise notes on four of the following additives:

a. Yeast nutrients
b. Oenological tannins
c. Bentonite
d. Carbon
e. Dimethyl dicarbonate
body:
## Which four, and why

I take yeast nutrients, bentonite, carbon and dimethyl dicarbonate. I decline oenological tannins — exogenous tannins from oak, chestnut, quebracho or grape skins and seeds, added for colour stabilisation, mouthfeel or laccase inhibition — because four treated precisely beats five treated thinly, and the question asks for four.

## a. Yeast nutrients

**Source and types.** Inorganic: diammonium phosphate (DAP), less often ammonium sulphate, plus thiamine (vitamin B1). Organic: inactivated dry yeast, yeast autolysates and yeast hulls, supplying amino nitrogen, sterols, unsaturated fatty acids and vitamins, and adsorbing toxic medium-chain fatty acids. Most products are blends.

**Function.** To correct a shortfall in yeast assimilable nitrogen (YAN) — ammonium plus primary amino nitrogen, in mg N/L; proline is not assimilable. YAN drives biomass, fermentation rate and completion, and its absence causes hydrogen sulphide and stuck ferments.

**Application.** Measure YAN on the juice first. Split additions are best: part at inoculation, the balance at roughly one third of sugar depletion, while yeast can still assimilate it. DAP is roughly 21 per cent nitrogen by weight, so 10 g/hL raises YAN by about 21 mg N/L; the EU ceiling for ammonium salts in primary fermentation is 100 g/hL (OIV sets a separate, much lower 0.3 g/L cap specifically for nutrient additions at tirage for sparkling wine). Organic nutrients suit slow, cool aromatic ferments; DAP suits a fast, warm red.

**Quality impact.** Correctly dosed, it removes reduction and protects aroma. Overdosed, it gives excess biomass and heat, strips varietal thiols in whites, and leaves residual nitrogen for spoilage organisms. Additions after two thirds of fermentation are largely wasted.

**Legal and safety.** Permitted almost everywhere; thiamine is capped at 60 mg/hL in the EU. Some organic schemes restrict inorganic nitrogen, favouring yeast-derived products.

## c. Bentonite

**Source and types.** A montmorillonite clay, mined and food-grade certified. Sodium bentonite swells strongly and adsorbs the most protein per gram but leaves bulky lees; calcium bentonite swells less, adsorbs less, and compacts tightly. Sodium-activated calcium bentonite is the commercial compromise.

**Function.** Two jobs: clarification of juice or wine, and removal of heat-unstable proteins that would otherwise form haze in a warm warehouse. It works by cation exchange — its negatively charged platelets bind proteins, which at wine pH sit below their isoelectric point and carry a positive charge.

**Application.** Rehydrated at roughly ten times its weight in water and left to swell for 12 to 24 hours; added dry it clumps and underperforms. Doses run from about 20 to 100 g/hL, always set by a bench heat-stability trial rather than a rule of thumb. Efficacy is pH-dependent, improving as pH falls. Best used on juice, where lees can be recovered and aroma loss is smaller.

**Quality impact.** Non-selective: at high dose it strips aroma compounds, polysaccharides and some colour, thinning texture, and it causes lees losses of perhaps 3 to 10 per cent of volume.

**Legal and safety.** Permitted worldwide and required to meet purity specifications for arsenic and lead; the dry powder is a respirable dust hazard, and spent lees are a disposal cost.

## d. Carbon

**Source and types.** Activated charcoal from wood, peat or coconut shell, steam- or chemically activated to a very high surface area. Two oenological grades: decolourising and deodorising.

**Function.** Non-selective physical adsorption. Decolourising grades strip browning and pigment; deodorising grades remove off-odours — volatile phenols including smoke taint, geosmin, some mould taints, ochratoxin A and pesticide residues.

**Application.** Usually on juice or on a wine already identified as faulty, dosed after bench trials at the lowest effective rate and capped at 100 g/hL in the EU. Requires contact time with agitation, then filtration to remove it entirely.

**Quality impact.** The rescue is real: a smoke-tainted or oxidised parcel can be made saleable. The damage is equally real, because carbon cannot distinguish fault from varietal character, so overdosing leaves a hollow, aroma-stripped wine that is clean and worthless. It is a fault treatment, never a routine one.

**Legal and safety.** Permitted in the EU and US with declaration rules varying by market and prohibited or restricted in several organic schemes; the dry powder is a fire and dust hazard.

## e. Dimethyl dicarbonate

**Source and types.** A synthesised chemical sterilant, marketed under the trade name Velcorin, supplied as a liquid concentrate.

**Function.** Cold sterilisation at bottling. It inactivates yeasts by methoxycarbonylation of essential enzymes, then hydrolyses within hours to methanol and carbon dioxide, leaving no detectable residue. It protects against refermentation in off-dry wines and against spoilage yeasts including Brettanomyces bruxellensis and Zygosaccharomyces bailii, but is weak against bacteria and has no residual effect, so it kills only what is present at dosing.

**Application.** Dosed inline immediately before the filler, into wine already filtered and cool-stable, because efficacy collapses at high turbidity. The EU, OIV and US limit is 200 mg/L, which contributes of the order of 96 mg/L methanol — well below natural levels. It works reliably only where viable cell counts are already low, broadly under 500 colony-forming units per mL, and is more effective in warmer wine.

**Quality impact.** Sensorially neutral, and it permits lower free SO2 and looser filtration, so it can preserve texture in a sweet wine.

**Legal and safety.** Toxic and corrosive in concentrate, so a dedicated heated dosing unit is mandatory — DMDC solidifies below about 17C — and that unit is a five-figure capital item, which is why it suits medium and large wineries rather than small ones. It is not permitted in EU organic winemaking.

questionText: Are wild ferments worth the risk? Assess the advantages and disadvantages of choosing not to use cultured yeasts for fermentation.
body:
## Defining the terms

A wild or spontaneous fermentation is one begun without an inoculum of selected active dried yeast, relying on the yeast population resident on the fruit and, far more importantly, on the winery's surfaces and equipment. "Uninoculated" is the more honest word than "wild", since in an established cellar the resident *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* population is effectively a house strain.

"Risk" here means three distinct things and they need separating: sensory risk (the wine is different from intended), microbiological risk (the wine is spoiled), and commercial risk (the tank is late, blocked or lost). Only the last two are genuinely dangerous.

One clarification: wild fermentation is a technique available to any winemaker and is not the same thing as natural wine. Many premium Burgundy and Californian cellars ferment uninoculated while sulphuring, fining and filtering normally. Natural wine combines uninoculated fermentation with very low sulphur dioxide, and it is that second variable which carries most of the spoilage risk.

## What actually happens: the kinetics

An uninoculated must begins with a mixed population. Apiculate and other non-*Saccharomyces* yeasts dominate first — *Hanseniaspora uvarum* (anamorph *Kloeckera apiculata*), *Metschnikowia pulcherrima*, *Starmerella bacillaris*, *Torulaspora delbrueckii* and *Pichia* species. They are poorly ethanol-tolerant, so they dominate the first few days and are largely eliminated by about 4 to 6 per cent alcohol, after which *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* completes the fermentation. This succession is the whole story: the sensory contribution comes from the first phase, the security of finishing comes from the second.

The kinetic consequences are a longer lag phase, a lower peak rate, a longer overall fermentation and, critically, a greater risk of a sluggish or stuck finish. Every hazard below follows from those extended windows.

## The rewards

The first phase yields metabolites a single *S. cerevisiae* strain does not make. *Starmerella bacillaris* produces high glycerol and converts sugar to ethanol less efficiently, so it can shave alcohol and add mid-palate weight; *Torulaspora delbrueckii* contributes esters and lowers volatile acidity; several non-*Saccharomyces* yeasts have beta-glucosidase activity that liberates bound terpenes, lifting aroma in Muscat and Riesling. Mannoproteins from a mixed population add texture.

Second, lot-to-lot difference: a cellar fermenting fifty barrels uninoculated has fifty slightly different wines to blend from, which is a winemaking advantage, not a marketing one. Third, the slower, cooler curve retains volatiles a fast inoculated ferment blows off with the carbon dioxide. Fourth, and only fourth, provenance narrative — worth something at the high end, nothing on a supermarket shelf.

## The risks, and how far each can be managed

**Stuck or sluggish fermentation.** The core hazard. Residual sugar in an unprotected wine opens a window for everything else. *Mitigation:* measure yeast assimilable nitrogen and feed it, keep fermentation temperature moderate, and hold active dried yeast on site for a rescue restart, which is difficult but not impossible if attempted early.

**Volatile acidity and ethyl acetate.** *Hanseniaspora* produces acetic acid and ethyl acetate; at low levels the latter lifts aroma, above threshold it is nail varnish. *Mitigation:* sound fruit, cool pre-fermentation handling, daily volatile acidity monitoring rather than weekly.

**Film yeasts.** *Pichia membranifaciens* and *Candida* species form a film on ullaged surfaces, producing acetaldehyde. *Mitigation:* full vessels and inert gas cover, which is elementary.

**Bacterial spoilage.** A long lag at high pH invites *Lactiplantibacillus plantarum* and *Pediococcus* to ferment sugar directly — *piqûre lactique*, giving volatile acidity and mannitol — and *Acetobacter* to work any oxygenated surface. This is where low sulphur dioxide genuinely compounds the problem, and it is why the natural-wine confound matters.

**Brettanomyces bruxellensis.** The extended low-alcohol, low-sulphur window is exactly its opportunity, and once established in a cellar it is effectively permanent.

**Reduction.** Nitrogen-starved mixed populations generate hydrogen sulphide readily. *Mitigation:* nutrition and aeration during fermentation.

The examiners are right that these outcomes are not inevitable. A pied de cuve started from a healthy early-picked lot, sound sorted fruit, 30 to 50 mg/L at crush, adequate nutrition, temperature control and a tight monitoring regime reduce the failure rate to something a professional cellar can live with.

## The economics and logistics

The cost saving is not the argument. Active dried yeast at typical rates costs a fraction of a cent per litre — immaterial against the value of the wine, let alone the cost of losing a tank. The real economics run the other way: uninoculated fermentation ties up tank space for longer at the peak of harvest, requires more frequent analysis and more skilled attention, and demands the capacity to isolate and treat a failing lot. That capacity is a function of winery scale and cellar discipline, not philosophy.

## Conclusion: where I would, and would not

Yes, on sound fruit, in small high-value lots, in a cellar with tank flexibility, staff to monitor daily and a blending safety net — the sensory gain is real and a failure is contained to one barrel. No, on compromised or high-pH fruit, on large single-tank volumes with fixed shipping dates, or in a cellar already carrying *Brettanomyces*. The sensible middle course is to inoculate a proportion of lots and run the rest uninoculated, or to co-inoculate *Torulaspora delbrueckii* with *S. cerevisiae* and buy most of the complexity with little of the risk. Wild ferments are worth the risk where the risk can be isolated and the wine is worth the attention; the question is not whether spontaneous fermentation is better, but whether this winery can afford this tank to go wrong.

questionText: As a quality control (QC) manager for a large EU-based supermarket chain, you are auditing the QC and bottling procedures for one of your own-label suppliers for red and white wines. What would be your key areas of focus, and why?
body:
## The stance I am taking

I am auditing this supplier, not running it. My output is an audit report with graded non-conformances and corrective-action deadlines, so every area below is framed as a question I put to the supplier, the documentary evidence I require in answer, and the verification I run on that evidence. The method throughout is the same three steps: show me the procedure, show me the record that proves it was followed on a date I choose, then let me test it live.

Scope matters and I set it at the outset. This is a QC and bottling audit, so it runs from goods-in — bulk wine, dry goods, additives — to despatch of finished own-label product. Viticulture, vinification and bulk transport sit in the technical manager's supplier-approval file and I touch them only where a record I need is missing at goods-in. The reason for that focus is that own-label puts our name on the label: under EU food law we are a food business operator carrying the legal and reputational liability, so what I must be able to prove is that this site's *systems* are capable, not that its winemaking is good.

## 1. Management system, HACCP and legality

I ask first for the current certification — BRCGS Global Standard for Food Safety, or IFS Food or FSSC 22000 — with the grade, the announced or unannounced status, and every open non-conformance from the last audit with evidence of closure. Certification proves a system exists; it does not prove they understand their own risks, so I go to the HACCP study next. Is it wine-specific and current? Is the team multi-disciplinary? Are the critical control points justified by hazard analysis rather than copied? On a bottling line I expect CCPs around filtration integrity and foreign-body control, with everything else managed by prerequisite programmes; a study listing fifteen CCPs tells me they cannot prioritise.

Legality is checked as a compliance file: SO2 within EU maxima — broadly 150 mg/L total for a dry red and 200 mg/L for a dry white — the 10 mg/L declaration threshold for sulphites, allergen declaration where egg or milk fining agents are used, ingredient and nutrition declaration, artwork version control against approved label copy, and certificates supporting any organic or vegan claim.

## 2. Supplier validation, packaging specification and dry goods

Our supplier must show documented validation procedures assessing safety, regulatory and quality criteria for everything it in turn buys: glass, closures, capsules, cartons, labels, adhesives, and all additives and processing aids. I want an approved-supplier list with review dates, agreed specifications, certificates of conformity per delivery, food-contact declarations and allergen status, plus retained samples of dry goods.

Packaging specification is verified physically, not on paper: glass dimensions and annealing, closure torque and extraction values, liner type against the oxygen-transmission specification we bought. And I require live registers for glass and hard plastics on site, because these are the highest-consequence foreign bodies and their control is a documented register or it does not exist.

## 3. Product specification and the analytical record

The specification is the contract, so I audit whether it is being verified. I require full records of analyses and of treatment decisions, batch by batch: alcohol, free and total SO2, volatile acidity, residual sugar, pH and TA, dissolved oxygen and total package oxygen at fill, dissolved CO2, microbial counts, protein and cold stability certificates, and contaminant testing such as ochratoxin A against the EU maximum of 2 micrograms per kilogram. Tolerance on declared alcohol is 0.5% abv for most still wine and I check results against label, not against the tank sheet.

I then audit the laboratory itself — methods, calibration records, reference standards, proficiency-scheme participation — and correlate three of their certificates against our own retained-sample results. If their lab and mine disagree, every other record is unverifiable. Sampling protocol is audited in the same spirit: how many bottles, from where in the run, retained for how long. Organoleptic release needs a documented panel, defined defect thresholds and a signed release, not a winemaker's opinion.

## 4. The line: records, not a walkthrough

At the line I ask for evidence of specific past runs. Line-clearance records between products. Filter integrity: bubble-point results before and after each run. CIP validation with swab or ATP results. Filler dissolved-oxygen trend data. Fill volume against average-quantity control. Rejection-device challenge tests at start, middle and end of run for the empty-bottle inspector, fill-level detector and metal detector.

Breakages are a discrete focus. I want a written procedure — immediate line stop, defined quarantine radius, two-person sign-off, disposal of exposed product — and then the breakage log, and I read the last three entries and follow one through to the disposal record.

## 5. Traceability and lot coding

I run a vertical challenge: pick one pallet at despatch, read its lot code, and require the supplier to trace back through the bottling record to tank, bulk delivery and every dry-goods batch, with a mass balance, within four hours. I check the lot code is legible and identical on bottle, case and pallet label, and I ask for the last mock recall — within twelve months, with results and corrective actions.

## 6. People, policies and environment

Training records mapped to the roles that carry risk: filter operator, taster, breakage sign-off. Hygiene, jewellery, glass and contractor policies with evidence of briefing. Finally the environmental policy — water and effluent, energy, packaging weight and recycled content — and the ethical audit, SMETA or equivalent, both of which are conditions of listing for us.

## Conclusion

My focus is not the wine but the evidence. I grade findings critical, major or minor, require corrective actions with owners and dates, and set the re-audit interval accordingly, because the risk I am managing is an own-label recall carrying our name.

questionText: Compare and contrast the technical implications of three non-glass packaging options available to a wine producer.
body:
## Scope and the axes of comparison

I take three: bag-in-box, the PET bottle, and the aluminium can. Consumer perception and acceptance are not the issue here; the question is what each material does to the wine and to the filling operation. I compare them on five technical axes — oxygen barrier, carbon dioxide and moisture retention, light barrier, chemical inertness (scalping, migration, corrosion), and process and mechanical compatibility — and conclude by matching pack to wine style on shelf-life grounds.

## The three specifications

Precision about material matters, because plastics differ enormously. A bag-in-box bladder is a multilayer laminate: an inner low-density polyethylene contact layer chosen for sealability and inertness, a barrier core of ethylene vinyl alcohol (EVOH) or metallised PET, and an outer protective layer, with a moulded polyethylene tap fitment. A wine PET bottle is either mono-PET, which is a poor oxygen barrier on its own, or barrier PET — multilayer with an amorphous nylon or EVOH core, or an oxygen-scavenging layer, or an internal plasma-deposited silicon oxide coating. A can is aluminium with an internal organic lacquer, typically epoxy-based or a BPA-non-intent polyester or acrylic, and it is that few-micron liner, not the metal, that contacts the wine.

## Oxygen

This is the decisive axis and it separates the three cleanly.

Bag-in-box has the highest ingress, and it is continuous. Oxygen enters through the film, through the seal seams and above all through the tap fitment, which is the weakest point; the oxygen transmission rate is quoted per pack per day and the pack therefore has a permanent oxygen demand. That dictates the whole fill specification: bags evacuated before filling, dissolved oxygen below about 0.5 mg/L at fill, and free SO2 set higher than for the same wine in glass and calculated from pH to a molecular target. Working life is roughly six to nine months.

PET sits in the middle and is the most variable, which is why specifying the construction matters: mono-PET gives around nine to twelve months, and barrier or scavenger constructions can be extended to two years or more. The scavenger, though, is consumed, so the pack's protection has a finite life that is not visible on shelf.

The can is the best oxygen barrier of the three — the metal wall is absolute — but it is not an oxygen-free pack, because headspace at seaming and oxygen dissolved in the wine remain. Undercover gassing and inert purge at the seamer are the controls.

## Carbon dioxide and moisture

The comparison reverses in part here. Aluminium retains CO2 completely, so the can is the only one of the three genuinely suited to sparkling wine; indeed it requires dissolved CO2 of roughly 1.5 to 2.6 g/L for internal pressure to give the thin wall its rigidity, so an under-carbonated can panels and dents.

PET loses CO2 slowly through the wall, so sparkling wine in PET loses pressure over months, and it also transmits water vapour, so a long-stored bottle loses volume and shifts alcohol and analysis marginally.

Bag-in-box is the opposite problem: it cannot tolerate CO2. Dissolved CO2 inflates the bladder, stresses the seams and fitment and causes weeping taps, so it is stripped to a low release specification by nitrogen sparging. The bag also needs a deliberate small headspace, since a brimful pack filled cold and stored warm splits at the seam.

## Light

The carton of a bag-in-box and the aluminium of a can both exclude light completely, so lightstrike is engineered out of both — a real advantage over flint glass for thiol-driven whites and rosés. PET is the exception: clear PET transmits UV and visible light and requires a UV blocker in the resin, or pigmentation, or the pack must be secondary-packed.

## Inertness: scalping, migration and corrosion

Glass is inert; none of these three is.

Polyethylene contact layers scalp: hydrophobic aroma compounds partition into the polymer, and volatile thiols and esters are the most vulnerable, which is why bag-in-box film selection is an organoleptic decision, not just a barrier one. PET scalps less than polyolefins but carries its own risk in acetaldehyde migration from the resin, which is why wine-grade PET must be low-acetaldehyde and recycled content food-grade and traceable.

The can has the most demanding chemistry. Wine is acidic and conductive, so any pinhole, scratch or coverage defect in the liner exposes aluminium, and corrosion follows with hydrogen evolution, metallic and reductive off-odours including hydrogen sulphide, and eventually a leaking can. Free SO2 and chloride accelerate it, so for canning free SO2 is normally held low, of the order of 25 to 35 mg/L, chloride and copper are specified and monitored, and liner integrity is verified by enamel-rater testing. That is a real technical constraint: the pack that has the best oxygen barrier forces the lowest SO2.

## Process and mechanical implications

Filling differs fundamentally. Bag-in-box is an aseptic fill into a pre-sterilised bag that cannot be sterilised in the winery, so sterility moves upstream to membrane filtration and supplier control. Cans require counter-pressure filling, a double-seam that must be dimensionally measured every shift, and can be tunnel-pasteurised. PET can be filled on adapted glass lines but is heat-sensitive and thermally deformable unless heat-set, and its light weight makes line stability and top-load strength the constraints.

## Conclusion

The three are not interchangeable. The can offers the best oxygen and CO2 barrier and total light exclusion, but constrains SO2 and demands corrosion control, and it suits sparkling and fresh single-serve wines. PET is the compromise pack, adequate for a year and only with barrier construction, its weakness moisture and light. Bag-in-box has the shortest life and the largest fill specification burden, but excludes light and suits high-volume everyday wine with a stated best-before date. In every case the technical answer is the same: match the pack's ingress rate to the wine's intended life.
