questionText: Discuss the evolution of the négociant business format in Burgundy over the last 15 years, explaining the contributing factors. Are current conditions financially sustainable?
body:
## What a négociant is, and how long it has been there

A Burgundian négociant buys grapes, must or finished wine and sells it under its own name. The format has three sub-forms that behave very differently: the négociant-éleveur, which vinifies purchased fruit; the éleveur proper, which buys wine in cask and raises and bottles it; and the négociant-manipulant scale buyer working in regional appellations. None of these is a courtier — a broker who matches seller to buyer for commission and never takes title — and none is a domaine, which bottles wine from vines it owns or leases. The distinction matters commercially because the négociant carries inventory risk and input-price risk that the courtier does not, and lacks the fixed fruit cost that the domaine enjoys.

The format is old, not new. The Beaune négoce was the mechanism by which Burgundy reached export markets for two centuries: Bouchard Père et Fils and Champy date from the eighteenth century, Bichot and Drouhin from the nineteenth. Domaine bottling is the recent development, spreading through the twentieth century and accelerating from the 1970s and 1980s — which is where the common error about négociant origins comes from. Even now a large share of Burgundy's crop never sees an estate bottling line: many growers sell grapes or bulk wine to the négoce or deliver to a co-operative, and that structural fact is the raw material of the whole business.

## The evolution, and what drove it

**Micro-négoce arrived.** The most visible change of the last fifteen years is the proliferation of small négociant labels founded by trained winemakers without land — Benjamin Leroux and Lucien Le Moine among the established names, with a long tail behind them. The driver is land price: Côte d'Or vineyard became unbuyable on a winemaker's earnings, so buying fruit is now the only realistic entry route. The format's virtue is that it needs a cellar, not a balance sheet.

**Established houses grew their négoce arms.** Where a house owns vineyard, it uses that as the quality core and buys fruit for volume and range. Jadot, Faiveley, Bichot and Drouhin have all expanded holdings while continuing to buy, and I treat their owned vineyard as part of the négociant model rather than as a domaine case: it is a hedge against input cost, not a separate business.

**Supply became the binding constraint.** A run of small vintages — hail in the Côte de Beaune in the early 2010s, the April frosts of 2016 and 2021 — took fruit off the market repeatedly. Growers stopped selling surplus, and grape and bulk prices rose sharply. The négociant format is uniquely exposed to this, because its cost of goods is priced by scarcity it cannot influence.

**Contracting changed shape.** The response has been to secure fruit without buying land: multi-year grape contracts, métayage and fermage arrangements, and equity in growers' operations. Négociants now compete for supply rather than for customers, which is a reversal of the historic position.

**Capital arrived and consolidated the top.** Groups have bought houses — Boisset's long accumulation, and Bouchard Père et Fils passed to Artémis Domaines in 2022. So the population is a barbell: many more small négociants than fifteen years ago, and greater concentration of value in a handful of well-capitalised houses. The number of négociants has not fallen.

## Are current conditions financially sustainable?

Not uniformly, and the split follows the structure above.

The pure-play négociant with no owned fruit faces a squeeze at both ends. Its input price is set by an appellation-scarce raw material bid up by better-capitalised competitors and by growers' own opportunity cost, while its selling price is capped by the consumer's ability to compare it with a domaine bottling of the same climat — which usually carries more prestige at similar money. Between 2015 and 2022 that gap was papered over by demand: Burgundy prices rose fast enough that expensive fruit was still profitable. Since 2023 the fine-wine market has cooled and Asian demand has weakened, so houses that contracted fruit at peak prices are selling into a softer market, and higher interest rates have made the multi-year inventory financing that élevage requires materially more expensive. That combination — peak input cost, softening output price, dearer working capital — is not sustainable, and I would expect failures and absorptions among mid-sized, vineyard-light houses.

Three models remain sound. Integrated houses with substantial owned or leased vineyard internalise the fruit cost and can average their margin across the range. Micro-négociants with negligible overhead, allocation-based selling and no salaried staff can pay high fruit prices because they have almost no fixed cost to cover. And volume houses working in the Mâconnais, the Châtillonnais and regional appellations still buy fruit at economic prices, because the scarcity premium is concentrated in the Côte d'Or.

The format itself is not in question — it is the mechanism by which most Burgundy reaches the market and it will remain so. What is in question is the vineyard-light, Côte d'Or-focused, inventory-heavy version of it. Restoring its economics needs a run of normal-sized vintages, longer and more secure fruit contracts, and a willingness to move down the appellation ladder rather than defend a price the market has stopped paying.

questionText: What will be the likely impact on the global wine industry if health warnings about cancer risks become increasingly mandatory on wine labels? Discuss the implications of such changes for producers, marketers and consumers.
body:
## Scope, and the position I take

By a mandatory cancer warning I mean a government-specified statement linking alcohol consumption to cancer risk, carried on or with the container. The regimes in play sit on a spectrum, and where a market lands on that spectrum matters far more than whether it legislates at all: an off-label digital disclosure reached by QR code; a sentence added to the existing back-label legalese; or a rotating front-of-pack warning with a pictogram on the tobacco template. Only the third materially changes what a shopper sees at the shelf, and I assess the question on the assumption that the direction of travel is from the first towards the third.

My position has two parts. First, the label itself is a second-order shock. Its first-order significance is that it settles, in law, the proposition that alcohol is a carcinogen — and once that is settled the same public-health apparatus reaches the levers that actually move volume: excise, minimum pricing, advertising restriction and retail availability. The implications should be assessed as the leading edge of a regulatory package, not as a packaging problem. Second, the effect will be deeply uneven. It accelerates a bifurcation already under way, pressing hardest on the commercial tier that is already in structural over-supply, and least on fine wine, whose buyers are the least deterred.

## Producers

Compliance cost is real but it is the least interesting consequence. Wine already carries market-specific mandatory text, so the machinery exists; the burden falls disproportionately on small and mid-sized exporters running many short label runs, while a multinational amortises a plate change across millions of bottles. The predictable structural response is more bulk shipping and in-market bottling — which favours scale, and adds one more push towards the consolidation already visible in Australia, Chile and South Africa. Producers selling into a single domestic market absorb almost nothing.

The material threat is demand meeting an over-supplied base. Vineyard area is being removed under public schemes in Bordeaux and reduced under commercial pressure in South Australia, Chile and South Africa, precisely because volume in the commercial tier is falling. A warning that shaves a few percentage points from mature-market volume does not land on a balanced market; it lands on one already removing vines, and it converts a cyclical surplus into a structural one. Grape prices in unbranded fruit-supply regions — inland Australia, the Central Valley of California, parts of Mendoza — are where that pain is felt first, by growers with no route to the consumer.

Two producer responses are more interesting than cost-cutting. The first is alcohol reduction, because several proposed regimes scale the warning or the tax to alcohol content, which turns lower ABV from a stylistic choice into a regulatory advantage. That means earlier picking, cooler sites, varieties and clones with lower sugar accumulation, and partial de-alcoholisation — all of which carry quality costs that need honest weighing rather than assertion. The second is premiumisation. If drinkers drink less, the rational commercial answer is to sell them better wine less often. That is genuinely available to producers with a story, a place and a brand; it is not available to bulk suppliers, which is why the same regulation is an opportunity for one tier and an existential threat to the other.

## Marketers

A front-of-pack warning is a message on your pack that you do not control and cannot answer. It compresses brand differentiation into the space that remains, and every marketer reads the tobacco sequence — warning, then larger warning, then plain packaging — as the precedent. Brand equity built on visual distinctiveness is therefore more exposed than brand equity built on relationships, provenance or trade advocacy.

It also closes a positioning territory. Wine's soft health halo — the Mediterranean diet, resveratrol, a glass a day — becomes unusable and, if deployed, actively dangerous. Marketers must move the claim from health to pleasure, craft, place, food and moderation. The on-trade is a partial shelter, since the warning is not seen by the glass, and so are DTC and hospitality channels where the message is a story rather than a shelf.

The judgement I would make is about trust. The tobacco industry's response to the evidence destroyed its standing permanently. Where the trade has publicly resisted labelling, as it did through Ireland's legislative process and around the EU's Beating Cancer Plan, it buys delay at the cost of looking like an interested party arguing with cancer researchers. I would argue for the opposite posture: accept the labelling, own the moderation message, and spend the political capital on the levers that matter more commercially, such as excise structure and advertising rules. There is also a genuine benefit here. A mandated, standardised statement ends the competitive uncertainty about what a responsible producer should say, and gives a rationale to lower-alcohol and no/low line extensions that previously looked like an admission.

## Consumers

The response varies more by market and by drinking pattern than by anything else, and treating "the consumer" as one person is the fastest way to get this wrong.

In mature Anglophone markets — the UK, US, Canada, Australia, the Nordics — health literacy is high, per-capita consumption is already falling, and younger cohorts drink less than their parents did. Warnings here confirm a shift rather than cause one, but they are an accelerant, and the strongest effect is on light and occasional drinkers, particularly women targeted by breast-cancer messaging, who have least attachment to the category. Heavy drinkers, the volume that matters, respond least to information and most to price.

In the traditional European producing countries the warning collides with identity: wine is food, agriculture and regional employment, and the political resistance in France, Italy and Spain will be far stronger than the behavioural change. In East Asia the evidence is instructive. South Korea has carried a cancer-specific warning on alcohol containers for years without the category collapsing, which supports the view that labels alone shift awareness rather than behaviour; China's wine decline has been driven by economic conditions and the retreat of banquet and gifting culture, not by labelling. Mexico already requires prominent health warnings on alcohol, and consumption there has continued to grow from a low base. In emerging markets such as India, Brazil and Nigeria, wine is a small, urban, aspirational category, and a warning arriving at the same moment as the category is being built is a heavier brake than the same warning in France.

There are real consumer benefits, and they should be conceded. Awareness of the alcohol–cancer link is low almost everywhere, and the people who benefit most from disclosure are those least served by existing health communication. A shift towards drinking less but better is also, awkwardly for the industry's rhetoric, exactly where wine's margin lives.

## Conclusion

Increasingly mandatory cancer warnings will not, on their own, cause a step change in global wine consumption; the international evidence from markets that already carry them does not support that. Their real impact is threefold: they legitimise the alcohol-as-carcinogen frame that will justify the pricing and availability measures that do move volume; they accelerate the collapse of the commercial tier while leaving fine wine largely intact; and they force marketing off health territory permanently. The industry's best response is not to fight the label but to concede it early, cut alcohol where quality allows, and defend the ground where wine still wins — place, craft and the table.

questionText: How is the global wine industry adapting to changing societal attitudes towards alcohol consumption, and how should it respond to the challenges and opportunities these changes present?
body:
## Terms and scope

Three terms need pinning down before anything can be assessed. **Changing societal attitudes** here means the shift from alcohol as an unremarkable, daily, socially expected product to one treated as a discretionary health risk — a shift driven by health-authority messaging, generational change, and the arrival of alternatives that meet the same social need. **Moderation** is ambiguous and the ambiguity matters commercially: it can mean fewer drinking occasions, less volume per occasion, or lower alcohol per serve, and these three have completely different consequences for a producer's mix. **No/low** I take as the trade does — de-alcoholised or low-alcohol products, which in the EU since the 2021 reform may be labelled as wine, alongside partially de-alcoholised wines and naturally light wines.

The scope point: this is a supply-chain-wide question, not a product question. A Languedoc co-operative member, a Napa cult estate and a multinational brand owner face the same social shift with completely different exposure, and I structure the second half around that.

My position, stated up front: the industry's adaptation so far has been overwhelmingly product-led, and product-led adaptation is the weakest available response, because it treats a change in the meaning of drinking as a change in the specification of the liquid. The correct response is structural — fewer litres produced, more value per litre, and a rebuilt case for the occasion rather than the bottle.

## Part one: how the industry is actually adapting

**Product reformulation.** The visible response is no/low, plus lower-alcohol styles, plus lighter categories. De-alcoholisation by reverse osmosis, spinning cone and vacuum distillation has moved from a fringe technology to standard equipment at scale, and every major brand owner now has a no/low line. Alongside it sits a quieter and more effective shift: earlier picking, cooler sites and cooler regions, and the promotion of naturally moderate styles — Vinho Verde, German Riesling Kabinett, Moscato d'Asti, English and Tasmanian sparkling. Assessment: the second movement is working better than the first, because it sells wine rather than a substitute for it.

**Category and portfolio shifts.** Sparkling has held up far better than still, because it is occasion-led rather than volume-led; Prosecco's growth and the rise of pét-nat and canned sparkling both belong to this. Rosé's success in the US and France is of the same kind. Meanwhile brand owners have been divesting commercial volume brands and buying premium estates. Assessment: this is real adaptation and it is rational, but it is a rearrangement of the same declining pool.

**Supply-side restructuring.** The most consequential adaptation is the least discussed: vine-pull and area reduction in Bordeaux, South Australia, Chile and South Africa, plus co-operative consolidation. Assessment: painful, slow, politically fraught, and the only adaptation that addresses the actual problem, which is that the world plants for a consumption level that no longer exists.

**Marketing and policy posture.** Responsible-drinking messaging, moderation partnerships and no-alcohol serve suggestions have been adopted broadly. Assessment: much of it is defensive and unconvincing, and where the trade has publicly disputed health evidence it has damaged its own credibility for very little delay.

## What no/low can and cannot do

This deserves scrutiny rather than enthusiasm, because it is where most of the industry's optimism is parked.

First, the arithmetic. Even bullish projections for no/low wine growth do not offset the decline in the wine market as a whole; a category growing fast from a very small base cannot fill a hole in a very large one. Second, the red-wine problem: de-alcoholisation works acceptably on aromatic whites, sparkling and sweeter styles, where sugar and CO2 rebuild body, and poorly on dry reds, where removing alcohol leaves tannin hard, aromatics stripped and texture hollow. That excludes the largest single style block and, with it, a whole swathe of consumers. Third, occasion mismatch: no/low wine performs in retail and at home, but sells weakly in restaurants, where wine's margin and its cultural transmission both live. Fourth, price and margin: consumers resist paying wine prices for a product with the excise removed, while de-alcoholisation adds process cost, so the category is structurally squeezed. Fifth, an unmentioned tension — de-alcoholisation is energy-intensive, and a producer with a public carbon-reduction target is adding an energy-hungry unit operation in order to chase a health-driven consumer. Those two goals are in direct conflict and almost nobody says so.

Growth in the no/low category is overwhelmingly concentrated in beer, whose flavour architecture survives alcohol removal far better. My verdict: no/low is a legitimate portfolio hedge and a way of keeping a brand present in a moderating consumer's repertoire. It is not a category answer, and an industry that treats it as one has mistaken a line extension for a strategy.

## Part two: how it should respond

**Fix supply before demand.** The first duty is to stop producing more wine than the world will drink. That means continued area reduction concentrated in the lowest-value fruit, contract discipline, and honesty from co-operatives and regional bodies about which vineyards have no economic future. Every other response is undermined if a surplus keeps commodity wine cheap.

**Compete for the occasion, not the shelf.** Wine's remaining advantage is the table. Moderation reduces frequency, so each occasion carries more weight, and the industry should invest in food pairing, hospitality, by-the-glass programmes and smaller formats — 500ml bottles, half bottles, cans, preservation systems — that let a consumer drink one good glass rather than avoid a whole bottle. This is portfolio and distribution work, not reformulation.

**Segment the response by scale.** A small estate cannot fund a no/low line and should not try; its response is direct relationships, hospitality and price. A regional co-operative's response is supply reduction and diversification into juice, spirit base or contract processing. A multinational's response is portfolio rebalancing, no/low as a hedge, and the political and scientific engagement that only it can fund. Prescribing one response to all three is the standard error.

**Treat developing markets as a separate strategy.** In India, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico and parts of South-East Asia, wine is a small, urban, aspirational category with no inherited drinking norm to defend. Here the challenge is not moderation but access, price, temperature control in the supply chain, and duty. Growth is genuinely available, and the industry should not export mature-market defensiveness into markets where the category has not yet been built. China is the caution: its decline was economic and cultural, not health-led, and misdiagnosing it as moderation would produce the wrong response entirely.

**Get ahead of the regulation.** Health-authority messaging and policy — labelling, excise, advertising limits, availability — will shape long-term demand far more than any product launch. Accepting labelling, publishing ingredients and nutrition, and moving marketing off health claims are cheap concessions that preserve the credibility needed to argue about the expensive things.

## Conclusion

The industry is adapting mostly by reformulating the product and rearranging its portfolio, and only reluctantly by cutting supply. That is the wrong order. It should respond by shrinking production to match a permanently smaller market, defending the occasion rather than the volume, differentiating its response by scale and by market maturity, treating no/low as a hedge rather than a rescue, and conceding the regulatory ground it cannot hold in order to keep credibility on the ground it can.

questionText: You are tasked with creating a wine blend that represents the essence of humanity's wine culture. Which grapes or regions would you include, and which winemaking style and packaging would you use, and why?
body:
## The essence I am trying to bottle

Humanity's wine culture is not the sum of its famous bottles, and a blend that tried to sample greatness would only represent the last two centuries of European commerce. I define the essence as four things, and every decision below answers to one of them.

**Continuity**: wine is one of the oldest technologies still practised in something close to its original form, and the vine that carries it is still propagated by cutting, so the plants in the ground are physically descended from ancient ones. **Travel and adaptation**: wine culture has never stayed where it started; it moved with trade, empire, migration and faith, and every time it arrived somewhere it was changed by the place and changed the place back. **The shared table**: wine's social function — hospitality, ritual, negotiation, mourning — is more universal than any style. **The graft**: since phylloxera, almost every vine on earth is two plants joined, an Old World scion on an American root. Nothing better expresses a culture that survives by combining.

That definition has consequences. The wine must be modest in alcohol and built for food, because the table is the point. It must be led by places that are usually spoken about last. And it must not be a luxury object, because a culture belonging to everyone cannot be packaged for the few.

## The blend

A red-fruited, savoury, moderate-alcohol blend of six components, around 12.5% alcohol:

**Saperavi, Kakheti, Georgia — 30%.** The anchor, for continuity. Georgia's qvevri tradition is the most direct living link to the earliest winemaking, and Georgian qvevri winemaking is inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. Saperavi is also a teinturier, so it earns its place technically as well as symbolically, giving colour and acid spine to everything else.

**Areni, Vayots Dzor, Armenia — 10%.** Pale, high-toned, red-fruited, from the region of the Areni-1 cave in Armenia, the oldest known winery site. It contributes lift and perfume where Saperavi contributes weight.

**Xinomavro, Naoussa, Greece — 10%.** For travel: the vine moving into the classical Mediterranean, and with it the idea of wine as a subject of conversation rather than only of consumption. Structurally it adds tannin and a savoury, tomato-leaf register that keeps the blend gastronomic.

**Pais, Maule, Chile — 15%.** Dry-farmed bush vines, brought by missionaries, farmed for generations by smallholders and dismissed as worthless until recently. Chile's old Pais vines are among the oldest continuously producing vines in the Americas. This is travel and adaptation with its uncomfortable colonial half included, and it puts a small grower rather than an estate at the centre of the wine.

**Cinsaut, Swartland, South Africa — 20%.** Old bush vines under South Africa's Old Vine Project, which certifies heritage vineyards of 35 years and older. A French variety that became a Cape variety, and the parent of a variety created there. It gives fragrance, light tannin and drinkability, and it brings an African component that is not a token.

**Marselan, Ningxia, China — 15%.** The newest chapter. Marselan, a French cross, has become the variety China has most convincingly made its own — proof that wine culture is still being founded, not only inherited.

North America is present in the blend without a component: the rootstock. Every one of these vines except the ungrafted Chilean and Greek material stands on American roots, and I would say so on the label rather than adding a seventh wine.

What I have excluded is as deliberate. There is no Bordeaux, Burgundy, Rioja or Tuscan component. A blend that includes everything represents nothing, and those regions already speak for themselves; the tension between authenticity and commercial popularity is resolved here in favour of authenticity, and I accept the cost.

## Winemaking

Components are vinified separately in their own regions, by their own growers, and shipped in bulk for assemblage — the blending itself being the point, since assemblage is the one winemaking technique that is unambiguously about combination.

The Saperavi is fermented and macerated in qvevri, as a living practice rather than as a museum exhibit; the qvevri portion is what makes the wine taste of the definition. Everything else ferments with ambient yeast in concrete and old, large-format oak. No new oak: new oak is a nineteenth-century European signature and would smother five of the six voices. Whole bunches in the Cinsaut and Areni for perfume and freshness. Alcohol held near 12.5% by picking for flavour rather than sugar, because the table demands a second glass. Sulphur used minimally but genuinely — a wine claiming to represent everyone cannot afford to be faulty, and fault tolerance is a niche taste, not a universal one.

This is where authenticity and innovation collide, and I resolve it openly: qvevri, ambient ferments and old vines are heritage; transcontinental bulk shipment and assemblage are unambiguously modern. The wine is honest about being both.

## Packaging

Packaging carries as much of the argument as the liquid, so it is not one decision but five.

**Format.** Three, deliberately. A 750ml bottle for the ceremonial and gifted occasion; a 250ml single-serve can, which is how a great many people under thirty drink and which suits moderation; and a 3-litre bag-in-box for the everyday shared table, which is where most of the world's wine is actually drunk. A single premium bottle would contradict the definition on the first page.

**Materials and footprint.** Lightweight glass well under the industry average, because glass weight is the largest single lever in most wines' carbon footprint; the can and bag-in-box are lighter still. Components shipped in bulk and filled in-market, which cuts freight and, usefully, spreads the work.

**Closure.** Certified natural cork on the bottle, screwcap on nothing here because there is no bottle line that needs it, and the bag-in-box tap otherwise. Cork is chosen because the cork oak landscapes are themselves a cultural landscape sustained by wine demand; the trade-off is a residual taint risk, and I accept it knowingly rather than by default.

**Label and message.** No château, no Bacchus, no coat of arms — those symbols encode a hierarchy the wine is arguing against. The motif is a graft union. The name appears in Latin, Georgian, Armenian, Chinese and Arabic script with none dominant. Full ingredient, nutrition and origin data sit behind a digital label under EU rules allowing ingredient and nutrition information to be carried on a digital label, in many languages. Growers are named; the brand owner is not. Type is set large and high-contrast with braille embossing on the bottle, because accessibility is inclusivity made concrete rather than claimed.

## Conclusion

The blend is Saperavi-led, six-country, moderate in alcohol and gastronomic; the winemaking is qvevri-anchored, oak-neutral and assembled; the packaging is three-format, lightweight and multilingual. Each choice is answerable to the same four-part definition — continuity, travel, the table, the graft — and where the choices conflict with commercial logic, as the exclusion of the European classics and the bag-in-box both do, I have chosen the definition. A wine that represents humanity's wine culture has to be one that most of humanity could actually open.

questionText: Analyse the major ethical concerns in the production of wine.
body:
## What I mean by ethical, and by production

An ethical concern in this context is not simply something undesirable. I take it to mean a harm that is imposed by the way wine is made on a party who has little or no power to refuse it, and which the price of the wine does not compensate. That definition does three useful things: it separates ethics from mere sustainability accounting, it puts the powerlessness of the harmed party at the centre, and it gives me a basis for ranking rather than listing.

By production of wine I mean the vineyard, the cellar and the inbound supply chain that serves them — labour, land, water, agrochemicals, energy, packaging materials — up to the point the wine leaves the winery. I exclude the health consequences of drinking and the ethics of alcohol marketing. Both are serious, but they are ethics of consumption and of communication, and folding them in would let a producer's actual conduct disappear behind a debate about the product.

## How I rank them

Four criteria: the severity of harm to an identifiable person; the number of people affected; the urgency, meaning whether the harm is happening now or is a risk to the future; and whether the harmed party can exit or object. On those tests I rank labour first, agrochemical exposure second, water third, and systemic inequality fourth — though inequality is arguably the cause of the other three rather than a peer of them.

## First: labour

Wine is one of the most labour-intensive crops in commercial agriculture, and the work is seasonal, physically punishing and largely done by people with the least bargaining power in the economies concerned: migrant, undocumented or contracted-out. The harms are direct and current — underpayment, unlawful hours, unsafe or squalid housing, heat exposure, and in the worst cases trafficking. Recent prosecutions in Champagne over the housing and treatment of migrant harvest workers were significant precisely because they occurred in the most prestigious and best-capitalised appellation in the world, which disposes of the argument that this is a problem of poor regions.

It is not confined to Europe. South Africa's wine industry still carries the legacy of the dop system, in which farm labour was part-paid in wine, and its consequences for tenure and dependency have outlasted the practice. California's harvest workforce faces heat and wildfire smoke exposure with limited employment protection. Contract labour is the common mechanism everywhere: it places a layer between the estate and the worker, so the estate can hold a certification and still not know who picked its fruit.

This ranks first because the harm is to people, now, who cannot leave, and because it is the one concern where a producer's own decisions are decisive. There are counter-examples worth naming: New Zealand's Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme created a regulated route for Pacific Island workers, showing that the alternative to exploitation is administrative effort rather than higher prices alone.

## Second: agrochemical exposure

I treat agrochemicals as an ethical rather than an environmental question first, because the earliest and most severe harm falls on people — applicators, their families, and the neighbours of vineyards. Vines receive more fungicide than most crops because they are grown as monocultures in humid climates, and the exposure is chronic. A case in Bordeaux in which children at a school beside a vineyard were affected during spraying is the kind of event that turned this from a technical matter into a public one, and vineyard-boundary buffer rules in several countries followed.

It ranks second rather than first because protective equipment, timing rules and spray technology genuinely reduce the harm, whereas labour abuse requires a change of intent. But it carries a dilemma that deserves stating: copper is permitted in organic viticulture but capped in the EU because it accumulates permanently in soil. The organic grower avoids synthetic residues at the cost of a persistent heavy metal, and there is no clean answer available.

## Third: water

Water ranks third because the harm is severe and often irreversible, but it is concentrated in specific regions rather than universal. Where vineyards draw from over-allocated basins the wine is being made at the expense of the communities and ecosystems sharing the resource — California's groundwater legislation and the Murray-Darling basin are the clearest examples of the public catching up with the problem, and irrigation-dependent regions in Chile, Argentina and parts of Spain face the same arithmetic. The ethical sharpness comes from the fact that an export vineyard is exporting water in liquid form from a water-stressed country, and the people who lose access are not the people who drink the wine.

## Fourth: systemic inequality

This is the least discussed and, I would argue, the most structurally important. Three strands. Land ownership: in South Africa, Chile and much of the New World, vineyard land is held in patterns set by colonisation, and ownership rather than employment is where the value accrues. Supply-chain power: grape growers routinely sell below the cost of production because a co-operative, a négociant or a retailer sets the price, and no discussion of a grower's environmental practice is honest without noting who takes the margin. Access to sustainability itself: certification costs money and administrative capacity, so the smallholder in a developing region cannot afford the credential that would earn the premium, and the ethical badge concentrates among those who least needed it.

## Dilemmas, technology and unintended consequences

Nothing above has a costless solution, and the strongest signal of a serious answer is saying so.

Mechanisation removes workers from chemical exposure, heat and back injury, and removes their jobs in regions where vineyard work is the only employment; it is available in the Languedoc or inland Australia and impossible on the terraces of the Douro or the Mosel, so the regions with the least capacity to mechanise are the ones most dependent on manual labour. Precision spraying and sensor-based application reduce chemical volumes and require capital that excludes small growers. Lightweight glass cuts emissions and raises breakage. De-alcoholisation, promoted as a responsible product, is energy-intensive.

The point is that most ethical improvements in wine transfer the cost to someone, and the ethical question is usually who.

## Certification, transparency and greenwashing

Certification is the main mechanism the industry offers, and it is doing less work than it appears. Schemes have proliferated to the point of consumer meaninglessness, most audit practices rather than outcomes, and many are self-declared. Critically, the dominant schemes are environmental: a wine can be certified organic and have no labour standard attached at all. The exceptions prove the gap — WIETA in South Africa and Fairtrade certification exist precisely because the environmental schemes did not cover people. The greatest ethical risk here is substitution: a label that lets a producer, a retailer and a consumer all feel the matter has been dealt with.

## Conclusion

The major ethical concerns in wine production are, in order, the treatment of the people who do the work, the chemical exposure of those same people and their neighbours, the appropriation of water in stressed regions, and the ownership and power structures that determine who can afford to behave well. I would demote carbon emissions and packaging — real, but wine is a small contributor to a diffuse harm, and the industry's attention to it is partly because it is the easiest to measure and the least confrontational to fix. If one concern deserves the industry's next decade, it is labour: it is the most severe, the most immediate, the most within producers' control, and the one that certification currently does least to reach.

questionText: To what extent does wine's cultural heritage remain relevant to younger consumers around the globe?
body:
## Two definitions

**Wine's cultural heritage** is four inheritances, and they behave very differently, so separating them is the whole argument. The *material and legal* inheritance: appellations, classifications, cru hierarchies, and the estates and families that hold them. The *practice* inheritance: transmitted technique — qvevri, solera, foot-treading, bush vines, ancestral-method sparkling. The *ritual* inheritance: wine's place at the table, in religion, in hospitality and celebration. And the *codified-knowledge* inheritance: the tasting vocabulary, the critic and sommelier apparatus, service etiquette, and the exam and certification culture I am writing inside.

**Younger consumers** I take as those between legal drinking age and roughly thirty-five: late Generation Z and younger millennials. That band is a demographic fact, not a market segment, and the difference matters. What actually predicts behaviour is three other axes: the maturity of the wine culture they were raised in, their disposable income relative to housing costs, and their level of category engagement.

My answer to the question, stated now and defended below: wine's cultural heritage remains highly relevant to younger consumers — but its function has inverted. Heritage as *narrative, craft and discovery* is more relevant to this cohort than it was to their parents. Heritage as *authority, hierarchy and status* is close to irrelevant, and in places actively repellent. The industry's problem is not that young people have rejected heritage; it is that the institutions holding the heritage keep offering it in the second mode.

## The segments, and what they actually want

Three engagement segments cut across every market. The *indifferent majority* drink little, choose by occasion and price, and have no relationship with heritage of any kind; for them the question is nearly moot. The *curious social drinker*, the largest addressable group, wants a story that makes a choice feel considered, discovery that can be shared, and no risk of being made to feel ignorant. The *enthusiast minority*, smaller but influential and now global rather than Western, wants exactly the depth heritage offers — but sourced directly, from the grower, not mediated by an institution.

Their stated values are legible: authenticity, provenance, environmental credibility, transparency about who made a thing, and a preference for the small over the corporate. Their contradictions are equally important, and a sweeping account misses them. The same cohort drinks less alcohol but pays more per bottle. It is anti-status in rhetoric and intensely status-conscious in practice, having simply moved the signal from the famous label to the obscure one. It says it wants sustainability and reliably chooses on taste and price. And within one age band a Lagos or Mumbai professional entering the category, a Parisian graduate leaving it, and a Shanghai enthusiast rebuilding it have almost nothing in common.

## The evidence from other cultural sectors

The clearest signal that heritage still works comes from outside wine. Specialty coffee took the most technical, origin-obsessed, hierarchical framework imaginable and sold it to this exact demographic at a large premium, by presenting it as craft and discovery rather than as connoisseurship. Vinyl records returned as a physical, effortful, deliberately obsolete format. Food went further: sourdough, fermentation, masa, and traditional Asian preserving techniques became aspirational for a generation whose grandparents abandoned them. Fashion's growth areas are vintage, repair and archive.

The pattern is consistent. Young consumers embrace heritage presented as *technique with a human author*, and reject heritage presented as *rules with a gatekeeper*. Natural wine is precisely this move performed within wine: old vines, indigenous varieties, pre-industrial methods and minimal intervention are heritage in substance, but they were marketed as counterculture, and they succeeded with the cohort that classified-growth marketing could not reach.

## How this varies around the globe

**China** is the sharpest case. Its status-driven Bordeaux boom collapsed after the anti-extravagance campaign, and younger Chinese consumers have shown little interest in inheriting a wine culture that was about gifting and hierarchy. What is emerging instead is domestic: Ningxia and Yunnan producing a heritage that is being made now, in their own lifetimes, which is a far more attractive proposition than being an audience for someone else's.

**Korea and Japan** show substitution rather than rejection: younger Korean drinkers have moved decisively towards whisky, highballs and craft spirits, categories that modernised their heritage storytelling faster than wine did. Japan's younger drinkers engage with wine through food pairing and through domestic Koshu, which is a heritage claim of their own.

**Latin America** shows heritage being locally owned rather than imported. Brazil's Serra Gaucha was settled by Italian immigrants and its young consumers can claim that lineage as theirs; Uruguay's Tannat belongs to the asado; Mexico's Valle de Guadalupe has built an identity around a food scene rather than a classification.

**India and Nigeria** show the limiting case: wine arrives with no inherited local ritual to attach to, so the ritual inheritance is unavailable and the material inheritance is meaningless. Here relevance depends entirely on the practice and story dimensions, and on whether wine can attach itself to local food and occasion.

**Georgia** is the most encouraging evidence in the question's favour. Georgian qvevri winemaking is on UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list, and amber wine has become genuinely fashionable among young urban drinkers in cities with no Georgian connection at all — heritage travelling successfully because it was received as strange and craft-led rather than as canonical.

**Europe** is where the material inheritance is strongest and youth engagement weakest. The Burgundy climats, the Champagne hillsides and cellars, the Alto Douro and Tokaj all hold UNESCO World Heritage status, and per-capita consumption among young French, Italian and Spanish drinkers has fallen furthest. Heritage as institution has the least traction where it is most concentrated, which is close to a proof of the argument.

**South Africa** adds the ownership dimension: heritage is only relevant to those permitted to claim it, and the emergence of Black-owned brands and young Black winemakers is doing more for wine's relevance to young South Africans than any appellation history could.

## Where heritage has to be reframed

Three reframings are available and mostly unexploited. *Sustainability*: old vines, dry farming, indigenous varieties and low-input traditional practice are simultaneously the oldest heritage and the best environmental story, and almost nobody sells them as one thing. *Inclusivity*: whose heritage is canonical is a live question, and expanding the canon beyond Western Europe is both honest and commercially useful. *Novelty*: obscure heritage varieties and revived methods are, to a new drinker, new — heritage is the industry's largest untapped source of novelty.

The competitive set determines the stakes. Against hard seltzer and RTDs, which have no heritage at all, wine's inheritance is a decisive advantage. Against agave spirits and whisky, which have modernised their heritage storytelling and built it around people and places, wine is losing on execution rather than on assets. Against not drinking, heritage is close to irrelevant.

## Conclusion

To a substantial but conditional extent. Graded against my four inheritances: the practice inheritance and the ritual inheritance remain highly relevant, and are wine's strongest assets with this cohort globally; the material and legal inheritance — classifications, hierarchies, château prestige — is of low and falling relevance outside a small enthusiast minority; and the codified-knowledge inheritance is the actively harmful one, because its function is to sort people into those who know and those who do not. Heritage is not the problem. Heritage delivered as authority is, and the regions with the most of it are the ones losing this cohort fastest.
